Impressive development of the P.K.O. in 1936.

[Economy — the Postal Savings Bank P.K.O. (PKO, Pocztowa Kasa Oszczędności).]
(J.T.A.) At the press conference of 21 January 1937 the president of the P.K.O., Director H. Gruber, gave the public the following interesting information:

Despite the unfavourable conditions that arose in 1936 on our money market in connection with the financial events on the European market, the specific [?] activity of the PKO again developed favourably.

The total sum of deposits grew in 1936, compared with the previous year, by 13,981,942.60 zł. and reached a sum of 895.7 million zł. The total deposit sum achieved puts the PKO in first place among the large financial institutions in Poland. Our institution collects about a third of the total sum of deposits in Poland.

The savings department shows in the year under report a not large deposit difference [?], amounting to 13 million zł. This must to a great extent be ascribed to the outflow of the largest deposits, which [—][?] a demand [?] for investments and passed over to cheque deposits, which grew by 29.6 million zł. This phenomenon must be regarded as favourable. The total [savings] deposit sum reached 663.7 million zł. at the end of 1936. The number of savings books grew in the year under report by almost 408 thousand, reaching 2,287,800 at the end of 1936. Thus there is one PKO savings book for every 15 inhabitants.

In cheque turnover the total turnover sum grew by 576 million zł. and amounted to 28.1 billion zł. The number of cheque accounts also grew (by [?] 1,490), and it amounts to 71,991 accounts.

The dynamics of development of life insurance show growth [?] both in the number of policies and in the insured sum. In the 6 and a half years of its existence this department has reached 125 thousand insurance policies for a total insured sum of 183.7 million zł.

The credit operation of the PKO, including [—] the purchase of fixed-interest securities ('Alush' [?] — an operation to support the life of the capital with cheap long-term credit), amounted in 1936 to a sum of 696.1 million zł., and together with the life-insurance department 723.9 million zł.

The corresponding credits, among which we count credits against pledges and securities, discounting of bills of exchange and acceptances, 'text' [?] credits and loans on [—][?] of insured policies, grew together by 5.6 million zł., reaching 43.1 million zł. at the end of the year. It is also worth drawing attention to the operation of crediting small-scale tourism, which began in the year under report.

The 'text' [?] collection (incasso) department accepted 425 thousand items for a total sum of 61.5 million zł. Compared with the previous year this department showed an increase of collection items by 27 thousand pieces.

Summing up the information given above, we see that the activity [?] of the PKO takes account of the middling possibilities of the country, to help a section of society and also beyond the borders of our country, making possible among other things the [—][?] of strengthening the ideas of thrift and life insurance; and as the holder of enormous sums that are the property of small savers, it converts them in the PKO into capital that returns to economic turnover in the form most responsible towards our economic organism — in the form of sound, economic, long-term credit.
The commandments / How to guard against influenza

[Health — advice against influenza.]
We draw attention to the fact that in order to guard against influenza one must:
Avoid mass gatherings.
Not stay in overcrowded [?] and cramped cinemas.
Not greet one another by shaking hands.
Not stand close to a person who coughs and sneezes.
Not overtire oneself too much.
Not change the temperature suddenly, as for example sitting in one's [outdoor] clothes in a warm room and then immediately going out into the street.
If one begins to feel unwell, one had better lie down in bed and not hurry to go out into the street.
The Last Attempt

[Będzin — Talmud Torah and kehilla; opinion piece.]
S. Fürstenberg.
When, six months ago, I called the first "Talmud Torah" meeting in the kehilla, the number of those present fell far short of the number of invitations sent out — but my initiative to restore and reorganise the Będzin Talmud Torah (T"T) was met with due enthusiasm by those assembled, who were recruited from the "Aguda" [Agudat Israel] and Orthodox representatives; and so I believed that the success of the task I had undertaken was assured, that the sin of their apathy until now could be forgiven them, along with the "existing" [?] expression of indifference; and therefore, when I came with my restoration project — and I came not empty-handed, but with a fully completed renovation of the T"T building and with a proper pledge for the future too — I believed in their enthusiasm and regarded it as true, sincere joy [?] of gratitude for awakening them from their drowsy, unjustified indifference. So I believed, and so common sense dictated, for just as fish must [?] have water, so is the task of a rabbinate [?] towards a Talmud Torah; for who should take care of poor Jewish children, if not specially declared Aguda activists and plain Orthodox Jews? But the disappointment was not long in coming. The enthusiasm of the "Torah-faithful" quickly cooled; they did not at all carry out the obligations they had taken upon themselves regarding the restoration plan [?]: they neither gave the declared sum themselves nor even tried to obtain it from someone else; they no longer even came to any meeting. They simply sobered up, made a business calculation and came to the conclusion that the "deal" does not pay. This is the sad truth about the "partisan" Orthodox, for whom the Torah is merely a means to an end, a weapon, "a spade to dig with", to decry and fight other classes and groupings — be it on political or [?] competitive grounds.
And this same tragedy is being played out around the Będzin T"T, which finds itself between "hammer and anvil": on one side the intelligentsia, the so-called "sinners" decried by the Aguda, against whom, it seems, one cannot have great complaints for [?] being indifferent to the T"T (but no more than indifferent, for they are, after all, the "[?]"); and on the other side the official political Orthodoxy (against the unofficial ones one can have no complaints at all, because they are inactive), which according to its motto, according to the inscription on its banner, should have been the stormers, awakeners and self-sacrificing fighters for a T"T. The misfortune, however, is that they have "their own kreplach" [their own interest] (that being the "Yesurei [sic; for Yesodei] HaTorah", which could, God forbid, suffer one day) if the T"T were reorganised and raised to the proper level — open competition... And therefore the Będzin T"T, for political-commercial reasons (albeit with the best of intentions), must remain in a [?] state of eternal death throes; true... it must not die (that would already touch their prestige), but live — by no means, for then it could become dangerous.
But the question arises: "And these sheep, what have they sinned?" What is to become of the 400 forlorn, poor T"T children? Are they to become abandoned street urchins and illiterates in every field? And what are the poor, despairing parents to do, for whom, lacking a bite of bread for their nearest, paying tuition fees is a legendary illusion? Are their own political, competitive motives already the golden altar on which one may sacrifice 400 young Jewish souls, and force a whole section of their parents to give up their last bite of bread for tuition fees and thereby increase their despair still further? Where is the sense of decency, morality and ethics?
The answer to these questions will have to be given by the general meeting called for Tuesday, under the unambiguous, clear motto [?] "restoration or liquidation"; and let everyone weigh the responsibility of the moment and take account of the fact that the general meeting of the T"T is the last attempt.
Who Is Guilty. (To the general meeting of the "Gemilut Chesed Fund.")

To the general meeting of the "Gemilut Chesed (Free-Loan) Fund."

At last we stand before the general meeting of the Będzin "Gemilut Chesed Fund." At last a date has been set from which one will have to draw a line under the past and begin a new activity [?], a new work, both for the benefit of the members and for the benefit of the interest-free fund, which is able, under good and conscientious management, to bring enormous benefit to impoverished Jewish Będzin.

But it is easily said: draw a line under the past and from now on open [?] new pages and keep new accounts, as if nothing had happened before.

Well, had the leaders up to now understood the crimes they caused with their disorderly management, they would have stepped aside as the guilty ones [?], and their place would have been taken by new people, people with initiative and clean hands, to whom one could, of course, entrust [?] the important institution. But the trouble is that they do not understand, or pretend not to understand, that they must vacate [?] the place so that others can take it.

We also know that at the general meeting people will operate — secretly, of course — under the slogan "shmor li ve-eshmor lekha" ("guard me and I will guard you"): do me a favour here, and I will come to your aid at the first opportunity; and by this system the members will be "worked on," as long as they vote for this or that person.

And here the matter must be clarified [?]. Everyone must take account of the fact that, on the one hand, the interest-free fund is an institution that has nothing whatsoever to do with politics, whichever trend it may belong to; and on the other hand, one must not forget that one must not climb with a healthy head into a sick bed. If the same people, or part of them, get in again — people whom one wants to persuade that they "owe only God their soul" [i.e. are entirely blameless] — the institution will not be raised to its proper state; and if it — as we hold — never stood at the proper height, it will now have every chance of going downhill. This must be remembered well.

At the previous general meeting the chairman declared that everyone who does something makes mistakes, whereas he who does nothing makes no mistakes. One may agree with these words, but only in the case where a mistake is actually [—] made; at the given moment, however, no mistake was made — rather, a disorderly management was conducted, whose consequences led to embezzlements that are material for the public prosecutor, so that the whole board sits in the dock. This must be learned by heart.

It is interesting how petty people are and how they do not understand their tasks and responsibility. Here a board member, who once even occupied the chairman's seat there, shouts that it is not he who is guilty but the clerk; along comes the clerk and says that the boy or the [—] is guilty. What a "Chad Gadya" story they want to make of those who should be responsible for Jewish groszy!

Yes, guilty are all who ran the institution, and first and foremost the elected representatives whom the people trusted. We know that not all are directly guilty of the sad events that brought the useful institution to its present state. But they must know that they bear the same responsibility as those who are directly guilty, for if they sit there they were obliged to react to every event, and if impermissible deeds took place, they had no right to play the role of extras.

The town even has the right to hold responsible for the deeds that occurred also the Joint [JDC] of Warsaw, for it is simply impossible to understand how they could let it come to the present state. After all, the institution is under its control, under its authority, [—] — so how could the embezzlements be allowed to happen?

We kept silent the whole time, and perhaps even too much, in fact; and that because, being far from making sensations out of our [—] problems, we did not want to cause harm to the useful institution, reckoning that the leaders would understand how to save the situation. Unfortunately they did not manage to do so, and therefore they bear all the consequences on their conscience.

So then, the whole board sits today in the dock, and none of them should accept any mandate, for all of them are guilty — it makes no difference whether directly or indirectly.

Let the members remember that the institution must remain non-partisan, and it must be handed over to such hands as will know how to guard the integrity of so useful a fund, for it is the most important institution for the masses of the people, for whom it can achieve much in today's hard times.

The main thing of all is that people of various trends should be represented there. And here a warning must be made: offices should not be taken by people who are out for nothing more than wearing ribbons [?] [i.e. honours only], for in that way one does not work oneself and does not give the opportunity to admit [?] such people as could achieve something.

Our Gemilut Chesed Fund must now be renewed and revived. Therefore let honest people, with initiative and will, set to work — people to whom Jewish honour and the existence of the Jewish masses are dear.

R. Les.
The Flu Has Helped...!

[Sosnowiec — humour, monologue.] Y. Oberżanek
(Monologue of a Sosnowiec Jew).
Whatever you say[?] — the flu! My neighbour says the flu was invented by the doctors; for them it is a charm for a livelihood. As soon as people start coughing and sneezing and there begins a series of stabbing pains and vomitings and other "-ings", the doctors hear [?] — a "[?]"!
And I say just the opposite: the flu is a fine thing. The flu is a charm not only for the doctors' pockets but for a simple flesh-and-blood mortal too. I don't know how you regard[?] the flu; me, for example, the flu has helped. Thanks to the flu I have been freed from my troubles, from plagues and nuisances, and I have a few weeks of rest — may it go on like this, sweet Father!..
You think I'm touched[?] in the "upper storey"? I'll tell you the story in detail ["podrobnie"]:
As soon as the flu became the fashion, I pictured the years[?]; wherever I came, I was stopped at the door:
— Sorry, you can't come in!
— What happened?
— Flu!
I came with a bill of exchange to collect a debt — the lady of the house blocked my way:
— Flu! A flu with complications.
— Flu? That's all I need. All the good things I already have — only a flu is missing. I wished a full recovery and ran off as if demons were chasing me.
I came to a neighbour of mine who had taken from me, out of the wall[?], a small interest-free loan — I found him lying in bed with a bandaged throat, face down, his back covered with cupping glasses; go and talk when instead of a face you have... a back with cupping glasses!
I phone a merchant about a bit of goods. I ask him:
— Panie, what's new?
— It has gone up — he answered.
— Gone up? By how much?
— It's very high!
— How high?
— 38 point 6.
— What 38? Whose is this "pekl", then?
— My wife's!
— So why has it suddenly gone up so much with her? What kind of article is it?
— A [?] article! It's very modern and sells well; if you like, you can take it from her as is.
— What is the article called?
— Flu! — the merchant answered me.
Wherever I go — flu and flu. I go into the café ["tsukernye"] to drink a glass of tea, I sit at the table and wait. Much good it does me to drink with so much waiting[?]. Only after an hour of sitting and knocking "Panie Ober!" does a fellow appear with a [?] as red as a beet, his throat wrapped in a woollen scarf, like a cantor before the High Holidays.
I ask him: Panie Ober, how long will I wait?
— Until I take the thermometer out from under my arm — he answered.
Only yesterday I dropped in on my wife's friend ["koleżanka"], and she was very glad to see me.
— Good that you came, I've been waiting for a man's hand like for the Messiah.
— A hand? For a doctor?
— What do I need a doctor for, the doctoring is going to my head!
— For bridge?
— Stop with the bridge, I badly need your hand, a real ["prawdziwa"] man's hand.
— What for?
— I want you to massage me, rub my back "the manly way" ["po męskiemu"].
— What do you mean, I should rub your back? What am I, a masseur? — I asked her.
— Don't talk so much and get down to the job — she answered.
Well, I ask you: how can one be such a swine — a Jewish woman needs a man's hand, how can one refuse her such a trifle ["drobnostka"]? I rolled up my sleeves and set about the massage. After the massage she wanted me to take her temperature; after taking the temperature she gave me her pulse. After the pulse she gave me a spoon so I'd look into her throat, whether she hadn't got "enlarged tonsils" ["powiększone migdały"]. I saw it was a story without end, that she might yet tell me to rock[?] the baby as well — so I took my feet under my arm and ran wherever my eyes carried me.
Wherever I came I met[?] flu; in whatever house I came, they answered me:
— Przepraszam, flu! Everywhere the beds were rumpled. Everywhere people were snoring, gargling, sneezing, coughing[?], sweating, backs with cupping glasses, thermometers under the arms. Everywhere the doors were shut; I come to a debtor — he lies face down and tells me to talk to... the back with the cupping glasses; I come to the café — the waiter sits with the thermometer under his arm. I come to my wife's friend — she tells me to rub her back, gives me her pulse and tells me to look at her "enlarged tonsils". Not a grosz can one collect, and I have to pay, because I don't have the flu.
What does one do? It's bitter; what advice can one give oneself. If only I too were sick with the flu, I too would be rid of the plagues, they'd leave me alone too.
In the midst of it, as I'm thinking this over, an idea strikes me. Where is it written that to lie down in bed you really must have the flu? Can't one get into bed, wrap up one's throat in perfect health and put on, you know, the act?
And indeed I didn't think long: I laid myself down in bed, wrapped my throat in a woollen kerchief, set out around me[?] little bottles and pills ["pigułki"], a [?] machine, liniment ["francówka"], turpentine, cotton wool, gauze, iodine, a box of cupping glasses, bandaged my head with a towel — and there, with good luck, I have a flu and a half!..
What else did I do? On the door I pasted a slip of paper with the words:
"Please[?] do not enter, contagious flu!"
Now I lie in bed like a count. Not a living soul [lit. "living bird"] shows up — no creditors, not the landlord, not the distrainer ["sekwestrator"], not the bailiff ["komornik"]. As soon as they come up to the door and see the little notice[?] on the door, they fly off as if demons were chasing them; and if somebody does risk his life and comes into my room, he sees what a "state"[?] I'm in, wishes me a full recovery and goes his way.
My neighbour says the flu was invented by the doctors as a charm for a livelihood. And I say the flu is a fine thing. Thanks to the flu I am rid of all the plagues and nuisances — the flu has helped.
We Must Pass the Exam

[Będzin — interest-free loan fund (gemilut chesed); opinion piece before the annual report meeting.] In 2 days' time, this coming Sunday, we, the citizens of Będzin, members of the Gemilut Chesed fund, will, after the lapse of 2 years, again be called upon to hear a report and to elect new trustees ("baalei-batim"), into whose hands we must anew[?] hand over the management of this interest-free credit institution, so important in today's hard times.
We are accustomed to regard the day of the annual general report meeting as a day of judgment. On that day the board must give its voters an exact account of how it has administered the public funds entrusted to it: whether it has used[?] them properly, i.e. for the purposes[?] for which these sums were designated; whether it, the board, properly guarded the public capital so that it should not be diminished; whether it made use of all possibilities and opportunities so that the public treasury should grow further; whether it truly relieved with these funds the need of those who depended on this help[?]. What obstacles the board met in its work, and how and by what means these obstacles were removed or avoided; what was done at all during the term of office, and in what state the whole public cause stands today.
The judge is the general meeting — the voter, the member of the fund, to whom the board reports and must report everything exactly, with full illumination of all the circumstances. Defenders and accusers come forward: the former lay on the scales all the good deeds of these trustees[?] of the community; the latter want to accuse and hurl all the sins the board has committed; and from all the arguments that both sides hurl it becomes clear whether the existing board is to be judged for punishment or for grace.
Very[?] often, however, it happens that the judge himself forgets, at the important moment of the accounting, his important role, his main task, for the sake of which he sat down on the seat of judgment. He loses the cold-bloodedness, seriousness and concentration of a judge, and is himself drawn into the camp of the defenders or the accusers; and then a hasty[?] struggle breaks out between 2 fighting sides, which ends in a perversion of justice, and the holy, important cause that was the object of the meeting's concern is harmed — sometimes even to the point of collapse.
We now stand on the eve of that day of judgment, and find it necessary and important to remind the judge of his exalted role.
Both the defenders and the accusers do[?] come with facts in hand when they argue, but beneath the arguments of both sides lies a hidden[?] intention to cover up the truth, and the judge's art is to unravel[?] and extract the pure truth; and only the pure truth can direct the judges to the goal of putting the public cause in the state that is desired for the community.
The judge must therefore be patient and serious, hear everything with gravity, take into account the whole complex of circumstances and, most importantly[?], not let himself be distracted for a single minute from the main purpose for which the judgment takes place.
We must remember well, and not forget even for a minute, that we live in a time when all the foundations of our existence are shaken; we stand on a swamp[?], the ground under our feet is disappearing[?] unnoticed[?]. The only support for those who are sliding into the abyss of want and need, poverty and hunger, is the Gemilut Chesed fund, and we may not for one moment forget our cool reason, our calm composure, in order to arrive at the conclusions and results that are most favourable for the existence of the fund and its further development.
"The Gemilut Chesed fund is truly holy[?]," said the late Yehoshua Thon of blessed memory, who died not long ago, "one may not approach it with dirty[?] shoes of party-[—] personal ambitions." [—] honour and prestige, [and][?] personal caprices must be set aside when the interest of the community is at stake.
If the board has justified the trust placed in it — if it has not only [not] harmed the common interest but has also contributed the full measure of its abilities for the benefit of the cause entrusted to it — then it deserves a great "yasher koach" and full trust for the future. But if the board did not understand the essence of the duties laid upon it, and has even harmed the public cause through its unserious, superficial attitude and indifference — then it must leave [—] with honour[?], [—][?] that it should not continue[?], and in its place better, more serious and more capable workers must[?] come.
The judge called "general meeting" must now be mature and pass the exam, which consists of the following:
1) To show full calm and cold-bloodedness when hearing the reports on the past period.
2) To conduct the discussion in the form of matter-of-fact and instructive criticism.
3) Not to let oneself be led onto the slippery path of personal[?] interests, of playing out[?] caprices and ambitions, or group and party interests.
4) To consider with full gravity the importance of the Gemilut Chesed fund, in today's cruel historical moment, for the broad masses of the people, and to hand over this rescue institution into the best hands that the town [—].
I believe that the serious moment and the great importance will lead us onto the straight path, and that we will pass the exam successfully.
S. S.
Technical Jubilees in the Year 1937

In the year 1937 there will be a great commemoration[?] of technical jubilees. In many branches of modern technology and industry great celebrations will be held this year, and the world will make great preparations for the jubilees of various inventions that have brought much good to the world.
Here we shall content ourselves with listing the most important jubilees falling in the present year, according to the records of the „ערכית“[?] (probably: the archive) of the Leipzig Fair. Some of these inventions deserve to be written about at length and in separate articles, which we will bring in our series „Technical News“.
Porcelain will celebrate a great jubilee this year. In the year 1687, i.e. exactly 250 years ago, porcelain was brought to market for the first time. True, the Chinese already knew hundreds of years earlier the material from which they made porcelain, but only single pieces were made, which cost a fortune and were bought only by the kings and nobles[?] of that time. The porcelain we have today in every home is only now[?] turning 250 years old.
A hundred years ago, in 1837, Morse invented the telegraph with its signs, which are used to this day all over the world.
Fifty years ago, 1887, the first automobile was invented.
A seeming trifle — the needle, used for sewing in the four corners of the world, began to be manufactured for the first time 125 years ago in an English steel factory. This trifle caused an upheaval throughout the whole world.
In 1817 the bicycle[?] was invented — first with three and then with two wheels; it is now 120 years old.
Ninety years ago, 1847, the first sewing machine was invented, which today is used even in the camps of wild tribes. In the same year the first rotary press was invented, without which no modern newspaper in the world could be printed today.
Seventy years ago, in 1867, Nobel invented dynamite. With this invention he made such[?] a great fortune that he founded his famous Nobel Foundation, which, as is well known, gives away every year part of the profits for special great achievements in the field of various sciences.
In the same year the secret of making reinforced concrete („iron-concrete“) was also discovered; without this invention it would not have been possible to build today's great modern houses and skyscrapers, which stand only thanks to reinforced concrete.
A hundred years ago, 1837, matches were brought to market for the first time. Over this invention there is to this day a dispute between the French, who say that their countryman made the invention, and the Hungarians, who say that the Frenchman bought the invention from their countryman and passed it off as his own work. A few months ago the Hungarians erected in Budapest a monument to the Hungarian inventor of matches.
In 1877 Edison invented the phonograph. For years he carried it around and nobody wanted to believe that it would be a business worth manufacturing.
Forty years ago, 1897, Marconi made the first attempts to telephone without wire, and thereby laid the first stone of the edifice called radio.
Also in the year 1817 [sic; read 1897] the diesel engine was invented, which is used today in all the power stations of the whole world.
Z. Haber, Vienna.
Heard and Seen.

[Sosnowiec and Zagłębie — weekly feuilleton.] By Ben Amotz.

An explicit "kal va-chomer"...
For several months now the committee for rescuing the Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec has been trumpeting to the "societies": "Jews of Sosnowiec, help! The Jewish hospital is going under!"
And the Jews of Sosnowiec — as we well know — possess a strong "sense of hearing"; they respond at once to signal calls whenever it is purely a matter of the common good. Here is living proof[?]: the campaign to build a municipal bath-house (the "sinners" call it, in the old fashion[?], — a mikveh..) has after all brought unheard-of, gigantic[?] results. Had it not been for the severe cold and frost (which froze the hearts of the rich — [unclear Hebrew phrase][?]) the building would long since have stood finished, and only then would the "Kashrut Committee" have shown its abilities...
And with the same zeal, with the same fire, the relief campaign for the hospital is indeed[?] proceeding too. The "people" bring money as once to the Tabernacle, and so that there should be no surplus, i.e., [squandering][?]. So that the "people" should not give as much as is needed, the committee refuses to accept small donations and sends them back to the "givers".
— What? You don't believe it? Here is the writer of these lines, a living witness, having seen how the president of the committee sent back a donation of... three złoty. We had a small complaint to him: how so[?]? After all we have the saying "whether one gives much or little", one gives more, another less, the main thing is the good will...
— Yes, I [think] so too[?], but "our conscience" does not let us take a donation of three gulden from such a person — an educated man, by the way — who owns no more than half a house; true, on Magruszewska[?] Street, but still it is no more than half a house.. Well, can we — says the president — be so cruel as to take someone's "last" few gulden?..
— We did not believe — chimes in a member of the executive — that the hospital campaign would "succeed so well". True, the campaign had merits, merits, when the [Prowizer][?] immersed himself in the mikveh every day, so that the "fine Jews" would have no grievances that the "Agudah ideology" is not tolerated by the committee... But one cannot have any complaint at all against the Jews of Sosnowiec, who "do not refuse": you barely come to them and they open their purses and give "with a cheerful countenance"...
— How much, for example, have you already collected for the campaign?
— "If we add up the promises of 'we'll give soon', we already have, [so to speak][?], a sum of three thousand zł...
And to collect such a sum in Sosnowiec — says the executive member with pride — is a colossal job, for you must not forget that "Yasha Kalb" could not drag more than eight thousand zł. out of Sosnowiec — do you hear, gentlemen[?]! Just remember — "Yasha Kalb"!...
And the "argument" is a convincing one; it is, after all, an explicit kal va-chomer: if "Yasha Kalb" did not drag out more than eight thousand zł., should a committee engaged in a hospital campaign collect more than 3 thousand zł.?...
— An explicit "kal va-chomer"...

A "secure livelihood"...
Jews are a stiff-necked people; they do not let go of their "[—]"[?]. In the struggle of suffering and pain the Jew takes the cup in his hand and cries out "Ve-hi she-amda"...
For example: when the peasant cast[?] an eye on the Jewish market stall, the Jews immediately found themselves a "new livelihood":
— they open "clubs".
And the "clubs" are of various kinds[?]. There are, for example, "Stzheroshiski[?] clubs", a place of rest for the "[—]"[?], in plain Yiddish — the "[—]"[?]; an ordinary mortal cannot get in there, because there they "study" from evening till morning...
Then there are "clubs" where one also reads a newspaper, and from time to time a "scientific" [—] is organised, and on the Hanukkah[?] days one also snatches a game of cards.
Lately a new sort of "club" has appeared on the Jewish street; the content is almost the same as all the "clubs" — it is wholly steeped[?] in "Ober Eichel" [a card of the German pack — i.e. card-playing], only the garb is a national one, or more precisely — a "Zionist" one...
We are in the premises of the Zionist organisation in Zagłębie. In which town, we will not say, because it is all one[?] — they play everywhere. — In the first room, by the way [—], it is as cold as at "zero point"[?]; around the stove stand several young people, members of "He-Halutz Ba'al Melacha" [the artisans' pioneer movement], who are[?] unemployed and dream of certificates [immigration permits].
— Why is it so quiet here, [—]? — we ask the young people.
— That's why it is cosy over there, in the next room — answers one of them.
And it is indeed true. In the next room it is bright and warm; the little tables are occupied by the "[—]"[?], whose minds work in earnest, so as not, God forbid, to make a "wrong move" and have all the work, God forbid, go to waste.
We look around and our eyes come to rest on a large notice hanging on the eastern wall.
Probably — I think to myself — this is a notice connected with some kind of cultural work in the "club"; and why not — the verse says "man does not live by bread alone"; apart from "playing" there are Jewish problems too.
And we were mistaken: the large "notice" is simply the by-laws of the "club", for a "club" without by-laws is, after all, like a "match [—] without [—]"...
And willy-nilly[?] we must admit that these by-laws contain several points that deserve attention; moreover, it is fitting to publish them for the "broad public"..
For example: the Christian merchants have striven from the first moment to have the [restrictions][?] on merchants abolished and to keep the shops open until 9 o'clock on the eves of holidays. Quite differently, however, do the bosses[?] of the "club" understand it: they have permitted that on the nights before holidays one may play until 2 a.m...
These by-laws contain a further[?] series of "important" points, such as that "players may not bring their own cards but must use the club's cards", etc., etc.. But we mention this only in passing, by the way[?]; the main thing is that we live in a "practical epoch". For example: when an organisation wanted income, it had to organise a [—], lectures and the like. But today — one no longer needs to bother with[?] such "foolishness"; one can[?] very easily get income for the organisation: you rent premises and open a "club", and there it is — a "secure livelihood"...
Among Jewish Youth

[Sosnowiec — feuilleton; Jewish youth, marriage and dowry.] By P. Blumenkranz (Sosnowiec).
A conversation among grown-up, independent and educated girls. First they talk about their day-to-day occupations, about prospects; little by little[?] they chat about film stars, until they come to the main point.
One says:
— I studied abroad, my parents are poor, I struggled, gave a lesson in exchange for a lunch, lived on the fourth floor, wrote a master's thesis — and today I earn a hundred zł. a month, and father[?] wants still more. I gave away my best years, and all of it cannot replace a dowry...
— With them[?] it is different — the second chimes in — I knew a student in Warsaw from a Hasidic home, a genuinely Semitic type, no beauty, with a long thin nose. She met a Christian, an engineer, and they got married. The girl suffered[?]; she did not know how to tell her parents about it. So she hit upon this ruse: she bargained with her father and said to him: You[?] know I have no wish to become an old maid; I have an acquaintance, but he does not belong to our people. I'll give you a year's time; if within that time you do not give me a bridegroom, I'll marry the gentile. And so it happened. She did not convert; she took a civil "ślub" [wedding], but the father, on hearing of it, died of a heart attack.
— But one cannot blame the Jewish young men so harshly — a third speaks up, one who has money and for whom the fear of "old-maidhood" is not so strong — the Jewish young men have no other way out, all gates are closed to them, they have no possibility of settling themselves. They finish a university and then wander about looking for work addressing envelopes, or become collectors for a philanthropic institution.
— Not true — the first objects — Jews[?] are materialists, a fact: in our town a well-situated architect, after spending many years with a girl, refused to go to the wedding canopy because at the last minute he found out that his bride did not have as much money as he had thought. Jewish young men love with the head and not with the heart — the opponent[?] goes on bitterly — they spend years with a girl and behave diplomatically, so as always to have a [—] out of the "[—]" [—]. They [the Christians], however, do not calculate; they are not so calculating — they meet and marry, without the money...
— Yes, you exaggerate — the well-to-do one defends them — some really are materialistic, but the majority truly has no other way out; they need money to get settled. Marrying Christians, i.e.[?] without converting, creates complications: what will these people do, e.g., with their children? Tragedies arise. The enthusiasm vanishes[?] sooner or later and grey life [—]. In this case it is much [—] for the "Jewess", who often [—] in her own home and is insulted by her own children (it goes without saying that I am now entirely leaving aside the national aspects, which are a separate chapter).
The girls spoke with fervour, all [—] together. The older ones, with flaming cheeks, angrily — their years full of disappointments — protested; the young ones with curiosity[?] and a light [—]: they had not yet given up their hopes. They brought examples, argued, quarrelled, until they got stuck[?] on one case[?]: "he" wanted to sell himself for money; she has red cheeks and thick legs, finished a vocational school and started running around with boys at less than[?] 15 years of age. "He" knows all this and paid no attention to it — she has money, so it works!
•
Three of them sat over cold tea. One says:
— You know that I like her, she is charming, I feel very good in her company, but at home it is mortal danger: my father would [bang?] on the table[?] and raise a commotion[?]: "Two strangers are going dancing[?]! You are both paupers and will raise a new generation of strangers." And my father wears me out[?], and at the same time I depend on him; every day I must hold out my hand to him.
The second argues:
— What nonsense you're talking! Do you know what seven circles of hell I went through until I managed to finish mechanical engineering abroad? My mother could not send me a single grosz, and I did everything: taught Hebrew, worked as a librarian, slept[?] in a synagogue, [—] — all in order to become independent. I came home and now I hang about idle and empty-handed. They propose matches to me. Sometimes I go to the dressed-up houses: they whisper[?] about me, look me over like a horse at the market, feel me with their eyes, watch how I hold the knife, whether I don't cross one leg over the other, whether I don't play with the [—], whether I don't kiss the hand of the triple-chinned[?] Jewess too softly[?]. Once they matched me with a "blondynka", i.e. an artificial one, with pretensions to film (her photograph was once in the weekly "Kino" as one of the "[—]"[?]); she wanted to impress me with her knowledge and at the same time[?] humiliate me — she starts[?] talking at length[?] about the "[—]" of Greta Garbo and Hepburn, Marlene Dietrich and Brigitte Helm, then about the best film singers, and she lists: Jeanette MacDonald, Grace Moore[?] and Marta Eggerth; she pours out names until everything starts getting mixed up in my head: [de] Havilland, Lombard, Rainer, Sidney and on and on. After all this she asks me who is more "sexy": Clark Gable, Gary Cooper or Fredric March.
— Right — the third interrupts, he too having "studied" — but how does one get settled after all? Money is an unworthy thing, but as long as it exists — the landlord wants, after all, for the flat only[?] this [—] "cover", and you won't replace it with the most beautiful stars of "Young Werther". And won't you start quarrelling with your wife the very next day if you go hungry? There is no domestic peace without a livelihood.
— True — the first sighs — when I starved abroad and gave lessons in the cold attic room, I strove to take my life into my own hands, to determine its further course. But nothing came of my [—]. I have one way out: to take a dowry and start dealing in bicycles or car parts, become a merchant and start signing bills of exchange. My father, it seems, is right; I shall be forced to close a transaction with a rich "calf": she will give me money, and I will give her the title on the invitations of philanthropic institutions — "Mrs. Engineer"...
•
They would probably have gone on talking a long time over the cold tea, but the orchestra began to play an English waltz, and it was a pity to let it pass, especially when there is a small crowd: nobody disturbs, and one can make a few minutes of one's own[?] fantasy. Ah...
For the annual Yavetz campaign

For the "Keren HeChalutz HaMizrachi".
On Sunday, 31 January, the annual campaign for the fund of the religious pioneer — the "Keren HeChalutz HaMizrachi" — begins.
The campaign will be proclaimed on 18 Shevat ("Motza'ei Shabbat Kodesh", Saturday night), on the yahrzeit of the Jewish scholar and religious-national thinker[?] Rabbi Ze'ev Yavetz of blessed memory, whose aspiration was to create a religious-national generation of workers in Eretz Israel.
The "Keren HeChalutz HaMizrachi" has the task of supporting the spiritual, physical and vocational hachshara (training) of the religious pioneer, and the olim and pioneers without means at the time of their aliyah to Eretz Israel.
Because of the present political situation in Zionism, the hachshara work must today be properly reorganised, so that the pioneers can go on finding their proper place there.
The latest events in Eretz Israel have shown that "Kfar Yavetz" [printed "Kfar Ybetz"] must be enlarged and developed.
It is especially important nowadays to send to Eretz Israel trained pioneers, men and women[?], who have gone through their hachshara in agricultural work.
The Keren HeChalutz HaMizrachi provides the financial means for this.
The Jewish population of Zagłębie and Upper Silesia has always[?] responded warmly[?] to the appeal of the "Keren HeChalutz HaMizrachi" directorate and has warmly[?] supported this important fund.
The pairs of collectors who will visit Jewish homes will find a cordial reception and will receive from everyone a donation according to his means.

A shepherd becomes a film star.
Randolph Scott made a rare career in a very short time. Born and raised on a farmstead (a farm) in California, he spent his childhood years in the distant fields and steppes together with the herds of cattle and horses. Once a film cameraman came to the steppe to shoot newsreel footage of a peasant festivity[?]. He took a great liking to the young Randolph Scott and took him along to Hollywood. Within a short time Scott was already playing in the so-called cowboy films. Now he is playing one of the leading roles in the film "Azoy[?] roys in di royn[?]" [Yiddish title, reading uncertain].
Oneg Shabbat — Torah novellae, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Yitro)

Torah novellae, remarks and anecdotes on the portion of this week.
Collected and edited by Yehuda.
Parashat Yitro
—o—
a) "And he bowed down and kissed him" (18:7)
"...Moses kissed none but his father-in-law; hence they said: a man should be ready to honour his father-in-law." Mekhilta.
R. Eizel of Słonim once had words with his father-in-law, R. Barukh Yosef. Flying into a rage, the father-in-law says to him:
— You should show me respect! You are indeed a Torah scholar, but "a man is obliged to honour his father-in-law"!
— Father-in-law — R. Eizel answers him — the Mekhilta does not say "a man is obliged to honour his father-in-law" but "a man should be READY to honour his father-in-law", that is: to be always ready, and when[?] the father-in-law has "eaten you up"[?], [—] go to the pillow[?] in the window[?] — then [—]... [end of the retort hard to make out; reading uncertain].
—o—
b) "...and out of the hand of Pharaoh, who delivered the people from under the hand of Egypt" (ibid., 10)
Pharaoh, it means, helped the Jews and rescued[?] them from the hands of the Egyptians. The Egyptians always wanted to slaughter[?] the Jews, and Pharaoh was the "righteous one"[?] who restrained[?] the popular wrath — just as the heads[?] of the pogrom states behave in all times...
Imrei Chen.
—o—
c) "And it came to pass on the morrow that Moses sat to judge the people" (ibid., 13)
"...this section is not written in order." Rashi.
Why is the section about judgments in particular[?] written out of order?
Because in matters of judgment we sometimes see the "nivshei dukhsana"[?]: if someone once takes money from somebody unlawfully[?], in the course of time circumstances arise and he has to give the money back in various ways to the one he robbed — that is "there is no earlier and later": sometimes one pays for a robbery of fifty years ago. That is why "there is no earlier and later" is hinted at here.. for a robbery, its time comes in the end.
Avodat HaGershuni.
—o—
d) "And shalt show them the way wherein they must walk" (ibid., 20)
"'And shalt show them' — this is their livelihood (see Rashi, that this means parnassa); 'the way' — this is acts of loving-kindness; 'they must walk' — this is visiting the sick, etc." Bava Kamma 99.
Instead of judging the people in their quarrels, provide them with ways of making a living, loving-kindness, and take care of them with similar things.
Leket Amarim.
—o—
e) "Visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children" (20:5)
"But is it not written 'the children shall not be put to death for the fathers'? How so? When they hold the deeds of their fathers in their hands, and when they do not hold the deeds of their fathers in their hands." Berakhot 7.
Today's children — a great man once complained — are "holding the deeds of their fathers in their hands", that is, they hold their parents' deeds and conduct in their hands: for when the father wants to do something, he asks what the son will say about it... In this way the children hold their parents' deeds in their hands.
Gibborei A"G[?].
—o—
f) "And they stood afar off" (ibid., 15)
[Pri?] Even when they find themselves far away, they should still remember and stand close[?].
Botzina[?] de-Torah.
• • •
"Come, ye children, hearken unto me" — Psalms 34.
It does not say "come in, children" (bo'u) but "go, children" (lekhu); this means: even when you go away from me — go, children — hearken unto me — you should still remember just as well[?] and listen to my words.
R. Shmelke of Nikolsburg.
Deaf Sub-tenants

[Humour — "Der Kokh-lefl" page.] ["Der Kokh-lefl" (The Cooking Ladle) — humour and satire. Compiled by Amutsli.]
Motl is a Jew who is more of a pauper than a Jew; when Motl has enough for the Sabbath, he is happy, he is a second Rothschild.
Motl also has a wife. And the wife is 15 years older than he is; he says she is 20 years older. So they are forever quarrelling[?]. They tear at each other like two cats in one sack, and since there is no livelihood either, they quarrel even more.
One may say that of the 24 hours a day and night contains, Motl quarrels with his wife for 19 hours. 5 hours they sleep, rest up, so that tomorrow they can go on quarrelling.
Motl also keeps two sub-tenants. He has to keep sub-tenants so that he need not pay the rent by himself.
Both sub-tenants that Motl has kept ever since he has been Motl, ever since he has been a pauper, ever since he has been quarrelling with his wife — have been deaf.
Motl takes in no sub-tenants who can hear; he takes only deaf ones, so that they will not hear how he quarrels with his wife.
When you talk with Motl's sub-tenants, they say that Motl lives with his wife like two doves in love...
B. Kovner.
Sayings about Women

[Humour — "Der Kokh-lefl" page; aphorisms.]
Truly faithful wives make family life as sublime as the Holy Temple. Unfaithful wives make family life as charmingly[?] interesting as a theatre.
—
With wives in whom the thirst for love flickers and burns, the husband constantly eats a quiet supper.
—
To abandon a wife one must be a person without a conscience; not to love other women one's whole life, one must be a person without a body and without life.
Og, King of Bashan.
A Leavened "Ma Nishtana"...

[Humour — "Der Kokh-lefl" page; satirical poem on animals and slaughter.]
Hear a story, enough to make you burst:
In the Viennese[?] "Rushpushnik"[?] they want to make [—][?]
for the cattle and for the rams —
so they can lean[?] a little on the sofas..
and not stay lying on the ground, rolling about like a drunkard,
for you must know that the main thing, the essence,
is not to cause the poor beasts, the poor things, any heartache, any pain,
but everything must be done "humanely" and "humanitarianly",
according to law and rule —
as befits, in this "epoch", the bovine species...
here too[?] the new ropes for tying may now be used —
and some say that from now on the flaying will be more refined...
"and the slaughter of [—]"[?] —
even the revolver-automatic is already ready to shoot..
Only one thing still troubles me, and I ask a question:
— Why is it somehow, on the scales[?], "people below and oxen above"?
Why do people lie [—] alone in poverty[?]
and above all, why[?] does one warm[?] the animal soul?!
The difficulty bothers me and I truly ask "Ma nishtana" — what is different?
Why do they give people potatoes, and the ox — the ottomans[?]?..
A Delegate's Speech

[Humour — "Der Kokh-lefl" page; satire on the Mizrachi conference.]
At the Mizrachi district conference in Sosnowiec
...I am from [—], it makes no difference where; I actually want to give you a report, although I had no intention at all of giving a report, because what sort of report do I have to give, when in general everything is without any account. But never mind, in short — I thought to myself: since we are at the [—] report, I will give a report from our town.
Yes, the report is not a proper report; if the public does not want to pay [membership dues?][?], then where is a report to come from? And again, about the activities carried out during the year, the C.C. [Central Committee] surely knows the report. Therefore I think the guilty party is the C.C., which gives no certificates [immigration permits], because if there were certificates the members would pay sooner and the report would be as it should be. So, I do not want to go on at length, since the delegates from other towns also want to give a report; therefore I am cutting it short and wish that at the next conference there will be a bigger public and there will be a better report...

The Festive Reception

[Humour — "Der Kokh-lefl" page; satire on the influenza epidemic, the doctors and the sick fund.]
For the great guest — the flu.
At last the Doctors' Association in Zagłębie has succeeded in arranging that the distinguished guest should come to our coal-and-iron industrial district as well.
Where has he not already been — beginning with America, then across the ocean to England, France, Belgium, Germany, and where not. Everywhere he filled[?] the hearts of the doctors with joy, everywhere he foretold them a good future and a secure livelihood — and at last our doctors too have begged and obtained that the guest is here.
The flu has visited Zagłębie. The young doctorlings rub their hands and rejoice: Be welcome, O you fulfiller of our dreams.
The sick fund has appointed a special reception committee, which after a series of meetings adopted the following resolutions:
To prepare a hundred metres of "[—] of the [—]"[?]; to engage several house caretakers (dozorcy), who are to pour this liquid into small bottles and distribute it among those who wish to be privileged to have the great guest — the flu — visit them.
For the convenience of the public it was resolved that the flu-"holder"[?] should simply send in his photograph. These photographs are to be forwarded within a week to the doctors so that they can give their opinion.
To heat the stoves in the out-patient clinics, so that the visitors will not get bored[?] when they have to sit there for 24 hours.
To buy telescopes for the doctors, so that they can look, for example, from [—][?] to a patient in Old Sosnowiec, or from the brewery to a patient at the New Market.
In addition, an amnesty has been proclaimed for the insured: they need not report before they have a 40-degree fever.
Those Above with Those Below

[Humour and satire — "Der Kokh-lefl"; the ritual-slaughter law, ghetto benches at the universities.] Those Above with Those Below.
Once, "the topmost of the shtoysl" [?; unclear expression, apparently "the top of the heap", the most important part] and other upper parts — let us say, like a head — were aristocrats... The "above" conducted the "below"...
Today it is quite different: the lowest part leads the topmost part around by the nose. Take, for example, the slaughter law. It made the "zadek" [Polish: backside; here also the hindquarter of the animal, affected by the slaughter restrictions] into the very "topmost of the shtoysl"; the un-porged "zadek" is on everyone's lips today. A whole "ya tebie vam" [?; probably Polish "ja tobie dam" — "I'll show you!"] — everywhere is full of "zadek"...
Take, for example, the fact that the Endek [National Democrat] students do not want to sit together with Jews and have [?] even held a plebiscite about it — whom are they forbidding [?] here, if not the Aryan "seat-part"? With them too the "seat-part" leads the "shel rosh" [the head-tefillin, i.e. the head]...

The Beautiful Benvenida (12)

[Serialized novel — Benvenida, the Venetian ghetto, Spain and Turkey; instalment 12.] (12) The Beautiful Benvenida
A novel that took place in the first Jewish ghetto and stirred up the governments of Spain and Turkey.
Philip the Third was then King of Spain. When his father died, he took over together with the inheritance also a war, which was then being waged between Spain and [printed "in" — apparently a misprint for "and"] England on one side and Spain and Holland on the other. In order to be strong on the war front, Spain entered into an agreement with Turkey on military neutrality and mutual trade. Nathan's father, Shlomo Ashkenazi, was the diplomatic intermediary.
The war ended; the courtiers of Spain then realised that Turkey gains more from this agreement than Spain. Now they incited the king to withdraw from the agreement, and as an argument they put forward:
— Spain can renounce [?] the agreement on the grounds that diplomats from Turkey meddle in the internal life of Spain, when something of it concerns another country.
— An example?
— The captive Benvenida...
Allegedly [?], Spain had the right to demand from the Venetian government that it send back runaway Marranos from Spain, and a diplomat from Turkey, Nathan Ashkenazi, stood in the way.
King Philip the Third was a weakling and a "valti" [?], and the courtiers did with him whatever they wanted. What was going on in his kingdom did not interest him; his energy was mainly occupied with plans for whether he could get this or that court lady as a mistress. Under his rule Spain went downhill; the country, as it were, began to rot; it lost its foreign trade. Its universities, which had formerly stood in the educated world of other countries, lost their lustre. People then began calling Spain "the rubbish bin of Europe". Morally it had sunk very low. One constantly heard of scandals. It was a wild [?], lustful life. When the king's attention was drawn to it, he giggled [?], and to show the Christian world how pious he was, he incited the Inquisition to be even more brutal than it had been. The Grand Inquisitor at the time was Fernando Valden [Valdés?]; in many details he went even further and acted more savagely than the historically notorious [?] Torquemada a hundred years earlier. He had three Englishmen, Protestant Christians, seized in Spain, and even without a trial burned them alive, drove them onto a pyre of the Inquisition, although this was against the agreements Spain had with England. It was on the point of England declaring war on Spain again, and in order to prove to England that it had not been a domestic act but a religious one, King Philip the Third incited the Inquisitor Valden to demand [?] that all Marranos be persecuted wherever they might be. The question of Benvenida in Venice reached the royal court, and the Inquisitor stormed that the Venetian government be required to send Benvenida back immediately, and the king had already begun to rage, in the name of piety, that his diplomats should gain influence in Venice so that it would come about as quickly as possible.
Because of the court politics that had become entangled here around Benvenida's fate, a compromise was reached between king and Inquisitor: the Spanish ambassador in Venice was to assure the leaders of that government that Benvenida would not be handed over to the Inquisition; she was to be sent back to Spain directly to the royal court.
At the same time there were rumours, and they came from the ghetto [?] in Venice, that King Philip had learned from his ambassador that Benvenida was a great beauty, that her splendour was not being extinguished in the stone prison cellar in which she was held, that she was blooming there like a fresh flower, and that he wanted to have her at his royal court in order to force her to live with him as a mistress.
The king indeed let his ambassador in Venice know that he should promise everything and let Benvenida in prison know that the most magnificent room in his palace was waiting for her.
All sorts of reports reached the ghetto about the struggle being waged over Benvenida, and prayers were said in the synagogues of the ghetto that her heart should not grow weak, that she should endure all sufferings and reject all offers.
Benvenida's first protector, Abraham Carpi, met constantly with leaders of the Venetian government in the name of Nathan Ashkenazi and encouraged them not to accept the offers of the Spanish royal court.
At the Sultan's court in Turkey and at the royal court in Spain Benvenida was talked about [?], and the ghetto of Venice was tense.
After Nathan Ashkenazi's visit to the Grand Vizier, the mother realised that she would have to come to her son's aid. The situation around him had become serious: he is accused of being disloyal to the country, of having acted treacherously as a diplomat in Venice — and this could bring catastrophe on him and on the whole family, and indeed on all Jews. The accusations helped the Grand Vizier to reinforce the campaign he had begun to remove [?] Jews from all access to the Sultan's court. He planned a whole series of laws against the Jews, even a law forbidding Jews to wear clothes that aristocratic Turks wear. How could this end? The mother took him [?] to the Sultan — but on condition that he never see Benvenida.
— You are cutting my heart as with knives — Nathan Ashkenazi said to his mother — you are throwing me into the torments of hell, you are taking from me every interest in life. But one thing I ask of you, and you must fulfil it: the beautiful Benvenida must be saved; she must not be sent back to Spain. The Sultan must stand up for her.
(Conclusion follows.)
A union between the “Agudah” and the Radomsko Hasidim?

[Będzin — rabbinate and community.] (Page banner: “What’s New in Zagłębie?” — Friday, 17 Shevat 5697 / 29 January 1937.)

Będzin

M. Lewin as rabbi — the Radomsko rebbe’s brother-in-law as moreh hora’ah.

In this connection a consultation took place among the Sochaczew Hasidim, at which it was decided that in place of the above-mentioned deceased, who had been a Sochaczew Hasid, the Rabbi of Koziegłowy should be appointed moreh hora’ah — he being, as is known [?], one of the few true geniuses of Torah.
For this purpose a delegation was elected, which brought this decision to the chairman of the kehilla council, Mr. Rinski.
The latter, having heard out the delegation’s demand, chose [?] to declare that “between the ‘Agudah’ and the Radomsko Hasidim an agreement [?] has been concluded, according to which R. Mendel Lewin will be appointed rabbi and the Radomsko rebbe’s brother-in-law, R. David Halberstam, moreh hora’ah”...
Who decides whether to send a sick person to hospital — the doctor or the secretary?

[Będzin — health and municipality.] Addressed to our town councillors.

Jewish residents of Third of May Square come to our editorial office and relate:
A Jewish woman, walking across the courtyard of Cukerman’s house, slipped. From the hard fall on the pavement she suffered a haemorrhage. The doctor who gave her first aid declared that the woman must be taken into hospital as soon as possible. The same was also established by the doctors Jur-kew [?] and Kaszybowicz [?], who had been [?] to the municipal doctor, Mr. Bigli [?], about the case; he ordered that a “visit” be carried out.
And here begins the most interesting part. The official who carried out the “visit” “established” that the woman need not be sent to hospital at the municipality’s expense. Even though a group of neighbours had confirmed with their signatures that the woman is poor, the secretary of the Health Office would not issue the “skierowanie” (referral) [—] [?].
When the patient’s condition grew worse from hour to hour, Dr. Weinzieher was called; not only did he refuse to take a fee for the visit, he also ordered that the patient be admitted as soon as possible to the Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec.
Hence the question: who has the main [?] authority in the matter of sending a poor sick person to hospital — the doctors or the secretary of the “Urząd Zdrowia” (Health Office)?

"We want to spend the night here, at home it is cold"

So several boys begged the board of the Talmud Torah.
The following scene, which mirrors the great want prevailing among Jews, took place in the local Talmud Torah.
On the above-mentioned day the board gathered in the Talmud Torah, where a board meeting was to be held. Before leaving, those assembled noticed several boys lying on the hard benches in a corner of one of the classrooms.
"What are you doing here? Why don't you go home?" the chairman of the Talmud Torah asks them.
The boys burst into tears and say:
"We want to sleep here, at home it is so cold..."
The board members then collected a few zlotys among themselves and distributed them among the children, who only then went home.

Terrible Want among the Jews of Kielce

[Kielce — community; social relief; winter.] [Page banner: "Life in Kielce"; date boxes: Friday 17 [?] Shevat 5697 / piątek 29 stycznia 1937 (Friday, 29 January 1937)]
More than a thousand families have registered for coal.
Last [?] Wednesday the kehilla hall in Kielce was packed with thousands of poor people, men and women, as well as small children, who had come to beg for a little coal. The crush was indescribably great, and the [—] cries [?] of the [—] and unfortunate paupers [?] [—] to the very heart of heaven. Every single one wanted [?] to get into the kehilla office to collect the slip [?] for the half "metr" of coal [a metr = 100 kg, i.e. 50 kg], because [—] [—] to [—] the [—], in order to warm a little their [—] and [—] bodies, [—] by the cold.
Among the thousands of Jews one noticed many dozens of [—] [—] people who only a few months ago had themselves been donors; these [?] come-down [?] families stood among the great mass of people so that at least they would not be noticed so much. More than one of them had tears pouring from their eyes. Such a picture of Jewish want and suffering had never been seen until now. The number of needy always reached five or six hundred families, but now the number of those in need has reached a thousand, twelve hundred families, i.e. close to 5,000 souls — and nobody had reckoned with that.
In the kehilla office, while the coal coupons were being issued, Messrs. President Piotrkowski, Dr. S. D. Ejzenberg, parnas Meir Ejzenberg and others were on duty.
Because of the great crush, the commission moved over to the "Linat [?] Cholim [?]" beit midrash.
The distribution lasted until 5 in the evening. Up to this hour close to 500 "metr" of coal [c. 50 tonnes] have been given out. But that is like a drop in the ocean against the immeasurable [?] and indescribable poverty that now reigns among the Jewish population of Kielce.
The coal campaign must be continued. All those registered should [?] receive at least half a "metr" of coal. But there is no money, and the only hope is that the Jewish population of Kielce, and first and foremost the well-to-do Jews, will respond warmly [?] to the great cry for help of the thousands of poor Jews. Everyone must contribute to the coal campaign. No excuses whatsoever will be accepted. The campaign must be brought to a close with great success — the quicker and the sooner, the better.
A Sensational Divorce at the Kielce Rabbi's

[Kielce — rabbinate; local chronicle.] Because of the... great frosts...
A divorce at the rabbinate is, properly speaking, no news at all. But a divorce because of the... great frosts — that really [?] is quite considerable news, and that is why today's divorce has become the sensation of the day.
The story of this sensational divorce is as follows:
As every week, this Monday [?] too a young merchant set out for a few days to the neighbouring small towns in the private [?] car of a well-known firm. As always, this time too he took a heartfelt leave of his young wife. Knowing [?] that her husband would come back from the road only on Friday towards evening, she invited to her place her good "pshyatshel" [?] [Polish przyjaciel, friend] S., who used to visit her almost every evening.
Because of the great frost the car broke down beyond Busko, and the merchant, unable to drive any further, had, having no choice, to go back home to Kielce.
He reached home on Wednesday, around 12 at night. While still in the courtyard [?], he noticed that there was still light in the bedroom; he was sure that his little wife was still reading the newspapers with their various serial novels. Opening the door of the flat with his spare key, he found there, in a very "important" [?] position, his wife's "friend". To his question what he was doing here so late at night, the "guest" replied that he had come to "warm himself up" a little by the stove...
The "friend", of course, left the flat at once. What happened next we do not know, but what is known for certain is that in the coming days the divorce will take place at the Kielce rabbi's — and all because of the great frosts..

The Price-List Question Still Topical.

Recently ordinances of the administrative authorities concerning price lists (cenniki) have again appeared. The matter is therefore still topical. The Union of Chambers of Commerce in Warsaw has published special brochures containing the ordinance on price lists; the brochures can be obtained at the Merchants' Association.
The brochure reproduces the ordinance of the Minister of the Interior of 20 February 1923, which imposes on owners of storehouses, shops, dealers, restaurants, confectioneries and in general on enterprises of every kind the obligation to hang up price lists. The obligation applies both to retail and to wholesale trade.
The price lists must be in a visible [?] place, so as to enable the consumer to acquaint himself with them. In some branches it is impossible to write out price lists, because the number of articles is very large, and in such enterprises there may be, instead of a price list, a price book. Besides the price lists, the articles themselves — the goods proper — must also be marked with prices: every article (sort, gatunek) must bear a ticket with the price.
Every business must also keep invoices to show in case the authorities demand them.

Sosnowiec Is Called to Deeds!

Sosnowiec is hosting today two distinguished guests: the well-known leader of the Zionist movement in Poland, Dr. Yitzhak (Ignacy) Schiper, and the delegate of the Keren Hayesod Directorate, Mr. Gerbowski [?], who come to us on a mission of the Keren Hayesod.
Dr. Y. Schiper is one of the figures [?] of modern Jewish historiography in Poland, who has created monumental works on the economic history of the Jews and, besides that, a whole series of valuable scholarly treatises on various subjects of Jewish life in Poland.
Dr. Y. Schiper is today one of the leading personalities of the Zionist movement in Poland. For over 35 years Dr. Schiper has devoted his tremendous erudition, his learning and knowledge to the Jewish people, its hope and its future.
Dr. Schiper, who began his public career in one of the remote Polish provinces in Galicia, is one of the most effective, most capable and most devoted fighters for the liberation of the Jewish people and for the rebuilding of the Land of Israel.
Needless to say, Dr. Schiper is one of the most brilliant speakers in the Zionist movement, and every [?] public appearance of his is heard with the greatest interest.
Mr. Naftali Gerbowski [?] is one of the ablest Zionist activists in our country, and in the course of his long and fruitful activity he has succeeded in drawing large means from the Jewish public for the efforts on behalf of the upbuilding of the Land of Israel.
Last year Mr. Gerbowski visited the Land of Israel, and during his lengthy stay there he diligently studied life in the Land of Israel in all its forms. It will therefore be very interesting to hear from so splendid a speaker as Mr. Gerbowski a lecture on his impressions of our old-new land.
The mission of the distinguished guests is of great importance. They come to us at a time when we in the Land of Israel face new economic possibilities and very important political events. The two factors are closely bound up with each other, because with the strengthening of every economic position we give force and content to our political demands. It is therefore to be expected that the Jewish public in Sosnowiec will duly understand and appreciate their important mission and will answer the call of the Land of Israel with deeds.

A Stormy General Meeting of the Będzin "Gemilut Chesed" Fund.

[Będzin — interest-free loan fund, general meeting and elections.] As was to be foreseen, the general meeting of the Będzin interest-free loan fund aroused great interest. Although the barometer showed 20 degrees of frost, and the meeting took place in the "Orphanage" (Beit Yetomim) on Sienkiewicza Street, the number of participants still reached 125 members.
A few days before the meeting, consultations were held among representatives of various economic organisations about putting forward a united list of candidates. The "Agudah" and the national camp "mobilised" their forces within the bounds of their possibilities, because in essence it was not so much [?] about the fundamental principles of the fund as about taking revenge on, or rehabilitating, the person who had stood at the head of the institution. To this end the "Agudah", which defended that person, brought down the leader of the "Agudah", R' Itche Meir Levin, to influence the representative of the "Joint" [JDC] to change the "Joint's" attitude toward that person.
As said, the course of the meeting was stormy. On the floor the dirty laundry of the public mess [?] was washed, during which dramatic moments occurred. Outbursts [?] turned the whole discussion into a combat arena, and when the strength of the fighting sides had already weakened (it was midnight), the drama was ended by a declaration of the "Joint" representative, who came with a new "He held the mountain over them like a barrel": "Not one member of the present board — his voice thundered — may be elected to the new board, because so the 'Joint' wills it, and if you assembled do not comply with our demand, we will destroy the fund."
It turned out that "the people" did not fully accept the "we will do and we will hear", and re-elected 6 members of the old board.
The chairman Mr. Rubinlicht opens the meeting and announces that a proposal has been submitted to invite [?] Mr. Rigski as chairman of the meeting. Here breaks out
The First Storm
from the opposing side, which proposes Mr. Landner [?]; a scandal arises, which is liquidated by the "Joint" representative Mr. Taraszczański, who takes over the chair and invites to the presidium Messrs. Rigski, Landner and M. [?] Dafner, and as secretaries M. [?] Kaner and A. Ralnicki.
Then Mr. Rubinlicht receives the floor for the report on the activity in the years 1934 and 1935/36. In his introduction Mr. Rubinlicht stresses that the main point of a report is whether the business functions — and the figures show that in 1934, 626 loans were issued for 115 thousand zł., and in 1935 — 604 loans for 112 thousand zł. In general the board was active in all fields.
Speaking of the balance sheet, Mr. Rubinlicht says that we live in a time when very many defraudations and embezzlements occur, and the "disease" has also caught hold of the fund, where an official defrauded [?] nearly 8 thousand zł. But the board cannot be reproached for this. The fund's loss over the course of its existence amounts to 22 thousand zł. Besides this there are doubtful debts amounting to 19,000 zł.
After the reading of the audit committee's minutes by the secretary Mr. Rusinek [?] there begins
The Discussion.
The opening is made by Mr. Yitzhak Landner [?]. He criticises the management so far and appeals not to elect the existing board. Then board member Mr. Avraham Leib Grinwald comes forward with "revelations". He relates that apart [?] from the "fine" complaints in town about the fund, he turned many times to Mr. Rubinlicht, but each time Mr. Rubinlicht "calmed" him. Because of this the board members Hugowski [?], Balimowski and Grinwald informed the "Joint" in a letter about the doings going on in the fund.
A sharp speech of accusation is delivered by Mr. A. Liter [?]. He throws the whole blame on the chairman Rubinlicht, who permitted such criminal doings. If the chairman — says Mr. L. — knew that a period of defraudations "reigns", then why did he not think to check whether the same thing was happening in the fund? Don't let yourselves be talked into it — cries Mr. L. — that something was done in the fund [by the board]; one must not blame the board, but the chairman of the fund.
In the same sense speak Messrs. Herszlewicz and G. Landner. A little sobriety is brought in by the statement of Mr. Yitzhak Feigenblat. The blame — says Mr. F. — is also borne by the "Joint", which as a partner in the fund pretended not to know and tolerated all the doings committed in the fund. Mr. F. reminds Mr. Liter that when Mr. Bauszykowski [?] had to be removed, speeches of praise were then delivered for the very same Mr. Rubinlicht.
Mr. Rigski declares that the concept of
"Thou shalt not stand idly by the blood of thy neighbour"
compels him to take the floor. The whole criticism from the opposing side — he says — is only because Mr. Rubinlicht did not want to be in the Zionist headquarters [?].
Messrs. Kilsztok [?] and Aharon Barnblat [?] also speak; the latter says that thanks to the fact that Mr. Montag [?] gave [?] Balimowski [the post], the "fine" doings were discovered.
Board member Mr. A. H. Balimowski has a grievance against the editors of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung", which came out with the slogan that none of the existing board, who do not have clean hands, may be elected again. Mr. B. gives a series of details about the reasons for which he received a post, and about the unsuccessful [?] interventions with the "Joint" concerning the fund's situation.
Mr. A. Klajman states that because of the "heated" [?] atmosphere the elections should be postponed. — Mr. Ralnicki also agrees with this opinion.
Board member Mr. Hugowski [?] is sincere in his speech against Mr. Rubinlicht, and he says: we are waging a fight against Mr. Rubinlicht because he sells out the most vital [?] Jewish interests. Mr. H. [?] agrees that not one of the existing board may be elected.
Then Mr. Rubinlicht receives the floor to answer the opposition. But right at the beginning a sharp exchange of words takes place between him and Liter. Only thanks to the energetic action of the chairman is the incident liquidated.
Half of Mr. Rubinlicht's answer is
Self-Praise.
He points out [?] his great merits in the public field, giving away his money and also his time. Therefore he dismisses the gentlemen of the opposition, who — he says — are not grown-up enough to criticise him. Anyway, the demagogic speeches are because he did not want to be in the Zionist headquarters [?].
Regarding the management of the fund, Mr. Rubinlicht is of the opinion that from time to time the "Joint" should have carried out an inspection of the activity.
After that the chairman Taraszczański "takes"
The Word of Peace.
Everyone's eyes are turned to the speaker, from whom a "statement of principle" was expected. But how disappointed [?] the assembled were when the speaker launched a general attack on the whole board in general and on the chairman in particular. It is not true — he says — that the whole tragedy of the fund begins with the defraudation by the official Wirman [?]; the tragedy lies in a series of factors, in various positions, in various fields. A curse has rested on the fund from the very beginning: thefts, robberies, lawlessness, chaotic management, and [?] the board is to blame, which was elected already 3 years ago to put the fund on its feet; but instead of restoring it, a criminal negligence was practised, which was only discovered thanks to the shameful deed that the [?] soul, Liter, committed toward board member Mr. Balimowski.
Passing to Mr. Rubinlicht's unfulfilled responsibility as chairman, Mr. Taraszczański addresses Mr. Rubinlicht with the following words: "Mr. Rubinlicht raises himself above the heads of the opposition, which also does not mean the good of the fund, and resigns as the fund's further leader."
Then the speaker turns to the innocent board members and says: "You truly have not sinned, but if in your [—] [?]
The Torah Scroll Fell,
you must fast. Not one of you — cries the speaker — may be elected to the new board; this is the position of the head office of the 'Joint', and from this position we shall in no case retreat. But [?] if you, dear Jews, will not reckon with our decision and will not want to understand the reality of the fund, and elect those whom we do not want, we shall withdraw all the credits from the fund, and of the fund there will remain no remnant or survivor. On the other hand, if you do accept our command, we shall build up the fund, giving it the revolving credits."
Then the new budget draft is presented by Mr. Sahbin [?], providing for an expenditure of 10 thousand zł.; it is adopted without discussion.
It is already past midnight. The assembled do not hurry home and wait for the last item — the elections. Several lists figured in the elections. The elections brought the following unexpected results.
