were elected: Szymon Fürstenberg, Marek Szajn, G. Landner, M. Rozenker [?], M. Grinszpan [?], A. H. Balimowski, M. M. Jagodski, M. Hampel [?], L. Frachcwajg, Sz. Fridler, M. Galer [?], Sz. Rozenker [?], M. Kaner, H. Grojger [?] and M. Y. Frachcwajg.
Deputies: Sz. Albojm [?], M. Lask, M. Dafner, Sz. Plates [?], A. Ralnicki and M. Rozenbaum.
Audit committee: A. Perlmuter, A. Wajsberg [?] and Ch. Erlich.
With Strengthened Forces

[Kicker in a box:] On the general meeting of the Sosnowiec Small Traders' Association.
Next Sunday the general meeting of the Small Traders' Association takes place in Sosnowiec. Naturally, people are quite indifferent to the traditional annual meetings, where the report on the past year is prepared[?], the statistics, the income and expenditure — and with that the matter is done. Then one moves on: a plan and a budget are drawn up for the coming year.
These are all things one knows in advance, and it does not draw the members to spend a couple of hours on something that yields nothing...
It is quite different when there are certain ambitions: when one man needs to trip up the other a little, pull a chair out from under him, grab the "power" — now that is a matter. But when everything is in order, when people don't tear into each other properly and there will be no chance to "have some fun"[?], when no one will "show"[?] the other — so that one might get some enjoyment — then why go, and why spend the time?
This is roughly how general meetings are treated among us. No sooner does an institution reach a certain level and look after its members than the members no longer care to come and hear a report, to see what has been achieved and what has, quite possibly, been neglected and must be improved in the future. Among us people go to meetings only when there is some "fun"[?] to be had. Otherwise everything is left to God's care — who has a head for such "foolishness".
And therefore it is worth drawing the members' attention to the fact that, since you have an association which concerns itself with your interests and takes care to fulfil the necessary tasks of your professional interests, you must — exactly as you demand it of your association — stand on guard and protect the integrity of your leadership.
Your institution can be a fortress for you only if you take an interest in it, if you want to know what is being done and what is not, because everything is at your expense and on your "account". You must take an interest in the fate of your association at every opportunity, let alone at a general meeting.
Today you have a well-organized association with nearly a thousand[?] members, carrying on a many-branched activity which demands penetrating[?] ever further into the inner ranks of the small-trading community.
So there are enough serious questions to be raised at today's meeting. Therefore both your voice and your counsel are needed.
Incidentally, the management has sinned a little — for the sake of the shaky[?] "domestic peace" among the members — as a result of which the statistics were somewhat neglected[?], especially in the area of the sections.
As said, one must stand on guard and protect the integrity of the people's institution, so that it can work for the benefit of its members and their interests.
Let these words of ours be taken into account on the eve of the general meeting, so as to avoid unwanted frictions in the future and to preserve the good name which the institution deserves to bear.
Dr. Popuri.
The kehilla must not be burdened with new officials

[Będzin — kehilla and rabbinate; article.] Soon after the passing of Rabbi Reb Yehoshua'le the dayan, of blessed memory, a revival set in among our kehilla 'diggers' [intriguers]. Negotiations and machinations with a peculiar aftertaste began in connection with the just-vacated post, and judging by the liveliness and bustle noticeable among our crew, one may believe that one fine day we will stand before an accomplished fact: we will have been 'granted' [?] a new moreh-tzedek [rabbinic judge], some home-grown one...

And here we must cry out in good time: no new dependants! At a time when the situation of the gmina [community] is so sad, when the employees, despondent and downtrodden, knock day after day at the thresholds of the gmina and do not receive their pay — there are some who are owed salary for 18 (read: eighteen) months and more — there can and must be no talk of further burdening the already overloaded budget. It would be a cruel murder with respect to all the kehilla employees, who go hungry with their families and whose poverty and dejection have reached the highest degree, if, instead of thinking about realising and collecting [?] the budget revenues so as to be able to meet the obligations towards them, one should try to burden the budget even further with a fresh item. No! Not for a single moment may this happen. The 'bluni' [?] [vacancy] created by Reb Yehoshua'le's passing can be covered in a simpler way, one that involves no new costs. The rabbinate can be completed by co-opting the moreh-tzedek of Czeladź, Rabbi Lewental [?], who figures in the budget of the Jewish gmina in Będzin and whose co-option will involve no new expenditure. One should follow the example of Sosnowiec, where the rabbis of Pogoń and Katarzyna [?], who also figured in the budget, were drawn into the work of the Sosnowiec rabbinate, and no [?] fresh people were taken on; rather, they preferred to be able to be in order with respect to the dependants already there.

Between Czeladź and Będzin communication is nowadays so eased and speeded up that they form almost one city, and the Czeladź rabbi can officiate in Będzin without any difficulty.

This is the natural way, demanded by all honest-minded people who are familiar with the sad situation of the Będzin gmina.

With this proposal we incidentally aim [?] to curb the appetites of [seekers of] an easy little income, or simply to provide [?] for some [?] ..., because every action in that direction will meet with sharp resistance from the entire Jewish population.

It is also to be hoped that the honest parnassim and councillors [?] will stand on guard and will not allow any machinations, but will agree to the above-mentioned plan, which is the only realistic and honest way.

X.
Incidents.

[Zagłębie — public life; article.] The serious gangrene bacilli of our public life, especially in Zagłębie, are — incidents.

There is not a single little corner of our public life in Zagłębie that is not eaten through by the 'incidents' bacillus, which has gangrened and atrophied the power of resistance and the activity of our day-to-day life. Wherever you look and wherever you turn — everywhere one finds it, the disease, like a decline, and it brings with it all sorts of stumbling-blocks and complications...

We will not point out today where the disease we have touched upon reigns; we will have to take upon ourselves, on occasion, the difficult mission of doing so. It would, however, have pleased us if we could point to a few specific spots where the 'disease' reigns, so as to be able to draw attention and alert the public: 'Contagious [?] — entry forbidden'.

Unfortunately our town is, in this field, at a generalised stage. Therefore we generalise the question of incidents, which we discuss from a general public standpoint.

If our words strike the right place and find due understanding, it will gladly [?] please us. If, however, our appeal is somewhere received with displeasure, we are prepared for that too. We must do our duty and draw the attention of the Jewish public of Zagłębie to the danger that incidents spread in the bodies [?] in which our public life is concentrated.

We must, however, state that the disputes and quarrels that arise in any public work whatsoever are mostly carried over from the private sphere. At a meeting or some other gathering, conflicts suddenly break out [?] that have nothing in common with the activity of the given circle.

Incidents for their own sake [on principle] — would be a gratifying phenomenon; on the other hand, such incidents are a curse when they bear a personal character.

G. L.
The Cry of the Poor...

L. Fajgenbaum [Feigenbaum]
(A picture of the times).
I was walking wrapped in my winter coat, huddling against the enormous cold that raged in the street. The strong wind lashed my face without pause, and the ever-growing frost pierced me to the bone.
I dragged myself like a shadow through the almost[?] empty street, which, because of the strong, enormous frost, looked as if it had died. Here and there people appeared, almost bent double [lit. folded in three]; they strode quickly, almost ran, and quickly vanished.
And the frost grows and grows, and the wind too became stronger and stronger.
For a moment I stuck my head out of my coat and saw before me a little stove with burning coke, around which a few people stood warming themselves.
So I too went up to the little stove, to warm my stiffened[?] limbs.
The glowing coals gave off a pleasant warmth around them, reviving those who sought to warm their frozen limbs with that warmth.
I had almost forgotten my surroundings, for I was thinking then: will this glowing fire really be able to drive away the great, strong frost, the enormous cold?
Suddenly something, something shattering, woke me from my reverie. I heard weeping.
It was the weeping of a small child, whom a woman held in her arms, wrapped in dirty rags.
I shuddered.
— Woman — I addressed her — how do you dare go out into the street with such a tiny child, with such an innocent soul, when such cold is raging?
She slowly raised her face to me, and I saw eyes full of tears, eyes full of suffering...
— Who lives? — she said to me — here, to this fire, I have come with my little babe to warm up. At my place, in my hovel, it is cold; for weeks now no fire has burned in the empty stove, and here it is so cold, so frosty!
— At night, when I lie on my bed, I try to warm my child with the warmth of my body, my tormented body, and by day, when I feel my limbs dying from the cold, I come here to revive myself with a little warmth.
She burst into convulsive weeping; her body trembled so with pain.
And they both wept for a long time — the poor woman and the little babe; the echo of their terrible weeping carried far, far over the empty street and surely reached the Throne of Glory..
She wiped away her tears, calmed her child a little and said to me:
— Sir [panie], come with me and I will show you my home.
I went with her. We passed through streets and alleys and stopped in front of a house on a desolate[?] street.
The little house looked as if it had collapsed.
She knocked on a door. A hoarse voice asked who it was, and the door was hastily opened.
We went inside[?], and I froze at the sight of the terrible picture:
In the broken beds lay several children wrapped in dirty rags; trembling from cold, they burst into convulsive weeping and wailed[?]:
— Mama, we are so hungry, give us bread..
— And did you bring coal?
— You promised us that today you would finally heat the stove, that today we would finally have a little warmth!
I looked now at the unfortunate children, now at the unfortunate mother and at the mute witness, the ice-cold stove with its black gaping[?] holes, and I went out into the street.
Like a wild man I began running from house to house, from room to room.
Oh, what terrible, shattering and heartrending pictures my eyes saw!
— Hunger, want, poverty, cold! Oh! What a cruel cold!!
A cry tore itself out of my heart.
— Gevalt! Where are our communal workers, our communal providers?
Do they not see what our poor brothers and sisters are going through? Do they not hear their terrible cry? Do they not feel their terrible suffering and pain?
— No!!
They are blind to the terrible hell, deaf to the shattering cry, their hearts are petrified against feeling their suffering and pain.
Sated, in their warm homes, these providers sit and do not think at all how to improve the situation of these poor, these unfortunates.
— You communal workers, who are entirely sunk in the swamp of political and party struggles and strife — does the fate of your poor brothers and sisters, who are condemned to perish from hunger and cold, not interest you?
Help, help for your poor brothers is needed now!
A broad campaign must now be undertaken on a large scale, aimed at providing[?] our brothers with a bit of coal.
— Coal, black coal for our poor, so that they do not freeze from the cold!
In Sosnowiec at least a few individuals have undertaken a campaign on their own responsibility and by their own hand, and are running it somehow. Although a well-organised campaign would be needed, so that everyone could be provided for.
But why is such a Jewish town as Będzin entirely silent?
Will there really not be found in such a town a few people, honest, compassionate, who would undertake to organise such a campaign?
Remember that your poor are waiting impatiently for your help!
Hundreds of thin little children's hands, hundreds of darkened faces are turned to you. Help them, do not let them perish from hunger and cold!
They are waiting for your help!
Will they have to wait long?
Polish Jews and the Upbuilding of Eretz Israel.

Prof. Z. Brodetsky (London)
Specially for the "Zaglembier Tsaytung".
(On the proclamation of the Keren Hayesod campaign in Sosnowiec.)
It is no easy matter for me to appeal to Polish Jewry for new efforts on behalf of the Keren Hayesod. I also know the economic situation of the Polish Jews so well that I can[?] understand what such an effort means for them, and for that reason I do not do it with a light heart.
If I nevertheless feel obliged to say a few words about the Keren Hayesod campaign, I do so for 2 reasons: first, because Eretz Israel calls and demands the greatest sacrifices, and second — because the response of Polish Jewry, precisely because it finds itself in such a difficult situation, will be greater and stronger than the response of the Jews in other countries.
I know[?] in advance that the enemies of Zion, and also people from our own camp, will say: "Good, Eretz Israel calls — but why are[?] its gates being closed?" This question does not stand up to criticism. True, emigration restrictions exist, but no obstacles and difficulties whatsoever are news to us. They have accompanied us from the very beginning of our work of liberation, and we have never had any illusions.
We face a hard struggle. A struggle for the unlimited right to build[?] our national home according to our will. We have no doubts whatsoever regarding the existing political difficulties, and precisely because the struggle is so hard we say: "Keren Hayesod"! Why? Because the Keren Hayesod is one of the strongest weapons in our hard struggle. Through the Keren Hayesod our unbroken will and determination to remove all political and economic obstacles find their most prominent expression.
Protests sometimes have an effect[?], but the most effective political argument is deeds! Our conquests in Eretz Israel up to now are the strongest bastions[?] we possess, and these conquests we owe, first and foremost, to our national funds.
Because a successful campaign for the Keren Hayesod is — apart from our constant upbuilding work being done in Eretz Israel — also an important act of great political significance, I have the courage to appeal to the Polish Jews to support the campaign now under way.
We are well aware what a sacrifice it now is for every average Jew in Poland to contribute to the Keren Hayesod. Precisely for that reason his contribution is all the more important and significant. Only such a sacrificial effort is the most convincing.
Regardless of all obstacles, we have won for ourselves a strong position in Eretz Israel. Our political strength has grown thanks to our creative work in Eretz Israel. All attacks on our holdings[?] we must repel with new positions in Eretz Israel. Experience teaches us that these have indeed been the most effective weapon in our struggles so far. Only thanks to the methods of ceaseless, untiring work do we have over 400 000 Jews in Eretz Israel. In the future, too, concrete upbuilding work will be the foundation of our hard struggle.
These methods find their expression in the Keren Hayesod and through the Keren Hayesod. I am convinced that the Jewry of Zagłębie will rise to the greatest effort in this year's Keren Hayesod campaign, in this decisive year of our upbuilding of the land.
I deeply believe that the Jews of Zagłębie will, in this historic hour, manifest their unbroken will for the upbuilding of Eretz Israel by a fitting participation in the campaign for the Keren Hayesod.
Inventions that were not made this year.

[World — science and technology; article.]
The number of inventions made in the year 1936 is even greater than in the year 1928, when people literally counted on inventions. There is today [?] not a single country in the world where every day a number of patents on new inventions are not registered, of which people think that any moment now they will bring salvation to the world and overturn everything that has been devised until today.
According to a statistic of the Leipzig Fair, about a thousand inventions are registered every day in the whole world; of these 700 are not registered at all, because the official of the patent office points out that such a patent already exists, or that the new object is not worth registering at all. Of the remaining 300, 250 stay lying idle, because no moneyed person can be found who would want to exploit the inventions.
But the remaining 50 inventions a day, which amount to about 17 thousand a year, with which various trials are made — more than 90 percent are lost; barely one in a thousand makes its way in the world.
But what is one to say to the fact that, for instance, last year the world was afflicted with 400 patents for new — trouser buttons, with more than 1000 little machines for the kitchen household, and with 100 new protective remedies against nosebleed, of which not even one is any good?
Therefore the great inventions were not made last year either, although people had reckoned that any moment now they would shake worlds with the inventions.
For years, for example, people have been working to find a glass that can be kneaded and bent and will not break; more than 30 such inventions have been made, but not one of them is any good yet.
People hoped to win power from the wind and from the sun, which we have so much of for free, so that all the railways and machines of the whole world could be driven by it; companies were founded, everything possible was done, but for the time being it has not succeeded.
People reckoned on gaining power from the waters of the seas, to be used for technical purposes; test stations were built that cost a heavy fortune — for the time being nothing has come of it.
People hoped to find the "eternal light" — matches or small electric lamps that would burn forever; for the time being the world has not been blessed with it. Some technicians even boast that they did in fact succeed, and that the match companies and the electric-lamp companies bought the inventions from them and destroyed them at once, so that their business should not go to ruin. Whether this is really true, or whether it is merely an advertisement, cannot for the time being be ascertained.
People hoped to find pills that would contain all the substances a person needs [?] for nourishment. The benefit was [?] that people who have no money, or desire, or time to spend on eating could swallow such a pill and be full with it [—] a whole day.
That too has not succeeded. Perhaps people feared [?] that nobody would buy the [—], because man — as it seems [?] — has more pleasure from the preparations for eating than from eating itself?..
There are many more such inventions that might perhaps have brought the world some benefit, but for the time being they have not been devised, although chemists and technicians from the four corners of the earth have been working on it for years, day in and day out..
Z. Haber, Vienna.
A little feuilleton. "And they departed from Makheloth and encamped at Tahath" (Masei, 33).

[Poland — satirical feuilleton; ghetto benches and the slaughter law.]
Three of them came to heaven with complaints: a poor man, "Aleinu" and a mamzer.
The poor man complained that [?] in the beit midrash he always stands by the door and the rich men stand turned to him with their behinds. So in heaven they gave him satisfaction: at "Bo'i be-shalom" [in the Friday-night service, when the congregation turns toward the door] everyone will turn around to the door and he will have the rich men from behind.
"Aleinu" complained why it is precisely at him that people spit; so he too was given satisfaction: on Rosh Hashanah people no longer spit but sing "Aleinu" with special honour.
The mamzer complained why it is written "A mamzer shall not enter the congregation" [Deut. 23:3] — is he then guilty of his parents' sins? He too received satisfaction: the mamzer will become a dozór [kehilla board member], and the kahal will come to him.
But a fourth one also came to heaven: the "if-you'll-pardon-me" [a polite euphemism for the backside], and he argued:
— I carry the whole person on me, and if the head has bad thoughts — they beat me; if the hands do bad deeds — they smack me. If the heart lusts, sins — they spank me. And if one wants the brain to understand better — they let me have it again, because when you hit below, it goes up above. Why does such a punishment befall me?
In heaven they answered: your time too will come.
And the time has come.
The Endek students want to separate themselves [?] — separate benches. It is not a question there of who is more intelligent, who studies more diligently, understands better and knows more, but of where the "if-you'll-pardon-me" should sit down, because the "if-you'll-pardon-me" is more important than the heart and the head.
The "if-you'll-pardon-me" need not necessarily belong to a human being; it now counts for cattle and oxen too.
So [?] a little cow comes to heaven with an accusation: I am the [—] [?] with an [—] [?], I rock the little calf, I give milk to people, I supply the fattest piece of meat — but it is not over me that the shochet says the blessing, it is not I who have the privilege of being fried in better pans.
And now the time has come for the lower part of the animal too: the ministry wants [?] special controls on the bovine "if-you'll-pardon-me", and trustees will watch over what happens to the lower part; newspapers write leading articles on the problem of the "if-you'll-pardon-me"; the "Agudat ha-Rabbanim" rack their brains, hold confidential meetings — you think about Torah and wisdom? No — about the "if-you'll-pardon-me", about a remedy for the lower part of the animal.
Long live the "if-you'll-pardon-me"!
A. Szwarcer.
In the Jewish "Ubezpieczalnia" [Insurance Fund].

(From the series: A stroll through the Sosnowiec institutions)
By Ben Amotz.
The Out-patient Clinic.
Our visit does not take place in the municipal out-patient clinic, nor in the "Ubezpieczalnia" [the social-insurance fund], but in the out-patient clinic of the "Linat ha-Holim" in Sosnowiec.
On[?] entering the clinic, one is reminded[?] of the look of the old-time heders. A wide door opens[?], as of a steam-bath, and we are already inside, in the premises of the "Linat ha-Holim".
The institution has no more than 2 rooms. One room is given over to the clinic and the other is a "universal room". For example, in this room are the "waiting hall", where the sick wait to be received by the doctors, the office of the "Linat ha-Holim" and... a passage to the doctor.
We are invited into the "office", where the miracle of "they stood crowded yet bowed down with room to spare" holds sway[?]... On a narrow "strip" of the premises, fenced off by a "barrier", sit the daily "dyżurny" [person on duty] of the board and the secretary with 2 assistants, and besides them the nurse [pielęgniarka] is "on the move"...
In the "waiting hall" there is a din as at a railway station where homeless people wait for the train. The door gets no rest from the applicants, from opening and closing. Even the calmest person would need a nerve doctor... The little children, too, cry "in anger at the world order" and do not stop squealing, even when their mothers walk back and forth across the "hall" humming them a little song.
Brisk activity reigns around the office "barrier". Here "current" work is dealt with, such as issuing medical utensils, taking in the medicines the doctors have prescribed, and "light" patients also receive medical help. "I am already an expert," the secretary explains to us, "and I already know how to give remedies for headaches and other 'homely' ailments."
The secretary, you should know, is not merely a "znawca" [connoisseur] of illnesses; he is also a great "psychologist": the first moment he meets an applicant, he already knows whether he is telling the truth or not. "It happens many times," he says, "that a messenger comes asking for a 'utensil' for a sick person who is not a member of the 'Linat ha-Holim'. When one is healthy[?], one does not want to know that such an institution must be supported with a couple of groszy a week; but when one falls ill and needs medical utensils, then all of a sudden one remembers that such an institution exists, which sends out[?] utensils on loan 'bla yorim'[?]. But I just take one look 'at the messenger's nose' and I know that they want to 'pull a fast one' on me..."
The door opens hastily. In comes the doctor of surgery, and a few minutes later the doctor of internal diseases; the clinic room is well lit and the applicants are received.
"At other times," we are told, "the number of patients is much greater than today; the reasons are the severe frost and the prevailing influenza epidemic, and when the sick can no longer come, the doctors who work in our clinic have to go to them..."
"How many patients received help in this clinic during the past year?" we ask.
"We cannot yet give an exact figure for the overall help, because we have not yet drawn up an exact total. But the number of those who received help in the clinic reaches nearly 3 000..."
Three thousand!
And at that moment the Jewish tragedy was mirrored before our eyes, which is the outcome of our fragmentation, our divisions[?], of party politics and petty personal ambitions — which, thank God, have not reached at all into the four cubits of this institution; the contagious diseases "sappahat and baheret" have as yet no hold within the walls of this so modest clinic, and thanks to that[?] a sick Jew has a place where he receives help, where he is received with a smile and a good word, where he is not treated as a stranger — and not only a few individuals, privileged ones, alone[?].
Three thousand!
A sad figure! But sadder still is that "Jewish society" does not take stock and does not appreciate the importance of this small but very important work, which a few individuals, people of the "folk", have created and who will not rest content with the mere creation, but breathe a spirit of life into the great camp of poor sick sisters and brothers.
And where would these people obtain relief for their sufferings? At the magistrate's [town hall]? There, after all, they are not registered as unemployed; there they all figure as "kupcy" [merchants] or at the very least as "handlarze" [peddlers]...
"But why don't you see to getting other premises?"
"We have been trying," says the chairman, "for more than a year to find suitable premises that would meet the tasks of our clinic. Unfortunately, all doors are shut to us; some fear takes hold of the Sosnowiec house-owners when they hear the 'terrible' name 'Linat Holim'. We don't want alms from anyone; we are ready to pay rent like the best tenant, but because of this 'fear' the clinic has to exist in such miserable[?] conditions."
And as we leave the institution, the [—] turns to us with a request that we appeal to the Sosnowiec house-owners not to be afraid of the "Linat ha-Holim", which lacks not money but the main thing, the soul —
— suitable premises...
Pity — or a Debt of Honour? (On the members' recruitment campaign for the "Beys Yesoymim")

(On the members' recruitment campaign for the "Beys Yesoymim" [orphanage]).
Among the most important problems of our time, the question of the rational upbringing of our children — of turning them into honest and useful members of society — occupies, without any doubt, one of the most prominent places.
If for the child who is brought up by his parents at home the question is not so acute, it is, however, painful and serious with regard to the children who are unprotected, orphaned. But such a difficult problem cannot be solved by a handful of communal workers, however energetic they may be and however dear the matter may be to them; this is a task for the whole of society, for all its strata, and only with united forces will it be possible to accomplish something in this field.
And it must not be merely for the sake of the commandment, merely a matter of alms. Do not make of a child's misfortune an affair of charity for your [—][?] soul.. It is a debt of honour of every conscious and honest person, of everyone who is at all capable of suffering and feeling.
And finally the moment has come when the question of providing the Jewish orphan with the most necessary, the most indispensable — must be put clearly and sharply before the [—][?] society.
One must not for a minute [—] that the orphans have to be maintained. Society must not be indifferent and apathetic towards them, for the orphans are victims of the time in which we live, and it is not they who are guilty that cruel fate has struck precisely them.
As is known, the "Tsenriger"[?] [probably a misprint for "Bendiner", i.e. of Będzin] Jewish society is in general apathetic to all cultural and educational problems as problems of national self-help; it does not know — or does not want to know — that there, at Sienkiewicza [Street] 19, in the bright and splendid rooms of the orphans' home, a fresh, dear, warm-hearted Jewish youth lives and creates; that there a healthy, industrious generation is growing up, raised in the spirit of national culture, of honest and productive work. A generation that is being armed with professional knowledge and practical education for the hard struggle of life to come. A generation that perhaps receives a much healthier and more rational upbringing than most of our own "fortunate" Jewish children.
The care of orphans, which has been understood so rightly and has already cost so much money thanks to individuals of the Będzin Jewish community ["gm."][?], must not be allowed to deteriorate, must not shrink, must not be left to a handful of activists; the contributions of society towards the "Beys Yesoymim" must and need to be increased.
For this purpose the board of the institution has proclaimed a members' recruitment campaign; the number of members must be increased. New forces must join, all should[?] stand in defence of the lonely child and orphan. The population must provide the possibility of strengthening the institution, and we believe and hope that precisely now the full understanding has already ripened for the great cause of true child-protection[?] and orphan care, and that the call for help will receive the strongest and widest response.
Y. P.
Two Funerals (A Tale for Every Town)

[Feuilleton — satirical story; community, rich and poor.]
By P. Blumenkranc (Częstochowa).

A panic, a commotion in town; the walls are plastered with posters from societies large and small, listing the virtues of the deceased; all the seats of honour — as president, vice-president and plain distinguished member — with which he had been favoured throughout his long life are enumerated in the notices. Even societies to which the deceased had never paid anything could not withstand the temptation and put up posters about the great loss to the Jewish population. The posters of the "Malbish Arumim" society indeed tell of the great misfortune that has befallen the Jewish public, and they say:
"With great pain in our hearts and with bowed heads we announce the death of the great communal worker and founder of our society, A.H. [?]."
The commotion kept growing. Jews, poor folk, talked in little knots about how much the kehilla would [—] [?] demand for the burial plot, and wagered [?] with wit and doggedness, as they once did over the Russo-Japanese War: fifty th[ousand] [?] — certainly! — a little Jew, a shammes [?] from a [—] [?] shtibl, gets heated.
— Some reckoning, to take money — a cigarette seller [?] butts in — what is fifty thousand? From whom, then, should the kehilla take if not from such rich men? Why, he is giving his daughter a [—] [? dowry] of a hundred thousand gulden!
The Mishnah reciters fussed like Hasidim over the matzot on the eve of Passover; they swayed over their Mishnayot and droned out into the world.
The grand Hevra Kadisha Jews, who do not simply go to just any dead man, gathered in [—] [?] with the [—] "[—]" [?]; they combed their beards straight and sighed solemnly.
Strictly speaking, one ought now to tell the "life story" of the deceased, to show that the public knows whom to honour; but it would take too long, and since today's public has no patience and no longer wants to read even about gangs and Mrs [?] Simpson, we shall at least briefly relate the fruitful life of the deceased and his untiring public work.
One trait [—] adds to his character and portrait [?]: he was always consistent and far-sighted.
In his youth he fell in love with a pretty girl, but since he had no [—] [?], he married an ugly woman, who did, however, bring him a house as a dowry. Already then he duly appreciated the value of money and did not let himself be dazzled.
But only here does his fruitful life really begin. Being predestined to a life of [—] and [—] [?] activity, he starts trading and goes bankrupt, until he attains an important place in the mercantile world.
It must be said to his credit that, being capable and resolute, people always had to pay him their debts, while he for his part merely promised — just as an ambitious and practical man should.
But his ambitions were interesting and had a wider scope. In time he indeed builds himself a factory, takes on a "silent" partner with money, and when he sees that the factory has established itself, he tells the partner to go. The "silent" partner runs to lawyers, wants to sue — and it doesn't work: our dead man had foreseen all these things and bought everything in his own name.
And it came to pass one day (until then the vayehi had been a good sign) that he began to look around him and realise that one should not live only for oneself, that a man should not occupy himself only with his material affairs. He at once bought a candelabrum for the synagogue and had his name engraved on it. Then he donated [—] [?] for the doors of the beit midrash, gave coal for the winter-relief campaign, and began to [count?] [?] as a philanthropist.
Lately his business had become very ramified, and so "the respect" for him grew, for despite his busyness and constant occupation he still found time for communal affairs. The best proof of how busy he was lately is the fact that he was forced to hand over the management of his houses to strangers, and this unfortunately caused [many?] [?] evictions, of which the landlord can, God forbid, in no way be suspected (evil tongues, of course, interpreted it differently, but all that was out of envy).
• • •
As you see, it is no wonder at all that his death made such an impression. The women indeed dressed up in [—] and [—] [?] and ran to the funeral.
— The son, the educated one, is stone-rich — the women whispered "quietly" — they say he married a countess "of flesh and blood" [Polish: hrabina z krwi i kości — a born countess]; people come from afar to look at his "palaces".
Cabs and carts, buses and motor-cars stood in rows; whoever had no money ran ahead to the cemetery to hear the speeches.
Meanwhile the women snatched a [—] [?] at a [—] [?] and had a good cry. The first eulogy was given by the president of "Somekh Noflim", after him the rabbi, whom one uses [?] only for funerals when rich men die...
The rabbi closed his eyes and expounded with verses from which it emerges that the death of the deceased must be lamented and bewailed. He also hinted that the great misfortune happened because the women transgress the three women's commandments... The women burst into loud weeping, and the whole public felt lost before the great loss that had so suddenly and unexpectedly befallen the population.
• • •
When the public was already going home, tired from pushing and weeping, they met a second funeral on the way. Since it was already dark, the carter was in a hurry. The coffin "ran", and the mourners ran after it.
The public looked at the funeral and wanted to know who had died.
— What do you mean who — answers a little Jew in a cotton robe — no important man has died, since the kehilla earned nothing from him, that I can guarantee.
— You can tell by the children's [gait?] [?] what kind of rich man he was — jokes a Jewish woman.
— Now it makes no difference, now he is as well off as [—] [?] — says a crumpled little Jew as if to himself — as Job said: "Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither", what...
— All right, no difference — a Jew disagrees with him — as long as one lives one must have, and even after death there is a difference. After all, the rabbi did not go to the funeral of the poor man. Only there where one can... za pieniądze [Polish: for money]...
When the coffin was brought to the cemetery it was already dusk; the gravedigger was in a great hurry, angry at the [—] [?] funeral: "The pauper couldn't have died tomorrow [?]." He even permitted himself to dig shallower: just [—] [?]; everything went very hastily [?], as when one wants to wipe out the traces of a crime. A little boy, small and thin, began, by dictation, to sound out syllable by syllable the Mourner's Kaddish. His older sister lay on the grave and wept into the fresh mound of earth.
Their mother, broken, whispered tearfully: her husband died as early as yesterday, and because of Goldsztajn's funeral he lay [unburied] until this evening; she had no strength left to weep; she sways from side to side like a broken branch and murmurs:
— Moshe, how could you leave me? Wouldn't it have been better if I had lain [?] in your grave?
Her husband, the melamed, taught a few boys; he lived in a damp attic room in one of Goldsztajn's houses. The administrator wanted to evict the melamed, but the bailiff (komornik) had so far not carried out the eviction, because the melamed had lately been lying ill in bed.
— And what will happen now? Where shall I go with my little worms?
She sways, and her shrunken, dark face merges with the shawl she wears on her head.
The little girl lies on the mound of earth and weeps into it:
— Daddy, daddy!
The little boy stands at a distance, looking with curiosity at the commotion, barely grasping what is going on here. Suddenly he presses against his mother and clutches her dress with his thin little hands:
— Mummy, I don't want to go home without daddy, I'm afraid!
• • •
At the Goldsztajns' the rooms are noisy, lit up everywhere as if for a celebration. Chance [?] people come in and out; the sons, paunchy and grown, look askance at the noise; [—] [?] note on the posters: "No condolences, please" — and that's that.
They go round [—] [?]. A Jew, a sharp one, nudges his acquaintance and says to him quietly:
— Just look how busy they are; they are surely calculating the shares of the inheritance.
— [—] [?] what is there to say. There's enough to share out — I'd wish myself a tenth of a share!
At the cemetery the watchman [?] was hurrying people along:
— Off with you, go! It won't bring him back to his feet, enough weeping, I'm a human being too, enough burying for today. Little girl, you'll finish [?] your crying at home — that's it! — — — —
A Successful Achievement

"Lean?" ("Whither?"), staged by pupils of the Jewish Gymnasium in Sosnowiec.

The management of the Sosnowiec Jewish Gymnasium prepared, in honour of the recent Fifteenth [of Shevat], a spiritual "orech"[?] [probably meant: feast/meal], a true spiritual delight (oneg ruchani), which the visitors will long remember. It is not the first time that the pupils of the gymnasium have appeared on the stage of the Sosnowiec municipal theatre. The productions arranged by the school have always stood at a high level, but this time the theatre event surpassed every expectation.

The leitmotif of the play "Lean?" is the question mark, which stands before our eyes in all five scenes of the play. We wander without a goal, and now we join the ranks of the eternal wanderers, fresh [?] people who thought that their road of wandering had already come to an end. But a brutal hand thrust them out of their rest and drove them along the further road of wandering, with distant brothers from the East. The prophet Ezekiel saw on the rivers of Babylon that even the dry bones still have hope — and lo, the prophecy has been fulfilled: out of the already dry bones of Diaspora Jewry there has grown a fresh generation, a generation of enthusiasts and idealists, who took the trowel in hand and set out on the road of renaissance, of rebuilding, sweeping along with them the poor wanderers, the most[?] inspired circles of the Jewish people, the Hasidim and "fariyngs"[?] (in the fifth scene). All the finest, best and most fruitful forces of the people, under the leadership of the greatest Jew of our time, answer the question mark that hung over our heads the whole time — whither? There, where the young halutzim lead us, there, where our old-new home is being built. "If you will it, it is no legend." That is the short content of the play "Lean?".

All this was illustrated with the pearls of Jewish folk music and Hasidic melodies. The author, director and musician Mr. Mgr. Kab[—]uki[?] made use of the purest[?] motifs of the Bible (Ezekiel 37, "By the rivers of Babylon") and of the so close and dear Hasidic mysticism and folklore (Havdalah, Elijah the Prophet). The stylised Hasidic dances were captivating, the solos[?] were masterly[?], so that one simply did not want to believe that these were children, pupils from the third class of the elementary school up to the eighth-year gymnasium pupils; some of them gave the impression of fully[?] mature artists.

In the hall there reigned a rare[?] quiet and deep concentration. Therefore the management of the Sosnowiec Jewish Gymnasium deserves a great "yishar koach" and thanks for the great pleasure it prepared for us, and we wish them further success in their national and all-round educational work.

B.—T.[?]

A Little Letter from a Zagłębie Merchant.

[Humour — the "Kokh-Lefl" page; satirical letter on the economic crisis.]
A little letter from a Zagłębie merchant.
My friend! This week the komornik [bailiff] comes in to me and sticks little labels on all the furniture and on all the walls.
— What are they good for — I ask him — these labels?
— So that — he tells me — nobody touches it.
— If so — I say to him — perhaps you could stick such a label on my wife too?
— What for? — he asks.
— She's going to Zakopane, and I want nobody to touch her...
How is business? Not hard; I've found a remedy for my creditors too: when they come to dun me, I treat them to "tea-shots"[?] — I scald them with hot tea.
On the whole one mustn't[?] complain, for what more does a man want? "Children, life and sustenance" [bney, khaye u-mezoney]; well, children — that, thank God, I have, and not just plain "children" but footballers, goalkeepers [bramkarze] and boxers. "Life" — that I have like this: I have a wife; she lives anyway, and she takes my life away from me. If God helps and gives me "sustenance" as well, it would be very good indeed.

Flu — 3 zł.

The Beautiful Benvenida (13)

A novel. What happened in the first Jewish ghetto and stirred up the governments of Spain and Turkey.
The mother took him to the Sultan. When they were already at the court, in the corridors of the Sultan's palace, the decree met them[?] that Jews may not dress like aristocratic Turks, and especially he, the son, who was dressed in clothes like the diplomats, in a white silk robe with a white silk turban on his head, would now have to change[?] his clothes. In any case he had already been excluded from the diplomatic corps, he no longer held the rank of a diplomat, there was a demand that he resign[?] and he could no longer appear before the Sultan. The mother barely managed to obtain that he be allowed once more to appear before the Sultan together with her and in the clothes in which he went about.
She was a modest and a clever woman and had never interfered [—][?] in this or that law proclaimed by the Grand Vizier of the Sultan's court. At their audience before the Sultan the mother mentioned nothing here[?] about the son's no longer being admitted to him. The Sultan was friendly to the son of Mrs. Ashkenazi, who had saved him from the grave smallpox illness; but, broken in spirit, Nathan Ashkenazi could not convey to the Sultan everything that was on his heart. The mother spoke for him:
— Only one request we have, for a daughter of our faith. She is a Marrano woman[?] from Spain and is in a prison in Venice, and [—][?] for the honour of Turkey, that she not be sent back to the Inquisition in Spain.
The Sultan at once called the Grand Vizier to him. When he appeared, Nathan's mother told him straight away:
— My son withdraws from the diplomatic corps; [?] there may be a libel against him that he did not properly serve the interests of his country — he is content to step down.
After a whole series of explanations, in which Nathan Ashkenazi too took part, an understanding was reached that the libel against Nathan Ashkenazi would be "smothered", that he would not be put before a court of the palace; that the Turkish court would try to intervene for Benvenida, but in order that everything[?] connected with it could be settled without international complications, Nathan Ashkenazi must fulfil the condition that he would keep entirely[?] away and never even try to see Benvenida.
So it came about. From the Turkish court a messenger went to the ambassador of Spain in Turkey with notice that the Sultan took an interest in the imprisoned Benvenida — that she be freed and handed over to the ghetto in Venice. And a messenger also went to the ambassador of Venice in Turkey with such[?] a message in the Sultan's name. The royal court of Spain was at that moment in a situation in which it was better for it[?] to comply with a request of the Sultan, and the Venetian government too had an interest that it should end so.
Benvenida was freed from the Venetian prison and came into the house of her first protector, Abraham Korfu[?]. At the same time[?] there was an order from the Venetian government to the leaders of the ghetto that no celebration, no special fuss should be made over Benvenida's liberation. Nathan Ashkenazi withdrew from all public life in Turkey; he became a forever broken man, his dream of love was not realised, though[?] his heart was soothed by the fact that Benvenida was free, that she had been saved from the Inquisition.
Benvenida received her liberation with deep gratitude to fortune[?] that had brought it about. But she remained forever longing for Nathan Ashkenazi, the man whom she had seen only once, in a side-room of a hall where an aristocratic ball was taking place, where she had been led in secret, and since then [—] in her an eternal song of love.
Years later, when the story of her captivity was already as good as forgotten, Benvenida hired herself out as a washerwoman on a ship that sailed from Venice to Turkey. Perhaps she would succeed in taking one more look at her liberator, the man for whom her heart says an order of prayers. She did not see Nathan Ashkenazi again; in Turkey she heard that he had died.
Before her return journey to Venice she brought candles to a synagogue in Constantinople, to be lit in memory of Nathan Ashkenazi. The congregation wondered:
— A servant, a ship's washerwoman, and[?] from another land, prays for the soul of the son of Shlomo Ashkenazi!
She explained to no one who she was.
When exactly his yahrzeit was she did not know; she adopted the day on which she had seen him, and every year on that day she lit candles in all the synagogues of Venice.
Like a lonely saint she lived all her remaining years, and with a holy tenderness she kept Nathan Ashkenazi's memory.
Whatever money she had, she always gave away to charity, and all of it in memory of Nathan Ashkenazi.
After her death many children of the ghetto were named after her; there the nickname "the beautiful Benvenida" and even "holy Benvenida" went around.
(The End).
A “peace” conference between the Agudah people and the national camp on the rabbinate question. The matter is to be decided by a committee of householders.

[Będzin — community, the rabbinate question.] On Saturday night a conference took place in the kehilla offices, at which the question was discussed of how to bring about peace within the kehilla council over the rabbinate question.
The initiator of the conference, the council chairman[?] Mr. Rygski, declared that the aim of the conference was that, for the sake of peace, the national camp should agree that R' Mendel Lewin be elected as “deputy rabbi” (“forrabbin”). As compensation, the Agudah is ready to give an undertaking that during the present term no rabbinical elections shall take place.
To this the representatives of the national camp, the council's vice-chairman Mr. Landger[?] and Dr. Spgelag[?], declared that at the present moment they are not authorised to give their consent to any concession whatsoever, but if in the end an agreement is indeed to be reached, the national camp must obtain a member in the local rabbinate.
After a lengthy discussion it was resolved to hand the matter over to a committee of town householders. On the Agudah's side the committee is joined by Messrs. Paltiel Unger, Moshele[?] Szpira and S. Rozenblat[?]; from the national camp, Messrs. Chairman Fürstenberg, L. Buchweitz[?] and Moshe Lewin.
The obligation of the Torah “monopolists” towards the Talmud Torah...

[Będzin — community, Talmud Torah.] On Tuesday a meeting took place in the kehilla offices under the chairmanship of President S. Fürstenberg, at which the question of rehabilitating or liquidating the Talmud Torah was discussed.
A small number of members took part in the meeting (of the “Torah monopolists” not a single one came) and a few of the “common folk”.
President Fürstenberg, in his report on the state of the Talmud Torah, gives a survey of the activity during the several months since he took over the management. It turns out that the temporary board, which in its time was created solely from Orthodox Jews with the rabbinate at its head, did not even come to the meetings and, above all, did not even fulfil the monetary obligations it had taken upon itself. It is a disgrace and a shame — says Mr. Fürstenberg — that from the Orthodox magnates, who really ought to take an interest in the situation of the Talmud Torah, barely 600 zl. was collected, while from a few “sinners” 3000 zl. was collected. My indictment is against[?] the whole of Jewish society, which takes no interest in the 400 children who are being educated in the Talmud Torah.
Regarding the situation in future, various proposals are made. The most far-reaching is that of Mr. Szmul Lewin: that all houses of prayer be closed until such time as such a[?] sum is collected as will be the foundation of the Talmud Torah. Later the proposal is formulated very clearly[?] and logically by R' Rafał Lewental (son of the moreh-tzedek Lewental), who says that a certain contribution must be imposed on every individual for the sake of the cause, and whoever [—][?] refuses it shall be cast outside the camp.
Taking part in the discussion are Messrs. Grünwald, Dr. Piekarski, Najmark, Janowski, Kaminer and Ch. Erlich. The last declares that the “Agudah” is interested in the Talmud Torah being [—][?] because of the competition from the “Yesodei ha-Torah” cheder. The only way out is for the Talmud Torah to be transformed into a “Talmud Torah ha-Klali” (general Talmud Torah), where children of well-to-do parents would also study.
The proposal is received with great satisfaction by the assembled public.
After the discussion the chairman sums up the proposals brought in and declares that the Talmud Torah hangs in the balance between existence and ruin. For this reason he has put together a list of candidates from among his sympathisers. If — he says — the list is accepted, he will continue to stand at the head of the Talmud Torah; if not, he hands the Talmud Torah over into the hands of the Orthodoxy.
The proposal is put to the vote, and the whole public unanimously agrees to the board[?] that was proposed[?], and with that the meeting is closed.
She strolled across the market with a shovel on her shoulder and earned 10 zl. An interesting wager between a young man and a girl.

[Będzin [?] — town life.] On Tuesday, in broad daylight, the residents of the Old Market suddenly saw a well-known Jewish girl, lightly dressed, strolling across the market with a shovel on her shoulder. Acquaintances ran up to her and asked: what is this?
— I'm earning right now — the girl answered — 10 zl.
As we are informed, a wager of 10 zl. had been made between the girl and a young man. The young man had declared that if the girl would stroll across the market with a shovel on her shoulder, he would give 10 zl.
The girl accepted the “offer” and made the deal.
Festive services.

[Zagłębie — state occasions.] On the name day of the President of the State, Prof. Ignacy Mościcki, festive prayers were held in the synagogues of Zagłębie.
In the Będzin synagogue the moreh-tzedek Fridberg and the director of the gymnasium, Mr. Eighorn[?], spoke
Sosnowiec — Proposal to Expel Jewish Doctors from the Doctors' Association. / The Proposal Barely Gets 2 Votes.

Last Sunday the annual general meeting of the doctors' association in Zagłębie took place. At the meeting a proposal was put forward by a member to expel the Jewish doctors from the association. The discussion around the proposal lasted about 3 hours. The converts [baptised Jews] spoke out most strongly against the proposal. The proposal is put to the vote and barely gets 2 votes.
On the other hand, the proposal passed that the „Ubezpieczalnia“ [social-insurance institution] should take on 10 percent Jewish doctors.
At the same time, in the hall of the technicians, a meeting of Polish doctors took place, at which it was decided to separate from the Jews and to found a separate „Society of Polish Doctors“.
Talks on the necessity of creating such a society, in order to defend themselves, were given by Doctors Guriński[?] and Reiss. (The latter was the candidate of the Jewish ex-servicemen; the board of the Jewish ex-servicemen in Będzin in particular went to great lengths for him, calling on the Jewish voters in special leaflets to cast their votes for the „lover of Israel“, Dr. Reiss..)
Elected to the board were Dr. Zamenski[?], Dr. Reiss, Dr. Bieńkowski[?] and Dr. Bren.
An Unusual Din-Torah before Rabbi Szwarc. / A Christian Has a Grievance against a Jew: Why Does He Allow His Daughter to Make a Match with a Christian...

Last week a Christian came to Rabbi Szwarc and declared that he wished to summon a Sosnowiec Jew to a din-torah [rabbinical court case].
— What claim do you have against the Jew? — asks the rabbi.
And here the Christian tells the following story:
„My brother's son, still a schoolboy, goes walking with a Jewish girl, the daughter of... And since my brother is greatly distressed that his son will not obey him and stop walking with the girl, we have decided to summon the girl's father to the „Rabin“ [rabbi]. Perhaps the „Rabin“ will prevail upon the father to influence his daughter in the way that we cannot influence our brother's son...
The rabbi, having heard the request, informed the girl's father that he should come to the din-torah at 4 o'clock.
But not only the father — the whole family and the girl came before the appointed time and told him that the whole story is a lie; the Christian is simply persecuting the girl, from which she suffers a great deal.
The unusual din-torah did not take place, however, because the Christian who had demanded the din-torah telephoned to say that, since his brother, the father of the „bridegroom“, had fallen ill, he could not come to the din-torah.
Jewish Women, Help Relieve the Distress of the Jewish Masses.

In connection with the notice in the „Zagl. Tsayt.“ [Zaglembier Tsaytung] we turn with a warm appeal to the Jewish woman whose children do not suffer[?] from hunger [and] cold, that she help in the urgent campaign of necessary winter relief for poor Jews in Sosnowiec.
Our town, with the Jewish community numbering 17,000 people and a whole series of institutions — although their boards have over 50 active members — is not prepared for the struggle with the situation and with the terrible distress of the Jewish population. It is already February, and apart from promises[?] and meetings, nothing has been done so far for the poor Jew.
That is precisely why we turn to the women, as mothers of healthy and well-fed children, with the request for help in the work. We must put right what is bad, without looking to anyone; we must give coal and potatoes to those who need them.
Thanks to the initiative of a few people, headed by Mr H. Załdman[?] and Dr. Rozendowski[?], 120 korzec [a dry measure] of coal have already been distributed.
If the women cooperate, we shall with complete certainty ease the situation of the pauperised Jewish population.
Women interested in the matter are asked to report their readiness to cooperate by telephone, from 10—12 to Mrs Dr. Rozendowska[?], number 62244, and between 10—13 to Mrs Dr. Brodzińska[?], number 62224.
Sosnowiec Already Has 11 Licensed Kosher Butcher Shops

When the ritual-slaughter law came into force, 4 licences for kosher meat were allotted to the local town.
In recent days the number of licences was increased to 11.
General Meeting of the Small Traders.

Next Sunday, the 7th of this month [7 February 1937], the annual general meeting will take place in the premises of the local Small Traders' Association, at which a series of points will be considered that are of great importance for the interests of the smaller merchants.
Unheard-of conduct

[Page section heading: "Life in Kielce" — Friday 24 Shevat 5697 / 5 February 1937]
Of the Jewish "representatives" at the economic conference at the local starosta's.
A few days ago the Kielce starosta [district head] convened a fairly large conference of representatives of the Christian and Jewish merchants' and craftsmen's organisations. The conference, at which the head of the tax office, the labour inspector and the director of the "Ubezpieczalnia" [social-insurance fund] were also present, was called in order to hear the opinion of the said representatives on economic matters and to become acquainted with the economic demands they put forward.
The representatives of the Christian and Jewish craftsmen submitted a detailed memorandum in which they demand, among other things, that the authorities curb illegal craft work, i.e. not allow those craftsmen who hold no craftsman's cards to work.
The "Jewish representative" Mr. Nisinowicz[?],
a councillor of the Kielce Chamber of Crafts, demanded that supervision be stepped up over the meat smuggled in from other towns by such[?] persons who hold no licences (patents) and pay no taxes..
The Christian councillor Mr. Brudek, in the name of the Christian and Jewish shoemakers' guild, turned to the head of the tax office with the complaint: why does he not make use of the information supplied to him concerning the great[?] smuggling by the shoe merchants. He further complained: why do the Jewish shoe merchants force the Christian shoemakers to desecrate the Sunday holy[?] day. To the labour inspector — why does he not protect the interests of the shoemaking workers; and to the director of the "Ubezpieczalnia" — why does he not compel the shoe merchants to insure the shoemaking workers with the sickness fund.
Councillor Brudek delivered the said speech to the representatives of the authorities, as noted, also in the name of the Jewish shoemakers' guild, and that in the presence of the Jewish representatives of that guild, who, it seems, gave their consent...
The only one who answered Mr. Brudek was the delegate of the Jewish Small Traders' Association, Mr. Górski, who rejected Mr. Brudek's "pretensions" and put forward a series of economic demands concerning[?] the good[?] of Jewish commerce. On that occasion Mr. Górski also called on the Jewish representative of the shoemakers' guild to make a statement that the Jewish shoemakers' guild does not associate itself with Mr. Brudek's words. The Jewish representative did not do so...
The representative of the Merchants' Association, Mr. Kan[?], agreed with Mr. Górski's opinion and declared that the Jewish Merchants' Association, too, would submit a separate memorandum.
The officer for trade and crafts, Mr. Mgr. Bleczyk[?], replied to such complaints of Mr. Brudek and declared that it is impossible, in such bitter times as now, to ruin a poor[?] craftsman at one stroke by the methods demanded by Mr. Durek [sic, = Brudek], with the consent of his Jewish colleagues...
The starosta thanked those present for taking part in the conference and declared that he would from time to time hold such economic conferences, and that the representatives of the authorities would take a positive attitude to the demands put forward, which would be taken into account as far as possible.
The coal campaign must be continued!

The coal campaign for the more than one thousand poor Jewish families in Kielce, in which Messrs. President Piotrkowski, Dr. M. D. Eisenberg and parnas M. Eisenberg take a very diligent interest, is already nearing its end. So far close to 700 families have benefited from the coal campaign; for the remaining 400 families there is no coal left — money is lacking.
Those of middling means, among them a few rich Jews, gave proportionately; on the other hand, the greater part of the newly risen war-profiteer magnates have still given nothing at all to the campaign. These fat[?] Jews, who came to Kielce as paupers and amassed[?] considerable fortunes here, have stopped their ears to the heart-rending cries[?] of the thousand poor and unfortunate Jews.
But the leaders of the coal campaign must not give up; the campaign must be continued, and at any price several hundred more metres [100-kg units] of coal must be collected for the remaining[?] Jews. Everyone must stand by[?] this urgent campaign; there is no time, for Passover is approaching and one must already think in good time about a kimcha [de-Pischa, Passover flour] campaign.
Distraints on poor Jews over birth and death certificates

This week the municipal (magistrat) bailiffs carried out distraints on poor Jews for debts for birth and death certificates. For a death certificate the magistrat charges 7 and a half złoty; for a marriage certificate (the minimum) 20 złoty. These fees are being collected unlawfully, for, as we are informed, the magistrat has no resolution to charge such high fees — and that in such bitter times as now.
Unfortunately there is no Jewish representation in the Kielce magistrat that could protest against such conduct. The only thing we can do is to turn to the Voivodeship Office in Kielce, as the supervisory authority, that it take an interest in this question and not allow such high fees to be taken from the poorest strata — especially since the magistrat indeed has no lawful resolution for it.
Chosen by fortune.

[Photograph: portrait of a man in a hat and spectacles]
Mr. Shmuel Weringfelder[?], whose photograph we print above, was blessed by fortune at the drawing of the fourth class of the 37th State Lottery. On his quarter-ticket, number 177 374, fell a prize of fifty thousand złoty.
The sum he has now received from the General Directorate of the State Lottery will secure his existence for his whole life, and he will also be able to expand his business and at the same time help his relatives.
Many people dream of improving their situation, but one must remember that only he who holds a lottery ticket can win in the lottery. On the 18th of this month the drawing of the 1st class of the thirty-eighth State Lottery be[gins]. The Directorate has now introduced many innovations which give players still more chances to win. Already in the 1st class of the 38th lottery there are, besides the 5 daily prizes of 20 thousand zł., 1 prize of 100,000 zł., 1 prize of 50,000 zł., 2 prizes of 15,000 zł., 5 prizes of 10,000 zł. and many others besides.
In the 4th class, just as until now, the main prize is one million zł.
One should therefore obtain a ticket in good time, for owing to the great demand such may run out.
General Meeting of the Jewish Tailors', Hatters' and Furriers' Guild in Kielce

[Kielce — artisans.] Last Saturday night the general meeting of the Jewish tailors', hatters' and furriers' guild (cech) took place.
The meeting was opened by Mr. Sz. Lejchter, who explained the significance of the meeting, which had been called in connection with the new, approved statute.
Mr. Nuta Wajsman was elected chairman of the meeting, and as secretaries — Messrs. Laches and Sz. Garfinkel.
The activity and treasury report was given by Mr. Lejchter. Then a discussion [?] was held on the report, and afterwards a vote of discharge (absolutorium) was expressed to the old board headed by Mr. Lejchter.
After the budget [?] for the year 1937 was approved, a new board was elected, with a starszy [guild elder] (Mr. Lejchter) and a deputy starszy (Mr. N. Wajsman).
The board consists of Messrs.: A. Lewi, K. A. Wajcman, Ch. Richter, Sz. Garfinkel, Sz. Hofman, Ch. Szmulewicz, Ch. Laches, Ch. Gerstenfeld, J. Lerer, Sz. Szlach, M. [?] Hefter [?], J. L. Mendlewicz, J. Fridman and J. Rozenholc.
Elected to the audit committee were Messrs.: G. [?] Kenigsberg, Ch. Tenenbaum, J. D. Hefter [?] and Ch. M. Cemacher [?].
The Impressive Erets-Israel Academy at the Teatr Polski

[Zionism — Palestine.] The Erets-Israel academy, which took place this [?] Sunday at the Teatr Polski, turned out very impressive.
The academy was opened, before a packed hall, by Adv. [?] Proks. Then Mr. Abraham Białopolski delivered a substantive lecture of about 2 hours on the present situation in Erets-Israel and on our tasks towards the national funds.
After the lecture the musical part began. Messrs. Mangel-Lewi and Bramsowicz [?] performed several successful numbers. The choir of the kibbutz and of "Hashomer Hatzair" sang various historical and Jewish songs, and Sara Czyżyk [?] of "Kibbutz Bar-Kochba" [?] performed "Masada" quite finely.
With the singing of "Hatikvah" the academy was closed at 12 at night.

Elected Communal Representatives in Sosnowiec Called to Take Over the Kehilla's Affairs

[Sosnowiec — kehilla.] Last Wednesday the commissarial kehilla administration in Sosnowiec received from the Starosta (district head) an order that by the 28th of this month the kehilla's affairs are to be handed over to the new kehilla administration.
The "Agudah" Protests...

[Będzin — institutions.] As we are informed, the following protests have been lodged against the general meeting of the "Gemilut Hesed" (free-loan) fund in Będzin.
The protests are: 1) from the rabbinate secretary Mr. Herzberg together with 15 members, who protest that Mr. Herzberg was not allowed to speak at the meeting; and 2) from the "Agudah" (Agudat Israel), which points out that Mr. Taraszczyński [?], as an employee of the "Joint", was not permitted to be chairman of the meeting.
The Keren Hayesod Campaign in Sosnowiec Is Going Successfully

[Sosnowiec — Zionism.] Despite the counter-campaign by a certain quarter, this year's Keren Hayesod campaign is enjoying great success. The collectors are received everywhere with a friendly welcome, and the number of pledgers grows from day to day.
A Teacher — Only a Catholic

[Olkusz district — antisemitism.] In the village of Krasszyc [?], Olkusz county, a meeting of the Catholic organisation was held on the question of teachers in the public elementary (powszechne) schools.
After a lengthy discussion a resolution was adopted that teaching duties in the schools must be performed only by religious people and not by Jews, Masons, etc.
Through the mediation of the local priest the resolution was forwarded to the bishop's curia.
Applications for Permits for Goods from Abroad

[Sosnowiec — economy.] The Chamber of Commerce in Sosnowiec informs us that until the 15th of this month applications are being accepted for bringing in goods from abroad under the allotted quota for the months of March and April 1937.
Demanding the Lost Property with a Revolver in Hand...

[Będzin — crime.] On Friday towards evening a Christian bought goods for 3 złoty in the stationery shop of D. Gutensztajn in Będzin. On Saturday night, as soon as Mr. G. had opened the shop, the same customer came in and demanded that they return to him the spectacles he had left in the shop.
Despite Mr. G.'s repeated declarations that he knew nothing about it, the customer would not give up his demand, and he showed Gutensztajn that he was carrying a revolver...
Mr. G. then went out into the street and called a policeman, who only then calmed down the "heroic" customer.
Poultry Slaughterers Want to Be Paid for „Nadliczbowe“ [Overtime]...

[Będzin — kehilla; ritual slaughter.] The greater part of the poultry dealers in Będzin have always been privileged in that the poultry shochtim came to them to slaughter poultry at daybreak. This privilege, however, the poultry shochtim now want to abolish, and they have turned to the kehilla administration with a demand that for such a „duty“ they should receive a special fee from the poultry dealers.
The kehilla administration agreed to this „just“ claim and decided that for every „duty“ the poultry dealers must give the shochtim one and a half złoty each.
The poultry dealers will by no means agree to this, and as a result a sharp conflict has broken out between the poultry dealers and the kehilla administration.
