One-Time Donation Drive for the Będzin Talmud Torah.

[Będzin — Talmud Torah; education and welfare.] The new administration of the Talmud Torah, under the chairmanship of its president Mr Fürstenberg, held its constituent meeting, at which the presidium was elected.
As president — Mr Sz. Fürstenberg, vice-president — Max Langer[?], treasurer — M. M. Janowski[?], and honorary secretary — Sz. Lewkowicz[?].
President Fürstenberg, reporting on the rehabilitation of the Talmud Torah, points out that the first task of the new administration is to carry out a one-time collection of money, and at the same time also a recruitment drive for new members.
For this purpose a list has been drawn up of the well-to-do part of the Jewish population, whom the delegates of the Talmud Torah will visit.
The meeting also dealt with the question of shmura flour, which is sold every year at the Talmud Torah. On this it was decided that this year the rabbinate should issue a strict prohibition on shmura flour that will not be bought
flour that will not be bought at the Talmud Torah.
It was also decided that on the first Saturday night after Purim a tea evening should take place in the premises of the Talmud Torah, to which the notables of the town will be invited.
An Elegant „Woman of Valour“ Who Turns Everyone's Head.

[Sosnowiec / Radom — crime; courts.] A curious trial took place in recent days. It concerns a „famous“[?] heroine, Goldenguber[?] Welbajan[?], a permanent resident of Sosnowiec. She is accused of blackmail.
Until not long ago she sat in the Częstochowa prison, having been sentenced to a full year for blackmailing a well-known person from Radom.
Mrs Guber[?] had passed herself off in that area as the wife of[?] a senior court official; thanks to this she moved in the most elegant circles, and she managed to „draw in“[?] more respectable gentlemen into [—][?] loans...
Among others she drew into her net the engineer G. from Radom and squeezed out of him the sum of 1000 zł. It was for this very thing that the court sentenced her to 1 year.
Now, after she has served her sentence in the Częstochowa prison, 2 new trials await her.
A Holiday in the Middle of the Week

[Będzin — Zionism / Keren Kayemet.]
(From the Eretz-Israel bazaar in Będzin)
Grey Jewish life has been livened up a little thanks to the Eretz-Israel bazaar. For a whole week the bazaar made itself heard in town. Every day another event (impreza) with fresh attractions; the Jewish public had somewhere to come and spend time among their own, in a homely and pleasant[?] setting.
The start[?] fell on the “first night of yom-tov” — the opening of the bazaar. It is by now almost a tradition that whatever “Będzin arranges”[?] comes out decent and harmonious.
The beautifully decorated hall of the “Beit Yetomim” [orphanage], where the bazaar is housed, is packed full with a varied public, headed by the town’s notables; a festive mood prevails.
On the special tribune sit Messrs. President[?] Fürstenberg, Dr. Weinzieher, Advocate Warsglas[?], Mrs. Ts. Szajn, Mrs. Hitner[?], Y. Wygodzki and G. Landner.
After the orchestra of Folk School No. 2 plays the Polish and the Jewish anthems, three strokes of a hammer are heard, and the representative of the Keren Kayemet committee, Mr. A. Liwer[?], delivers the opening speech, in which he expresses thanks to the bazaar committee and especially to “WIZO” for their cooperation.
On behalf of “WIZO” the president, Mrs. Hutner, gives a warm greeting.
Then Advocate Warsglas[?] is given the floor for his lecture “The tasks[?] of the Keren Kayemet at the present moment”. The speaker gives a survey of the disturbances in Eretz Israel from 1929[?] to 1937 and comes to the conclusion that the latest disturbances have improved[?] the economic situation of the chalutzim in the field of labour[?] with Jewish employers.
Then Mr. Liwer[?] announces that the honour of cutting the ribbon is being handed to the public worker Mrs. Ts. Szajn.
Moved by the honour, Mrs. Ts. Szajn speaks about the importance of the redemption of the Land (geulat ha-aretz) and, amid strong applause, cuts the “special” ribbon of the bazaar.
The assembled public besieges the kiosks of: KKL, “WIZO”, Kibbutz, “Ha-No’ar ha-Tsiyoni”, the firm Goldfeld and “Gordonia”. The best impression is made by the “Gordonia” kiosk; especially unique is the “Degania colony”.
Places of honour[?] at the bazaar are occupied by the picture exhibitions of the painters Shmuel Ziegler and Artur Wiger[?].
Very successful was the second part of the programme, a concert by the singer Mrs. Distenfeld and Pinush[?] Zusman. Mrs. Distenfeld sang very beautifully “Eli Eli”, “Der Rebbe” and other Jewish songs, which had great applause, and she had to sing an encore (“bis”).
———
On Sunday a “five o’clock” [tea party] took place. The public enjoyed itself, went into dances (rikudim)[?], and the cash box took a handsome income.
———
Monday was dedicated to the youth. Several hundred young people gathered and spent a few hours listening to a lecture by Mr. Bergman and recitations by L. Lewin, Tusze[?] Gutman and others.
———
Tuesday was a “WIZO day”. In the afternoon a children’s performance took place. The programme consisted of recitations and dances, performed in the best way by the children of the “Gan Yeladim” [kindergarten]. The little ones enjoyed themselves greatly.
Later the same day an “Evening for the Jewish Woman” took place. The well-known artist Chanan[?] Lewensztajn took part and brilliantly performed a series of Yiddish recitations. Mr. Bergman spoke about the work of “WIZO” in Eretz Israel, and the pianist Miss Epsztajn played several compositions.
———
The bazaar committee also took care of the “bridge ladies” and arranged a “bridge tournament” on Wednesday evening.
———
On the whole the bazaar has caught on very well; the takings at the kiosks are good.
Great success is enjoyed by the picture exhibition of S. Ziegler, who is represented this time by a series of first-class Palestine pictures, such as Jerusalem, Haifa, Safed, a Yemenite synagogue, the Western Wall, etc.
The picture exhibition will close next Sunday.
What Is the Broad Gesture For?

[Będzin — Kehilla.] (The Będzin kehilla has become “active”: the budget has been drawn up[?]. — It is going downhill. — The system of “shmor li [ve-eshmor lekha]” — what use is there in the big expenditures?)
The Jewish kehilla of Będzin has become active — it has drawn up[?] the budget; for apart from fixing the budget one does not even know that it exists; for as to doing something for the good of the population, easing the conditions of its members, [bringing it] closer[?] to [—] — about that nobody cares at all, and about [—][?] all the parnassim couldn't care less [lit.: it lies in their left side-lock], since after all this has nothing to do with rabbis, dayanim, shochtim and cantors. Introducing a little order[?] has nothing whatever to do with politics, and if not politics, if not business — then why the work, why bother[?]? Who [would bother[?]] with it, and who would want here [—] the parties [—][?]?
From time immemorial, when a householder held a celebration in Będzin, [—][?], for whatever he did not want to do, he could not satisfy the klei-kodesh [the religious functionaries]. But that was once, not today; today all these deeds have reached their culmination point. If a Jew permits himself to make a wedding or a bris, it is by no means ruled out that a mess[?] will break out, that the joy[?] will turn into a quarrel, that the cantor will run away and the mohel will not come, or that a caricature of klei-kodesh will get mixed up with all kinds of beggars — [—][?] and “gevurah”, so that the celebration is ruined and then a general discontent arises, which produces the opinion that one must not set up a chuppah in Będzin.
Granted that this damages the material interests of the Jewish population — that is understandable: people travel out, buy there, and Będzin suffers the loss. But even if we disregard that, which is a great wrong, the question arises: how can one let it stay like this[?]? Why should one degrade oneself so far? Why must[?] one flee the town when one has to make a wedding? Has one no respect[?] for the old traditional Będzin, which, with all its shortcomings, has enough beauty and antiquity? A Będzin Jew has an open hand, knows how to appreciate and has understanding for the community. So why drive him out of town with all his virtues? Why should he have to shake himself loose[?] from you because of the lawlessness you practise? Why does nothing interest you, parnassim and kehilla people of all currents, except what has to do with politics and with wheeling and dealing at the expense of the kehilla's shoulders?
You become “active” when you need to take money from your members, and then you reap a ready harvest; at the population's expense you set about enlarging the budget, giving raises here, wherever [—][?], and then one must ask: is now the time to raise pensions? Do you also raise the pensions of your officials and employees in your ritual enterprises? Has anyone even thought of raises? On the contrary, we know that in your own house you cut and make reductions — so how[?] have you become generous with kehilla money which in fact does not exist[?].
Granted even that there is no “pious” kehilla, but the people's money was created in times when one spared[?] every Jewish groschen, when a rabbi or a dayan or a shochet did not want to burden the community, when they contented themselves with bread to eat, and a garment to wear already counted as luxury.
Pensions are raised[?] [for people] [—] who have both the one and the other, i.e. who can manage with bread to eat and a garment to wear. So this is suddenly the “broad gesture”? And where did you get this money from? Perhaps you forgot that the shechita will give you increased revenues? If not — if it turns out a fiasco — how can you allow yourselves the planned budget? From whom will you take the money? Perhaps you will not pay out the subsidies to the social institutions which you put into the budget? Will you [—][?] here — since the items are merely demonstrative and in fact have no significance at all — then nothing remains but to tear a strip off the broad strata of the population. The question then arises: may you do this, can you do this, and will you pay for it by overstepping the measure[?], since in the end you will have fewer budget-payers[?] from year to year.
Incidentally, we would still have understood and perhaps agreed with you on a higher burden, had it concerned important matters that would bring the oppressed[?] masses positive benefit, first-rate help.
But since it is settled[?] — the gmina [kehilla] is not [—][?] and does not even think [—] of carrying out any relief actions at all — and if now, in the middle of winter, a coal campaign is created, it is for appearances' sake, so that people should think, for example, that it would be talked about and the newspaper would write about it, since it is calculated from the outset that by the time it happens it will be after the winter. But this is no news; it is not the first time that such pretences are made. Had they really wanted to carry out a coal action, they could have realised it three months ago; and so it is nothing more than an experiment to blind the eyes. If they wanted to be honest and sincere, that too would be no wrong,
for as soon as one has nothing oneself and has troubles of one's own, one cannot think of helping others.
Running the kehilla's affairs is, to put it mildly, bound up with rather great difficulties, for all around one is in debt, and obligations are[?] rather large. The wheel that is turned there is terribly complicated, and there is never an account[?] of the expenditures; and the most interesting thing is that, despite all this, efforts are made to have more expenditures, to give raises and even to engage new officials, who then lie on the kehilla's shoulders, and when there is no pension for them, they sue and obtain [—][?].
If they wanted to be honest and had the desire to work for the common good, they would not follow the system of the slogan “shmor li ve-eshmor lekha” [“you guard mine and I'll guard yours”]; then a modus of economising and reducing would be created. Honest parnassim would think[?] of cutting the expenditures, reducing the pensions, reducing both pensions and officials, for in the end the gmina today is nothing more than a “meysim-shtibl” [a house for the dead], and for that it is not worth sustaining so much energy and making such large budgets, which will weigh heavily on the citizens.
The gminas give the Jewish citizens nothing[?]; barely does a Jew need something from them[?], he must pay for every trifle anyway; nothing does he get[?] there for free. So what are the huge expenses for, what is the big apparatus for — who [—] benefit has from it.
And therefore one must react: since the population has no benefit from the institution — it neither maintains nor subsidises social institutions, nor does it reorganise[?] itself or try to adapt itself to the needs of its members — the budget should therefore be fixed at the minimal measure; everything that is at all possible must be reduced, so as not to burden the town with superfluous expenditures from which society has no benefit. Let this be well remembered at every budget item.
R. Lesz[?].
First of All — Collect!

[Sosnowiec — the Jewish hospital.] (Once more on improving the condition of the Jewish hospital.)

The campaign to improve the condition of the Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec is under way, and already a black cat has run across it [i.e. discord has set in]; and with us[?] in Sosnowiec nothing more is needed — the slightest jolt[?] can do harm to the useful undertaking.

It is possible that there are individuals who are out to harm the campaign; they have spread a rumour that debts, too, will be paid off from the money collected. Apparently, once the chairman of the campaign realised that this could harm the undertaking, he found it necessary to declare that it is an utter lie, and the situation has apparently been saved — although we, with our modest understanding, do not see the sin in paying debts that one owes.

But why waste superfluous words, why divide up[?] the inheritance before it is a reality? We are therefore of the opinion that first of all the campaign must be properly carried out, and only then will the consultations take place on what to use the money for.

We therefore hold that, first and foremost, the campaign must succeed. The matter must be worked through[?] intensively by the committee, and the [contributors?] must understand their sacred duty towards the only institution for the sick.

One cannot come to the public with rescue campaigns at every moment; it is therefore desirable that nobody should refuse to contribute — on the contrary, one must give with an open hand and a good heart, and show pity and compassion to the sick and suffering, who cannot help themselves in a time of trouble.

It may very well be that the hospital needs various improvements and changes that would benefit the community; it is possible that there are certain defects that need to be revised — but that is a later matter, to which it will be necessary[?] to return. First and foremost the “sick” hospital must be made healthy, and then we will have the courage, the strength and the boldness to demand changes that will improve the situation and the housekeeping, as well as the management of this important institution.

But meanwhile[?] the Jews of Sosnowiec must give money and see to it that the campaign is carried out generously and brings due benefit to the town.

This must be well remembered during the days of the campaign.

Dr. Papuri[?].
Come With Me

[Będzin — sketch: poverty.] J. Weinsztejn.
(Pictures of Jewish poverty.)

“Come, son of man, and I will show you how people live in such a Jewish community as Będzin; and when you see the cruel poverty with your own eyes, you will not wonder that your work is in vain — you would rather just look and keep silent. Let those who adorn themselves with the title ‘providers for the community’ take it upon their own account; let this terrible poverty call them to account.”

So my companion said to me, and led me further through the back alleys of the town.

He led me to the Podzamcze[?], into the “kingdom of poverty.”

What did I see there?

Believe me, the last thing I want is to use my notes to awaken pity for the needy among our communal workers. I am not so naive as to think that poverty can be eliminated by chance alms; I only want to share here the impressions the visit made on me.

Moshe Rewicz[?], the hero of today’s sketch, said nothing at first; he was silent. When I came to him like a curious rich man to take a look at “how beggars live.”

But I too was silent. The poverty of that house caught me in its clamps; I remained standing as if turned to stone; I was ashamed before my acquaintances, the Jews of Będzin, who can afford the luxury of not noticing such poverty crying to heaven, which reigns in the Jewish streets.

Moshe Rewicz!

Your[?] name will not enter history! You are no poet, no orator, no communal worker, not even an extraordinary beggar — you are a child of Bontshe Shvayg [Bontshe the Silent, hero of I. L. Peretz’s story]. The difference, though, is this: Bontshe was silent in the world of truth, when he stood before the heavenly court, while you, poor man, are silent in this world.

When some time ago your wife was taken away to the hospital, you merely accompanied her with tearful eyes — beggarly tears which, it seems, did not even roll[?].

And when a few weeks ago the evil wind knocked on your “palace,” you were the first to take in the frost with open[?] arms[?] — and accepted it with love.

Through the bare, holed walls the frost strolled proudly into your living grave and set about its “work”: first it froze the little hands and feet of your three small children, who go about almost naked; then it dared to fall upon your wife and quickly laid her low; her lungs did not hold out, and she, poor thing, succumbed.

* * *

The doors of the kehilla opened and a Jew came in.. Do few Jews come there? But such a Jew had not been seen for a long time. Wrapped in an old, patched “sli-bushi”[?], from which here and there dirty bits of cotton wadding stick out, looking like muddy snow that is already about to melt[?]. From under his pulled-down, patched fur cap (kutshme)[?] looked out two large, glowing, wrathful[?] eyes. Only in a Jew who has escaped from under the slaughterer’s knife can one see such eyes. With his dishevelled beard and stooped[?], he looked like a bad dream from a desolate world..

Moshe Rewicz had come for a “kvitl” [a slip, apparently a burial permit]. One of his three children had died — of what? What difference does it make? Whose business is it, and who asks him anyway? There were 3 and 2 remained.. an ordinary beggars’ statistic!

And the “kvitl,” of course, was given to him without a grosz.

And Moshe Rewicz was content at that moment. There are still fine people in the world who give out “kvitlekh” for free — first-rate people!

* * *

And “music” Moshe Rewicz hears at home almost every day..

I heard it too, this “music,” and it still shrieks in my ears like the whimpering voice of someone who is choking and is already near the end.

In Moshe Rewicz’s home there is a wooden bed that once had four long legs. But little by little its legs are shrivelling, just like Moshe and his household: coal for heating he does not have, after all, so each time he saws a bit off the bed’s legs and “heats.”

And when Moshe Rewicz sets about heating a little iron stove, there is joy in the room; the children forget their sick mother lying in the hospital, and their little sister who died, and they rejoice in the bit of warmth the little stove gives out for a while.

The father shoves a piece of the bed-leg into the stove, and the children help too: they pull straw out of the holed straw mattress (siennik) and push it into the stove; the mattress is nearly finished — and what if there is nothing to sleep on? Never mind: beggars’ children cannot live on the future alone; they must have today in mind as well. Let it be warm in the room for the time being.

The two literally naked children stand around the little stove and look at the fire, which quickly devours the few[?] straws and swallows even the piece of wooden bed-leg.

And while the children watch the fire with happy little eyes, a wind blows in from somewhere and the fire goes out.

And suddenly the joy in the children’s little eyes was hidden, and it became cold again. The frost[?] spread its dominion once more over Moshe’s home.

And the silent Moshe Rewicz let a curse escape his mouth at his children:

— May you be snuffed out! Why did you put the fire out with your straw?!

— — — — — —

Moshe, Moshe! You have nobody left to curse but your naked, hungry, sick, forlorn children!
To New Exertions, to New Sacrifices.

[Eretz Israel — Keren Hayesod.] Y. Gruenbaum [Yitzhak Gruenbaum].
(Special for the "Zaglembier Tsaytung").

The extraordinary campaign for the "Bitzaron and Bitachon Fund" [Fortification and Security Fund], which was meant to create the means to cover the budget of fortification and defence, has only just ended. It has only just called upon the Jews of all the countries of the world to give us the means to repair the damage caused by the bloody disturbances, to strengthen the Yishuv, which so proudly and heroically withstood a six-month struggle and siege — and now we return to the ordinary year-by-year work, whose aim is to procure as many means as possible for the Keren Hayesod for its ordinary budget, for its year-by-year work.

The struggle for our rights is not yet over even today. It is now concentrated in the Royal Commission [the Peel Commission]. Our Arab enemies are boycotting this commission; they do not send their representatives to testify before it, but their spirit hovers over the commission, and their attitude is evident in more than one question put to our representatives. Incidentally, they have openly declared that they are giving up the fight by argument — presumably[?] because they feel too weak for such a fight; they know very well that their arguments and accusations have proved unfounded. Nobody claims any longer that our building work in the country does the Arabs any harm, that it pushes out[?] the Arab peasants; it has already become clear to everyone that Eretz Israel is developing so fast thanks to our work of construction.

That is precisely why they are now threatening to renew the disturbances if their demands are not met. As is known, they demand that our work of construction be stopped and that Jewish immigration into the country be cut off. It is believed that this is because of fear of the growth of the Jewish Yishuv, of the emergence of a Jewish majority that will turn the country into a Jewish country. Means are being sought[?] to tear this fear out of Arab hearts. But it is not so much about their fear. It is more about the fear of the Mandatory Power, which takes the Arab threats[?] very much into account and seeks compromises to pacify them — and it goes without saying that these compromises can only come at our expense.

We must be strong in order to defend ourselves against these dangers. We showed during the six bloody months how significantly our strength has grown since 1929. We owe this above all to the intensive work of construction that was carried on in the meantime with the funds of the Keren Hayesod. In every field new positions were created and the old ones strengthened, with the means the Keren Hayesod placed at our disposal.

Now this must be repeated in an even larger form, at a faster pace. With this, and only with this, can we remove the fear of the Mandatory Power and convince it and the Arabs that the Jewish people cannot and will not renounce the realisation of its thousand-year-old dream of liberation, of redemption. They must come to see that no effort is too great for us, that no sacrifice deters us. It must become clear to them that our determination will not be weakened, whatever may happen. For all other roads are as good as closed to us, and only the road of building our home in Eretz Israel remains open to us, thanks to our struggle and our work of construction.

This road must and will remain open to us. For that the greatest exertions of our forces are needed. For that the untiring work in Eretz Israel and in the Diaspora is needed.

In Eretz Israel we stand, as our forefathers once did, with the trowel in one hand and the sword in the other. We are always ready — without letting go of the tools of building — to defend, rifle in hand, our right to a home of our own, to an independent life, to freedom. The Diaspora must give us the people and the means for the work, for the struggle. It must share in the creating and share in the fighting — both in times of bloody attacks and in times of peaceful construction work.

In almost every country of the world an embittered attack is being waged on our Jewish communities. Everywhere we stand under fire; our battle front stretches across the countries of our largest Jewish communities in Europe and ends in Eretz Israel. But almost everywhere in the Diaspora we are mostly defending a retreat, partial or total; only in Eretz Israel do we advance, ever further, ever faster, regardless of all stumbling blocks, of all disruptions. In this our struggle in Eretz Israel differs from the one we wage in the lands of the Diaspora, for it is bound up with establishing and building, with work and creation.

We are approaching the Keren Hayesod campaign without waiting to rest after the exertions of the just-concluded campaign for "Bitzaron and Bitachon". We have no time to rest. The bitter fate, the suffering of the Jews in the Diaspora, which grows ceaselessly, gives us no rest. And even more so the necessity to entrench ourselves in Eretz Israel, to strike roots still deeper in the ancient soil of our forefathers, to become still stronger, still more numerous, so that our final victory may be assured.

That is precisely why we call on you for new exertions, for new sacrifices in the Keren Hayesod campaign, which we are now beginning.
Eating, Then and Now

[Article — history of food.] In medical circles in the four corners of the world there were, some years ago, great disputes between two parties of doctors. One side argued that all the ailments with which our present age is „blessed“ come only from the fact that people today eat too much. The other faction[?] argued that we do indeed eat more than our forefathers, but the various diseases do not come from that, because poor people, who do not have the means even for[?] a single meal, are also struck by the „lean sickness“.
I am no physician and do not know which of the two parties is right; this much is certain: we eat today a great deal more than our great-great-grandfathers used to eat. Moreover one must not forget that in the past people allowed themselves to eat, because they did not worry about any „slim lines“; they did not rack their brains over whether it is better to stay thin or fat; they ate so as not to be hungry, and not in order to look prettier or younger.
Whoever takes a look in the archive of the Leipzig fair at the menus of the restaurants of the past centuries can see that in the past one ate a single dish — meat. That was the only food.
True, in every restaurant everyone received a portion of meat of half a kilo. In addition one ate „riin“[?] (perhaps rice) or flour (potatoes were introduced in our parts only at the end of the 16th century). No bread was served with the meat either, because wheat, from which we bake bread today, was only „invented“ in the 17th century. Flat cakes of flour were baked over the fire and eaten with the meat.
Soup was unknown. Only in the 17th century did England introduce soups of wine and of eggs with water. Neither tea nor coffee was brewed; since there were no spoons, people drank the broth slowly out of little pots (perhaps that is where the name „zup“[?] — soup — comes from).
Since forks did not yet exist then either, meat was eaten with the hands. In the greatest houses one would nibble a few cloves[?] of garlic after the meal; in the finer houses peas were cooked, which cost more than meat.
In every house wine or water was drunk from one cup, which passed from mouth to mouth. The lady of the house had constantly to refill the cup and take out the crumbs that fell into it from the food.
Tablecloths were unknown; people ate on wooden tables. The meat lay on [—] single platter, and each [—] cut off his share with a knife. Fine[?] [houses] had earthen [—] for the meat; in simple[?] houses [—] it was laid straight on the table.
Fruit or sweets after the meal were unknown; these were introduced only at the end of the eighteenth century. The first egg dishes began to be made some 150 years ago — „gepelegitsn“[?] (word unclear).
In every house a large bowl of water stood on the table; before and after the meal everyone dipped his hands into the bowl.
The master and the mistress of the house sat at a separate small table. The children sat with their parents only when they were of marriageable age.
Z. Haber, Vienna.
Heard and Seen

[Sosnowiec — satirical feuilleton; Zionism, kehilla.] By Ben Amotz.
— On both banks of the Jordan...
On the Jewish street there exists an organisation which is not[?] a "[—] of its kind"[?], as the organisation calls it, and which does not agree that the Jewish National Home should encompass the "measure" that was designated under the Basel Programme, but rather the holy Jewish land — "in its length and in its breadth", as the verse says — on both banks of the Jordan.
It is therefore no wonder that sympathy for the organisation among the Jewish population grows from day to day, and not only because of the above, but because of its deeds, which are good proof that only the members of the org. are called to be the builders of the Jewish National Home in Eretz Israel, and that they are the true emissaries of the Redemption...
And their deeds they carry out to perfection, because they bear within them the spirit of those Jewish martyrs who perished with the Shema Yisrael on their lips, and the new "redemption-bringers" spread[?] their idea of the "Kingdom of the Almighty" (Malkhut Shaddai) and of a democratic Palestine [—]...
And over the Keren Hayesod "academy" in the Sosnowiec[?] city theatre, too, there hovered the spirit of the "Kingdom of the Almighty", which halted the power of the "false prophets" — of those who wrap themselves in the mantle of Zionists while in fact being "secret emissaries from Madrid"...
And indeed, when the "truth" was spoken openly and freely, those who belong to the "false prophets" got "frightened" and slept[?] through the academy...
But "these weep and those laugh": some wept and some laughed. The organisers of the academy wept over the spiritual decline in the Jewish [—], and those who had managed to drive the "[—]" out of the theatre laughed..
It is only a pity that the "Narodowcy" (the Polish nationalists) did not know[?] beforehand of the spectacle that had been prepared. Oh, how they would have enjoyed it.. Possibly they would even have taken part in the "triumphal procession" of the new "redemption-bringers"... But [—], even without the "Narodowcy" the picture in the theatre was not an ugly one. Every one of the visitors recognised and admitted that the new Zionist organisation will, with its new ways, reach its goal, and the Jewish people will possess the whole of Eretz Israel, in its length and in its breadth, as it says in the verse:
— "On both banks of the Jordan".
—o—
A "Revealer of Deep Things" (Megaleh Amukot)...
Two years ago he was revealed, and only now[?] does Jewish Sosnowiec see[?] what a treasure was to be found in the town, and nobody had been a connoisseur of him...
All his days his conduct had been that of a true "hidden saint" (nistar); he never let his whole "self" be recognised. But the greatest mistake about him was made by the Zionists: they always patted their bellies[?] and boasted with joy:
He is one of ours..
But when the "nistar" was revealed, only then did the Zionists see — or, more correctly, begin to understand — the true meaning of the verse:
— "Thy destroyers and they that made thee waste shall go forth of thee"...
As soon as his 18-year-old dream came true, the "nistar" cast an "eye" on the national camp; with a generous hand he supported "exclusively" the Zionist organisation in general and the Jewish gymnasium in particular..
In order to be loyal to all the payers of the "etat"[?] (the kehilla levy), he also satisfied the needs of the religious part of the population: for it he created a "masarnia" (a pork-butcher's/sausage shop), regulated the shechita question, so that the most scrupulous of the scrupulous could eat kosher[?] "meat" without any misgiving, and from time to time he preached moral sermons to them, calling for mitzvot and good deeds...
Besides this he, the head of the kehilla, took care of the "maidens[?], daughters of Israel", and for Hanukkah the "daughters" received from him — oranges.
And so that the "great world" should be well informed of his great deeds, he managed to make a "golem" out of a two-legged creature, which followed him at every step, licked his boots in front of people, and imitated all his movements and opinions (later the master of the house came to suspect that the creature was becoming disloyal, and he drove him out).
But the greatest "satisfaction" the Sosnowiec Zionists got from him last Sabbath. In honour of Parashat Shekalim he came to the synagogue to deliver a sermon on today's "shekels" — on the new kehilla budget.
And long, very[?] long did the "farewell" sermon last; had it not been for the women of the women's gallery, who began to "[—]"[?] that he should stop already, the sermon would have lasted even longer...
And he told a great deal, real "revelations". For example, he gave to "understand" why, for instance, he had not paid out the preliminarily budgeted subsidies to the institutions and societies. He said it like that rich man who gave nothing to any charity because — so he said — he had many close relatives whom he must[?] support; and when a poor relative actually came to him, he showed him the door, because "the family — he [—] — blackens his face before the neighbours"..
And the head of the kehilla went the same "way". He did not pay out the subsidies for the gymnasium because "the etat[?] (budget) flows in only from the Orthodox, so he surely cannot give away Orthodox money to the Zionists"; and conversely, when he was asked for the subsidy for the Talmud Torah, he wriggled out with the excuse that "the Zionist money which he has to give to the gymnasium he surely cannot give away to the Orthodox"...
The "sensation" of the sermon, however, was the "secret" which he revealed in the synagogue, and it was a word in season, a timely word, a "remedy" for the Keren Hayesod campaign being conducted in Sosnowiec.
"Jews!" — he repeated several times — "I swear by my beard and sidelocks that the activists of the Keren Kayemet in Sosnowiec have a big appetite, and all the money collected in Sosnowiec is eaten up on the spot"...
And you may "believe" what he says, because this was not said by some simple flesh and blood, some nobody, but by a leader whose abilities were revealed only two years ago, a man who has discovered many things in Sosnowiec and has earned himself the name:
— "Megaleh Amukot" (Revealer of Deep Things)..
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Terumah)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Terumah
—o—
a) "Speak unto the children of Israel, that they bring me an offering" (Ex. 25:2)
Regarding charity we find: "Charity may be enforced" — in collecting charity one may even use coercive means. That applies to charity for suffering[?] individuals; whereas for the taxes of the Jewish state, even when building the Temple, one was not allowed to use distraint. One was not even allowed to demand sternly, only to ask. "Speak unto the children of Israel" — to speak and to ask... Imrei Chen.
* * *
Why is no blessing said over charity?
Because when one gives a poor man charity there is, after all, a curse in it — that a person has been left so low that he has to depend on another — so one cannot say a blessing over it, no praise to God... Rashba.
* * *
R' Abushel of Frankfurt distributed his entire fortune to charity. His intimates admonished him: [—] is "after fifty — [?] fine; after forty", and that is why the Sages said "one who spends lavishly should not spend more than a fifth" — and you distribute your entire fortune to charity?
R' Abushel replied:
— It is indeed the law that one may not give away more than a fifth; if one gives away more than a fifth one commits a transgression. But of charity it is said "the more charity, the more life" — charity brings life, so it is a matter of saving life, a matter of life; and to save a life one may commit even a Torah-level transgression, even desecrate the Sabbath — all the more so a rabbinic transgression, such as the prohibition[?] on giving away more than a fifth of one's fortune...
* * *
The Sanzer Rav also acted thus[?]. His children complained to him: it is surely a sin to give everything away! He answered them:
— The prohibition "one who spends lavishly should not spend more than a fifth" was said of an ordinary person; but I am a great sinner, and it is written "redeem thy sins by charity" — sins can be redeemed with charity; so I must give that much charity, in order to wipe away my so many sins... Dor De'ah.
* * *
R' Eliyahu Chaim Meisel was also a [—] giver of charity, and when at home they wanted[?] to hinder him in it, he said:
— I once committed the sin of "spending more than a fifth" — so I must indeed redeem that sin with charity; and since I keep on giving charity, my sin of "spending more than a fifth" grows stronger again — so I must buy it off anew with charity...
* * *
The Chatam Sofer once came to a stingy rich man of Pressburg for a donation. The rich man did not want to give. After much argument back and forth he agreed to give some donation. The Chatam Sofer stood up and said:
— Praise be to God!
The rich man wondered: I give to you, and you thank God?
To this the Chatam Sofer replied:
— In truth the money does not belong to man: "The silver is mine and the gold is mine, saith the Lord" — the money belongs to God. Only, in Berakhot folio 35 the Gemara says that when a man does God's will with his money and makes a blessing over it — the money thereby becomes his. But you did not want to give charity, you did not want to do God's will with your money — so the money is not yours, and what I took I took from God — so the thanks are due to Him...
—o—
b) "And badgers' [tachash] skins" (ibid., 5)
"...and it had many colours, therefore [Onkelos] translates it 'sasgona' — it rejoices and glories in its colours." Rashi.
The Tabernacle had a covering of many-coloured hide, and they even prided themselves on the various colours — "it rejoices and glories in its colours". This symbolises that all currents, all shades within Judaism must have a share in building the Tabernacle. The Sadigura Rebbe.
—o—
c) "And thou shalt make a candlestick of pure gold" (ibid., 31)
In Yoma 33 the Gemara says that the candlestick must stand opposite the table.
Because the candlestick symbolises Torah and knowledge, the table symbolises bread — working for bread — and the two must go together: "Torah study is good together with a worldly occupation". It is not good when one takes the bread, the livelihood, from the candlestick — from the Torah — and not from the table... R' Yehuda Leib Ginzburg.
* * *
It is quite possible that this is why the teaching of Hillel was more accepted by the people than that of Shammai: Hillel did not only sit and study, but also worked hard for a living. Every day — the Gemara relates in Yoma 35b — Hillel worked hard and earned a tropaik (a coin). Half he gave to the guard of the house of study to let him in, and half he gave his wife for their livelihood; and because he lived by the toil of his hands he was more accepted by the people than Shammai. The Ethics of Judaism (Moritz Lazarus).
* * *
"When thou eatest the labour of thine hands".
Happy is he who eats from "the toil of the hands" and not from "the toil of the brain" — who eats from the work of the hands and not from the work of the brain... Rebbe Mendele of Kotzk.
—o—
d) "And the Lord gave Solomon wisdom, as he promised him: and there was peace between Hiram and Solomon" (haftarah).
It appears that the whole wisdom of a king and ruler is — peace; in that the wisdom consists, not in quarrels and intrigues... Ralbag.

By P. Blumenkrants (Częstochowa).
"They Are Distributing" Coal...
(A present-day sketch).

The president of the society "Ezrat Aniyim" [Aid to the Poor], R' Michael Welinson[?], and the vice-president, R' Ajzyk Adler, had for years been travelling together to Krynica.
They used to travel at the time of the Days of Awe, and that for two reasons: first, things are a bit quieter in business; second, by then the poor people are already [—] (passage unclear in the original); there are of course other reasons too, only it is not convenient to put them on paper.
So, towards evening, the president and the vice-president were sitting in the Krynica woods. The president heaves a sigh and speaks up:
— R' Ajzyk, a good piece of work awaits us! Winter is coming and we haven't a grosz in the till. We must give timely thought to a coal campaign. I no longer feel up to supplying coal this year (R' Michael deals in coal). We must already start collecting; this year we will have, no evil eye, some 12 hundred needy.
R' Ajzyk gave the president a "sad" look and, wisely:
— Well, of course we must already start doing something; first of all one must carry out educational work, issue appeals, send them to the homes. I note, however, that I have no intention of printing on credit any more (for information: the vice-president is the owner of a printing shop). Enough[?] lending; you surely must know that I do all the printing at cost price[?] (ahem, ahem).
How the presidents spent their holiday is not our business; for that there are [—][?] days...
The presidents, however, on coming home, set to work at once. The president convened the board and, sticking his thumb into his waistcoat pocket, began:
— "Suri" [i.e. Mori] verabotai [Gentlemen], as you know the need among Jews is very great; the crisis is making a ruin of our brethren; those who were formerly givers will this year be receivers. It is our sacred duty to set about the campaign now.
The discussion truly lasted several hours; everyone agreed with the president and remarked on it at once, but nevertheless found it necessary also to describe the need among Jews. The "intellectual" of the board gave expression to it:
— "Gentlemen, the pauperisation of the masses grows stronger from day to day, the need in the Jewish street is indescribable. Gentlemen, my voice trembles, horror seizes me as I watch the foundations of our life totter. The antisemitic wave rages...
The president pointed out to him that he was not speaking to the agenda, and the "intellectual", nodding his head to the president to show he took the remark into account, concluded:
— "Gentlemen, I am not playing at [popularity?]; my emotional speaking is a result of my deep pain. We must come to the aid of our pauperised brethren. I support the motion of our honoured president to its full extent. Urgent help must be our motto, the command of the present hour!
When all the speakers had described the great Jewish need, people began looking at their watches, and the president came forward with a motion:
— I move that today's meeting be broken off; I am still tired from the journey.
The motion was adopted unanimously.
• • •
Three months later. The thermometer shows 20 below zero, the streets are as if dead, little iron braziers with coke stand on the corners, children do not go to school — it is too cold outside; other children have even greater privileges: they do not get out of bed, because at home the iron stove stands cold and terrifying...
R' Michael sent out a circular for a board meeting, which took place with a small number of members: one had gone to Zakopane, the second — on business, and three were only 7 days past the flu.
Before the meeting opened, the floor was taken by the board's only craftsman, who always upset the members with his impudent talk.
— Honoured assembly — he began — first of all I must protest against our president, who did not find it necessary to call the meeting earlier. For three months people deliberate, and meanwhile the poor are swelling from the cold.
R' Michael began to fidget restlessly on his bench: the impudence of that cobbler's lad!
The speaker thunders!
— How can you fall asleep calmly while hungry Jewish children are freezing from cold! How can you sit calmly in your bright, comfortable, well-heated flats while our brethren are dying of hunger! You have been meeting for three months now, drinking tea and joking, telling stories and news[?], but it never occurs to you that at that very time a mother is warming her child's frozen little hands with the breath of her mouth, that at that very time in the poor homes they pull the straw out of the bed to warm a little water.
— Today I went into a Jewish home — a cellar, not a home; the window stuffed with rags, the iron stove in the middle of the room cold, in the bed lie four children, only because of the cold; they are covered with a heap of old clothes; the mother wanders about the room[?] with a kerchief on her head as if she were mourning someone. She tells me that her husband has no work, they won't take him on in any Jewish factory; he is ill, he must stay at home, and he cannot bear to watch the children's suffering. Yesterday, when the children began to cry that they were cold, he began to beat his own fists against his head; his eyes were so terrible that I thought he had had a fit of madness. I ran out of the room with a curse on my lips and clenched[?] fists, with a curse directed at you, the sated, the contented!
There was shouting and panic; the president rings, the crowd yells.
— Quiet there, shut your mouth!
— Such an insolent fellow, such a thing has never been heard — fumes a Jew with a broad beard of the wealthy cut — our "man with a say"[?], just look at the rich man: "Does he give much? Or is he still owed money?"
— "To jest niedopuszczalne" [Polish: this is inadmissible] — bangs on the table an "aristocrat" — [call?] the guards!
The tumult grew ever greater, the president rang, and all shouted together until the meeting was broken off.
• • •
The second meeting has not been called for the time being. The president is not feeling his best and the vice-president is busy.
In any case, as I have learnt, a meeting will soon take place with the following agenda:
1) Minutes.
2) Jubilee of the president on his 10 years of activity.
3) General assembly.
4) Annual ball.
5) Protest against the craftsmen's member.
6) Repair of the premises.
7) Coal campaign: a) report on the work so far, b) plan of further activity, c) financial questions.

A doctor of the sick fund says — „it's nothing“.
A private doctor says — „it's serious, the patient must be examined again“.
With flu one must above all beware of complications. Medicine lists the following kinds of complications:
A kehilla elder gets the complication in the brain.
A public activist — in the heart.
A rich man — in the fingers.
A bank director — in the head.
A Jewish town councillor — in the mouth.
An official[?] — in the ears.
A merchant — in the pocket.
A cantor — in the throat.
A radical remedy for flu is cupping-glasses, but lately cupping-glasses are used on healthy people too. The Endeks [Polish National Democrats] put cupping-glasses on the markets, the tax office puts cupping-glasses on the merchants, the magistrate [town council] puts cupping-glasses on the Jewish institutions.
Whoever has flu must take a powder to sweat. Young couples may replace the powder with dancing.
The main thing is that one must rest after flu; therefore during flu it is good to be unemployed...

“Just Trade — Never Mind the Loss”

[Feuilleton — Jewish shopkeepers and trade.]
(From the series “Jewish Livelihoods”.)
One can get used to everything — to good and to bad, to cold and to warm; one can live like a human being, and one can also live like a worm.
In Sholem Aleichem there is a story about a melamed who raised a goat so as to have milk. But he begrudged the extra expense of feeding it; so he hit upon the invention of weaning it off eating.
And had it not been for the accident that the goat got ahead of him and croaked, it would — as this melamed assures us — have needed no feeding at all.
Why am I telling this?
Because of our shopkeepers, who have become — no evil eye — such men content with little, and have grown so used to living so frugally, that they need almost nothing at all.
All day long one gets by on [?] (“shvi psi”), an onion, a radish, a hasty [?] potato, just to keep body and soul together; of larger needs there is no talk.
So it is a simple and understandable thing: if you need nothing, there is no need to earn either, and the main thing is only “just trade — never mind the loss”.
And indeed day and night one is worn out [?], toiling, always running out of breath and in a sweat.
To sit down for a while and reckon up, to calculate what the goods cost, how many other extras add to the purchase price, shortages and losses — that, our shopkeepers consider superfluous. Better for them the less they reckon and know. As it is written: “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow.”
They do indeed tell of a certain man who all his days passed for a great merchant and ran his business the old way, just with “mine” and “yours”; he lived all his years a quiet, respectable life, raised his children and married them off with pedigree and pride [?].
But then he got a brainstorm [lit. a “Shma Koleinu”] — to bring a bookkeeper into his business. Well, well, he did indeed come to a nasty end.
He hired [?] a bookkeeper, a Litvak, who set to the work with relish: he sat a week, two, endlessly brooding and rummaging among the papers, toiling over the books, calculating, writing, writing and calculating, wrinkling his nose and furrowing his brow the while, and in the end, after sweating it out for about a month, the Litvak calls out to the merchant: “Reb Yid, be it known to you that you are bankrupt!” —
Do you understand such language? He had traded so many years without books and accounts, fine and well, had married off all his children in joy and contentment — but the moment he let the Litvak, the bookkeeper, into his business, he at once saw that he was, may it not befall us, a pauper seven times over.
All these tales about books and accounts are worth, to the shopkeeper, a blown-out egg. The main thing is the competition, God help us: he need only work and strive to take in as much as possible and earn as little as possible, so that the competitor earns nothing. The more one competes, the greater a merchant one is. And [?] a livelihood? For that there is surely a verse in the Chumash: “He who gives life gives sustenance” [Aramaic “man dyhiv khayey yahiv mezoney”, printed “dytiv”].
And our shopkeepers do trade according to this system. A few examples of our own:
Take, for instance, an article like sugar, on which the profit is reckoned in groszy.
What do our shopkeepers do to out-compete the other fellow? Very simple — they sell at cost. So what then remains for him for his trouble?
— What do you mean, what? The sack from the sugar; with candles — the wooden box; with oil — the tin can. It is much worse for him with articles such as cigarettes, tobacco and the like, which one must, poor man, sell at fixed prices, otherwise a fine threatens.
But a Jewish merchant finds a way here too, and here too he steers his way out so that he should not, God forbid, earn anything: you are surely curious to know his trick? — Very simple — he throws in a few matches for the customer, and so gets rid of the profit.
As for goods bought on credit, our shopkeepers make it even simpler: the time from receiving the “bill” to the due date of payment is counted as profit — what more does one need?
That might perhaps have been quite fine, but sooner or later the due date creeps up, and one must run to the bank, discount bills and beg that they be rolled over [?], “prolonged”. So one holds out [?] until… until one has to [?] get an interest-free loan, pawn a pledge, or even — until a moratorium. Having no choice, one sells goods below cost, just to be able to pay — and pay one must, so as to get a little fresh stock, for without stock one cannot stand on one's feet. That is called competing.
•
In a certain place our merchants gathered [to consider] [—] what is to be done, so that they could exist and live like human beings.
After long discussions, squabbles and wrangling [?], they came at long last to the decision that one must trade “with reckoning” and earn.
Meanwhile a quarrel broke out between the members of the merchants' organisation and the small-traders' association over which of them should carry out the campaign to [combat] [—] dishonest competition.
During the passionate discussion between “the greater light” and “the lesser light”, such a storm-wind broke out there that it extinguished the kindled hope that “our merchants will at last begin to live like other people”.
Yigdal.
Kehilla board. Decision to open a competition for a rabbi and a 'podrabin' [deputy rabbi].

[Będzin — kehilla.] This week the kehilla board of Będzin, which has an Agudist[?] majority, was very active; it held several sessions at which the 'most urgent' kehilla matters were dealt with.
The main point at every session was actually to consider the appeals against the kehilla tax (etat), but in passing 'important' questions were also considered, for example: fixing 200[?] zł a month for Rabbi Khamayres[?] for fulfilling the special function of a rabbi, and opening a competition for a rabbi and a 'podrabin' [deputy rabbi].
The competition question was dealt with at Tuesday's session. President Rubinlicht, reporting on the matter, 'appealed' to the Agudist councillors to leave the question of the competition to the new term. Our term — said Mr. Rubinlicht — ends in a few months anyway. It is therefore not worth getting drawn into a fight over the rabbinate.
This [unclear word: 'skatsilas'?], however, did not help 'to oblige' the president, but supported the proposal of the 5 councillors that the competition be published, because 'the town needs it'.
The proposal is put to a vote and is adopted.
From Betar's activity.

[Będzin — Betar.] On Saturday the declamation contest named 'We Want[?] New Sounds[?]' took place at the Betar club-rooms. The contest drew many young people from outside the organisation. First prize went to 9-year-old Teri[?], who recited 'El Male Rachamim'; the next 4 prizes went to Kaplnik[?], Galenwer[?], Blacharusz[?], Hwiska[?], and 2 prizes to Waks and Selcer.
The contest ended, to the great satisfaction of all present, with 'Beshuv Hashem'.
The 'wywiad' question at the city council plenum. House numbers must be illuminated.

[Będzin — city council.] The last city council session was rich in emotions. The discussions were 'hot', which led to the session being broken off.
Before the agenda, the rescript of the Voivodeship is announced, according to which house numbers must be illuminated.
The 'treat' of the agenda was the supplementary budget, which was also sharply criticised by the councillors Dr. Weinzieher, Mrs. Ts. Szajn, Grynhald[?], Zylberberg and others. The speakers cite a series of unpleasant facts brought about by the 'wywiady' [means-test inquiries], which establish that the persons concerned 'do not need' the support of the Magistrat.
By a majority of votes the budget is not adopted (it is worth noting that the budget has already been carried out and only needs the consent of the city council.
In connection with this the president declares that he is breaking off the session.
The new-born child 'held back' the eviction.

[Będzin — daily life.] This week a poor Jewish family was to be evicted from its flat. But at the moment the komornik [bailiff] came to carry out his duty, the 'lokatorka' [tenant] went into labour and gave birth to a child. Thanks to this the eviction 'was no longer carried out'...
The Heirs of R' Yehoshele, of Blessed Memory — Sue the Kehilla for the Debt in Court. — The Trial Is Set for Today.

[Będzin — kehilla.] The kehilla owed the late R' Yehoshele the dayan (rabbinical judge) a sum of 5000 zł. For this the deceased held a written document, and since the document had to be renewed so that the debt would not become "przedawniony" (time-barred), the heirs demanded from the kehilla board a fresh document for their father's debt.
Because the board put them off with lame excuses, the debt has been claimed through the court.
The trial is to take place today
Sosnowiec — Annual General Meeting of the Small Traders' Union.

[Sosnowiec — organizations.] On Sunday the annual general meeting of the members of the Small Traders' Union in Sosnowiec took place in the union's own premises.
Although ill winds are blowing upon Jewish merchants, and upon small traders in particular, the indifference of the merchant element to its own interests has remained as it was. This was shown by the slight interest in the meeting: of over 700 members, up to 80 came.
The highlight of the meeting was the visit of the president, Mr. Oliner [?], who, despite his poor state of health, came and opened the meeting with a short introduction, in which he thanked the board for its cooperation. Thanks to this the union has brought a member into the kehilla council. "Two years ago," says Mr. Oliner, "when I described the situation of the Jewish small traders, I did not imagine that the situation would grow even worse." As chairman of the meeting he proposes Mr. Chaim Unger.
The chairman thanks for the election and invites Messrs. B. Gszepkowicz [?] and Brandes to the presidium, and as secretary — editor S. Lewkowicz.
Before the agenda, the chairman, in the name of those assembled, expresses thanks to the president Mr. Oliner, whose public work is appreciated by the entire Jewish population, and greets him with the traditional "Baruch haba" (welcome)!
Advocate Frenohof [?] in his greeting stresses that the greatest honour for the president Mr. Oliner will be if such a board is elected as will continue Mr. Oliner's work for the good of the members.
In the name of the peddlers' [?] section Mr. Wajcberg [?] brings greetings.
The secretary, Mr. Zvi Glajtman, reads the minutes of the last general meeting and also the minutes of the constituent session, at which Mr. Shlomo Kimelman was elected honorary vice-president.
The report on general activity is given by the vice-president, Mr. D. Durkiewicz. The report shows that in 1936 the number of members fell by 66 and today stands at only 707 members. The board carried on intensive work in all fields and stood on guard to defend the members' interests.
Among other things it is worth mentioning the obtaining of a member on the appeals commission in the person of councillor Mr. A. D. Kiner [?]. "Unfortunately," says Mr. D., "one must stress that whatever has not been done is due solely to the apathy of the members, who come to the union only when 'the knife is at their throat'."
The report on the last convention in Warsaw and on the economic conference at the town hall ("ratusz") is given by the "gospodarusz" [?], Mr. S. Honigman, who cites a series of sad examples resulting from the fact that Jewish merchants are not organized.
Mr. Kiner supplements the report with a long "al chet" (confession of sins) addressed to the members, who show no interest whatsoever in the union and consequently do not know the board's many-sided activity.
The treasury report is given by Mr. Ch. Dwiński, whose report shows that the annual budget amounts to over 10 thousand zł. The union owes 4600 zł., and 3500 zł. in membership dues is owed by the members.
After Mr. Chaim Rabinowicz reads the minutes of the audit commission, the discussion begins, in which Messrs. Mlotek, Slabocki, Szwajcer, Kraśniewicki [?], Feldman and others take part. The discussion was not a matter-of-fact one and bore the character of almost personal accounts with the board.
In the reply on behalf of the board Messrs. Kiner, Durkiewicz, Honigman and the director of the union, Mr. Kac, take part; the latter delivers a strong speech of defence, in which he says that the union has fulfilled its national duties and has even defended non-members. Mr. Kac appeals that the idea of organizing should penetrate the merchants' ranks, for "if not now, when?"...
Then, at Mr. Kac's request, an absolutorium (vote of discharge) is granted to the outgoing board.
After fixing the budget at a sum of 13 500 zł., they proceed to the elections of the board, which gave the following result:
To the board: Ch. Oliner, D. Durkiewicz, S. Honigman, S. Kimelman, Ch. Dwiński, A. Ojzaz [?], S. Fererman [?], A. D. Kiner, S. Gsmajner [?], Ch. Rabinowicz and Herszkowicz.
Deputies: B. Rozenwas [?], Bernsztajn, Werdiger [?], Szapiro, Wajcberg, L. Szwajcer and Marga [?].
Arbitration court: Dawid Szwajcer, Ch. Unger, J. Grachazina [?], S. A. Pardes, B. Ruszepkowicz [?], D. Zylberman and Szenker.
Audit commission: Man, Altman and B. Jakub.
Under the item "free motions" a series of motions are put forward in honour of the president Mr. Oliner, and it is decided to arrange a jubilee celebration next month.
After that the session is closed.
The Trial of the Bomb-Throwers Postponed.

[Sosnowiec — courts.] The trial of 9 members of the Endek (National Democratic) party, charged with carrying out bomb attacks on Jewish premises, had been set for Monday.
The defence was undertaken by the advocates Czarazski [?] (Warsaw), and also Kichta [?], Kowarski, Lisewicz, Chodyński, Florowski and others.
Because several witnesses did not appear, the trial was postponed.
In this connection the defence put forward a motion to release from prison the accused Hinziger [?] and Zaprudzki [?].
The prosecutor spoke against it and the motion was rejected.
Large Assembly on the Kashrut Question.

[Sosnowiec — kashrut.] On Friday evening a large assembly took place in the "Yirbi Goes" [?] cheder on the question of kosher meat in connection with the ritual-slaughter law.
After many of those present had spoken on the question, it was decided to turn to the kehilla commissioner with a proposal that he should make clear that in matters of kashrut the main say should belong to the Va'ad ha-Kashrut (kashrut committee).
As is reported, the kehilla commissioner is categorically against private persons interfering in matters that lie wholly within the competence of the kehilla,
Trumpeldor Academy in Sosnowiec.

[Sosnowiec — Zionism.] On Sunday the local Betar is holding, in the hall of the municipal theatre, a Trumpeldor academy (commemorative evening) in connection with the 17th anniversary of the heroic death of Joseph Trumpeldor.
In connection with the "bar mitzvah" (13 years) celebration of World Betar, the academy will be attended by the netziv (commissioner) of Betar in Czechoslovakia, Magister Menachem [?] Begin, who is known as one of the best speakers, and by the orator well known in Zagłębie, Dr. Jakub Szester [?] of Kraków.
—o—
"The Jews in the Middle Ages".
Today, Friday, at 8 in the evening, the Zionist Org. is holding in its own premises a lecture by Dr. Jakub Szpinberg [?] on "The Jews in the Middle Ages",
The general meeting of the Zionist Organization

[Kielce — Zionism.] [Page header: Friday, 1 Adar 5697 — "Life in Kielce" — piątek 12 lutego 1937 (Friday, 12 February 1937).]
On Monday the general meeting of the Zionist Organization in Kielce took place in the premises of the Zionist club.
The meeting was opened with a short introductory speech by the honorary president of the organization, Mr. Alter Erlich, who pointed to the importance of the meeting, which had been convened on the eve of the 12th national Zionist conference.
After the deceased Zionist leaders — President Nahum Sokolow, M. Dizengoff, Dr. Y. Thon and Dr. M. Klimel[?] [probably Klumel] — as well as the deceased members of the local Zionist organization, such as Szymon Kajzer, Moshe Kalbstein[?], Józef Dajbak, Zelig Grossman and B. Szmulewicz, had been honoured by rising, a presidium was elected from the following members: Y. M. Rajzman (chairman), B. Saszenberg[?] and M. Goldberg (as secretary).
After the reading of the minutes of the last general meeting, which were approved by those assembled, the delegate of the Central Committee, Adv. A. Salbe, gave a strong lecture on the present situation in Zionism and on the problems of the 12th national Zionist conference. The speaker discussed, in a very matter-of-fact and quite clear manner, the question of the unification of the Zionist central committees of Congress Poland with Eastern and Western Galicia, and national policy in connection with the new orientation towards the democratic camp. Adv. Salbe also touched, among other things, on the questions of aliyah for the General Zionists, and ended his lecture with an appeal to the members to strengthen and consolidate the ranks of the General Zionist Organization. He also called on the Kielce Zionists to complete the enrolment campaign as quickly as possible[?] and to take part in the national conference.
The activity report was presented by Mr. Grandfel. In his speech Mr. Grandfel, as chairman of the organization, discussed comprehensively[?] the internal organizational and political questions of the organization. The report shows that all kinds of collections for the Zionist funds are carried out exclusively by the General Zionists of Group "A", who are actively responsible for Zionist work. So it is with the "Keren Hayesod", the Keren Kayemet and other special collections, and only very rarely does one see any help whatsoever from the other Zionist factions. This — says the speaker — obliges that the General Zionists should also enjoy the right to aliyah; unfortunately it is exactly the opposite: all Zionist factions, and first and foremost the left-wing factions in Zionism, enjoy aliyah — only not the General Zionists. This weakens the activity of the General Zionists, and therefore it is no wonder that organizational work has lately been so backward. Mr. Grandfel further holds that the 12th conference must change this situation and above all think about rebuilding a strong [unclear word, perhaps "and vigorous"] Zionist organization, which shall not depend on individuals, as has been the case until now, but on all the positive forces of the whole organization.
The first to open[?] the discussion, in the political and organizational sense, was editor Ch. Wielany[?], who in a longer lecture discussed all the problems of the organization, among them the unification question, which must find an appropriate solution at the 12th conference.
Also speaking were members B. Saszenberg[?], Wilberig[?], Mrs. Erlich, Ostrowicz[?] and others.
After a vote of discharge (absolutorium) had been expressed[?] to the outgoing board, a new committee was elected from the following members: Eng. M. Cukerman, Dr. Polak, A. Grandfel, N. Kajzer, editor Wielany, Y. Alter, A. Finkelsztajn, M. Zylber, M. Lewin, Mrs. Erlich, Mrs. L. Rozenberg and Mrs. Hajchendler[?].
As first[?] deputies, members: A. Klajman, G. Polinak and Ch. Tejtelbaum. One representative each of "WIZO"[?], "HaNoar HaTzioni" and "Halutz Ba'al Melakha" will additionally be co-opted to the new committee.
To the audit committee, members: Y. M. Rajzman, M. Lipszyc and Mrs. Erlich. To the party court, members: M. Cytryn, Y. Rotenberg and Ch. Sanszeszet[?].
After the closing speech of editor Wielany, the meeting was closed to the strains of "Hatikvah" at 2 o'clock at night.
Scandals and brawls at Abba Achimeir's lecture in Kielce

[Kielce — Zionism; Revisionists.] This[?] Sunday Abba Achimeir [printed "Abi Achi Meir"], accompanied by Dr. Lipman, came to Kielce; he was to appear in the Teatr Polski with a lecture on the topic "The struggle with the red Satan[?]".
The meeting was opened by Mgr. Chitlin[?]. Dr. Lipman was the first to give a short speech, and after him Abba Achimeir began his speech. In his well-known manner he attacked the Zionist Executive, which in his opinion is guilty of the present situation in the Land of Israel. He also did not spare words about the "Histadrut", etc.
During these words a good number of rotten eggs came pouring down from the gallery, from which[?] the air in the hall became very stuffy. At the same moment a pigeon also appeared, which [—] flew over the hall [—] belonged to the sermon.
From the gallery there was also heard loud whistling and squealing, as well as various shouts such as: "Down with fascism", "Down with the execution[?]-policy", etc. Because of this a mutual brawl broke out between the Revisionists and the "Liga" members present.
Seeing that it would certainly come to even greater scandals and brawls, Abba Achimeir had to break off the lecture, and the meeting was dissolved.
For 680 zł She Bought “Diamonds”

[Kielce — fraud.] From Tsar Nicholas's crown...
On Leonarda [?] Street, not far from Bank Polski, the Kielce woman Mrs. Keyle Ostałka [?] was walking past this Wednesday. At the corner of Sienkiewicza she was stopped by a young man, who held her up and asked her to lend him 20 zł. for a couple of minutes, which he had to give as a “deposit” to the Russian “aristocrat” standing there, who had a “kosher bargain” to sell: several “precious diamonds” that came from the crown of Tsar Nicholas... The young man, who introduced himself to Mrs. Ostałka as the “son” of the local jeweller Yitzhak Erman, promised to take her on as a “partner” in the “treasure”. Mrs. Ostałka went in to the Tschejgel [?] family, borrowed 20 zł. and handed them to Mr. “Erman”.
The young man “Erman” also asked Mrs. Ostałka to go over to his “father” in the shop, so that he would immediately send him the remaining 660 zł. The young “Erman” explained to Mrs. Ostałka that she could trust him with the 20 zł., because, “inasmuch and therefore”, he was a good “acquaintance” of her father's [?], and his “father” Yitzhak Erman prays together with “him” in the same beth-midrash, at R' Hirshl Zaniejski's [?]...
Mrs. Ostałka was sure that the young man's words were “holy of holies”; she handed him the 20 zł. and went off to Mr. Yitzhak Erman for the remaining 660 zł.
Coming back to Leonarda Street, she of course no longer found anyone... Only then was it explained to her that she had fallen victim to local swindlers, who have lately been rampant in Kielce and are cheating many people. Mrs. Ostałka reported the matter to the police.
Always All the Same.

[Kielce — State Lottery.] The best way to secure oneself prosperity is, without doubt, intensive and strenuous work, a sense of orientation and professional knowledge. But the natural striving of a person is the wish to acquire such means that, besides covering current expenses, he will also be able to secure his future, when he can no longer work so intensively.
Various means are used for this. Some want to acquire a fortune through financial operations, others try their luck at games. But only one game can truly become a source of wealth [?]; only that game gives a guarantee of a fair outcome and does not depend on any dark machinations, on any moods of the sun [?] or weather.
The road along which the luck of the player in the State Lottery runs is neither too soft nor too hard, neither too light nor too heavy; it is the same for everyone and ensures equal chances for everyone.
The safest and luckiest thing, therefore, is to buy a ticket for the first class of the thirty-eighth lottery and to count on a win. It may be that one will not have to wait long for the hopes to come true. [—]
The drawing begins already on the eighteenth of this month [?].
The Murderers of Shloyme Hersh Kirszenbaum

[Kielce — court; anti-Jewish violence.] Sentenced to 3½ years in prison.
Yesterday, Thursday, the Kielce District Court heard the trial of the two Endek [National Democrat] hooligans Chiliński and Baraszyński, who several weeks ago attacked, outside Kielce, the 56-year-old Jewish village trader Shloyme Hersh Kirszenbaum and beat him murderously; he died a few days later of the wounds, orphaning a wife with 7 children.
In the afternoon the court delivered its verdict, according to which both are sentenced to 3½ years in prison.
Constituent Meeting of the Board of the Small Traders' Association.

[Kielce — organisations.] This Sunday [?] the constituent meeting of the newly elected board of the Small Traders' Association took place. Adv. Stegla [?] was elected president, and Mr. Arnold Mink vice-president. The board comprises Messrs.: H. Pochel [?], Eng. [?] H. Piotrowski (secretary), Noah Laks, A. Y. Szejnfeler [?], A. Bojmsztajn, Motl Włosa [?], S. Zajączkowski, M. Krzęński [?], L. Wróbel, D. Zylberberg, A. Goldberg and Y. Wajsberg. As office manager — Mr. Górski.
Big Fire in Kielce.

[Kielce — disaster; mutual aid.] 10 Jewish families left without a roof over their heads.
In the night from Monday to Tuesday a big fire broke out at No. 8 Zagnańska [?] Street, in the house of Mr. Berl Raler [?]. 10 poor Jewish families have been left without a roof over their heads.
It is the duty of the Jewish public to take an immediate interest in the bitter fate of the fire victims, who, as said, are very poor people. Efforts must be made so that the fire victims receive loans from the Gemilut Hesed (free-loan) fund.
—o—
A Loan for House-Owners.
The Kielce Magistrate has received a loan of 100 thousand zł. to carry out sewerage and a water-supply system.

Elected kehilla representation in Sosnowiec takes over the administration on Sunday the 28th inst.

As we have already written, the local starosta [district head] ordered that the commissarial kehilla administration hand over the kehilla's affairs by the 28th of this month into the hands of the newly elected kehilla board and council.
In this connection the kehilla commissioner, Mr. Fenzer[?], sent out letters to the board and council of the kehilla, in which he informs them that they are to come on Sunday the 28th of this month at 6 in the evening to a meeting, for the purpose of taking over the administration of the kehilla in Sosnowiec.
Meeting on the rabbinate question in Będzin

As we have already written, the Agudah side put forward the proposal that the rabbinate question in Będzin be settled by way of a compromise, i.e. the „Agudah“ wants the kehilla council to give its consent that R' Mendel Lewin be elected as „podrabin“ [deputy rabbi], and in return the „Agudah“ gives up pressing for him as rabbi.
As a result a committee of 6 persons was elected, 3 from the national camp and 3 from the „Agudah“.
On Wednesday evening the first meeting of the committee was to have taken place; the „peace“ meeting, however, did not come about, because some members of the committee were unable to come.
—o—
Dr. A. Lipman and Mgr. M. Begin in Będzin.
This Saturday evening, in the premises of the Będzin Betar, the distinguished representatives of the NZO [New Zionist Organization] movement in Poland, Dr. A. Lipman and Mgr. M. Begin, will appear with lectures.
The registration books are to be kept on the kehilla premises

As we are informed, this week there took place a consultation of representatives of the national camp in Będzin on the question of the registration books [vital-records registers], and it was decided that the registration books should be kept on the kehilla premises, where the secretary of the rabbinate is also to officiate.
The decision was forwarded to Rabbi Chamayres[?], who, as is known, performs the rabbinical functions in Będzin.
—o—
The Agudah did not protest officially.
From the president[?] of the Będzin „Agudah“, town councillor Abraham Leib Grünwald, we have received a letter in which it is declared that the „Agudah“ as an official organisation has no connection whatsoever with the protest concerning the general meeting of the Gemilut Chesed [free-loan] fund in Będzin.
—o—
2 people fell into a cesspit.
In Landauer's[?] house on Modrzejowska[?] Street in Będzin, the boards of the privy gave way yesterday morning; at that moment Messrs. Yeshaya Ziegler and Leib Hersh Reich were there and fell into the pit.
It happened under the following circumstances:
Around 6 before daybreak, when Reich came into the Sochaczew [Hasidic] shtibl, which is located in the same courtyard, he heard cries for help coming to him from the privy, but as soon as he went inside to rescue Ziegler, he too fell into the pit.
With great effort they managed to rescue them from the danger.
—o—
Support the Purim campaign of „Beit Lechem“.
As every year, a Purim campaign will be carried out next week for the benefit of the „Beit Lechem“ society in Będzin.
One must bear in mind, however, that „Beit Lechem“ is the only institution in Będzin which, within the limits of its means, alleviates the great want that prevails in the Jewish street, and gives bread and challahs weekly to dozens of [—] [word illegible; probably „needy“] families.
The collection will be carried out by several collectors authorised for the purpose, from whom one must demand proper identification. Donations can also be handed in at the shop of president[?] A. D. Balimowski[?].
—o—
Meeting of Jewish productive org[anisations].
The branch of the „ORT“ society in Zagłębie is calling a meeting of all Jewish productive organisations, and also of public activists, for the purpose of starting a campaign for productivisation. The meeting takes place on Sunday at 3 p.m. in the club in Będzin.
