From the screen

"The Year 2000" — at the "Światowid".
The problem of whether technical civilization brings happiness to mankind or not — is the quintessence of this interesting and wide-ranging picture.
Wells in his work depicted the world after the greatest future war. Further on he wanted to show that technical civilization can be used in another way than to murder and destroy. The Air League, which was created after the great war, set itself the goal of bringing peace to the world with the help of the achievements of civilization.
But after the rebuilding of the world and the attainment of the highest stage of technical civilization, man rebels. The masses, so to say[?], do not want to consent to the rocket experiment to the moon. The masses rebel, but the leader himself sends his daughter on the first rocket, which is to connect [printed "farbundn"] with the moon.
The problem of the teleology[?] of technical progress is not clearly presented in this picture. The parents who sent their children on the first rocket stand and observe the little speck moving on high, and with the hope that they will after all achieve something, the film ends.
As already said, it is a picture of great scope. The battle scenes are organized on a scale not seen until now. [They] show[?] the whole horror of the future war. The technical scenes surpass the best films of this genre ("Metropolis", "Woman in the Moon", etc.).
The film also displays many satirical moments. In it the dictatorship system is discreetly ridiculed, and it shows what lust for power can bring about.
In general the picture is an event in the field of film and astonishes with its content and scope.
"The Jungle Queen" at the "Apollo", Będzin
The jungle queen is a young, beautiful girl who was born and grew up in the jungles, where at every step wild beasts and dangers lie in wait, [and] all kinds of natural catastrophes. The girl is an orphan from childhood. Her remaining friends are: a tiger, which she raised from a small cub, and a lively, nimble little monkey. Together[?] they lead their life in the jungle thicket, cherishing one another.
But a young, charming fellow from an English expedition strays here, and between the half-wild jungle girl and the young Englishman a love develops. Various "white"[?] disturbing factors interfere (the Englishman's fiancée, his companions, the local wild tribes), which are, however, finally overcome.
The director aptly handed the thread of initiative here not to people but to the jungle animals themselves. Help comes from the small, clever-eyed little monkey, which calls together all the jungle monkeys. Like a mighty, wildly overflowing torrent they pour over the huts[?] of the frightened people, destroying everything around them. Rescued from certain death are the jungle girl and her beloved, as well as all the other whites.

“There Are No People”

This is a slogan which[?] is lately repeated so often in our organisations and public institutions. They tell you there with regret that this or that prepared relief campaign was a fiasco, not merely because people refused to give — however bad things may be, there still remains a decent number of people who still gladly contribute to every collection, so that one cannot say the campaign failed because of that — but solely because there are no people for the work: everyone wants by every possible means to be freed from the role of a “tove’a” (solicitor, collector). And by the way[?], people complain lately that it is hard to convene meetings of the boards because the board members do not come — one may surmise that this is certainly out of the fear that hovers before their eyes lest duties be imposed on them, as one is used to putting it somewhat, “to go round the houses” and collect money; and this people do not want, so they run from it as from a demon.
It is a thankless role nowadays to be a “tove’a”, asking[?] others to give; much more comfortable is the role of the “nitba” (the one solicited), who always finds himself in a privileged position. He can — if you have after all taken upon yourself this task [—] to be a tove’a — make of you a “receptacle” into which to pour[?] all his grievances that he has against this or that communal activist and official, the very ones who refuse to reduce his assessment[?] (“etat”).
After all, he expressly stated in his petition that this year he did no business at all and lived on [—][?]. These cruel people[?] take no account of his situation, would not reduce his assessment[?] even by 10 zł., and on top of that sent the tax office to collect the unpaid assessment[?] from him by distraint. Can there be a greater murder than this — and you still have the nerve[?] — so the “giver” ends his refrain — to come to me for more money! And he gives you to understand that you should say “good day” [and leave].
The role of the tove’a is, as said, a much harder one; and although he knows in himself that he is a collector for the community and ought to be proud of the mission laid upon him, he nonetheless tries to avoid the reception that awaits him at a given[?] nitba, and — if he does not want to be exposed to personal insults as well — he must time the hour so as to find the nitba in the proper mood. Otherwise — in the best case, if it passes at all without incidents — the trouble is in vain.
And perhaps because a person, thanks to the many heavy daily worries and cares he has to bear today, is always agitated, and the minutes in which he finds himself in a good mood are very few — for that very reason there is a lack of people who would have the courage, in such a depressed mood, to trouble others for contributions, for a spirit of sacrifice[?]; and everyone, as said, hides from such missions. And if some are found after all, they are one or two, and on them falls the whole burden of carrying out the prepared campaign. It goes without saying that they are physically unable to do it, and so the campaign suffers a failure, and the consequences of the fact that “there are no people” stand out plainly.
“There are no people” is today a problem you come up against not only when it is a matter of dry money collections, but also, and perhaps chiefly, in various phenomena of public life.
As an illustration of the foregoing one can point to two such facts:
This week, before Purim, as has long been the custom among Jews, money is collected for various purposes. The “Linat HaHolim” in Sosnowiec has also kept up this tradition for a number of years already, and this year too it decided to send out a certain number of people to Jewish homes to collect money. This time, however, it turned out very hard to pick the required number of people, because not everyone wanted to be a tove’a, be it even for such an important institution.
And the same worry is shared by the “Beit Lechem” society in Będzin: there too they are anxious where to find people who would take part in the collection campaign for Passover.
In a word — there are no “people”!
A. L—s.
Our Gymnasia

[Zagłębie — education; opinion article.]
I intend here to touch on a painful educational question, which has already been dealt with countless times by various Jewish educators and scholars, namely: the problem of Jewish studies (limudei ha-yahadut) in the Jewish gymnasia. I believe that, although we are in the middle of the school year, this question must nevertheless be examined, in order to find[?] a proper solution for it.
Here in Zagłębie there exist fine Jewish educational institutions — the Jewish gymnasia — which in the course of their existence have succeeded in turning out many graduates, who, incidentally, occupy an important position in our Jewish public life. It is superfluous to praise[?] these schools, because Jewish Zagłębie knows how to value properly the worth of these institutions, which are the pride of the Jewish population of Zagłębie.
But — in the field of Jewish studies certain small reforms are, in my opinion, called for. True, both the pupils and the teachers show great signs of devotion and love for our national language — Hebrew — and for its literature; in the curriculum the Tanakh and the Hebrew language occupy an honourable place. One must admit that a love for our national treasures is being planted in the hearts of the pupils, and the teachers stand at the proper height of their tasks and fulfil their duty conscientiously and completely; nevertheless I wish to dwell here more broadly on this question.
"Jewish gymnasium" — these two words contain within them a synthesis of Jewishness and humanity, of Judaism and Europeanism. Parallel to this, the Jewish gymnasium must also, in the educational sense, be an embodiment of these two synthesised[?] parts.
There was once a time, in the "Hashpala" [sic, misprint for Haskalah] era, when the great Hebrew poet Y. L. Gordon threw into the Jewish street the well-known slogan: "Be a Jew in your tent and a man when you go out" — that is to say: it was then understood that Jewishness and Europeanness relate to one another as two opposites, as two contrasts. But that was a mistaken conception. Our maskilim lacked historical sense, for they did not grasp that Jewishness relates to humanity as a part to a whole, and that European culture is a fusion of Hellenism and Judaism.
Nowadays, or better said: at the beginning of our national renaissance era, a completely reversed slogan was put forward: "Be a Jew in your tent and a Jew when you go out" — that is, be a Jew both inwardly and outwardly. On the contrary, we must not be ashamed of our Jewishness, but proud of it.
Against what am I saying this?
What I have in mind is our young, growing generation, especially the school youth. These young people must absorb in large measure the freshness of our old and at the same time eternally new spiritual treasures, and find in them the whole content of their lives, so that the growing generation should know what we Jews possess and what we have given the world.
Some maintain that for the national education of our youth a superficial study of a little Tanakh and some acquaintance with the new Hebrew literature is enough; in essence, however, this is a fundamentally false claim, for we see that those who did not devote themselves broadly to Jewish studies but only superficially learned a little Hebrew and Tanakh — very little of it remained with them in later years, and no wonder: entry into our ancient literature, so rich in spirit, was not made possible for them; it remained for them a sealed book.
And conversely, all those who in former times, in their childhood years, studied Jewish learning on a broad scale and were occupied with the Talmud and its commentators — they later, on going over[?] to secular studies, remained fully[?] bound with every fibre of their soul to Jewishness and all its spiritual treasures; and even when studying at the universities they distinguished themselves in the various branches of science, thanks to the sharpening of their minds in the sea of the Talmud.
It goes without saying that I do not intend that a gymnasium should be turned into a yeshiva; I merely stress that Jewish studies, in the deeper sense of the word, must be properly utilised in the curriculum.
H. W-B.
*) Although the editors do not agree with all the author's arguments, we nevertheless give the article space, taking into account all circles of our readers. The Editors.
A Son a Doctor...

[Humorous feuilleton — Sosnowiec.] Told by a Sosnowiec Jew and passed on by Y. Oberżanek.
[?]To know this — what you call children. Having children — my grandmother, may she rest in peace, used to say — is no great trick; the trick is to bring children up. Oh, listen to this — what a trick my child-rearing is!
I am saying it about my own son, about my only son, the doctor.
— Feigele, I argued with my wife, what do you want to make of your son? He has, thank God, finished ("geskontshet" — skończył) school; we have to think about a purpose in life, put him to a tailor as an apprentice, so he will become a good craftsman. She got angry and started shouting:
— Not while I live! I don't need any tailors! Do you hear? I don't want any tailors!
— So what do you want to make of him?
— A doctor. My Simchale must be a doctor.
— A doctor? Do you even know what a doctor smells of [i.e. what it takes]?
— I know what a doctor smells of. A doctor smells very good. Ask me and I'll tell you what a doctor smells of... A handsome lad, like[?] gold, clever as the day, taking after me entirely; and when the women and the lady patients find out that there is a young, handsome doctor with a black forelock, with big black sideburns, who tells jokes and pays compliments during the "zbadań" [examination], the lady patients will start pouring in like hail, they will bring the 5-złoty and 10-złoty notes, he will become "slyne" [probably: famous, Pol. słynny][?] among the women; and if a young doctor becomes "slyne" among "the fair sex" — he is a happy man... What more do you need? I myself, when I feel a little unwell[?], I too look for a young, "slyne" doctor; I hate an old doctor whose hands tremble. A young doctor takes more trouble over a lady patient than an old doctor. A young doctor does the "zbadań" quite differently from an old doctor, a young doctor listens [auscultates] quite differently, he has wit, pays a compliment, this, that, "i tak dalej" [and so on]... And when Simchale is a doctor, he will indeed have a clientele ("patronye")[?]. He has all the "zdolności" [talents] to be able to attract the sick, weak women and "panny" [young ladies] who need a "complete recovery"...
— Yes, you are quite right, a doctor really is a good profession, but do you even know that to study to be a doctor one needs a "majątek" [a fortune]?
— I don't want to hear anything — my wife argued — Simchale must be a doctor! I won't eat, I won't drink, I'll give up everything, as long as I have a son a doctor.
Well, I saw it was a lost cause, so I took Simchale and sent him off to study.
My Feigele beamed with joy; whomever she spoke to, she said at every other word:
— My doctor, my Stefek.
When he came home on vacation, she invited ("poproshet" — zaprosiła) guests and introduced him:
— "Mój syn przyszły doktor" [my son, the future doctor] — and her face shone with joy.
Now he is already, thank God, a doctor; that is, a full doctor he is not yet; for now he practises on me and on my wife — we are his first patients.
Well, I have[?] a few bitter [lit. burnt] troubles from my doctor. Since he has no surgery ("cabinet") of his own yet, he has meanwhile made the surgery at my home. I am the patient and my wife — the maid. In the corridor he set up a little table with chairs — a "poczekalnia" [waiting room]; whole days I sit in the "poczekalnia" and wait... for a patient, and if someone rings at the door, my wife runs in a white "czepek" [cap] on her head to open the door.
On the first day, when he opened the "cabinet", he gave my wife and me a lesson in what we have to do.
If a patient comes in, I have to recount the doctor's virtues, how he is curing me, how he brought me back from the dead, and that I have been sitting here in the waiting room for a long time already, because the doctor has a big practice.
To her, the mother, he gave a lesson in how to receive a patient: if a patient comes in and asks:
— "Czy pan doktor przyjmuje?" [Is the doctor receiving?] — one must answer:
— "Pan doktor zajęty" [The doctor is busy].
— "Pan doktor ma konsylium" [The doctor has a consultation].
— "Pan doktor wyjechał do chorego" [The doctor has gone out to a patient][?].
But she must let nobody go: keep them, invite them into the waiting room, give them an old newspaper or a magazine to read.
Besides me and my wife he invited ("zaproshet") the whole family; they all sit in the waiting room, so that if a patient should happen to stray in, he will see what a big "practice" the young doctor has.
Well, so I really do sit whole days in the waiting room and wait; my wife in her cap stands "na pogotowiu" [on standby] and waits for a ring, and since the bell doesn't stir, we both sit, my wife and I — and wait.
These last days he has started "practising". Since he has no patients, he has meanwhile started practising on me and on my wife.
— Father — he says to me — you know that you are already a man getting on in years?
— Well, so what?
— Well, at these years — he says — all sorts of things happen to a person: water, kidneys, liver, heart, blood pressure, this, that, "i tak dalej".
— And what do you think I should do?
— Come, I'll [do][?] an analysis. The analysis shows what a person has. According to the analysis one knows how to treat.
Well, I obeyed him, I gave him my "material"; he wrapped it up like a costly bottle of champagne and did the analysis.
The next morning I ask him:
— Well, Stefek, what have I got?
He took out the "analysis" and started studying it, studying it this way and that, wrinkled his forehead and finally he says to me:
— Daddy, I must examine ("zbadać") you!
So I undressed and he got down to work. He went for the belly.
— Does it hurt you here?
— No, it doesn't hurt me.
— That's impossible; here, in this place, it must hurt Daddy!
— How do you know, Stefekl, that it must hurt me here?
— According to the analysis! The analysis says that you are dealing with women's things...
— Me? How does a male person come to women's things?
— That's what it says here, in the analysis! You see, Daddy, you have something in this place. If I didn't know you are my father, I would be sure that you are pregnant...
— Me? I am pregnant? A father can be pregnant?
— That's what it says in the analysis!
The end of it was that he was right[?]: it was merely a small misunderstanding — he had mixed things up. Together with my "material" he had also taken a bit of "material" from the mother, and what he meant to tell the mother, he told me; and that is how my son, the doctor, made me pregnant...
Well, I ask you, wouldn't it have been happier if I had a son a tailor, not a doctor? Had I had a son a tailor, I would have had a "korzyść" [benefit][?]; I have a son a doctor — he turns his mother into a door-opener and his father he makes — pregnant... And still my wife is content: she has a son a doctor...
Kimcha de-Pischa (Passover flour relief)

„Mi-shenikhnas Adar“ [“When Adar enters”] — already the hearts of many hundreds of Jewish families are beginning to pound, not, God forbid, over a tasty „hamantash“, but over the important and heavy matter — Passover. Not a few of them remain, poor souls, very sad (in contrast to „marbin be-simcha“ [“joy increases”]) and despondent, seeing no way out of their difficult situation. After all, the past year was so hard to get through. The cruel, frosty winter further increased the bloodletting [„dam ha-tamtzit“] and so starkly brought out the terrible, catastrophic poverty that rages in the dozens and hundreds of homes of the impoverished Jewish masses; and the help of the municipal institutions — already including [?] the help of the Jewish kehilla — is so small compared with the great destitution and the terrible reality of everyday Jewish life here. What more is to be expected in the future? Me-ayin yavo ezri [“From where will my help come?”] — with such and similar thoughts the forlorn, poor [?] and hidden paupers go about, dreading the approaching Passover.
„Mi-shenikhnas Adar“ — therefore the Jewish communal activists in Zagłębie, those who year after year take care of kimcha de-pischa for all the needy in Zagłębie, must this year gird their loins and step up their activity in this field. The kehilla must contribute a correspondingly larger sum, taking into account that this year the number of the needy has grown. Our well-to-do magnates must open their hands more widely, bearing in mind the great dearness that now prevails here in the most essential food products, which will surely affect matzot and other products. Our landsleit [townsmen abroad], in every place, must also remember their impoverished brothers and sisters in Zagłębie, who have been [?] struck by a hard fate, and among whom there were [?], perhaps not long ago, many „givers“, and who have now become „receivers“.
Together they must exert all their influence and help to create easier conditions that will relieve the hard, unbearable life of the poor Jewish masses in Zagłębie — at least for the time of the Passover festival.
A-B-R.
On the Problems of Our National Education

It is an old pedagogical rule that the education of the young generation must be bound up with the dominant idea in the life of the given community. All modern educators always strive to give education an essential content and to link it with a great idea; and a second important premise: education cannot and must not be abstract, but must be closely bound up with practical deeds.
The ideal that dominates Jewish life today is the national revival in our homeland — the rebuilding of Eretz Israel. And therefore it is self-evident that the Jewish school, seeking a way for itself, began to attach itself to the Eretz-Israel idea and to place it at the centre of education and of the curriculum. And just as our forefathers knew how to bind the Torah with everyday commandments, so has our present-day school bound the great idea of national renaissance with practical deeds for Eretz Israel and the redemption of its land. No abstract teaching can have the proper effect if it is not accompanied by concrete acts.
This important national mission — making education concrete and implanting in the Jewish child love and devotion to Eretz Israel — has fallen to the Keren Kayemet le-Israel [Jewish National Fund], which fulfils its mission hand in hand with the Jewish national teacher. The idea of redeeming and nationalising the soil of Eretz Israel, of making Jewish youth productive and settling it on the land, of creating a new type of Jewish farmer — an idea which found its symbolic expression in the Keren Kayemet — has contributed much to changing the psyche and character of the Jewish child of the exile; in the darkness that surrounds him a ray of light and hope has appeared, which dispels melancholy and awakens joy and faith in the soul of the young child.
Whoever watches with what joy and enthusiasm the child donates the groszy he has saved for the redemption of land in Eretz Israel, feeling that he thereby becomes a partner in the work of Creation, in the national work of rebuilding — will understand that it is not the child who gives to the Keren Kayemet, but the Keren Kayemet that gives the child an ideal and a content in life.
Now the head office of the Keren Kayemet in Poland has proclaimed a special propaganda week among school parents. Its aim is to explain to the parents the essential foundations of Eretz-Israel education and the important significance of the Keren Kayemet's work in the schools.
It is to be hoped that the broad masses of Jewish parents will take an interest in the problems of Jewish national education and will also, for their part, help to deepen and spread it among their children.
R. A.
What Rights Does the English King Have?

[World — England.] Without any doubt the London "Times", the paper of the greatest pre-[?]stige, takes first place in the journalism of the four corners of the earth. The "Times" does not have the largest circulation. It is printed in only 800 [?] thousand copies a day, and in London itself or in America there are papers with a daily circulation four times as large. But the "Times" is the newspaper the whole world reckons with. To be editor of the "Times" one must have a great, a very great privilege, and must be versed in much wisdom and a great deal of knowledge.
The "Times" is only 150 years old; there are [?] papers much older. But when anywhere in the world one wants to look something up — a matter, a law and the like — one looks into a volume of the "Times".
When an English judge, or even a non-English one, wants to look up something concerning a difficult point of international law, it matters to him what the "Times" said about it when the law came into force [?].
In a word: the editors of the "Times" are everywhere counted among those who know everything and deliver the best judgement on every matter.
Some years ago we sat at a press meeting of the Leipzig Fair and discussed the topics of the day. We talked about things that were topical at the time. The chairman then was Mister Doan [?] Stutts, the editor of the "Times".
One of us — the writer of these lines, I believe — expressed the opinion that the English king is there only to represent, and has no power whatsoever in the country.
The subject was topical then because the recently deceased King George the Fifth had suddenly fallen gravely ill, and the doctors feared he would die. The then Prince of Wales, the present abdicated king, was staying in Africa at the time, and it was feared that by the time he got home he would no longer find his father alive.
Mister Stutts sat with his pipe in his mouth and smiled — that kind of smile which shows that he is cleverer than you...
"You are mistaken, friends, if you think the English king has no power at all. On the contrary, the English king has the greatest power in the country. If the English king only wishes, he can:
send home all the officers and soldiers, and can sell all the English ships to whomever he likes and for as much as he likes.
In case of war he can, 'for the sake of peace', give away the whole [?] and thus hand over the whole of England to the enemy.
He can win back Brittany, which once belonged to England.
He can change any law as it suits him.
He can call up to the army whomever he wants, no matter how old he is.
With his telegrams and telephone calls, which by law are dealt with first, he can stop all traffic in the whole of England.
He can order his chauffeurs to drive so fast in town that no other vehicle would dare to be on the street.
As you see, the King of England has the greatest power, if only he wants to do something with that power. The only luck is that no king to this day has had any desire to use his power..."
Z. Haber, Vienna.
Homely Letters

[Będzin and Sosnowiec — feuilleton; community and institutions.]
With God's help, week of the portion "for it is a stiff-necked people" [Ki Tisa].
My friend R' Shlomo, may his light shine.
I have received your letter. Your letter made a heavy impression on me, for[?] from every line cries out the Jewish pain, the Jewish grief. There has never yet been — you say — such a time of trouble for Jacob: every day new tidings of Job, new calamities. But you must not take it so much to heart and be in so despairing a mood. Look at the old Megillah, which was read yesterday throughout all the dispersions of Israel, and you will calm down a little. In the Megillah you will find almost every word that we hear today in the Nazi press. The difference is only this: Haman of the Scroll of Esther demanded to make an end of the few Jews all at once. But in the 20th century this is done in the cultural manner; today things are settled day by day[?] more practically, today new Megillot are being written.
— And one more thing you must do, so that[?] you do not fall into melancholy: study closely the verse of this week's portion, "for it is a stiff-necked people." It is as though He stamped us with this "pedigree," and this "pedigree" is in our time very "useful" to us. True, we do not know exactly what use this "pedigree" brings to other Jewish communities; but it is clear, and we can say it openly and boldly, that "it is a stiff-necked people" applies to a great extent to our Jews in Zagłębie.
Here, for example, I will relate to you a fact from the very latest time. You surely know that a general meeting of the interest-free fund [gemilut hasadim] took place in Będzin. As the devil would have it, the persons who lately found great favour with a certain side were not elected to the board. Well, you will surely ask, what is all the noise about? But you are mistaken: with a "stiff-necked people" you will not get anyone to yield even the tip of a yod — even when the whole existence of the fund is put at stake, on the scales of life or death... Are you surprised[?] that Jews will risk their livelihoods? And whose worry is it anyway?
So they no doubt girded their loins and went out to battle. First of all they started writing, as they are called[?], "Dear-friend letters," in which a list of "sins" was enumerated, and therefore one has to begin again from "In the beginning"... As rumour has it, the latest demand was delivered not only in writing but also orally, and carried out on that Sabbath at midday, after the singing of "Yom ze mekhubad"...
Jews who are not versed in the "secrets of the Torah" of politics could not grasp why So-and-so son of So-and-so was running precisely on the Sabbath to carry out the holy mission. But those who stand close "to the helm" knew that "the midday was urgent," because in the evening the constituent session was to take place...
And not only the affair of the free-loan fund confirms that we are a "stiff-necked people"; in various fields we can easily prove it among ourselves. Take, for instance, this year's coal campaign, which was finished only this week — not because the coal committee stopped its activity, but because "simply there were no more needy people"...
And this is only thanks to the obstinacy and strong will of our communal delegates, who paid no heed to the sharp protests of the kehilla taxpayers, who demanded that the rabbinate question in our town must and should be settled before Purim, but took care first of all that the poor families with their children should not suffer from cold in the hard frost..
Successful this year will be the "kimcha [de-Pischa]" campaign: day after day consultations take place on how to organise the campaign; there is even a plan to open a competition for the best advice on the "kimcha" question. Yes, R' Shlomo, a "stiff-necked" people cannot be worn down[?]. The Jewish people — a great rebbe said — is likened to an olive: however much one squeezes it, one cannot squeeze everything out of it...
Sosnowiec too has not lagged behind in the field of obstinacy. If you do not believe me — "ask your father and he will tell you": ask the "Satan" of the kehilla and he will tell you that the whole time he laughed up his sleeve when, from various directions, it was pointed out to him that he should follow the example of his colleagues.
— "Not with Moshe!" [i.e. not with me] — his answer rang firmly. "With a mighty hand will I rule over you" — with the strong hand "will I lord it over you." What is more, in the "Ne'ilah" days, seeing that at long last he will have to move aside and make room for others, for the chosen, he issued a public proclamation in which he warns that none of the rabbis in Sosnowiec "shall lift up his hand" [printed "yarum"] — let none dare to kasher the ovens for Passover, except the one whom he will order...
— And today's Maccabees also stroll about[?] as children of the "stiff-necked people"... For several months now an obstinate struggle has been waged around the half-moribund sports club "Maccabi" in Sosnowiec. Three groupings are fighting: old Maccabeans, new Maccabeans (the "Nordia" bloc[?]) and Zionists. Self-evidently, none of the fighting sides intends, God forbid, to kill off "Maccabi"; on the contrary, each wants to breathe into it a "spirit of life" — only according to his own colour...
Optimists predict that "Maccabi" will not one day suffer the same fate that befell the child of the [?] faithful mother... But whatever happens, one cannot on that account give up the holy struggle. That could, after all, be an outright compromising of the "stiff-necked people."
— Your request that I report to you in detail about the "upheaval" in the Sosnowiec "Mizrachi" I unfortunately cannot fulfil, because I am very busy with the "[—]"[?] and the "party" interests that the new communal delegates will take over in the Sosnowiec kehilla next Sunday.
Meanwhile, have a good Sabbath, as wishes you your friend
Ben Amotz.
Oneg Shabbat — Parashat Ki Tisa

Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around this week's Torah portion, collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Tisa
a) "The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less than half a shekel... to make atonement for your souls" (30:15).
Since it is about "to make atonement for your souls", about atoning for sins, one might have supposed that the rich man should give more and the poor man less, for sinning — it is mainly the rich man who sins... — Imrei Chen.
b) "And galbanum" (ibid., 34).
"Rabbi Hana bar Bizna said in the name of Rabbi Shimon Hasida: any fast in which none of the sinners of Israel take part is no fast, for galbanum has a bad smell and yet Scripture counts it among the spices of the incense." — Keritot 6b.
Every fast in which none of the sinners of Israel take part: if those fasting cannot carry along any of the sinners of Israel, if they cannot exert influence so that through their repentance the sinners of Israel also repent — it is no fast; it is a sign that the fasters do not mean it with their whole heart. For when burning kindling catches well, damp, poor kindling also catches[?] together with it; and if the damp kindling does not catch any fire, it is a sign that the others also have no real fire in them... — Rabbi Israel Baal Shem Tov.
c) "Break off the golden earrings which are in the ears of your wives" (32:2).
Why did he not order them simply[?] to bring jewellery, but "the golden earrings which are in the ears of your wives" — why precisely the earrings?
Because in those times women's earrings represented idolatrous images[?] and talismans. When Jacob told his household[?] "put away the strange gods that are among you", that they should remove the idols from their house, it is said: "And they gave unto Jacob all the strange gods which were in their hand, and the earrings which were in their ears." So women's earrings were idolatrous images[?]; therefore Aaron ordered them to be brought for the calf... — R. Eliezer Ashkenazi.
d) "And he saw the calf and the dancing" (ibid., 19).
All along Moses thought: the Jews are making a calf, some new false doctrine has got stuck in their heads — well then, he will convince them. [—][?] And seeing the dancing, the dance — "he cast the tablets out of his hands and broke them", he threw away the tablets and broke them. As soon as it is a matter of dancing, not of a false idea but of dancing — then it is a hard thing indeed... — Leket Amarim.
e) "That He may bestow upon you a blessing this day" (ibid., 29).
"The Holy One, blessed be He, found no vessel that holds blessing for Israel except peace" — and here God ordered them to destroy the peace, to kill all the worshippers of the calf; so a promise had to come that even without peace they would this time also have a blessing, for such a destroyed peace is in fact the true peace.. — Nimukei ha-Ridbaz.
In honour of Purim.
f) "Even if all the festivals were abolished, the days of Purim will never be abolished."
Because the Hamans will never die out; they will exist forever... — Sefer ha-Hayim.
g) "When he showed the riches of his glorious kingdom" (Esther 1:4).
All his royal glory came from wealth; riches alone procured him honour. — Megillat Sefer.
h) "And the Jews undertook to do as they had begun" (9:23).
Once, at the Purim feast, a theologian came to the rabbi R. Yehonatan Eybeschütz; he used to hold disputations with him.
"Today is Purim," Rabbi Yehonatan tells him, "among Jews everything is turned upside down today. So let us also swap roles today: you will play the part of a Jew and put questions to me, and I will defend the Christians."
"Good."
The priest asks:
"Tell me, why do the gentiles celebrate carnival and Purim? What connection do they have with Purim?"
"Because had all the Jews been destroyed back then, there would have been no Christian messiah and no Christians."
i) "All the words of this letter" (ibid., 26).
Why did the author of the Megillah avoid writing a [divine] Name in the Megillah?
Because the Persian chroniclers did translate it, and in place of God's name they would have put the name of their idols... — Ta'amei ha-Minhagim.
j) "And King Ahasuerus laid a tribute upon the land" (10:1).
Why is "King Ahasuerus" mentioned and underlined here?
Because on Ahasuerus the Gemara (Megillah 11) expounds: "that all became poor in his days". The name Ahasuerus symbolises that everyone became poor in his time. So the verse underlines[?] that this came from the fact that "he laid a tribute". — Megillat Sefer.
Prof. Dr. M. Bałaban (on his 60th jubilee).

Polish Jewry — boldly put, the whole thinking Jewry of the world — has celebrated these days the jubilee of the 60th birthday of Prof. Dr. Majer Bałaban.
Dr. M. Bałaban is well enough known to the Jewish scholarly world in general and to the Jewish scholars in Poland in particular; the name of the jubilarian speaks for itself. It is enough to ask any secondary-school child who Prof. Bałaban is, and he will answer at once that thanks to his brilliant enlightenment[?] he came to know[?] the whole of Jewish history — from the four corners[?] of the world and above all of Poland. Even the greatest enemy of Israel, as soon as the name Bałaban is mentioned to him, must salute, must show respect.
At the University of Warsaw and at the Jewish Institute you will be told that Prof. Bałaban is a great man, a star, a brilliant painter, an artist of the Jewish past, the one who strengthens the Jewish soul...
With his artistic hand and brilliant mind he has shown the world that we Jews have been in the world, and above all in Poland, good citizens already 800 years ago. He has proved it documentarily from various archives. He has never tired of delving, of researching in all the libraries, archives, kehilla minute-books, which he has embodied with a soul that will never be extinguished!...
Every synagogue, holy place, cemetery, every tombstone of a Jewish hero[?] or victim has been recorded and immortalised in Jewish history for all generations — thanks to him.
Most honoured jubilarian! Every step, every glance, every deed of our forefathers you have embodied; on every stone, wall, street and town you have set a historical seal that we were here even before others. With factual, probative quotations and other writings you have shown that we helped to plough, sow, work, build and fight for this country — which has been shown, and the truth cannot be denied.
Generations will pass and come, and your magnificent work will remain immortal, just as your biographies of the rabbis of the Lwów and Kraków communities!
Your work on the leaseholders[?] — your work as a Jewish educator! Great indeed is the number of your pupils!
And how great is your name in the English historical society, and in the Polish one too!
And how beautifully your articles on our past read, and in what beautiful Polish you present all the Jewish epochs bound up with Polish life!
Nor have you neglected all our great men — rabbis, artists, poets, musicians. For all of them you found a place!
And together with the whole Jewish cultural world we give you, Professor Dr., historian, our blessing for length of days. May your talent grow ever stronger together with your health, for the benefit of Jewish wisdom and scholarship.
Graetz and Dubnow remain great men in Jewish history, and you — the greatest of the great.
Herman Szer, Będzin.
A Little Feuilleton. Shopkeepers Around the World.

Every country has its own peculiar kind of shopkeeper. Each shopkeeper with his own characteristic approach to the customer, with his specific manner.
You come into a shop and ask for, let us say, light-green silk, but the shop does not have that kind of goods. How does this or that shopkeeper react to it?
The English shopkeeper.
The English shopkeeper will hear you out coldly, phlegmatically; then he will solemnly, earnest-stiff and official, shake his head from right to left and say: "I am sorry" ("I'm sorry") — and that's it, the matter is settled.
The Parisian shopkeeper.
The Parisian shopkeeper will greet you with great enthusiasm, embrace you, "What do you need, my friend[?]" — and when he hears that what you need he does not have, he will not let you go. He will ask you: "For whom do you need the light-green silk? For your wife or for a... Then he will tell you a couple of piquant anecdotes from the bedroom, and only after that will he tell you that he does not have the goods.
The American shopkeeper.
The American shopkeeper looks at you, and his first thought is: haven't you come to rob him?
When he is convinced that you are a quiet customer, he sizes up how much you are worth, and when he hears that you need something he does not have, he tells you that only yesterday he had a whole warehouse, where he sold out half a million metres of "re-vign"[?] silk, and if you will wait a quarter of an hour, his factory will be finished, which will produce every hour six million metres a day. He has spent a couple of million dollars on advertising. Good-bye.
The Jewish shopkeeper.
The Jewish shopkeeper simply gets frightened: aren't you a tax official or a bailiff; his[?] eyes rummage — aren't you carrying a bomb? When he finds out that you are a simple, quiet customer and you need light-green silk, he lays out dark cheviot before you.
When you tell him that you want only light-green silk, he tells you it's all the same. When he sees that he cannot convince you, he leaves you standing, he "doesn't know you", and he starts quarrelling with his wife.
From the Book Table.

„Yung Zaglembye" [Young Zagłębie]
A collection of poems, „Yung-Fon" [Young Banner] publishers.
At a time when the book market is quiet and complains about the crisis, a little book — and a Yiddish little book at that — is an event.
„Yung Zaglembye" is the name of the new booklet that has appeared here. The first thing that catches the eye is the beautiful and well-suited cover by the young artist S. Z. Boym. It is a good poster with much expression, and if we take into account the thankless material in which the cut was made (linoleum-cut), we must be grateful to the artist.
Apart from the cover, the booklet is in general quite aesthetically produced, and one wants to look into it.
According to the poet's ideological attitude to his work, we can divide the participants of the poetry booklet into individualists, that is, those who give in their creation only their personal experiences, such as Szykman, Danziger, Blat; and problematists, that is, those who give poetic form to their [—] attitude to all topical and social problems, such as: Klajman, Boym. The poets Wisman and Tug-shayn[?] belong to neither of the two groups — better said, they belong to both: they try to write on both kinds of themes, without forgetting their individualism. Let us try to discuss the direction of the participants of „Yung Zaglembye" according to the groups into which we have divided them. The whole poetry of Hershl Danziger, as well as that of the individualists, revolves only around his own person, and just like each of them, he too has unjustified claims on the reader, who is not much moved by the poet's experiences, because he looks in poetry for what is topical for him.
Danziger is in places inconsistent; his poetry is still very young; in general — a young talent who can develop.
The second — A. Blat — is represented by two poems, and rather weak ones at that. The first, „Memento[?] mori", is the pessimistic flutter of a beginner; the second, „The Ballad", is — in both form and rhythm — much better.
Leyzer Szykman, as we see from his writing, can be called the poet of suffering. We can have compassion for him as a person — as a poet he is not convincing. Among the most literarily successful belongs the picture „Sadness". In the poems „Khoygirer"[?] and „Smuggler's Song" he tries to carry himself over to a different theme, but he remains only[?] an abstract photographer.
Dovid Wisman, a young poet, long since deceased, is a lyricist, a beautiful talent. He remains a lyricist even when he describes himself as one of the mass. His poem „Sorehn"[?] is very tender and beautiful, the form perfect. The poem „Ikh un Efroim" [I and Ephraim] is successful in content. It is the cry of a blind man who suddenly sees. He... sees nothing around him except a sea of light. His untimely death is a loss for Yiddish literature.
The last of the group is S. Tugshayn[?]. His themes are old, the form weak. He has inclinations toward small-town philosophy. His poem „Let Us Storm" only calls to the storm, but does not storm. We would advise him to open his eyes and change his themes.
All those of the above-mentioned group we can reproach for nebulousness[?] and pessimism in their poetry. These are no merits, as was once thought in the time of Romantic literature — these are rather faults.
Efroim Klajman belongs to the second group. His poem „Khayim Gurnik" is poetically weak. We have the impression as if he had forced himself to dress his ideas in poetic form. We write[?] ideas, although his poem is idea-less. His hero Khayim is in the end not resolute and asks himself: „Whither?" His second poem, „Jews Wander", is the product of a direct experience-construction[?] which strongly affected the poet. The dynamics and rhythm — strong, the language — beautiful. The poem is the opposite of the former one: not forced, and therefore good.
Most absolutely of the represented poets stands out Tuvia Boym. His themes are straightforward and mainly topical. There is not, in his three poems, the slightest attempt to want to interest the reader in his personal experiences. He aims throughout to express what he feels.
A biting satire is the poem „Two Overproductions".
So much about the themes. As regards the purely artistic side, the energetic rhythm of the poem must be underlined. The poet also has a few painterly effects. Perhaps in places the lofty tone, which weakens the poetry, is disturbing.
Adding the above-mentioned merits — the beautiful cover, the aesthetic appearance of the booklet, as well as the colourful Zagłębie representation — one can recommend it to the reader.
Skeptikan[?].

Ezekiel 34.

And you, dear shepherds,
where is your flock?
On mountain and valley without pasture —
is that no question to you at all?
The fat little lamb you have eaten,
the lean ones forgotten,
the sick not healed,
the lost not counted,
the hungry not fed till sated —
thin as a leaf.
Meat, wool
you want without number;
my flock is scattered through the world —
meanwhile you count the money.
You, the latter ones,
learn from the former ones:
the Vilna Gaon preferred to become a plain “reb”
rather than be a rabbi.
Reb Zushe [—] cries:
“Better forget about a raise,
I do not want to be a glutton!”
And in Zagłębie, in the holy communities,
the quarrel tastes delicious.
I beg you, holy rabbis,
don't be my enemies;
over the Megillah I ask your forgiveness —
today I am very drunk.
Our “friend” should break his neck!
I wish you ad de-lo yada;
after all, on Purim you too take
a little brandy, surely —
don't be angry,
it's Shushan Purim in the street.
B. Dinerman.
A Heder Boy Again

The pills worked.

An old 80-year-old Sosnowiec sinner[?] came to a doctor to ask whether there was not some means of becoming younger. The doctor prescribed him pills. Every night before going to sleep he was to take one pill. Out of great joy he gulped down[?] the whole little box of pills right on the first night.
Next morning they could by no means wake him up. Only with great trouble was he roused. Seeing his relatives and acquaintances at his bed, he mumbled:
— I'm already feeling better, I'll get up soon, only I won't go to heder today.

The New Megillat Esther

Interpreted according to the latest fashion — by Leyb Stabinski.

1.
“When he showed the riches of his glorious kingdom.” For 180 days the showing of Ahasuerus's wealth to the people lasted.
Why? Ahasuerus wanted to show his people that he need not come to them for a “pożyczka” [loan]. In this way he wanted to win the people's sympathy.
2.
“Unto the custody of Hegai, keeper of the women, and let their ointments be given them.” From this one infers that when women have every good thing, one man can keep watch over them; but when they lack their luxuries, a hundred men cannot keep watch over one wife...
3.
“And he cried with a loud and bitter cry.” Once Mordecai cried out and his cry was heard; today Mordecai cries out and he remains with his crying...
4.
“Let the king and Haman come unto the banquet.” Once, when Queen Esther gave a ball, she “ate up” Haman[?] at the ball; today, when Haman gives a ball and[?] celebrates his pleasures, Mordecai comes with Esther uninvited.

"A pig, my child, is a person who, when you invite him to come as a guest, goes and comes."
Dalphon and Vaizatha.

[Purim feuilleton — satire on communal leaders.] (A Purim tale dedicated to our communal workers)
When King Ahasuerus issued the verdict that the Jews of Shushan might take revenge on their enemies, take away their property and hang Haman with his ten sons, the Chevra Kadisha took a stand and argued: without a little glass of liquor we don't go to work; and looking at them, the same was argued by the Chevra Nos'ei ha-Mitah [pall-bearers' society], the tailors' society [?] and other Jewish societies of the royal residence city of Shushan.
And Mordecai had to give in; he called a porter and ordered him to roll out a barrel from King Ahasuerus's wine cellar, and therefore, while hanging Haman and his sons, the fellows were a little too [—] [apparently: tipsy].
Nevertheless everyone carried out his work to perfection. Only one, because he was a little drunk, somewhat neglected his work. He tightened the ropes around the necks of Dalphon and Vaizatha too weakly, and because of this negligence we now have something to sing and tell about to this very day.
The first to notice that the whole crowd that had hanged Haman and his sons had gone away was Vaizatha. He took another good look around and convinced himself that there was not a living soul around the gallows.
From above, from the gallows, a quiet sigh was heard.
— Who's sighing up there?
— It's me, Dalphon — the other answered weakly.
— You're alive, brother Dalphon?!
— And who are you, then?
— I, Vaizatha.
— You know, a fool is stronger than iron: they hang him and he is still alive!
— And how did you save yourself?
— Don't you know, brother? A poor man doesn't even have the luck to die easily. As bad luck would have it, they made me too big a noose — from Heaven [printed so] they assumed I had a fattened neck like my brothers.
And when Vaizatha had already torn himself loose from the gallows, he did not know how to climb up and rescue Dalphon. He was afraid to bring a ladder, because someone could come along. So Dalphon said to him:
— Listen, brother, our brothers have wide pockets, so do as I say: crawl into Arisai's pocket, from Arisai you'll crawl into Aridai's, from Aridai's into Aspatha's [printed "Ashpatha's"], until you reach me.
When both had been rescued, the two brothers began to consider their present situation.
— What do I do, Vaizatha, about your face — said Dalphon — wherever you go, they'll recognise the fool by your face?
— For that I have a plan: I'll grow a beard. But what do I do, Dalphon, about your "gait"? Wherever you go, they'll recognise Dalphon [the pauper, from Hebrew dalut, poverty] by your walk.
— That doesn't matter at all. Everyone who sees my walk will think I'm a Jewish intellectual and won't bother me.
And the next day, when the crowd had already sobered up from the previous night's liquor and everyone had gone back to his daily work, they noticed that in the royal residence city of Shushan a Jew with a broad beard was wandering about, together with a ragged intellectual, and both were idle.
So a meeting was called, and it was decided that Vaizatha, the supposedly respectable Jew with the beard, should become the chairman of all the kehilla benches, and Dalphon, "the Jewish intellectual", should become a secretary.
That is what the Jews of Shushan did, and so from them we have nothing left to sing, to tell or to read — nothing Megillah-like at all.

Our Brothers Overseas Ease the Financial Plight of the Jewish Philanthropic Institutions in Our Town

[Będzin — charity, aid from abroad.] The editorial office of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" has received 788.25 zł. from Chicago.
Only a few months ago [?] our editorial office received from the Relief Society in Chicago 175 dollars, which were distributed among the Jewish philanthropic institutions in our town and also to the Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec. But the above-mentioned society on the other side of the sea has also not forgotten that the festival of Passover is approaching and that one must come to the aid of the institutions that are in need of material help, which should give them the possibility of fulfilling their tasks.
And when the representative of the Będzin Mutual Aid Society, Mr. Bernard Szlipka, was in Będzin on a visit to his relatives, the society gave him 125 dollars and the Ladies' Society in Chicago 25 dollars, together 150 dollars, which are to be distributed exclusively to philanthropic institutions in Będzin.
This week Mr. Szlipka visited our editorial office and handed over to us the above-mentioned sum in złoty at the special dollar rate.
In agreement with Mr. Szlipka the sum was divided in the following manner:
Orphans' Home — 157.65 zł., Talmud Torah 157.65 z., Linat Holim 157.65 zł. (i.e. 30 dollars each), the Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec 105.10 zł. (20 dollars), Beit Lechem 78.82 zł. (15 d.), Malbish Arumim, the Ladies' Society, Menachem Avelim, TOZ and Hakhnasat Orchim 26.27 [?] zł. each (5 dollars each).
The fine deed of our brothers overseas should serve as an example for our local "landslayt", for those who do not want to hear the call for help on behalf of the déclassé Jewish masses in general and of the institutions which, because of their bad material situation, cannot help those who turn to them for help.
In our name and in the name of all [?] the social institutions we express our warm thanks to the [g.] donors in Chicago and say to them a hearty yasher koach.

An Outrageous Act by a Municipal Bailiff (Sequestrator)

[Kielce — Municipality, Kehilla and Welfare.]
Life in Kielce
Friday, 15 Adar 5697 — 26 February 1937

The attitude of the Magistrat (municipality) towards the Jewish population and Jewish institutions now oversteps every limit of human tact.
A few weeks ago the 70-year-old Zelig Grossman died. The funeral costs were covered by the kehilla — or rather by the Magistrat, which is obliged, on the basis of the binding[?] regulations on social welfare, to reimburse the kehilla for the funeral expenses of poor Jews, and the Kielce kehilla indeed applied to the Magistrat on that account.
This week, however, the Magistrat placed a distraint on the household goods of the widow Grossman, demanding that she pay 7 zł. 50 gr. in death tax for her husband.
The kehilla had issued Mrs. Grossman, who incidentally is supported by public relief, a certificate stating that her husband's funeral was held at the city's expense and that she, the poor widow Grossman, is maintained from the public fund.
On that basis Mrs. Grossman did not have to pay a single penny, as the law explicitly provides.
On Tuesday, however, the Magistrat's bailiff came to Mrs. Grossman's flat and wanted to remove her things from the home. When Mrs. Grossman showed him the said kehilla document, he angrily tore it up and began carrying out the things.
Having no choice, the poor widow had to scrape together in a hurry the few złoty from the neighbours, and paid the death tax.

Trial of the Desecrators of the Jewish Cemetery Postponed

[Kielce — Cemetery and Courts.]
Last Saturday the municipal court heard the trial of the young hooligans who desecrated the graves and broke the tombstones in the Jewish cemetery in Kielce. In the dock sat: Stanisław Każ[?], Stanisław Bans, Stanisław Ger, Władysław Fric and Mieczysław Kardynał — all aged 14 to 16. The five said juvenile hooligans are accused of profaning the cemetery and of selling chains and other pieces of iron from the graves of the Jewish cemetery and from the Evangelical cemetery.
None of the five accused admitted to breaking tombstones in the Jewish cemetery. On the other hand they did admit that they had sold the iron stolen from the Evangelical cemetery for two zł. thirty gr. to Mrs. Rojze Goldgrub, who also sat in the dock.
A number of witnesses were heard, among them the secretary Sokołowski, M. Korngold, the gravedigger of the Jewish cemetery Jankel Borolawski[?], and the authorized officer of the investigation office, H. Klesik, who established that the shameful act in the Jewish cemetery had been committed by the five said hooligans.
After a short deliberation the court decided to adjourn the trial until 18 March and to summon as a witness the superintendent of the Evangelical cemetery.

Terrible Distress among the Jews of Kielce

[Kielce — Economic Distress.]
Dozens of respectable Jews disguised themselves on Purim night and went round collecting alms.
Yesterday, on Purim night, hundreds of Jews were seen in the streets of Kielce going round collecting alms. Among the collectors were also seen dozens of respectable Jews who only a few months ago were themselves among the givers.
The same was noticed among the masqueraders on Purim night. In one house a certain person was seen of whom nobody would have imagined that he, poor man, would come to need support.
People knew, and know, that the poverty among the Jews of Kielce is very great, but that the distress is so terrible — of that surely nobody had any idea.
