The End Crowns the Work

There is an old Latin expression, „Finis Coronat opus“ [„the end crowns the work“]: whatever course anything, any undertaking or work may take in the process of its creation or genesis, the most important moment is the end, the conclusion, the finale. If the matter has ended well, everything is to be welcomed, however painful the birth of the thing may have been; if the end is a bad one, the whole process of development is worth absolutely nothing, however easy and pleasant it may have been. And how rightly[?] the Greek philosopher „Solon“ put it: „in every phenomenon one must look only at how it ends“.
We Jews of Będzin lived through the last half-year of 1936 in a nightmare, which went by the name of „the Gemilut-Hesed affair“. Eleven years ago a Gemilut-Hesed (interest-free loan) fund was created, with the aim of combating the severe consequences of the lasting economic crisis. The purpose of the fund was clear to everyone. The idea of helping impoverished Jews with interest-free loans found an echo in all the hearts of Będzin's Jewish population, and through common will and cooperation the G"H fund was created and developed rapidly. Its capital grew quickly, and together with the capital grew the local help given through it. There were times when the fund was a model for many towns in Poland. But then came impure people, who desecrated the sanctuary and brought the fund to a decline. We, citizens of Będzin — onlookers from the side, but also genuinely interested in the integrity and proper functioning of so important an institution — were truly grieved by the sad situation that had arisen, which also brought us shame and fear of sad consequences. The categorical position of the „Joint“ — that all those standing at the helm, during whose term of office the wrongdoings had occurred, must be removed to the last man, otherwise it would break off all relations and credit links with the fund — truly alarmed us.
The stormy course of the general meeting; the results of the elections, which satisfied the demands of the „D.D.K.“ only to 60—65 per cent; and also the combativeness of a certain group, which after the elections wanted to diminish[?] the results and did not stop even at using such means as have long been branded by the Jewish people as shameful and for which people suffered for years in the „3 letters“ — all this seriously alarmed us, cool-headed and objective people. Victory is a tasty morsel, and we trembled lest both sides would stubbornly insist on winning the fight, and the one truly defeated would be the needy Jew, because he would be left without a fund.
But the father of the fund, the „Joint“, is after all a father, and its emissaries do not lose their heads: they give up the fight where the common cause is in danger. The categorical position of the „Joint“ was softened; the will of the population, expressed through the elections at the general meeting, was recognised as sovereign, and the newly elected board was called to work. It turns out that the new choice was in fact very successful. The new board, with Mr. Mark Shein[?] Gross[?], set to work with great seriousness and full sincerity. A series of meetings of the board and the presidium has already been held, and loans have already been distributed to some 70[?]—80 families for a large sum. The „Joint“, too, is fully satisfied with the serious activity of the new board and has promised to return to the fund in the coming days all the moneys withdrawn, even with a surplus. Calm and a democratic attitude prevail on the board. All this gives us the certainty and full belief that for our sorrow we shall have much joy. For it is to be hoped that soon the G"H fund in Będzin will again be raised to the level at which it stood in its most flourishing period.
The matter has ended „well“ (be-khi tov), and we welcome this finale from the depths of our heart, and we call upon the entire Jewish community of Będzin: remember your dear and important rescue-institution („placówka“) — the Gemilut-Hesed fund — and strive with every possible means to strengthen its power.
S. D.
Crafts among the Jews (On the Question of Building Vocational Schools in Zagłębie)

[Zagłębie — education and crafts; opinion.] At the present moment, when Jewish society is imbued with the idea that our growing youth must be made productive and given the opportunity to learn every kind of craft that will secure their existence in life, it is important to take a look at our distant and near past of life and creation in the field of crafts, in order to know how handicraft was regarded among us then and what place it occupied in Jewish society.
Society's attitude toward the craftsman was not the same in all periods of our national life: there were times when people who earned their living from a craft very often occupied the place of honour in society, if intellectually they were worthy of it; on the other hand there were times when the craft degraded a person and he was looked upon as one of low rank...
In fact, the Jews, from the very beginning of becoming a people, displayed their great talents for crafts, and when the Tabernacle had to be built, there were soon found among[?] them all the necessary craftsmen and even such outstanding artists as Bezalel and Oholiab, of whom today's world of art would not have needed to be ashamed either.
Also in the time of our exile in Babylon we see that the crafts were in the hands of intellectual people of high culture.
How far the Jews had a sense for crafts we also see from the fact that in the Talmud it is stressed at every opportunity that a person must learn a craft in order to draw his livelihood from it. "Love work" ("Ehov et ha-melakha") — love the work of handicraft.
All this proves that at all times the Jews were imbued with the spirit of crafts, and that in former times culture and crafts went together.
Quite different, however, was the situation of the craftsman in the recent past: crafts among the Jews fell far down from their former throne and gave no honour to the one who drew his livelihood from them.
That was in the period of the second half of the last century, when Jews, for various reasons, declined strongly in cultural terms, gradually neglecting our old culture and not joining our new culture, to which only a select few devoted themselves. Schools[?] for learning crafts — it did not occur to anyone at all. So the [—] of teaching crafts was handed over to private craftsmen, who for the most part stood at a very low level in their whole[?] way of life; therefore it is no wonder that society showed no respect to the craftsman class and also ignored them in communal life.
The situation became better after the war years, when access to the schools became possible for poor children too; all children receive an elementary education, and the more capable one [—] great knowledge, so that the young craftsmen, when they came to learn a trade, were already armed with a great deal of knowledge. Therefore it is now no rarity to see a number of public activists who are craftsmen, occupying an important place in public life.
The craftsman is esteemed in society according to his individual intelligence, like everyone else, and many parents from very distinguished, well-pedigreed families, who once looked upon the trade of handicraft with disregard, now strive with all their might to make their sons and daughters into intelligent craftsmen, whatever trade it may be, because in recent years only people with a definite trade have remained in their positions, occupying also an honourable[?] place in society, at a time when the great rich men — "people of air" — were knocked off[?] the surface and thereby also lost their former position in society.
Therefore the command of the hour now is to build as many vocational schools as possible, also for girls, who have suffered even more than the boys from the world upheaval. Once a woman did not need to think about independence: she married and the husband provided the livelihood; today not every young man is able to take upon himself the burden of family life, because unemployment (lack of livelihood) among Jews is too great, and only independent women with a definite trade have suitors; and that is precisely why the only aspiration of every woman is to learn a trade — it secures her existence in all places to which she may have to emigrate, and emigration is, after all, now on the agenda.
And if now a vocational-school building is to be added here, it deserves to be welcomed by all strata of the population; the initiators have understood the needs of the hour and of the generation, and adapted themselves to the new aspiration for an institution (placówka) for young intelligent craftsmen.
Mordechai Zylberblat.
The Road to “Popularity”... (A Conversation of Sorts).

[Satirical essay — society and culture; feuilleton.] By P. Blumenkranc, Częstochowa [?].
The question of how to become popular is truly complicated, and at once [?] various difficulties arise, e.g.: what does popularity mean? Is the beginning of popularity really one and the same [?] for everyone? Are the same rules valid for all fields of work — for a musician as for a man of letters, for a painter as for a public activist, for an official as for an antisemite, etc. [?]. And [?] the matter is quite a hard one, so we must find a formula that will at least have certain points of contact with every field and with every mortal.
And it is precisely this formula that our present conversation is about.
After some deliberation we arrived at the strange conclusion “that the most fitting (at any rate one of the most fitting) answers to the question is: to become popular one must be a ‘socher’ [merchant], i.e. a musician plus merchant, a writer plus merchant, etc. But what does it mean to be a ‘socher’?
Here a small philological digression.
“The meaning of the word ‘socher’ is to go around; the merchant is called ‘socher’ because he goes around selling his wares (‘Otzar Yisrael’). The word socher comes from Chaldean [?]; socher means to encircle, to go around.”
The word socher, as said, means to go around, to encircle, i.e. to plead, to persuade and to adapt oneself.
If we translate all this into our present-day language, it turns out that one can run [?] a business for, say, thirty years and never attain the knack [?] of a true merchant.
For, as we have already mentioned, a merchant must know how to adapt himself, to efface his very self for the sake of the customer, to incarnate himself in him; for just as a writer describing a thieves’ scene must be transmigrated into a real thief, so the merchant must, e.g., sometimes transform [?] himself into a 20-year-old young lady who has to meet a young man in the evening; she wants, say, something pretty and “[?]” for little money, and he must fit it to her, talk her into it and sell it.
At other times again he must be transmigrated into a man in the “[?]” months, who wants to be obliged [?] etc. [?].
For clarity, at least one concrete example of a true and [?] merchant such as one meets every day.
A “patient” comes into a haberdashery shop and wants, let us say, “Swedish” gloves. As it happens there are no Swedish gloves in the shop. If the shopkeeper is a schlemiel, he says:
— Unfortunately I have no Swedish gloves — and that is the end of the customer. If the shopkeeper has a bit more practice but is still far [?] from perfect, he answers: at this minute I don’t have them in stock; tomorrow I am getting a large selection, the newest of the new — thinking meanwhile that he will snatch a pair of gloves somewhere; one must not let a customer go.
But if the patient falls into the hands of a true merchant, he will not leave without gloves. The merchant will lay out gloves of every kind before him and at the same time give him to understand that “Swedish” gloves are altogether impractical and not solid; indeed he does not stock them because he has a better clientele and must suit their good taste. He will talk so long and so broadly until the patient leaves the shop loaded with shopworn leather gloves, old-fashioned shirts, tasteless ties and the like.
The patient does not feel [?] that the merchant is “cheating” [?]; on the contrary, he takes leave [?] like our [?] and buys...
* * *
Now, what does the advantage of merchant-mindedness look like in non-commercial fields?
Well, let us take writers.
A young hungry poet sits in a garret and writes little poems wept out of him [?], of which (at best) one in ten is accepted for printing free of charge. He cannot do otherwise: he polishes every word, waits for moods, checks, polishes — and starves.
A second one, quite often also with talent, acts differently: many newspapers come out; one must reckon that in every daily instalment a girl must [?] be raped — and at once he produces novels and supplies the readers with “[?]”, because the reader’s heart craves it.
A second [sic] mercantile writer calculates:
— What, there is a war in Spain? I already have a story about a young man who was in the trenches and tells about Franco’s [?] [?] beautiful women, love affairs, intrigues, so that people will wait [?] with bated breath for the next “instalment” and read it even while peeling potatoes.
It happens that there is no paper in which to print about the boards [?]; so one publishes one’s own, and in order to remind the public of the earlier [?] paper, one launches [?] [?] and [?] with sharpness [?] (if it pays) or [?] — when one finds on the other side [?] a certain loan [?]. And there is something to eat and drink...
A painter, for example. Not being [?] a merchant, he can paint landscapes, still lifes and genre scenes all his life, and possibly [?] no one will hear a word about him.
But if he manages to drag along some shikse [gentile girl] or to make a real “[?]” of a “[?]” reviewer — then everything is all right.
And so on ad infinitum, for since the foundation of foundations today is the collective (totalism, in the foreign tongue), one must today please the collective, or the one who regards himself as the collective’s guide — in a word, cultivate the mercantile sense...
* * *
Such examples we could bring ad infinitum — for the time being we wish to conclude with the hope that this short conversation will at least lighten a little the hard [?] road of some of those who strive for popularity, and incidentally also help explain the strange phenomenon that our Jewish merchants, the little merchants, are surrounded by so much envy and begrudging.
Apparently they are envied for their developed mercantile sense, which, as we have clearly shown, is a means to be [?], the vestibule to every hall. And therefore one fights [?], because by developing in the people the striving-urge one can achieve extraordinary results in other, purely spiritual fields; one can activate the slumbering spiritual forces of the people,
A Chance That Obliges to Deeds... / (Addressed to the Sosnowiec Kehilla Administration).

[Sosnowiec — kehilla; editorial.]
At last, after a long period of commissar rule in our kehilla, Jewish Sosnowiec has obtained the possibility of taking into its own hands the stewardship of its autonomous institution, the kehilla, in the persons of the public representatives it has elected. There is already a new kehilla leadership, which, immediately after taking over all the business from the outgoing kehilla commissar, set about fulfilling the duties laid upon it. We, too, can therefore say that we have already lived through the period of commissar rule, connected with the person of Mr. Tencer, and now we are entering a second one — the period of a democratic kehilla leadership, to which we attach many pious wishes[?] and hopes...
On the first period we have no intention, in this connection, of wasting superfluous words. A more exact assessment of the latter we already gave in one of the earlier issues of the "Zagl. Tsayt." [Zaglembier Tsaytung]. We therefore wish to proceed to discuss the forthcoming[?] period of the newly elected kehilla. It must, however, be said a priori[?] that the well-known agreement[?] between the two election-contending[?] sides in our town most probably saved the situation and made it possible for the elected public representatives to take over the leadership of the new kehilla.
That was the only way out of the eventuality, to hand over at least[?] the Sosnowiec kehilla for the long term into the hands of the elected public representatives.
But — and here we reach the most important part of the following[?] article:
It is clear that Jewish kehilla life in our town has been given a chance — and an effectively good chance at that — to introduce a series of important and first-rank necessary institutions for Jewish public life in Sosnowiec. Let the present kehilla administration remember that our shattered public life needs[?] not only spiritual food and clergy[?]. There is a broad field for achievements, and it is entirely[?] on the ability of the present kehilla that the success of, and the recognition by the local public for, their achievements depend.
There is a chance, which, however, must not be squandered[?] for nothing. From an elected "kehilla leadership" relatively more is expected, and the responsibility is greater, much greater. First and foremost one must have before oneself a plan of serious[?], sensible[?] deeds and forthcoming tasks.
More concretely about the tasks of the new kehilla in Sosnowiec — another time.
L. K.
It Is High Time to Reflect. / (More on This Year's Passover Campaign).

[Zagłębie — relief and Passover; article.]
Only a few weeks separate us from the holiday of Passover, and as this holiday approaches the worry grows. It is therefore now already high time to give it some thought.
We have had to live through the hard winter months. It will be no exaggeration if we say that 90 percent of the needy, who ought to have received public aid, a little coal to warm their frozen limbs — did indeed freeze in the hard winter days, because that, unfortunately, is what our public aid has looked like lately: it consists for the most part of... prescriptions, plans for the future and the like.
But why touch again on this [—][?] matter[?]! It seems that it is enough when sad facts speak for themselves. It is therefore hard to write in the form of again turning to the Jewish population for help. We, the Jewish people, have after all been designated "merciful sons of the merciful" — but unfortunately lately the feeling of compassion among us, too, has been blunted. Should one now unfold the Jewish distress and write about it — it seems this is superfluous, since, as said, the distress itself cries out[?]. As is, after all, well enough known to all, the number of those needing public aid has unfortunately not diminished, but on the contrary increased; poverty has lately forced its way into a large number of respectable[?] Jewish families and has become a permanent resident...
And one should note here that if they starve and freeze the whole year — which is, it seems, not one of the pleasant things — it is nevertheless a sacred duty that we must see to it that at least for the eight days of Passover they can be made to forget their great worries, and be torn for a short time from the sharp claws of the distress that has gripped them. With a clear conscience we shall be able to celebrate the holiday only when we know that our impoverished brethren, who languish in hunger the whole year, are also sitting at the festive table, provided with the articles of first necessity.
Year after year a Passover campaign is carried out by the Zagłębie kehillas, and the philanthropic institutions also carry out a Passover campaign. This year, however, this relief campaign must be carried out with more energy and effort.
There will have to be more givers and larger gifts, because unfortunately this year there are more receivers. Not a single Jew who has but the possibility of giving may exclude himself from the campaign.
We would also turn[?] to the proper authorities, that there be a just and rational distribution, for we have a rule: "One does not investigate [those asking] for food"...
This year's campaign must be governed by the slogan: if you are not a receiver — you must be a giver!
B. M.
Outlandish Records

When one learns of the outlandish records reported every day in the newspapers of various countries, one clutches one's head and asks: would it not be more fitting to send these people to a madhouse? Surely it cannot be that people with normal senses should undertake to set such crazy records, and that normal people should still admire them and pay for these follies.
A few months ago, in a small American town, a man won a bet: in 30 minutes (one glass[?] after another) he drank no less than five hundred litres of beer.
Charles Potter[?] in Sydney (Australia) won a bet by drinking at one go 12 large glasses of beer while standing on his head.
In Buenos Aires (Argentina) a man bet that he would drink at one go half a litre of castor oil. He won the bet, but what his stomach said about it we do not know.
In Galvan-Isle[?] (South America) a man has just turned 82 who for 50 years has eaten nine eggs every day; that is, to date he has eaten 165 thousand eggs.
In Písek (Czechoslovakia) a young peasant won a bet by eating at one go 123 large Bohemian dumplings (kneydlekh).
Sam Hart[?] in Florida (America) ate within one hour no less than 168 "bagels"[?], and it did him no harm whatsoever, as the local papers say.
A few years ago a coffee firm from Brazil exhibited at the Leipzig fair. To show how good its coffee is, a man at the exhibition stand drank 100 cups of coffee a day for 8 days running.
Or what do you say to fasting[?] records [—]: in Michelka[?] (South America) two peasants, under the supervision of hundreds of spectators, fasted for 26 hours on end. Also a record...
In Chicago a man sat for 26 hours on a block of ice, until he was taken off to hospital with a 40-degree fever.
In Linz (Austria) the police a few weeks ago locked up a "record-collector" on whom were found, in his pockets and around his body, 300 small bottles, 80 pipes, 50 knives, 30 spoons, 15 forks, 10 broken pairs of scissors and 3 kilos of old newspaper. The police at once took this "record-collector" off to a madhouse, and thereby did the wisest thing it could possibly have done.
From various quarters, however, such crazy, wild records are paid quite well. The Metro Goldwyn film company in Hollywood, for example, keeps a whole menagerie of such "heroes".
Boston Bean[?], for example, is champion[?] at eating at one go 12 litres of "baked beans".
Rudolf[?] Rigler eats within one hour no less than 24 roast veal cutlets.
Klem[?] Beck eats at one [—] 20 kilos of all kinds of fish.
Matt Grenbriden[?] eats at one go 8 kilos of Italian noodles.
Metro Goldwyn also employs Tom Magnus, who drinks at one go 22 litres of beer.
American cinemas are now showing a man, Eland[?] by name, who eats at a single lunch 16 cutlets with 6 kilos of potatoes and washes it down with 15 litres of beer.
And this film has been running throughout South America, almost everywhere, for months already, and the public does not tire of seeing this record, for which the film company paid quite handsome fees...
Z. Haber[?], Vienna.
Heard and Seen.

[Będzin — weekly feuilleton; charity, rabbinate.] By Ben Amotz.

"Let there only be takers"..
We receive a delegation from the "Beit Lechem" society [poor relief] in Będzin. And probably[?] for the first time it happens to us that representatives of a philanthropic society, and especially of a society with such a "brand" as "Beit Lechem", do not come before us and sing their lament, which every time ends with the cry:
— Help! We are going under!...
On the contrary, this time the representatives of the above-mentioned institution came with "smiling faces"; their faces beamed with joy, exactly as if the big prize had fallen into their lap.
— What do you want? we asked the delegation (naturally after a longer talk about "important" matters).
— We have come to you so that you announce the good news in your paper that this year's Passover campaign of "Beit Lechem" will surpass all campaigns so far; for this purpose we have colossal possibilities, so that the needy part of the local Jewish population (if only they will ask...) will be provided this Passover with all good things.
At first we did not have much faith in what the members of the delegation were telling us, for we know how the newly risen rich relate to all institutions, and especially to "Beit Lechem" — the institution that busies itself with such "trifles" as stilling the hunger of neglected families... But when the delegates laid out before us the collection sheets, on which are recorded the collections in the shtiblekh [Hasidic prayer rooms] last Purim for the benefit of "Beit Lechem", only then did we have reason to believe that what we were hearing is the plain truth...
And so that the Jewish public should know what income this year's Purim campaign brought "Beit Lechem", it is worth mentioning at least a few "shtiblekh" that "distinguished themselves" in this field.
We will begin with the Ger [Góra Kalwaria] "shtibl" (not with the "branches", where the income was also not hard-won[?], but with the shtibl of category A, number one...), where no less than 40 (read: forty) groszy was collected; then "come" the Radomsko and Sochaczew "shtiblekh" (we again mean the "first classes" here...), where it "fell" in half-złotys...
The "record" in this field was set by the Aleksandrów "shtibl", where from just two donors there came a whole 22 (twenty-two) groszy; the rest of the congregation was in any case already exempt from giving, because after all "Beit Lechem" gives out for Passover nothing more than various products, so one can surely have no complaints that in a "shtibl" where several dozen Jews pray more than 22 groszy should be collected...
The delegation, which all the while spoke with great enthusiasm about the generosity, still wanted to show us a series of "brilliant" lists, among them also the list of the town beit midrash, where the collection brought 5 (five) groszy; but we no longer wanted to hear the "figures that speak volumes", and simply agreed with the delegation that their "joy" is well-founded: they are, so to speak, rid of a burden on their heads — where to take money for Passover; the only "worry" of the board is
— let there only be takers...

"Everyone can — egal [all the same]"...
The conversation takes place on the tram, between a few Jews riding from Będzin to Sosnowiec. "Bending" one's ear to overhear what the Jews are talking about is not necessary, because when Jews talk, whether on the tram or on the train, one hears them even in the next carriage.
The two talkers are: 1) a well-known parnas [board member] of the Będzin kehilla, who is head and body in Sosnowiec, but whose "weight"[?] is in Będzin — more precisely, in the Będzin kehilla, when meetings of the kehilla council take place... and 2) a young fellow, half Mizrahi, half Orthodox, but above all a strong opponent of the Agudah's policy in Będzin on the rabbinate question. Around "them" — several[?] Jews with bowed[?] heads say not a word, but listen with relish and smile roguishly. They take special "pleasure" when the young fellow relates details of Sunday's meeting devoted to the rabbinate question in Będzin.
— I'm amazed at you — the young man says to the parnas — that you go along with the "Agudah"; after all, you are some sort of "postępowy"[?] [progressive] person. So where does your love for the "Agudah" come from?
— "What, no fool"[?] — the parnas exclaims with a laugh — why do you meddle in the business of rabbis; what difference does it make which rabbi it will be: this one can do as well as that one, and that one can do as well as the other. Big difference — Agudah, shmire[?], "Mizrahi"
— "Everyone can — egal"...
The "argument" is not a new one. In the book "Nifla'ot Hadashot" (if I am not mistaken) a parable is told of Rebbe Reb Bunem [of Przysucha] of blessed memory, who was asked the following question. The Gemara says "whoever makes himself mute or blind, etc." — whoever pretends to be mute or blind does not die before he is punished with that very thing. So the Hasidim asked: and how is it when someone puts on the rabbinic mantle — a shtreimel with a silk zhupitse [long coat] — and says: I am a rebbe?
To this the above-mentioned rebbe answered with the following parable:
In a small town there was a drunkard who wallowed day and night in the gutters from drunkenness, which caused his children great grief. Finally the children decided to make the following experiment with their father. Bringing him home once from the street drunk, they laid him to sleep in a bed that stood in a specially tidied room and put priest's vestments by the bed.
The drunkard, waking from his sleep in the morning, suddenly saw that he was in a splendid room and that priestly clothes lay before him; moreover, a servant comes in, bows humbly and asks:
— Does the Reverend Father wish to dress already?
— What[?], what is this, a dream or reality? Me a priest? But then I am indeed a priest, since the vestments lie ready before me.
— I will make one more test whether I am a priest — the drunkard decided; he went up to the bookcase, took out a book and began to read...
...Naturally, the book was entirely foreign to this "priest", but that did not weaken his certainty that he is indeed a priest.
Ay — he says — so what, I can't [read]?
— Because "not everyone can"...
And with exactly the same "argument" the parnas answered the young man, who wanted to influence him not to follow the ways of the "Agudah" on the rabbinate question.
But the young man did not succeed, because the parnas is also well "versed" in the rabbinic world, and he is convinced that it makes no difference whatsoever which rabbi it will be, because
— "everyone can — egal"...
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Vayikra)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Vayikra
—o—
a) "And He called unto Moses" (Lev. 1:1)
In Moses' generation there were the tribes, the elders, Aaron, Bezalel and Hur, but of all the righteous the Holy One, blessed be He, called only to Moses, because Moses fled from authority, and "whoever pursues authority, authority flees from him, and whoever flees from authority, authority pursues him." Midrash Tanhuma.
• • •
Once there came to the Chafetz Chaim of blessed memory R' Shmuel Rakthiim[?], a well-known [—][?] Jew who had found favour with Marshal Piłsudski, whom he had once rescued[?] in the Tsarist times. The Marshal remembered it of him and did him good all his days[?]. He used his standing with the Marshal to do Jews many favours.
He was a simple Jew, but honour made him drunk, and he already craved to become also... a Sejm deputy. So in 1929 he came to the Chafetz Chaim and asked him to issue a letter and a public appeal (kol kore) that people should elect him a Sejm deputy. He gave him to understand that he only meant to do Jews favours.
Says the Chafetz Chaim to him:
The Midrash says: "Whoever pursues authority, authority flees from him, and whoever flees from authority, authority pursues him." As is known, the expression "whoever" (kol) comes to include something; and what does the "kol" come to include here? [—]: "whoever pursues authority" — even one who chases honour and authority for the sake of Heaven, even when he does not mean himself but only the sake of Heaven — honour flees from him; and "and whoever flees from authority, authority pursues him" includes even one who flees honour not for the sake of Heaven but because he organically[?] hates honour — even with such a flight from honour, honour still pursues the man...
(Heard from Rabbi Moshe Ir[?]esis.)
—o—
b) "Which is upon the altar" (ibid., 8)
"Could he bring wood from his own house? [No —] the wood and the fire too are of the public." (Menachot 22a.)
The public has a share in every individual's sin. The environment acts on the individual with its bad atmosphere; therefore the public must give fire and wood for the individual's sacrifice, because the individual's sin was caused by the atmosphere of the public...
R' Zvi Hirsch Kalischer.
—o—
c) "When a ruler sinneth" (Lev. 4:22)
"Happy is the generation whose ruler brings a sin-offering for his inadvertent sin." Horayot 10b.
So what does it have to do with the generation if the ruler brings a sin-offering for an inadvertent sin?
Because a person does not see his own faults, and if the generation is a sinful one, people flatter the ruler and are not exacting about his sins. It is otherwise, though, when the ruler brings a sacrifice for his sins: that is surely a proof[?] that the generation does not flatter him, and therefore — "happy is the generation"...
R' Israel Salanter.
—o—
d) "If a soul shall sin through ignorance" (Lev. 4:2)
"The children of Israel bring a sin-offering, but the gentiles do not bring a sin-offering." Torat Kohanim.
When a person sins against God, "between man and the Omnipresent", there is a difference between inadvertent and deliberate. Between man and his fellow, however, there is no difference: "a man is always forewarned, whether inadvertent or deliberate" (Bava Kamma 29).
When a gentile sins, he sins only against people, and therefore if inadvertent he is exempt ("and the gentiles do not bring a sin-offering"); but a Jew, even when he sins against people, it is also "between man and his fellow", because a Jew's guilt is, as a rule, thrown[?] upon all Jews; so every Jew's sin against people is a "sin between man and his fellow", and therefore he is obliged to bring a sin-offering even for an inadvertent sin.
R' Yoshe Ber of Brisk.
—o—
e) "And if a soul sin, and hear the voice of swearing, and is a witness, whether he hath seen or known" (Lev. 5:1)
If someone knows of a sin in another person, it is a sign — "and if a soul sin" — that he himself has sinned... A pure person knows of no sins — even with himself[?] — in his fellow...
Imrei Chen.
—o—
f) "And the priest shall make an atonement for him before the Lord, and it shall be forgiven him" (ibid., 26)
Of an anointed priest (kohen mashiach) it is not said "and it shall be forgiven him", because the priest atones for himself, and oneself one cannot and may not forgive too much...
R' Zadok HaKohen of Lublin.
"Victims" of the Spanish Revolution (A Humoresque)

I and my colleague Leizer went into a "rezure" [? probably a barbershop], where two apprentices threw themselves upon us, and in the blink of an eye we were already lying lathered up, and 2 razors were raised over us, ready for the "slaughter".
— Do you say, Moritz, that the "Republicans" will hold Madrid? — my lad called over to Leizer's lad.
— What[?] do you mean hold! A plague the Fascists will be able to accomplish [i.e. they will achieve nothing]!
— Meanwhile, you know, the Fascists keep pushing forward and are already [—] past "Mavala de Alarcón"[?]; a few more days and Madrid will fall.
— I don't give a hoot for yours[?]! How does "Mavala" come to Spain? It's just like from Segrushne[?] to Stockholm.
— You're an ignoramus in geography; take a look, you'll see[?] — he points with the razor at my nose — let's say that this is Spain, and on the other side — he says, running the razor over my left cheek — lies Madrid.
— Help, my nose, my cheek! I immediately glanced into the mirror and saw blood on my left cheek.
— Calm down, sir, you're spoiling my map. Now we come to "Alicante" — he takes a ride with the razor into my right ear — right after that is Franco's headquarters, and then you can already rend your garments and sit shiva over your whole Spain. Meanwhile the "Fascist" had crawled up to my throat...
— Just wait a minute — the "Republican" spoke up — it's not going that easily — you've completely forgotten that right here stands the "Basque government army".
— Help! — Leizer shouted — you've scraped[?] my mug[?]; take away the "Basque knife".
— "Malkariekh"[?]! He's an "ungeriger"[?] — the Fascist [—] — the customer can't stand your lies.
— He's against Fascism because he's no sucker (yold) — the Republican flared up[?] — you're showing him a false map.
— My map is false? Your map is false,
— If so, I'll show you right now what kind of face your map has.
Both lads went at each other like two wild oxen. The Republican ran in the direction of the Fascist map — towards my face, which looked like a ploughed field, and the Fascist — towards my colleague's face, which didn't look any better either.
Needless to add that we tore ourselves out of their hands as if from a fire and, with our bloodied "maps", barely escaped with our lives.
Avichayil[?].
—o—
The film "Moonlight Sonata" with Paderewski in the leading role.
We have already seen many motion pictures about and with famous musicians. They depicted either a certain fragment of the artist's life, or dwelt on one of the artist's principal works, to which a kind of romantic background was[?] invented.
The role of the artist was played by specially engaged actors. Thus films were created about Chopin, Beethoven, Schubert, Liszt, etc.
The newest film "Moonlight Sonata", with the world-famous Polish composer and musician Ignacy Paderewski, is formed[?] quite differently — both in its character and in its whole composition — from the musician-films so far. This is the merit first of all of the scenario-writer, who wanted to create something new, and then of the "[—]" director.
The action of this most interesting film takes place in the castle of an aristocratic Swedish family. Paderewski plays here a chance guest, using[?] his free time to perform his splendid concerts and musical works. It is truly admirable how this 76-year-old man carries himself freely and naturally before the camera, how clearly and sharply his diction rings, not to mention his musical performance itself.
Paderewski has revealed himself here as a first-rank actor. He appears without make-up on his face. Of his musical works which he performs in this film, one must mention Chopin's "Polonaise", Liszt's "Rhapsody", the first movement of Beethoven's "Moonlight Sonata" and the "Minuet" by Paderewski himself.
It goes without saying that the music is the main nerve of the film mentioned. It fills out its whole essence and character, blending in harmonious wholeness with the individual scenes and fragments.
In London, a few days earlier, the festive premiere of "Moonlight Sonata" took place, to which the most prominent personalities[?] of London came. Paderewski too came specially to the premiere of his first film, which is today the greatest artistic event in London. In Poland it is being distributed by the well-known film company "United Artists". It is already in Warsaw, and we shall have the opportunity to admire it all over Poland, also in Zagłębie.
S. V.
Musical Conversations

[Culture — music; serialized essay.]
A.
"The mirror of the folk-genius.
If one wants to recognise the essence of a people, its spiritual mentality and temperament, one must listen closely to its musical creations.
Among primitive peoples music has a special, ingrained trait of character, which finds expression on various occasions of their hard life, and which is a reflection of the unequal struggle they must wage with the elemental forces of[?] the wild African in the deep [—][?] horizon, with which they come into daily contact.
Music played an everyday role in antiquity; then it was an inspiring force, a religious factor in the life of the peoples. The various tones and sounds served as an accompanying resonator, and apart from the purely aesthetic side of the matter (the embellishment of divine worship, etc.) it had a decisive effect on the masses: the emotional element, the playing upon the strings of the enthusiastic thinking individual [?], the provoking in man of ecstasy, of religious trembling, birth [?], etc. [?], the passing away of man; likewise the most varied wild rites and customs of that time were wrapped in various sounds and tones: the bringing of human sacrifices to the numerous idols, the burning [printed 'farbregen', apparently for 'farbrenen'] of widows beside the grave of their deceased husband, and all the other savageries of the long-lasting barbaric era — all of it had to take place to the accompaniment of noisy sounds, so that [?] every act of life was closely bound up with the abstract little world [?] of tones and sounds...
Music also took on more concrete forms, whose shaping went through [?] a long, quite long path of development.
B.
Then, in the so-called "knightly" era, when the "new age" began to create its first conditions for flowering and development — the barbarities took on a more worldly appearance; the modern world order brought with it a more luxury-like view of music, whose refinement and ennoblement became a fact. Then music gained its great momentum, then it received the elaborate [?] content that made possible its later ascent; the progress of its spiritual expansion.
So it went on [?] in the 18th and 19th centuries, when it was the fashion that every self-respecting [?] aristocrat (not to mention kings, emperors and princes) considered it a point of honour to engage the best composer and the best fiddlers and pipers [?], so as to be able to boast: "Now [?] I have a kapelye [court orchestra] in my court."
It is, after all, well known that the magnates — the Liechtensteins, the Esterházys, and whatever else they were called there — maintained at their own expense the various musical geniuses such as Bach, Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven, etc. And not for nothing does one feel an enormous difference between Haydn, dependent on his high-placed bread-givers and on their caprices, and our own [?] Mendelssohn, the freely moving, uncramped music-creator, who is himself the master of his will and his creation — because he did not need to depend on others, being himself a member of a rich, distinguished family.
So one need not be any special "Mar bar Rav Ashi" [great expert] in the laws of music, because even an average, well-feeling music lover, hearing the illustrations [works] of two such contrasting composers [printed 'kompanistn'], will soon make out which of them was happy in his lifetime and which was not...
The enrichment of musical literature also helped to form a general social approach, a unified view of all the nuances and effects which, with their magic, grace and distinctiveness [?], further strengthened the rule of almighty music.
The culminating point of this was reached at the beginning of the 19th century; the arriving liberalist epoch began to bring forth its first shoots.
(To be continued)
Conductor M. Dawidson.
“The Cooking Spoon” — Oy, Ma Nomar

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-Lefl”; poem.]
The Cooking Spoon
Humour and Satire
Compiled by Amutslo [pen name].

Oy, Ma Nomar (“Oh, what shall we say”)
(a little of Khaye Pese's mysticism).

Oy, what shall we say, what shall we speak,
what then shall I tell you —
that we lie [unclear word: “ayngehirtshaft”]
in the earth, very deep, to go and hurry?

Oy, what shall we say, what shall we speak,
what news then shall we tell,
when all the news is good only
for the seven good laments!

Oy, what shall we say, what shall we speak —
what is there to conclude from it,
when all we have from the news
is only to... say and to sing?!

Oy, what shall we say, what shall we speak,
about all the seven weeks?
One can only hold one's belly laughing,
where does one get the means to make Shabbat...

Always the same thing remains for us:
Oy, what shall we say, what shall we speak..
It turns out we are talking to the lamp,
pleading with the candelabrum...

Oy, what shall we say, what shall we speak —
what then will one tell you
except[?] this great “pszykachs”[?],
that the “kimkhe bekasise” [pun on “kimkha de-piskha”, the Passover flour charity — “flour in the till”] is going
to hand out for the holiday..
Yakl ben Alekl[?].
People with Titles.

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-Lefl”; joke.]
— Listen, Reb Moshe, my family consists only of great people, hear this:
My wife is a doctor-surgeon — she “cuts” my [unclear word “naysn”], my son is an engineer — he measures the streets, my mother-in-law is a Dr. of chemistry — she mixes heaven and earth together, my son-in-law is one of the greatest writers — he writes promissory notes [veksl, bills of exchange], my daughter is an astronomer — she spends her time with young men under the moon and the stars, and I myself am one of the greatest mathematicians — I only “calculate” what the “unshand”[?] [perhaps “disgrace”/“circumstance”] has made of me...
Lejb Sztabiński.
At the Fish Market.

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-Lefl”; joke.]
An overheard conversation.
A Jewish woman (to the fishwife): Tell me, Yentl, what's the sense in dead fish being dearer than live ones?
Fishwife: Don't you know that, as it is[?] in the world, the living envy the dead...
Bar-Gesh.
Będzin Parnassim Have a Sense of Smell...

[Będzin — kehilla; satire.]
The “goniec” [messenger] of the Będzin kehilla comes in to a parnas he knows and hands him an invitation to a session of the kehilla council.
The parnas puts on his spectacles, reads through the agenda, and an angry grimace appears on his face.
— Why are you making a face? — his wife asks him.
— I got the invitation — answers the parnas — and I thought it was already about the real “business”, but meanwhile it concerns only a trifle.
— How much could it be? — the wife asks again.
— What do I know, maybe a fifty...
Stop Press.

[Będzin — kehilla; satire.]
Before closing this issue we received the confidential news that the kehilla board in Będzin has resolved that, in honour of Passover, the floor of the town synagogue [shtot-shul] shall be washed.
To the Fight Against Suicides!

[Sosnowiec — burial society; satire.]
The “Khaver shel Emes” society [burial society] in Sosnowiec is drawing up regulations concerning suicides, so that they shall not be given burial.
At last the right measures have been adopted against suicides. It is really a scandalous scandal: what is this — the bridegroom pleaded[?] remorse — bang[?]! — for 10 groszy of sublimate [mercury poison], and blessed be the true Judge! The wife did not want to “be bored” alone at home — crash! a pull by the rope and out[?]!..
The husband “gassed himself” on the Kaleushanka[?] [unclear place], deep, tap — and an end!..
A merchant was expecting a guest with a “yellow ribbon” and had nothing with which to “honour” the guest, so he lay down[?] to suck[?] at the gas pipe.
As long as you, rascals, were left at will[?], you “lived” a “good day”; now you will be taught manners — no more “mekhaye”!
When you feel like making a “wycieczka” [excursion] to the next world, you'll catch it. A stick and [?]? — “nie ma tak dobrze!” [Polish: it's not that easy!] From now on, when you have a “chrapka” [craving] to pay a visit to Paradise, it will go for you “stopniowo” [gradually]: first of all you will have to walk about in shoes without[?] soles, so that it can well[?] leak in and leak back out. It will have to start with a catarrh, and the “Kasa Chorych” [sickness fund] will give you [something] for the stomach. One must have cupping glasses and swallow pills, and, God willing, you will then do a “skhartl”[?]... — like respectable householders! But not when you want, when you feel like it — “nie ma tak dobrze”!
The First “Condition”

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-Lefl”; joke.]
Of an old bachelor.
A match was proposed to a stingy old bachelor. The bachelor-groom set the matchmaker conditions:
— She must be young, must have a dowry of at least 20 thousand złoty, and must... wear shoes size 37!..
— Why exactly 37? — the matchmaker wondered.
— Because I took 6 pairs of ladies' overshoes [latshn] in payment of a debt, and they are all size 37!

"Di menushetkes[?] makharonye[?]" — with the participation of the subtenant [sublokator].
"Domestic Peace" (Shalom Bayis) — from Monday to Wednesday.

[Humour — "The Cooking Spoon"; satire on the Spanish Civil War reports.]
Berlin. The insurgents are celebrating one victory after another. Any day now Madrid will be taken by the insurgents.
• • •
Paris. From Madrid it is reported that the government troops have won great victories. The insurgents have suffered great defeats.
• • •

The Last Will of a Well-Known Sosnowiec Manufacturer.

[Humour — "The Cooking Spoon"; Sosnowiec — satire on philanthropists.]
The following will of a well-known Sosnowiec [Sosnowiec] philanthropist has fallen into the hands of the "Kokh-lefl".
Children, you shall treat the employees humanely. You shall let them do as they wish: if they absolutely insist on working until 12 at night, you shall not disturb them, and if they strike even 3 years in a row, you shall let them do that too...
Since I find myself on the threshold of the World of Truth and I fear the final reckoning, I therefore demand of you, my children, that you draw up a list of all my pre-war debts which I remained owing to the Sosnowiec charitable societies, and settle them at 10 per cent. The pledge to "Linas Kholim" [society for nursing the sick], which I paid by mistake, do not forget to deduct from the settlement...
Sports Supplement

[Humour — "The Cooking Spoon"; sport — satire.]
Edited by a sportsman [sportowiec].
In the very near future an international swimming match is to take place in America.
As the "Kokh-lefl" sports[?] [sportozyink — reporter?] has learned, a well-known Sosnowiec merchant, who is bathing over his head... in debts, will travel from Sosnowiec to the match.
Boxing.
At a meeting of the Zagłębie boxers the critical situation of the boxing profession was discussed. The speakers complained that the number of spectators at the boxing matches is shrinking from day to day.
It was resolved that from now on there will be no boxing in leather gloves; from now on people will box with bare fists. After every match the ambulance [pogotowie] will take several battered[?] boxers to the hospitals. At a "podbródek"[?] [chin punch] a whole set[?] of porcelain will pour out of the mouth; at a "lewy sierp" [left hook] a bone will burst, or the nose will swell up like a pumpkin [bania]; they'll hit the way one should — they'll get a "skręt kiszek" [twisted gut] — let boxing be real boxing! That will surely be a "hit" with the esteemed public of spectators.
—o—
Three Jokes.
— Do you know the three jokes [vitsn]?
— Which ones?
— Kato-witz [Katowice], Sosno-witz [Sosnowiec] and Myslo-witz [Mysłowice].
Ugly and Beautiful Women.

[Humour — "The Cooking Spoon"; light essay — women and beauty.]
When the ugly one wants to be beautiful, she becomes uglier still.
They say that most beautiful women are foolish.
A hint of this is also mentioned in the Bible.
And it stands to reason: the beautiful woman is content with her beauty and neglects her other virtues, even when she possesses them.
Most of the beautiful girls in the schools neglect their studies; they think their beauty will cover the shortcoming of little education and even of little intelligence.
Most beautiful girls read little, because they are sure that with their beauty they will cover up their ignorance.
And if they devote themselves entirely to their beauty, if they put all their mind and all their soul into beauty alone, they do not sharpen their mind for cleverer, deeper matters, and they remain foolish.
It is told of a certain talented young painter that he has in his album portraits of many women, and few of them are not beautiful, not graceful and not charming [sic], but instead intelligence, education and a deep mind look out of them. When he was asked why he does not paint beautiful women, he answered that if he wanted to paint geese, he would go to the coop.
Of course, nowadays there are enough beautiful women who are no geese; there are beautiful women who are both intelligent and educated. Such beautiful women existed in all times, and in the salons they were always the exceptions[?]; but with many beautiful women it is accepted by a great majority of people that they neglect their other virtues because they devote themselves too much to their beauty.
Yet however foolish the beautiful woman may be, the ugly one who wants to make herself beautiful is more foolish still.
There is simply no comparison[?] in foolishness to an ugly woman who piles every trouble upon herself just to look beautiful; she does not reckon with what harms[?] her and with what makes her a laughingstock. It makes no difference to her that the powder with which she thickly smears her face makes her uglier still; the paint that she slaps on coarse and greasy makes her look like a painted lump of clay.
They tell a joke about a pious[?] [frimen] dealer who had worked his way up: he went to a painter and ordered a portrait of himself. When the painter named him a price, the self-made merchant replied: "Fine, I won't haggle with you, but don't spare [zhalevn, żałować] the oil."
It is the same with those ugly women who want to look beautiful: they heave beautiful clothes onto themselves without considering whether these suit them or make them look clumsy. A woman sees how young girls paint their nails — so she drenches herself in paint too and will not understand that the less paint, or the lighter the colour, the more beautiful and natural the nails look; on the contrary, she uses the very strongest blood-red paint, her coarse fingers look like slaughtered pigeons, and it is nauseating to look at them.
So it is with powder, with face-paint and with the clothes she heaves onto herself.
The English Queen Elizabeth was a lump of ugliness who was renowned[?] all over Europe for her ugly face. Had she had sense and held an open conversation with her beauty doctors, she could have heard from them a frank confession; perhaps she could have been made to look decent; in any case she could have been dressed and painted so that she would have the face of a human being and look somewhat prettier and more attractive. But Elizabeth would have slaughtered all the doctors had they merely hinted to her that she was not beautiful.
In order to look beautiful, the ugly queen dressed in garments that made her look even more hideous and even uglier.
It is known that she wore a garment that weighed a whole hundred pounds; she loaded onto herself silk, velvet, lace, gold, silver and precious stones — a whole hundred pounds of burden!
And just as the poor thing carried such a heavy burden on her body, so she also slapped onto her face a lot of paint, a lot of thick powder and such "beauty plasters" that [—] often made her look like a monkey. But since she had seen that beautiful women become even more beautiful when they deck themselves out in velvet and silk garments, how rich and elegant they look in their finery, how charming they look with their rouged cheeks, Elizabeth thought that the more paint she put on herself, the heavier her diamonds and gold pieces of jewellery, the more beautiful she would look, and perhaps with her beauty she would overtake those women whom nature has blessed with beauty and grace.
The beautiful woman — when the doctor adds something[?] to her beauty, she becomes more beautiful still; but the ugly woman, who wants to catch up and even overtake, looks more hideous and more foolish besides.
Kh.
Będzin — Meeting on the Rabbinate Question

[Section:] "What's New in Zagłębie?" — Friday, 29 Adar 5697 — piątek 12 marca [1]937 [Friday, 12 March 1937]
Będzin
Meeting on the rabbinate question
Appeal by R' Itshe Meir Levin [Yitzhak Meir Levin, Agudat Israel leader] to the rabbi of Koziegłowy not to put up his candidacy.
In connection with the fact that, together with the competition which the kehilla board published for a rabbi and a "podrabin" [?; deputy rabbi], the "Agudat HaRabbanim in Poland" also issued a ban that no rabbi whatsoever should put up his candidacy as rabbi of Będzin, the national[?] camp organised a meeting on Sunday in the "Nowości"[?] cinema.
Before a packed hall Mr. Yaakov Neumark [ניימארק] opened the meeting and gave the floor to Dr. S. Manela[?], who said among other things that the rabbinate fight was provoked by the Agudah camp, which rejected all proposals that could have avoided the fight.
Mr. Yitzhak Windrucki[?] divides the question into two parts: 1) whether it is permissible at all, in the present bitter times, to take upon ourselves the burden of a rabbi, and 2) if yes, what qualifications a rabbi must possess. With various arguments the speaker shows that first of all a rabbi must be, besides a religious authority, also an educated person whom both the Jewish and the non-Jewish world will respect. The speaker comes to the conclusion that the candidate whom the "Agudah" wants to impose on the Będzin Jewish kehilla does not possess the proper qualifications.
A strong speech is delivered by Mr. A. Liter[?]; he lifts "the curtain of the kehilla" and shows the assembly who they are, those who now stand at the helm of the kehilla, and how they fulfil their tasks with regard to Jewish need. The speaker talks about the conduct of the "farhete"[?] parnassim, to whom he says: "Woe will be to the parnassim who will help the 'Agudah' with their votes."
Then the floor goes to Mr. Wegrl-Landa[?], who says that he speaks in the name of the majority of worshippers in the Sochaczew shtibl. His appearance is a real "revolution". Speaking about the ban of the "Agudat HaRabbanim", he reports that besides the ban R' Itshe Meir Levin turned to the rabbi of Koziegłowy with a letter, in which he warns that the Koziegłowy rabbi should not put up his candidacy in Będzin, even for the post of a moreh hora'ah. "It is," he says, "the same story as in Sodom, where they chopped off the feet of a tall man so that a short bed would be enough for him..."
After the short speech by Mr. Szmukler (Warsaw), who points out the comic side of the ban of the "Agudat HaRabbanim", Mr. N. Langner[?] makes a speech in which he reports a series of facts about the kehilla's economy in general and the means by which the "Agudah", with the help of kehilla presidents, wants to impose Mr. Mendel Levin as rabbi of Będzin.
In the same vein speaks parnas Warszlewicz[?], and the chairman Mr. Neumark reads the following resolutions:
1) The great mass meeting, which took place on Sunday the 7th of this month in "Nowości", protests against the Agudah practice of the kehilla board of publishing a competition for a rabbi and "podrabin" at a time when the term of office of the kehilla has ended.
2) It protests against the "Agudat HaRabbanim", which has published a ban on the Będzin rabbinate. The meeting states that the published competition is, because of the ban, an illegal one.
3) The assembled protest against the impudence of a young man who wants to force himself as rabbi on so large a kehilla as Będzin without having the religious and secular qualifications.
4) The popular assembly calls on the kehilla board to annul the rabbis' competition, since the economic situation of the Będzin kehilla, which owes overdue pensions to its poor officials, does not permit it to commit itself to further unnecessary rabbis' pensions.
Tried to Sell "Diamonds" of Tsar Nicholas

An elderly Jewish woman who was walking last Tuesday along Modrzejowska[?] Street was approached by a young man who suggested that the woman buy diamonds from Tsar Nicholas's crown.
— Who are you? — the woman asked.
— I am Balimowski's[?] son — the "merchant" answered.
— Oh, you want to fool me already — the woman said — I know all of Balimowski's children; they are not "Balimaskis"... and leave me alone.

It takes place the day after tomorrow, Saturday night, in the halls of Public School No. 2.

Premier Składkowski Accepted Honorary Citizenship of Czeladź

At the last session of the town council in Czeladź, Mayor Brudnicki[?] informed the town council that Mr. Premier Składkowski has accepted the honour of being an honorary citizen of the town of Czeladź.
Sudden Death

On Saturday night the 26-year-old Avraham Welberg[?] of "Sheher"[?] died of a heart attack.
For formal reasons the funeral took place only on Monday at about 9 in the evening. It is worth noting that it took two whole hours until the hearse-wagon came from the cemetery..
The "Orphanage" Finally Gets a Repair... — Mr. Jakub Gutman Completes the Fourth Floor
As we are informed, Mr. Jakub Gutman has decided to complete the fourth floor of the "Beit Yetomim" [orphanage], and also to plaster[?] the whole building. The work is to begin right after Passover.
The Revival of the “Discount Bank”

In the premises of the local Small Traders’ Association, a general meeting of the members of the “Diskonto Bank” in our town [Będzin] took place last week.
The meeting bore a serious character, the discussion was a businesslike one, and one could infer[?] that there exists a public desire to revive this necessary financial institution.
With some 40 members present, Mr D. Gitler opens the meeting and proposes Mr Maks Landau as chairman, to which those assembled agree. Elected to the presidium are Messrs Herman Fride and R. Wohlhendler.
Then Mr M. Kaner reads the minutes of the general meeting in the year 1935, the report of the audit by the Auditing Union and, finally, a proposal to create a capital of 10 thousand zł. with which the bank would be active again.
From the report given by Mr Józef Ros it emerges that the bank today owes no more than 900 zł. On the other hand, the bank has a part[?] of its capital, as well as secure debts (receivables) amounting to a few thousand zł.
A longer discussion is provoked by the proposal of the Auditing Union concerning[?] that the bank should in future not engage in any speculation[?] in goods. The proposal is then adopted unanimously.
After fixing the new budget at 2,500 zł. a year, the chairman Mr B. Brand reports on the [unclear word] activity in general and on how to proceed against the former bank management, which to this day refuses to render an account of its activity.
After a short discussion it is resolved that the matter be dealt with by the new board.
Then the elections of the new board are held. The result is this. Board: Messrs B. Brand, Jehoszua Klajman, J. D. Lustiger, M. Rozenker[?] and J. Ros.
Deputies: Messrs M. Lenczner and N. Rajnherc[?].
Supervisory council: Messrs H. Stopnicki, D. Gitler, D. Gutensztajn, H. Bolimowski[?], H. Merin, N. Rechnic[?] and Sz. Rajchman.
Deputies: Messrs A. Feldberg and M. Lask.
Under the item “free motions”, thanks were expressed to the advocate Dr Rechtman for his help on behalf of the bank’s existence.

At the last session of the local town council a motion was put forward by the alderman (ławnik) Mr Director Mazur that from the new school year a commercial lyceum should be opened in Sosnowiec. The motion was adopted unanimously.

As we are informed, the question of abolishing the hitherto existing “autonomy” of the board of the “Chesed shel Emes” [burial society] is on the agenda of the present kehilla board. The point is that all income from funerals should belong solely to the kehilla.

Next Sunday at 4 p.m. the annual general meeting of the members of the House-Owners’ Association will take place in its own premises (Modrzejowska[?] 20). A number of very important questions concerning the house-owners will be dealt with.
Jewish Journeymen Are Waiting for Miracles

On Sunday, in the continuation school on Kilińskiego Street in Sosnowiec, the festive conclusion took place of a course for journeymen preparing for the journeyman’s examinations.
45 Christian journeymen completed it.
Also invited to the celebration was the “Kolegium Radców”[?] of the Kielce Chamber of Crafts in Sosnowiec.

Five Thousand Jewish Souls Are Waiting for Passover Aid from the Kehilla — An Appeal to the Jewish Public on the Same Matter[?]

[Kielce — Kehilla, Passover relief.]
[Page header:] „Das lebn in Kielce“ (Life in Kielce) — Friday, 29 Adar 5697 — piątek 12 marca 1937.
Only recently we appealed to the Jewish population of Kielce about the coal campaign, which, incidentally, thanks to the energetic work of several persons headed by [—] Piotrkowski[?], was carried out with unheard-of[?] success — and already we come again to the broad[?] Jewish public with a greater appeal!
[—] this time [—] concerns the important[?] Passover campaign.
If during the coal campaign over a thousand [—] families registered, then one can already [—] that at least 1,200 families, i.e. some 5000 souls, will [—] for Passover aid!
It is superfluous, believe us, to describe the terrible need that prevails today among the Jewish population of our town. It is no longer a secret to anyone that the bitter crisis has ruined a large part of the Jewish population, [—] of [—] and [—] former[?] well-to-do merchants, who have lost their entire fortune and today lie in hunger.
For these [—] needy Jewish families, in whose homes[?] [—] tragedies are played out day after day, our festival of freedom, Passover — if the needy[?] are not provided with adequate support — will be turned into a festival of mourning; and while we sit down on Passover night at finely laid tables and tell of the miracles of the Jewish redemption, the festival will be turned into Tisha b'Av for our unfortunate brethren.
The great care[?] of organising a large-scale Passover campaign has, as every year, been taken upon itself by the Jewish kehilla. Upon it, as the representative of the Jewish population, indeed lies the duty to see to the Passover campaign, adapted to present needs. The kehilla's financial situation, however, is, as everyone knows, exceptionally difficult, and without the help of the [—] Jewish population the kehilla will in no way be able to carry out a large relief campaign.
The Jewish kehilla has therefore turned with a request to the payers of the "etat" [kehilla tax] that they pay an a-conto (advance) on the new budget for the year 1937, which will later, after the budget has been approved by the supervisory authority, be credited against this year's kehilla tax.
A sum of at least 15 thousand zł. must absolutely be made ready[?], for besides providing Passover aid to the more than five thousand poor souls, a special soldiers' kitchen must, as last year, be set up this year too. The kitchen, which must be set up for various reasons, will cost three thousand zł. The kehilla must also provide food[?] for the prisoners, the poor children of the orphanage, the old people in the "Beit Zekenim" (old-age home), the sick in the Jewish hospital, the poor children in the public schools, and the Halutz kibbutzim must[?] be given matzot for the whole 8 days. For all this one needs, as mentioned, at least 25[?] thousand zł. — and where does one get such a colossal sum in so hard a time as now?
The only source from which the kehilla can put together the large sum is solely the "etat", on which every well-to-do taxpayer should pay an a-conto for the year 1937, as well as the various donations[?] that the Jews of Kielce will give especially for the soldiers' kitchen, about which the kehilla has turned with a written appeal to the Jewish inhabitants.
Let no one therefore fail to give his help to the Passover campaign. No excuses whatsoever may be taken into account. Everyone must support the campaign with whatever he is able. The kehilla does not ask for charity, only an a-conto on the obligatory etat tax, and precisely therefore every taxpayer has the duty [—] to pay[?] into the kehilla treasury the sum demanded of him — and only in this way can the Passover relief campaign be carried out.
The only support besides the etat which the kehilla asks of the Jews of Kielce besides the etat is the individual voluntary contribution to the soldiers' kitchen.
[—] on you, Jews of Kielce, first and foremost[?] on the wealthy, over 5000 Jewish souls are waiting. On you it depends whether our unfortunate brothers and sisters will, God forbid, have a festival of mourning or a festival of freedom!

Under the chairmanship of the Kielce Voivode, Dr. Dziadosz[?], a conference was held on starting[?] the investment (public) works in the territory of the Kielce Voivodeship and on employing the unemployed.

Mr. Chaim Sachel[?], the well-known communal activist of Kielce, was elected last Sunday as a councillor (Ratman) in the Sosnowiec[?] Chamber of Commerce.

Convention of the Invalids' Associations of the Kielce Voivodeship

Trade Unions and the "Kultur-Lige" Society Closed in Kielce

[Kielce — Police and politics.]
A few days ago searches and arrests were carried out in Kielce. About 40 persons were detained, mostly young people, as suspected of communism. Some of those arrested were released and the rest were put in prison.
In connection with the searches and arrests several trade unions were closed, namely: the leather-workers' union, the commerce and food-workers' union, which are housed in one locale, the needle-trade union, as well as the "Kultur-Lige" society.
On Sunday matzah baking begins.

[Kielce — Passover.] This coming Sunday matzah baking begins. For the time being 15 bakeries [will bake] matzot. The price of matzot is not yet known. Machine-made matzot will be prohibited by the Kielce [Kielce] rabbinate.
R. Yisroel Finkelsztajn, of blessed memory

[Kielce — Obituaries.] A few days ago Jewish Kielce [Kielce] accompanied to his eternal rest the well-known 90-year-old Kielce resident R. Yisroel Finkelsztajn, of blessed memory.
The deceased R. Yisroel Finkelsztajn came from a very distinguished (meyukhes) family. He was a grandson of the Shakh [R. Shabsai HaKohen] and of R. Yitzchakl of Lelów[?]. R. Yisroel Finkelsztajn was a Hasidic Jew in the full sense of the word and was well known in the circles of the old Kotzk [Kock] Hasidim. R. Yisroel Finkelsztajn was also a shrewd, sensible Jew, and even a few weeks before his death people still sought his advice on various matters.
He belonged to the remnants of the old generation (she'eriyei ha-dor ha-yashan). Such types of honest and Hasidic Jews are, unfortunately, no longer to be found anew.
A large crowd from all strata of the Jewish population of Kielce took part in his funeral.
May his soul be bound up in the bond of life (T.N.Tz.B.H.).

Public Tribune — 1. An open letter to R' Dudl Halberstam in Sosnowiec

As is known to us, you have, on the advice of a certain group, concluded an agreement with the Aguda-[?]-Ger clique of our town, which is supposed to have promised you the post of "podrabin" [deputy rabbi] in Będzin, and in return you are to help elect Mr. Mendel Lewin as rabbi of Będzin.
At the present moment it is not our task to explain to you how it is at all possible to elect you as "podrabin" when there is no confirmed elected rabbi; and how agreements with Ger Hasidim turn out[?] you will be able to see for yourself when this agreement is carried out — once they have already accomplished their part.
But we consider it our sacred duty, as long as there is still time, to draw your attention and to warn you against the ill-considered[?] step you wish to take only because certain irresponsible people want to lead you to it, and we tell you: remember that you are abetting a crying injustice which the Gerer are preparing for Jewish Będzin. Do you think that Będzin's Jewish public will keep silent and quiet when you help to impose[?], against the whole of public opinion (from the intelligentsia to all the Hasidic shtiblekh, among them the majority of Radomsko Hasidim), a young man who has never served in the rabbinate, to occupy a rabbinical post at all, and in particular in so large a Jewish community as Będzin?
Do you want to help such a person become the responsible leader of our town only because a group of Ger Hasidim wants to impose him by force, and you are being taken[?] as helpers in this unheard-of[?] scandalous game?
Do you really believe that the Jewish population of Będzin will let itself be sold by agreements and will silently look on?
Do you really want to come to us in town with the help of strife and hatred and settle among us by handing over all the important, serious religious, educational, communal etc. tasks into the hands of an unsuitable person?
Therefore, because your honour is dear to us and because we are convinced that someone wants to sully and compromise your good name, we tell you: do not become the target of strife and struggle, [do not] help[?] carry out impudent Gerer private interests.
Remember that everything is being presented to you falsely and dishonestly.
Jewish Będzin is boiling with indignation at the local historic crime which the Ger crowd wants to commit. We ask you: do not abet it, do not lend your hand to it — something for which you will be responsible.
With respect,
"Mizrachi" organisation,
Zionist Organisation,
faction of the religious bloc[?],
dozór members and parnasim,
"Torah ve-Avodah" organisation, Będzin.
2. An open letter to the kehilla president Mr. Rubinlicht

For 18 months now a sum of 1000 zł. has been lying with you privately, as the remainder of the burial-plot fee after the late Dr. Wasserzweig[?] of blessed memory.
We ask you: by what right do you keep a thousand zł. of kehilla money? Have you not found, in all this time, any purpose for which to use the 1000 zł.? After all, this year the kehilla could not supply any coal to poor people for lack of money, and now we again face the Kimcha [de-Pischa] campaign and there is the threat[?] that the poor population will again not be provided with matzot for Passover. Under such conditions it is in itself[?] an injustice that you should keep privately 1000 zł. of kehilla money which could have covered a considerable part of the Kimcha campaign.
We therefore demand that you immediately pay the thousand zł. into the kehilla treasury, as well as the interest for the whole period.
Jakub Neimark, Moshe Manele[?],
Nete Landner, Moshe Rozenker[?],
Cwi Herszlewicz[?].

The Communal Mission

What is happening with the campaign for the Jewish „hospital“? — Where is the total and why is it not being closed?
It is already half a year since a campaign was proclaimed here to improve the situation of the Jewish hospital. During this time the public was agitated, written to, lectured and begged: help your sick and suffering[?] poor people who lie in the beds of the Jewish hospital. Help [—][?], do not leave the institution in a catastrophic state of bad dependence[?], lest one fine bright day we learn that the hospital has been closed and no longer exists for Jewish patients.
For this purpose a broad campaign was undertaken, a committee of the most respected people in town was chosen, and preparations were made for the undertaking, which was intended[?] to obtain the sum the hospital needs in order to carry on normal activity.
Usually, among decent people, such a campaign is proclaimed for a set time — let us say four or at most six weeks. During the fixed period one works energetically, and then the total is drawn up and one sees[?]: so-and-so much has been collected — and the mission is concluded and finished.
With us, however, the matter looks quite different. Here nobody hurries and nobody closes, and in truth — why close at all, when the donors are positively waiting for it. They display so much skill at wriggling out until the deadline expires, and then there will be nobody left to collect, and one will be rid of a superfluous bother (kłopot), which Sosnowiec Jews need exactly like the fifth wheel on a wagon.
That is how one can excel[?], and nobody wants to yield to the other. With us — say the communal workers — you always have time to give, and we will not release you from the mission. With us you will not strike any bargain.
So it is with those who try[?] to wriggle out by artificial means. And what about the citizens who did give and who will still[?] give? They surely deserve a yasher-koach; it is not easy[?] to give nowadays[?], [—][?], when collecting groszy comes very, very hard, especially when our citizens have no heart to give — even if they want to, even if the feeling of pity is great and reaches right to tears. If it already reaches its culminating point, then the heart interferes, and God alone knows that with the best will the heart does not allow it, and „giving a heart“ cannot be carried out, because nobody can get inside and convince it what noble[?] hearts our Jews have — and may God guard and preserve us if one recounts[?] them.
Thanks are due only to a handful of citizens who knew how to appreciate the necessity of the campaign and fulfilled their duty like a debt they paid off. But the public at large — of course only those who are able to give come into consideration here — stands at a distance and will by no means let itself be influenced. These people either give „get-off-my-back money“ just to discharge an obligation, so that nobody will pester them, or else they give nothing at all and take no account of anyone or anything.
Characteristically: on every holiday we see in the „Zagl. Tsayt.“ [Zaglembier Tsaytung] lists of money from the American Jews originating from Będzin, as they remember to send to their poor brethren; and there[?], on the other side of the ocean, they also do not forget that in Będzin there is our hospital, and they do not miss any occasion to send in their contribution. And if those people remember our poor sick from afar — why should our brethren not remember them from close by? Should our better-situated citizens not be ashamed for the disgrace, for this disregard? Should they not take a moral lesson from people who work hard in America and still remember that we have a Jewish hospital — while here, where[?] one sees it, one does not want to know about it or look at it before one's eyes?!
It does not matter, upon my life[?]; the truth may always be told, however bitter it be. We know it from you[?], how no thing is too dear and luxury takes the place of honour; but as soon as[?] one has to put a hand in one's pocket and take out a donation for a charitable purpose, then[?] one becomes so penny-pinching and sighs so heavily that the delegates look for the door, and [—][?] it as a gain that they did not have to pay a proper contribution there.
These are not fantasies, not illusions imagined by the writer of these lines. Only living facts, which one encounters very often. Communal workers would[?] have much to tell you about such[?] facts.
An end must finally be put to this lawlessness. People who are able to give must be taught to know how to value honest communal activity when it brings benefit to the community; and if they do not want to listen to the sufferings of the poor and their grief and want do not interest them, then let it be known that they are separating themselves from the Jewish community, and there is no need to visit them and from the outset no reason to count on their help.
The campaign to improve the situation of the Jewish hospital has so far been a failure: it is neither stopped nor continued. It is high time to draw up the total and to know what it has brought[?]; then the verdict can be pronounced and we will see what kind of certificate our citizens have earned.
Let the campaign be closed after Passover. Thus during the holiday days all those who can give and have not fulfilled their duty should be visited, and then it will be possible to draw up the total, and we shall know who gave how much and who remained outside the camp.
Dr. Papuri[?].
