[Newspaper's own announcement: serial novel.] „The Living Dead Man“ (Der lebediker mes)
This is the name of the original, highly gripping erotic-criminal novel of Jewish life in Zagłębie, which begins to appear in our newspaper on Friday, the eve of Passover.
The novel „The Living Dead Man“ — this is a piece of quivering reality from Jewish life in Zagłębie. The remarkable, mysterious story began before the World War and continues to this very day. Many heroes depicted in the novel still live among us today.
The novel „The Living Dead Man“ reveals to the reader one of the most mysterious and tragic stories that happened to a Jewish family in Zagłębie. All the strange and sensational[?] events of the novel were created by life itself, which often surpasses the richest imagination of a human being.
In the novel „The Living Dead Man“ the ruin and downfall of a respected Jewish house is depicted, owing to the recklessness of a father who became entangled in an unhappy love with a Christian girl...
Against the background of this remarkable story, the novel „The Living Dead Man“ depicts Jewish life in Zagłębie before the war, during the German occupation, up to the present day.
The novel „The Living Dead Man“ by A. Zaglembier is written in a very popular, engaging language, and it reads from beginning to end with bated breath.
Read on Friday, Passover eve, the beginning of the new novel „The Living Dead Man“!
Itche Hener Is Hanging in the Attic!...

[Humour — a pre-Passover monologue.] A pre-Passover monologue by Y. Oberzhanek [J. Oberżanek?].

Why am I so torn to pieces? Why do I go about like a yesterday's [?] one?
What are you asking questions for? Don't you know it's before Passover? Don't you know of the exile we married men go through in the days before Passover?
In the old pre-Passover days, when [?] I didn't know [?] any better when we eat, where we sleep? — my home was a hell for 3 weeks, when [?] the beds were taken apart, the bedding stripped, the wardrobe emptied, the clothes in the middle of the room, the little chairs turned over, the windows from the doors [—], my wife with her head tied up in a towel, like a painter [?], lehavdil, and the whole day long clambering up a ladder like a circus acrobat with a sweeping brush, and "dusting".
And now the curses? The whole curse-water she poured out in the weeks before Passover, and what is more — when there was still a laundry going on at home, my wife began to scold and to speak in "the holy tongue".
— Itche Hener — she said — why don't you dare [?] go to the doctors of a strange death [?]! This is good tedium [?]. But [?] she mourns [?] like the red heifer; the whole "Yekum Purkan" was poured out on my head — may I not be punished for the words [?].
And later, when my missus began to speak "the holy tongue", I understood that the time had come for me to kiss the mezuzah on every white [?] door,
That was once, when my wife was the mistress of the house and I — the great giver [?].
This year, soon after Purim, my missus says to me: Itche Hener, where does it follow [?] that I must be the cleaner for Passover? Because I wear a dress and you the trousers? Once, when you were a merchant and had better business, I really had to work myself black; but now, when you've become "-less": livelihood-less, money-less, business-less, merchandise-less, and to add to your troubles, for shame [?], childless too — so why shouldn't you really take over my functions? Why shouldn't you clean for Passover?
Well, I saw that she had a just claim. Why really shouldn't I clean for Passover? Do I have better business, then? Is "frittering away" [?] my time for nothing better? And secondly, if I clean, my wife won't speak "the holy tongue", and I'll spare myself listening to the bit of pre-Passover curses.
So I agreed to my wife's proposal and began cleaning.
First of all I took on the windows, poured boiling water over the panes, and in one minute the panes were... smashed.
Then I took my wife's silk blouse out of the wardrobe and cleaned the panes with it.
Done with the panes, I took on the floors. I poured out several buckets [?] of water on the floor and everything in the room began to swim. Soon the neighbour who lives below me came running with a great outcry, that in his flat one has to walk around with an umbrella...
Finished with the floors, I took on the dishes; the glassware [?] I polished with a [paste?] "Yeshue Slagba" [?], and the pots I polished with my satin kapote so that they should have a "shine". The plates I scrubbed with sand, and the spoons, forks and knives I washed with kerosene; the ceiling I scrubbed with a "brush", and the "dusting" I did with my tallis-koton. From the beds I first pulled off the top cover, then the under cover, and in one minute the whole courtyard was full of feathers. The feathers flew like a heavy snow, and within a day the whole flat was fit for Passover, koshered — just sit down to the Seder...
After cleaning I took on the borscht — to sour Passover borscht — and before I could look round the borscht was [scraped?] [?]. The pot covered with a clean towel — and kosher for Passover...
When my wife came in from the street, she raised an outcry: schlemiel, good-for-nothing, [?], just look what you've done!
— What have I done? — I didn't understand what she meant.
— Why, you've pickled the peelings of the beetroots! Where did you put the beetroots?
— The beetroots? Threw them out!
But that's not the main thing — the main thing is the story with the attic:
The stories with the attics before Passover are surely known to you. One attic for 50 neighbours, and on one day all 50 wives want to hang [laundry]. Every woman does her wash — and how can 50 wives hang all at once?
They [?] climb up on tables and on benches. One shouts: I want to hang! and the other shouts even louder: they'll [?] hang tomorrow... One stretches lines and the other tears them down, one hangs on a lock [?] and the other tears down the lock; one shouts: [?], the other answers: [?]; one says: old gossip [yakhne], the other says: common slattern; one says: witch, the other answers — and so they pull each other by the tongue, on and on, until they make it up over the dishes...
That's all among women. They have a remedy: they make it up over the dishes and that's that. But what is the law when in the attic there is a strange man with a strange woman? A man surely won't [?] grab at a strange dish!
I'm actually telling this about [?] myself. When I had finished cleaning, I went up to the attic to hang out the wash.
— Reb Itche Hener — my neighbour Gele-Brane said to me — you won't hang now, now I'm hanging!
— I will hang all the same — I answered her like a real man.
— We'll see [?].
— Don't be a Cossack — I said.
— Don't be a [?] — she said, and began hanging her wash.
She hung and I hung too; she threw down my trousers, I threw down her bloomers ["reformy"], and she raised an outcry: Reb Itche Hener, clear off with your trousers! I shouted: come back [?] with your bloomers! And what was the end? My neighbour ran out with an outcry, and all over the courtyard she shouted: Help, Itche Hener is hanging in the attic!..
What happened later? Listen to what happened:
The whole house of neighbours came running together with the janitor [stróż]; they carried me down like a herring: one held me by the hands, another by the head, a third by the feet. The women shouted: Fie, not nice, a Jew at his age — committing suicide. — You should be ashamed of yourself, Reb Itche Hener; if there's no livelihood any more — so what's the fuss? A Jew must live with trust [in God] — and to hang himself, and in an attic to boot...
The end was that the one who hanged [the wash] was my neighbour Gele-Brane, and now I can't go out into the street: everyone points their finger at me: there's the one who hanged himself in the attic...
So, gentlemen, that's how a "he" becomes a "she" and a "she" becomes a "he"...
Not for the Sake of Honour...

(Concerning the new kehilla representatives in Sosnowiec).
At last the newly elected Sosnowiec kehilla has lived to see[?] itself admitted to the table to take the stamp[?] into its hands, so[?] that it can now begin to turn the kehilla's wheel.
For several months the newly elected parnasim waited for this occasion. Something placed itself between them and the building at Modrushever[?] [probably ul. Modrzejowska] 22. Not voluntarily[?] [—], because they were not allowed to get a word in. Twice lots were drawn; a third time further[?] new formalities were found; one way or another, it took a little too long. But better late than never.
On the contrary[?], the difficult labour of our new kehilla did it no honour[?]; it surely affected the kehilla's economy.
On the contrary, one must say that if all other public bodies had come to work at such a "tempo" as the new kehilla, they would surely not have got far nor achieved much. Public activity must have free momentum, broad scope, without delays[?]. Otherwise it is hampered, braked, atrophied[?].
In such a condition our new kehilla too now comes to speak and to act; how[?] hampered it is, and it is already more exhausted from waiting for work than from the wearying[?] work itself, more from doing nothing than from what it will yet have to do.
We therefore harbour no illusions [lit. "we put no little birds[?] in our bosom"]. We do not feed[?] ourselves on overly great hopes and expectations; we do not come now in advance with overly great claims on the managers of our new kehilla; we soberly assess their possibilities, in order that we may be able to put very great demands to them. We know that it does not depend on them, that life is stronger than all the good intentions with which they enter the kehilla. We also know that there are still material reasons because of which they[?] will in any case be unable to develop that great and broad activity which a Jewish kehilla like Sosnowiec deserves and befits it, so as not to shame its name.
We are far from being misled[?] and blinded. We foresee for our new kehilla a bitter and hard life, as dangers and strange perils [sakones umeshunes] have stood out on all sides. It will meet dangers enough in the period of its work.
We do not belong to those who would, out of love, sing praises of the new kehilla leaders and make their hearts light; but neither do we want to be the "bad ones" and make their hearts heavy. Yet we cannot refrain from telling the truth. The kehilla matter is too responsible a thing, since it has until now been taken too lightly; but the present hour is such that one cannot take such matters lightly — they must at last be taken seriously, with full awareness.
Let us believe that our new representatives do not lack this awareness; let us hope that they will take up their duty with complete sincerity, wanting to do something, and not merely to discharge an obligation and, for honour's sake, to bear the title of dozor [kehilla board member] or parnas.
A. Y. G—ski.
100 Years of Patents.

In the year 1937 it will be exactly a hundred years since all countries began to issue patents and in this way to protect all inventors, so that others should not copy their things and should not push them out of the market.
In these 100 years hundreds of thousands of inventions have been protected, the greater part of which turned out to be unimportant, and the patents were never used at all.
The first patent office was founded in New York under a law proposed by the then Senator Ruggles. He was also the one who received patent number 1, for a little wheel for small wagons[?] (later it turned out that this little wheel was no good).
According to a list from the archive[?] of the Leipzig fair, important patents were received:
In 1840 F.[?] B. Morse, for his telegraph signs, which are used to this day.
In 1876 Grim[?] received a patent for his telephone. Another telephone apparatus was patented a year later by Emil Berliner of Boston[?], and a third apparatus was protected by Edison in 1891.
In 1879 Brush patented an electric lamp, and in 1880 Edison patented a white[?] electric lamp.
In 1878 Edison patented the phonograph, and 15 years later, in 1893, he patented the first cinema apparatus.
In 1895 Gibi[?] Weldn[?] [probably George B. Selden] of Rochester patented the first automobile. The patent office, however, soon withdrew this patent, because the invention "was not practical"...
In 1906 two young men, the Wright brothers of Dayton, patented the first airship. But since they wanted to test the invention themselves, both of them fell and were killed.
In 1889 aluminium was patented "for all purposes". Until then aluminium had been very expensive and only jewellers used it, to work precious objects with it.
In 1903 Henry Howe[?] patented the "resht-vek"[?] machine for printing houses.
In 1852 the first ship that travelled under water was protected by patent.
In 1836 Samuel Colt protected the first revolver, and in 1862 the American Gatling patented the first machine gun. In the Spanish-American War both sides were already shooting with machine guns.
Nehemiah Howe[?] of New York patented in 1860 the first brake to stop a wagon when it goes downhill. In 1879 the American Westinghouse invented the brake that is now used on the railways.
In 1883 Ritty and Birch of Chicago invented the first cash register, and a firm from Milwaukee received in 1868 a patent for the first typewriter.
In 1849 the American Howe received a patent for the first sewing machine, and in 1869 McGaffey of Chicago invented the vacuum cleaner. But he had no money to manufacture his invention, so he did not use the patent. Only after the patent had lapsed did the big electricity works recently begin to manufacture vacuum cleaners.
The first electric flat-iron was invented by Henry Seely of New York in 1882.
The first razor apparatus was patented by Gillette of Brooklyn in 1904.
We have mentioned only the great inventions of the last hundred years. Thousands of inventions were never carried out at all, because no capitalists were found who would want to occupy themselves with them. Who knows whether these inventions too would not have brought about a whole upheaval, had the inventors had the luck to carry them out and not let their ideas go to ruin?...
Z. Haber, Vienna.
Passover Eve.

The frost has gone, the snows have melted, the ice is pouring away, the white world has vanished and a great wet earth covers its face. All around it is damp, grey and dirty[?]. And yet one feels that winter, with its colds and frosts, with its influenzas and its "klipes" [evil husks], is already gone, and the world now stands on "the eve of spring" — the eve of Passover.
The beautiful festival of Passover is drawing near — the symbol of freedom and happiness, the holiday when all, poor and rich alike, sit down at the table to entertain themselves with the bread of affliction; when Jews, sitting at their ease [reclining], laugh at all the Pharaohs with their "Come, let us deal wisely" and show a fig to all the Labans the Aramean with their demands "to uproot everything".
All these proud exclamations would have sounded like self-glorification had they not been preceded by the prelude of "Kol dikhfin" ["Let all who are hungry come and eat", from the Haggadah] as the social justification for the cries of triumph. "Kol dikhfin" carries within it the great secret of Jewish self-preservation.
"Kol dikhfin" has since long ago been realised in two other words: "maos khitim" [wheat money]. After paying in for the bread of affliction for those who have not got it, the Jew [—] for himself the moral right to taste of the "poor bread" himself.
This year the problem mentioned comes out in all its sharpness.
Want in the Jewish street is now much sharper. Prices are high; matzah costs 20 percent more than last year. The kimkha [Passover-flour relief] committees at the kehillas have set themselves the task of enlarging the grants, which must take the place of the necessary Passover products that will be missing this year from the tables of many needy people. To this are added the holiday meals for the Jewish soldiers of the local garrison.
It now depends entirely on Jewish society — on all those who are preparing for the holiday for themselves, who must help so that the kimkha committees can fulfil their tasks.
L. K-e.
Heard and Seen

Heard and Seen. By Ben Amotz.
In the ways of the "Aguda".
The well-known German rabbis who, at the time of the conference, founded[?] the "Aguda" in Poland (the organisation bore the name "Shlomei Emunei Yisroel", and later in the "simul"[?] was enlarged under the name — "Aguda"), are often mentioned "favourably" by the Jewish population. In almost all matters concerning the honour of the Jewish community, people acknowledge them, the rabbis, gratefully... For the "Aguda", which has taken the Torah monopoly into its hands, cares[?] completely for the religious institutions in general and for the institutions occupied with religious education in particular.
What the devotion of the "Aguda" to the Będzin "Talmud Torah" looks like is, after all, known to everyone. They do not, God forbid, content themselves with the great material support, but are truly heart and soul absorbed[?] in the institution, where hundreds of poor children are being brought up; at every call they stand ready as one man, and take an active part in all campaigns that have even the slightest connection with the existence of the "Talmud Torah".
And therefore their deeds are indeed appreciated by the Jewish population regardless of whatever[?] tendency, because, as they say, "the walls have ears" — it is known everywhere. Not only in Orthodox ranks, but even in the circle where religious matters in general and the Talmud Torah in particular are very little noticeable... And how far that circle of people regards the "Aguda" with the greatest respect is shown by the following fact:
A group of women social activists held a meeting with the aim[?] of taking part in the campaign to sell "galietkes"[?]. Among others, a social activist, the wife of a well-known Jewish lawyer, took part in the meeting, and she was asked to take part in the "galietkes" campaign.
— "Owszem" [certainly] — the woman answered — the campaign for the Talmud Torah is a very important one and I do not refuse my participation in the campaign, but on condition that those who stand at the helm of the "Aguda" take part as well.
— "And why so?" — the chairman of the meeting called out — the "Aguda" after all stands aside and takes no part in any campaign whatsoever for the Talmud Torah. On the contrary, there are such who are directly interested in the Talmud Torah having no means of existence..
— "Właśnie" [exactly] — the astonished woman then explained — that is precisely why I set my "warunek" [condition], because the deeds of the "Aguda" with regard to the Talmud Torah are known to me too, because I too go "oyfn velbo khng"[?];
— In the ways of the "Aguda"...
Happy are you, Israel...
Happy are you, people of Israel! These words "burst" from my mouth as I listened to the report of a meeting held by the community representatives of Rybnik.
At the meeting the kehilla budget for the coming year was discussed. While fixing the subsidy for the Fröbel school [kindergarten], which is maintained by the kehilla, one of the representatives proposed that Yiddish also be taught in the school. At first sight it seems that such a proposal ought not to provoke any opposition at all; but there was in the proceedings a "yavor"[?], in whom the "yavor-ish"[?] spirit still "spliet"[?], and he came out against Yiddish with a series of "arguments" that are well worth being published in "Aregravnik"[?] — above all the "argument" that "antisemitism in the world[?] stems from the Yiddish language"..
It goes without saying that the Yiddish language no longer needs the approval of such a "scholar". We bring the fact as material for the future historian, so that he may have an idea what sort of element had a say in Jewish communal life in the twentieth century.
— Happy are you, Israel..
"And you shall burn out the evil from your midst"...
In the portion "Ki Tetze" the commandment "u-vi'arta ha-ra mi-kirbekha" — you shall root out the evil from the Jewish people — is mentioned several times. The punishment, according to the Torah, must be applied to a stubborn and rebellious son, to a kidnapper, to one who brings an evil name upon a Jewish daughter; and if our Torah thus cares for the honour of a single person, how much more must one react when the most shameful libels are invented against the best and finest people of the Jewish community!
About two years ago there drifted to Sosnowiec a "brugiger"[?] soul, a man with a dark past, who succeeded, with the help of the until-now kehilla treasurer, in publishing a little sheet that is used 1) for blackmail purposes and 2) to revile[?] with the vilest filth-words those who keep their distance from him as from...
We consider it superfluous to enumerate even a minimum of the blackmail stories that this disgusting creature has carried out[?] since he appeared on the Sosnowiec pavement — not to mention that there is hardly a single public figure on whom this "Investigator" fellow has not used his mud-lexicon; but even such authorities as the Radomsko Rebbe, Rabbi Hager, Rabbi Chameides[?] and others, whom the scoundrel does not spare — just because they refused to put something into his paws..
And perhaps it also comes hard to us to deal with this soul in our newspaper. But we are forced to it, and those who pointed it out[?] are several Radomsko Hasidim from Katowice, who give us to read a whoring story, a shameful pamphlet about a certain Chaim Lewin, printed in the latest issue of the blackmail sheet published by Simchele M...
And a cold sweat pours over you as you read it through. And one simply wants to "tear kriah" seeing how far the Jewish printed word is being spat upon and demoralised by underworld people whose place ought to be in the vilest houses of ill repute..
— Where is the Jewish society of Sosnowiec? — asks the delegation from Katowice — where are the public activists? They bear responsibility, after all, for the deceitful deeds committed by the "Investigator" gang, because on them lies the duty to fulfil the commandment:
— "And you shall burn out the evil from your midst"..
Oneg Shabbat

Little Torah teachings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion. Collected by [—] Yehuda.
Parshat Tzav

a) "Command Aaron and his sons" (6:2)
"Said R' Shimon: Scripture must urge especially where there is a loss of money." Rashi.
One asks: what loss of money, what financial damage do the priests suffer in offering a sacrifice?
But what is meant (not as it is usually explained, that R' Shimon is referring here to the sacrifices) is what is said in verse 8: that at the removal of the ashes the priest must change his garments, so that the garments of the Temple should not get soiled while he busies himself with the ashes (as Rashi says there: "so that he not soil, in taking out the ashes, the garments in which he always serves"). So this is what R' Shimon says: Scripture must especially warn the priests where there is a loss of money to the sacred treasury, that is, to guard the penny of the sacred treasury. That demands extra diligence, for unfortunately priests and leaders were accustomed to treat sacred money lightly...
Shem Efraim.

b) "This is the law of the burnt-offering" (ibid., 2)
A burnt-offering comes only for sinful thoughts. Midrash Rabbah.
"Sinful thoughts are worse than sin" — Rabbi Reb Ber interpreted: "sinful thoughts are grave" — the fact that sinful thoughts weigh so heavily, so harshly, though they weigh no more than a mere thought — that comes "from sin", for no sinful thought comes to a person unless he has previously committed a sin. One who has never sinned does not have thoughts of sin come to mind.

*

The burnt-offering atones for arrogance, and therefore it is said of Aaron and his sons, of the leaders.. of those among whom arrogance is common...
Ktav Sofer.

c) "This is the offering of Aaron and his sons... on the day when he is anointed" (ibid., 13)
"No man becomes a head below unless he is made a head above." Every appointment and elevation is the result of a certain sin. Therefore "on the day when he is anointed", when the priest was anointed and raised to greatness, he had to bring an offering for that sin, because of which he was punished with being raised to greatness...
Imrei Chen.

d) "And the anointed priest that shall be in his stead from among his sons" (ibid., 15)
At a time when the priest goes about finding sins in others and orders them to bring offerings, he must see to it that not only he himself be clean of sin, but that his children too be clean. If his own house is not whole, he has no right to look for sins in another: "and the anointed priest in his stead from among his sons"...
R' Shlomo Kluger.

e) "And the flesh of the sacrifice of his thanksgiving peace-offerings shall be eaten on the day of his offering; he shall not leave any of it until the morning" (7:15)
Why are all kinds of peace-offerings eaten over two days and a night, while the thanksgiving peace-offering is eaten only for one day and a night?
Because to a thanksgiving offering one invites good friends and guests too, and with invited guests — said R' Eizel Charif jokingly — there is in any case nothing left to eat for more than a day and a night...

f) "And you shall eat no manner of blood" (ibid., 26)
"All" is an inclusion. Here it comes to include [?] human blood: that a person may not shed blood, for that is surely in any case no better than drinking the blood of an animal...
R' Moshe Leib of Sasov.

Despite the great expenses and the difficult situation of the Jewish press in general and in the provinces in particular, this year's Passover issue will nevertheless be much enlarged and will contain 12 pages.

The beloved Y. Oberushanek[?], in a feuilleton entitled "Yanek at the Seder", describes a seder at the home of one of the "[?] Jews".

Musical Conversations

[Culture — music.] By M. Dawidzon.

III.
The course of history has always had a strong influence on the lines of development of music, which remains forever the living expression of mankind's permanent process of creation. The ancient Greeks set up in their spiritual baggage a specific "kingdom of heaven" for art: these were 9 "apostles" [i.e. the Muses], to whom the various branches of art were "subject" (poetry, painting, sculpture, architecture, etc.); the apostles together formed the general "Muse", which was — and has also remained — the symbol of every fine art. Therefore, when one hears it said: "the Muse has struck up a tune in him", one does not necessarily mean that "he feels like playing or singing" — the same can also apply to poetry and to every other branch of the 9 Muses; but because the "little world of sounds" is more accessible and closer to the masses than any other branch of art, the concept "Muse" was broadened [?], was, so to speak, "popularised" [?], within the "narrow frame of mere music.
Incidentally, we Jews have a similar view on this matter to the ancient Greeks: only with the difference that we "approve" just 7 "apostles" — with us this is called the seven wisdoms.
Why Jewish ethics [?] did not recognise all 9 (like the Greeks and after them the Romans), but limited itself to the number 17 [as printed; read 7] — there are quite a few historical-psychological reasons for that; one of them: so important a branch as sculpture found, until not long ago, no echo whatsoever among the Jewish people; it is conceivable to claim that to a great extent this was the effect of the Torah's prohibition: "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image." This is not the place to treat the problem in all its details and minutiae. Meanwhile we "may" quite boldly "rely" on the "small" scope of the seven wisdoms...

IV.
So then, the world of sounds — let us call it by its universal name, the name the masses have bestowed on it — music, is a collaboration of three main properties embodied in it: 1) rhythm; 2) melody; 3) harmony.
Rhythm, or beat, is the guide according to which music is conducted. Melody is a successful combination of various tones that form the musical idea. Harmony, the connection of those sounds whose existence is founded on acoustic structure, plays the role of a content-bound [?] chordal unity. Schumann compared music to a game of chess, in which the melody is the queen and has freedom of movement and unlimited possibilities; harmony, on the other hand, is, as in chess — the king, who is bound in his steps. Because [?] on him hangs [?] success or fiasco; only he can say the final word....
Many live in error, thinking that the melody is a thing standing by itself, an independent spiritual specimen [?]; true, superficially it looks as if the composer first of all writes the melody and only afterwards "harmonises" it, i.e. accompanies it with beautiful-sounding chords; when one looks a little deeper [full stop as printed]. When one understands that first of all the harmonic "element" is born in the composer, and from it, from the harmonic whole, only afterwards do the small pieces "fall away", the splinters that create the melody... Therefore the motif of a people alone is not enough to recognise its character; although we know that a folk motif — both the poetry and the music of the folkloristic treasure — is in and of itself a mirror of the people's character, nevertheless it comes to expression much more distinctly when the folklore material is accompanied by the harmonic binding factor.
It is no wonder, then, that lately special attention is being paid to folklore, and in all the larger cities folk choirs are being organised whose task is to cultivate the spirit of the people, its joys and sorrows. All this among the nations of the world; among Jews, who are — as is well known — real "imps" [?] in the musical field, folklore has lately been badly neglected; and yet there were times when we could pride ourselves on the way our broad, many-branched folk treasure was preserved. Today we are living through different times. The raging waves of [as printed: "of what"] bring the Jewish person to a depressed mood, and in such a state of mind his ear cannot catch the strong encouraging tone of the all-embracing folklore colouring.
We must, however, remember that we have always had for this a unique, specifically Jewish method of healing: to seek in the spiritual treasures the strength that should fortify and cement us in the struggle for our existence; so too today, when we are the perpetual sacrifice of all the "burning problems" and harassments [?] of our generation; today, when the nightmare of insecurity presses on us from all sides, we must go on seeking [?] and searching, so that the spiritual [?] may move along the great and sure paths of Jewish history.
This opinion is without doubt something of a digression, a deviation from the actual theme; but proceeding from the standpoint that music is the surest means of concentrating the spirit, this juxtaposition will be understandable. As one of the ways leading to the people's source and to the regenerator of its strength, there is the long-tested way of f o l k  c h o i r s. The importance of such cultural institutions is known and quite evident. On the development of such Jewish choirs in the last 15 years in Poland — in the next article.

Among Matchmakers

(An overheard conversation).
— Have you perhaps, Reb Shmuel, a girl?
— I have, thank God, four girls, but I don't know what to do with them.
— Just give them here to me, and I'll settle[?] them for you.
— No, you didn't understand me. I'm talking about my girls, about my daughters, whom I would like to marry off, but I have no dowry for them; and you surely think I'll give you brides for your young men, [from whom?] you want to earn a matchmaker's fee. But it doesn't matter; I can give you brides too. Yes. First of all I need to know what sort of young men you have... what they do for a living.
And the first matchmaker began to list the virtues of „his" young men.
— I have a young man — he said — by profession he's an economist.
— What does that mean?
— He makes economies.
— Namely?
— He always goes on foot. You will never see him riding a tram or a droshky, because he is stingy with money. Besides, he eats only twice a day. Socks [„skarpetkes"], for example, he wears from one season to the next. Further, he never opens a window, because he saves, he says, on heating. In summer he doesn't wipe off his sweat, because the handkerchiefs get dirty from it. In short, a rare economical person... And he's looking for a girl who should, first, be pretty and clever, and on top of that she should have a hundred thousand zł. She may be an orphan too, because he hates, he says, dealing with inheritance matters.
— Yes, but what profession does he have? What does he do?
— Do — for the time being he does nothing, but he won't be lost in life, because he's a... sort of artist, he plays in the „Swe"[?]...

A Lesson for Married Men

When your wife asks you: „Yankl, what would you do if I died today?" and you answer that you would take your own life, you are a liar. If you answer that you will soon marry again, then you are an honest man.
But if you don't just talk and actually do marry, then you are the real idiot.
Bridegrooms

Told by a young lady from Sosnowiec.
As you see, I am already a girl getting on in years. There are many reasons why I have not yet married; the main reason is that I have no dowry. Parents I don't have; I even have relatives in America who take my fate to heart — but what of it: they are all "crisis" relatives. To my moving[?] letters one of them answered that unfortunately he can do nothing for me, because not long ago he "got rid of" (lost) about 50 thousand dollars in shares. According to his letter it turns out that I ought to have sent him something for Passover. The second writes me that he has bought a 6-storey house and is now squeezed[?] for money. But I am not entirely forsaken: instead of parents I have many "mothers", who take a very[?] great interest in me and give me from time to time — advice. One advises me not to dye my hair and lips, because it makes me ridiculous; the second advises me not to spend money on rags[?] (clothes), but to collect groschen by groschen, until in the course of years I will after all scrape together a dowry; the third counsels me to dress up, because — plainly[?] said — no money, so at least I should win on my own merits; the fourth advises me to throw out of my head my fanciful[?] thoughts about love-shmove etc. and turn to matchmakers.
From all this advice my head is a mishmash; they propose many matches to me, and every one of them comes to nothing, because money I have none.
I ask some of the bridegrooms: how come — such a healthy young fellow, with such healthy hands, you don't own a groschen to this day, and from me, a weak girl, you demand that I should have it? But I remain with my question.
Father in Heaven! How many sorts of young men have already passed through my room! All kinds of types, starting with "beginner"[?] young men in this line, with whom everything already goes like with an expert, and ending with those who are bashful, poor things, don't know where to put their hands, every moment take out the snow-white handkerchief (bought specially) and wipe the sweat, and tell me that in the morning it was very cloudy, one could have thought it would rain, but later it cleared up so much that the sun even appeared. With an experienced[?] eye I look over the young "sparrows"[?] and a kind of pity takes hold of me for them; I already lead them on[?] to a little chat. Somehow I please them all, but nothing comes of it, because almost all of them are "naked Adams" (penniless) and they need at least some money.
All these "pshipngtshes"[?] and [—] make a ruin of my last few groschen, and I decided to give it up, to sweep away[?] the business of dealing with the poor nudniks, from whom I can expect nothing more than heartache. I decided: if I am going to play the thankless role of a bride-girl at all, better to be a rich bride — it comes to nothing anyway, so let me at least for one evening throw poverty off me and live it up like a human being.
So I went to Katowice, where I can already do as I please and rely on my own wits. I introduced myself as having 5 thousand dollars and wanting to marry, naturally someone decent. You should have seen what matches they propose to me.
There pass before me, as in a panorama, applicants, whole lawyers, students, engineers. At the last ones I turn up my nose and wave my hand dismissively[?]: what is a Jewish engineer — he won't even earn water for his porridge, and all he'll do is measure the streets. There is also no lack of manufacturers, candidates for manufacturers — just give them the whole pharmacy —, merchant boys who only need to consolidate their fathers' businesses; in short — there is no lack of fresh goods. I am busy at my old trade — I have dates[?], but not with "pętaki" (good-for-nothings) like me, but really with the "śmietana" (the cream) of Katowice.
I catch a caress, a compliment, a kiss, first on the hand and later further; it goes like greased; the smell of money lends me the seventh grace; I am like a fish in water; I hear various languages in which they flirt with me; as a great [?] I must listen to criticism of literature, theatre and music; I must promise him to accept his invitation to the premiere. Sitting in the theatre I feel his touch every minute. After the performance he invites me to a first-class restaurant or café, orders a good supper; my young man crawls out of his skin[?] to please me and to flatter me, for he is well brought up; he showers me with compliments — I know that he is dancing around my money, but I forget about that: a life of the moment is also good. This affair[?] will cost him several tens of złoty, and that is my best revenge[?].
My role does not come hard to me; I have already learned to tell various liqueurs apart. I no longer lose my way in the menus, I already know what rich people like; I no longer have to say: "I rely on your taste." Meanwhile I snatch a little dance in company; they admire my good conversation, my pretty little foot, my bearing, etc.; the only bad thing is that the night vanishes quickly; day begins to dawn and one has to go back home. My cavalier has already ordered a taxi in good time and he takes me home. With a burning kiss on the hand the last act of the tragicomedy ends, and I remain alone in my desolate, lonely little room.
The next day I tell the matchmaker that unfortunately the bridegroom is not for me.
— How come? — the matchmaker wonders — such a young man!
— No, my dear man[?], with such capital I can attain something better; by the way, I have received a telegram from my brother in Palestine that I should get ready to leave for Eretz Israel.
— To Eretz Israel! — the matchmaker jumps up — why, that is certainly good, he will travel with you, he is also enthusiastic[?], he is also —
— No! — I cut him off in the middle — what do I need to take him along for? Won't I get the goods there?
That is how I take revenge on the bridegrooms for my lonely life, for my dashed[?] hopes and for my humiliations and for the wretchedness[?] of all our poor and dowryless sisters.
M. S.[?]

What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 7 Nisan 5697 — piątek 19 marca 937 [Friday, 19 March (1)937].)
Będzin
Bought the "pearl" of the Russian tsarina...
Last Saturday night, as Mrs S. was walking along Kołłątaja Street, a young man came up to her and suggested that she go over to the "Russian" standing in the same street and ask him why he will not sell the "żyd" [Polish: "Jew", derogatory] the "pearl". For her trouble the young man, who introduced himself as a jewellery merchant, promised to reward her well.
Mrs S., who took this on for "good money", went up to the person pointed out to her and put the question to him[?].
To this the "Russian" replied that he will not sell the "żyd" the "pearl" because he has no paper banknotes, and as for small coins, "he knows nothing of them, nyet".
When the woman came back with the answer, the "merchant" asked her: "Perhaps you [lit. they] have paper banknotes at home — exchange them for me, and if I make the deal, you will get a hundred-złoty note."
Mrs S., hearing of the "fortune" awaiting her — soon to the "fuler hakh"[?] [unclear phrase] — ran home quickly and told her son-in-law about the "transaction" she was about to make..
— If so — said the son-in-law — I am coming along.
When mother-in-law and son-in-law came out into the street, the "merchants" were no longer there. It turns out that when they saw the son-in-law coming along, they took "va-yivrah" [i.e. fled].
Yet there is no shortage of naive people who let themselves be caught in the net of buying "bargains". Such a victim later was Mrs Ch., who did indeed buy the "tsarist pearl".
The "secret" that she had been cheated Mrs Ch. discovered when she came into the shop of Mr Balimazski[?], where she wanted to sell the "pearl"..

Sosnowiec — General Meeting of the Jewish House-Owners

[Sosnowiec — Organizations; House-owners.]
Last Sunday, in its own new premises, the annual general meeting of the members of the Jewish House- and Lot-Owners' Association took place. The „attendance“ was small: of about 300 members about 40 came (including the board).
The president, Mr. M. Lubelski, who opens the meeting, speaks about the apathy of the members, who come — he says — to the association only when they find themselves in time of trouble. After the deceased — Advocate Gross, Maurycy Rajner, Ch. Oppenheim, Sala Halpern, L. Spiegel, S. Lampel, Israel Michal Berkowicz, Director Baruch, L. Federman, S. Aren — are honoured by rising, and sympathy is expressed to Mr. Feliks on the death of his brother, Igus[?] is elected chairman. Jakub Wolkan, who appeals that the meeting should bring the desired result, invites to the presidium Messrs. D. Wurkiewicz[?] and B. Rozengast[?]; as secretary — Mr. Berlinger.
The activity report is delivered by Mr. Skierczyk[?]. The report shows intensive activity on the part of the board. The report is supplemented by Mr. Lubelski, who enumerates a series of successful actions, among them also the office of kehilla president in the person of the vice-president I. Lejwerkowicz[?].

Then I. A. Chlewicki reads the minutes of the audit commission, after which absolutorium is granted to the outgoing board.

Life in Kielce — Danger That 5,000 Poor Jewish Souls Will Be Left Without Matzos for Passover!

[Kielce — Community, Passover relief.]
Life in Kielce
(Date boxes: Friday 7 Nisan 5697 — 19 March 1937.)
Danger that 5,000 poor Jewish souls will be left without matzos for Passover!
As we have already written, the Kielce kehilla has taken upon itself the great burden of carrying out the Passover campaign. To this end the kehilla administration has turned to the "etat"-payers (kehilla taxpayers), asking each of them to give an instalment[?] on account of the etat (kehilla tax) for the year 1937.
This is the only source from which the kehilla will be able to put together the sum needed for the Passover campaign, on which more than five thousand poor Jewish souls are counting.
For this year's Passover campaign the kehilla must have a sum of at least 15 thousand złoty. Otherwise there is a danger that hundreds of Jewish families will be left without matzos for Passover — and this absolutely necessary sum the kehilla can obtain only from the etat-payers.
To our greatest regret, the greater part of the etat-payers have not found it necessary to respond to the kehilla's request and will not listen to the desperate cries for help of the thousands of poor Jews.
Such disregard must in no[?] way be tolerated. All well-to-do etat-payers, as well as those who are not etat-payers, if they have any possibility at all of helping the Passover campaign, must show their help at once[?]. This is no time for deliberating — it is already late enough!
Already the S.O.S. calls of the five thousand Jewish souls resound loudly in the Jewish street in Kielce, calling on all of us not to forget them on our festival of freedom, Passover!
Christian Washerwoman Wanted to Concoct a Blood Libel Against a Hasidic Jew

[Kielce — Blood libel.]
A Christian washerwoman from a village near Kielce did the washing last week at the home of the Kielce Jew Pinchas Rozenberg. When[?] the washerwoman finished her work at about 9 o'clock, she asked to be allowed to stay the night there. Rozenberg's wife agreed to this.
At 10 o'clock Pinchas Rozenberg came home from the shtibl and, as always, got ready for supper. He sharpened the big rusty[?] knife, washed his hands [ritually], wiped his hands and began to eat. Meanwhile the washerwoman got dressed and left the house. To Rozenberg's wife's question of where she was going, she answered that she was going out to the yard and would be right back.
When an hour had passed and the washerwoman had still not come back, Rozenberg and his wife went out into the yard and began to look for her. They searched for her at all the neighbours' and did not find her. Rozenberg was therefore sure that the washerwoman had gone home to the village, and together with his household he went to bed.
At about 12 o'clock at night the police knocked at Rozenberg's flat and ordered him to open. Together with the policeman the washerwoman also came into the house. The policeman told Rozenberg that the washerwoman had reported at the commissariat that he, Rozenberg, had been preparing to "slaughter" her, and to that end he had sharpened the big knife, washed his hands and girded himself with the towel. Seeing all this the washerwoman took fright, ran away from the house and came to report it at the police commissariat.
Rozenberg told the policeman the whole story and explained to him that he had no idea of anything, that everything the washerwoman had reported was lies and falsehood, and that with it she had wanted to concoct a blood libel against him and thereby meant to cook up a whole mess...
After this explanation the policeman went away.
The next morning the washerwoman came to Rozenberg with her son and began making scenes, supposedly[?] he had wanted to "slaughter" his mother...
Rozenberg reported this to the police. When the police arrived, the washerwoman and her son had already left the house.
Prosecutor Annuls the Indictment Against the Chęciny Rabbi Bornsztajn

[Chęciny — Rabbinate, courts.]
At the beginning of 1936 several underworld characters from Chęciny lodged with the prosecutor's office a shameful denunciation (mesirah) against the local rabbi Bornsztajn and the kehilla dozors (board members). An inspection was carried out at the kehilla, and also at Rabbi Bornsztajn's. The kehilla books were seized by the investigating authorities, and an investigation was opened against the rabbi and the dozors. They were charged under Art. 286, i.e. with misappropriation of public funds. The rabbi and the dozors faced imprisonment.
Many witnesses were heard for and against the charge.
This week Rabbi Bornsztajn received a notice from the prosecutor's office that the charge against him has been annulled for lack of evidence.

Important for Business People

[Economy — banking.]
(YTA) The P.K.O. branch in Łódź accepts bills of exchange for collection at a preferential tariff and moderate [?] costs. Both branches of client service are of great importance for industrial and commercial circles, which will certainly benefit from these conveniences, which are very important for perfecting the administrative-organisational side of economic life.
Besides this, the Łódź branch of the P.K.O. runs the cheque-account department, which provides very many conveniences for merchants, industrialists, artisans and in general all persons who conduct transactions in cash. A cheque account at the P.K.O. is the best guarantee of the security of capital. Moreover, the holder of a cheque account can transfer money to all regions of the country without any additional fee.
Thus, for example, a merchant from Łódź can transfer any sum without any fee to the account of his client in Lwów (Lemberg); in this way he enjoys the ease, so valuable in trade relations, of turnover and of money transfers from one city to another. The secrecy of cheque accounts is, naturally, strictly guarded at the P.K.O.

Worth It, Upon My Life, to Give It a Thought

[Sosnowiec and Będzin — society and charitable institutions; article.] By L. Szpigelman [the paper's editor].
The notions of Sosnowiec citizens on how to support public institutions. — The parallel Będzin–Sosnowiec. — The "evil inclination" of becoming great.
Every one of us knows in what a difficult situation we find ourselves today, how badly off the Jewish community is, and with what pain the masses of the people manage to earn their daily expenses.
It is held that the best-situated corner in Poland is our Zagłębie–Upper Silesia, and perhaps that really is so. After all, we know that while elsewhere people go about idle and unemployed and there is nothing with which to get through the day, here with us, where there is productive [?] activity, something [?] also comes one's way [?] to keep body and soul together.
True, the majority of Polish papers go with the stream and strive to stir up [?] antagonism among the population; yet the Jew does not lose his confidence and lives in the hope that he will also get through the hard times that have arisen [?].
Proceeding from this standpoint, we must see to it, without any excuse, that public life and the most normal conditions are maintained. One must by no means say that because the situation is hard, because the situation is abnormal, therefore one should refrain [?] from supporting or maintaining this or that institution, this or that establishment. It must be just the opposite: because the times are hard, because the need is greater, precisely for that reason one must see to it to take more [?] interest in the hard-hit, who are the victims of the times.
It goes without saying that one should support and maintain only those institutions which bring benefit to the population, where order and honesty prevail, the institutions which submit themselves to public control; and if that matches reality — if the institutions are public-minded and honest and bring benefit to the community — then they must not only be supported and maintained, but one must see to enlarging them.
The few philanthropic institutions that exist in Sosnowiec were once founded on a small scale, in the hope that later they would be enlarged, beautified and broadened. Meanwhile we see exactly the opposite phenomenon: not only have the institutions not been enlarged, they have not become [?] more permanent and more productive; on the contrary, they have shrunk and the notions are small — at a time when the town has grown considerably and is no longer the Sosnowiec of old.
The Jewish population has also grown, and the institutions keep on shrinking.
And a remarkable thing: the writer of these lines often has occasion to draw parallels between the two sister towns, Będzin and Sosnowiec. In Zagłębie it is known that Będzin is a town with tradition; there is an attitude there towards everything of a public character; there are people who have understanding for the community and have a broad [?] gesture [?], a [—] [printed "א לוב" — ?], a good hand [?].
More than once we have occasion to visit the institutions there, and then one has to admit that one gains respect for the people, and at the same time feelings of pity are awakened that Będzin has become impoverished at the expense of the growing Sosnowiec.
We are far [?] from singing hymns [?] of praise and acclaim, for that is not the task of a newspaper and of the journalist; yet recognition must be expressed for a town where, notwithstanding that the Jewish population is becoming poorer and smaller, it can still create and build so much for the common good. Here, in Będzin an orphanage of four storeys has been erected, and now we hear that Mr Jakub Gutman — whom the institution cost [?] tens of thousands when he completed two storeys at once — is now undertaking to finish the fourth storey and to roof [?] the whole building. Or a Mr Fürstenberg [Szymon Fürstenberg], who single-handedly built a Jewish gymnasium, which is an ornament of Jewish Zagłębie; and now, it is said, Mr Chaim Szaj [?] is again going to build, single-handedly, a crafts school, and that too in a modern manner, as the Jews of Będzin like it.
Why do we bring these facts here? Precisely so that Jewish Sosnowiec should be ashamed and perhaps draw a moral from them. After all, there are more Jews in the town who are able to give than in Będzin, and yet here [?] people play at trifles and at miniature institutions.
On the contrary — what have the Jews of Sosnowiec really created in the course of recent [?] times? Nothing except the "Old-Age Home", which was realised thanks to a few wealthy men, while the great number of rich Jews to this day do not lift a finger.
Yes, in Sosnowiec people love to keep puffing themselves up, so that it should be thought that something is being done.
Where is the new building of the modern mikveh, whose campaign became known [?] all over Poland, and what has become of the campaign for the Jewish hospital? Everything for which people in Sosnowiec sacrificed themselves so greatly is done only so that the bells should ring and others should think that something is being done.
There is a "Linat Ha-Cholim" there, on the system of the small shtetls; it is cramped and small there, so that the outpatient clinic does not have the possibility of working properly; and not only is there no philanthropist who would give premises for the said institution — [they] forgo [?] and will not let any premises even for money. Truly clever and level-headed are our rich men — they are "ones who foresee the future"...
So close to Będzin, and such an enormous contrast.
There are neighbouring towns where the rich men compete with each other; each town wants to show the world that it is more capable and creates more for the common good.
Perhaps the rich Jews of Sosnowiec might acquire a good inclination and start competing with Będzin in the field of public work? Upon my life, it would be worth setting out on that road, and thereby they would show that they are no longer petty and can also turn [?] small institutions into large modern buildings and build what does not exist at all. At the same time we can assure the rich Jews of Sosnowiec that the contest [?] would not be any harder, because materially Będzin cannot compare with Sosnowiec.
Upon my life, it is a favourable opportunity, a propitious hour, and it would be worth seizing the moment in order [to rise] up to the proper height.
During the holidays [Passover] one could give this idea a thought.
A Pencil Note

[Feuilleton — Passover eve in the Jewish street.]
Cleaning up.
In honour of the holiday I took a stroll through the Jewish lanes. I wanted to witness[?] what the holiday-eve preparations look like there.
Fine, warm spring days. But in the eyes of the Jewish passers-by the winter still blows[?]. Not a spark of contentment and joy nests[?] in them.
People are clearing out their homes, airing the bedding, polishing the windows, but out of everything a kind of question mark emerges:
—?...
— A matzah-carrier has strayed in here. He carries the basket[?] of matzot; he looks so lonely, as if not of this world. Envious glances, soaked with pain and sorrow, pierce him from all sides; he is accompanied by the sighs and groans of Jewish men and women.
Tiny Jewish children, ragged and threadbare, run after him, pester[?] him and want to wheedle[?] a little matzah out of him — but they do not succeed. Disappointed, they run back, and their thin little faces express boundless grief.
Old and young Jews, ordinary craftsmen, wander about without a stitch of work. Driven by want and poverty, they look for some small earnings — and there are none.
As I approach them, my ears catch:
— Oh, where does one get the good old times...
And —
people are clearing out their homes, airing the bedding and polishing the windows —
Sh-R.
Janek at the Seder...

[Humorous Passover story — assimilated Jews return to Jewishness.]
Told by Y. Aberzhantsek[?].
When misfortune is fated, it comes right into the house; and when you are fated to have a spoiled Passover, they send you a neighbour named Janek.
You think Janek is not a Jew? You are mistaken — this Janek is a Jew. You will ask: how so? A Jew — Janek? The answer is: he is as much a Jew as I am. Hitler has reminded many thousands of such Janeks that they are Jews — the uprooted, the estranged, the runaways from Jewishness, those who were ashamed of the name Jew, the "nie tu i nie sam[?] żydki" [Polish: little Jews; 'neither here nor there'?], who choked on a single Yiddish word, the żydki who [—][?] with a bit of charm[?] and for whom the word "Żyd" was the greatest "obraza" [insult] — all these Jews have lately remembered that they are Jews and have come back to Jewishness.
To these very Jews belongs my neighbour Janek Karpaka[?].
This past year our Janek has become quite another man, unrecognisable. He hardly talks[?] with Jews but he tries to slip in a Yiddish word; at every opportunity he declares with pride: "Przecież ja jestem Żydem" [Polish: after all, I am a Jew]. After the [—] "[—]" [perhaps an allusion to the Przytyk pogrom] he even began, out of spite, to eat "koszerne" [kosher] meat, became a "regular"[?] at Jewish institutions and takes an interest in "Palestina".
His wife too, the Jankowa, has become muddled; she too already speaks "Yiddish". Just before Passover she said to my wife in "Yiddish":
— Me not katoliczka, me żydówka, me terribly[?] love ryby po żydowsku [fish Jewish-style — gefilte fish]!
One way or another she comes to my wife to ask questions: how one salts (koshers) meat, how long one must wait between meat and milk — a whole calamity!..
And he, Janek, for his part keeps plying me with questions: "Kiedy jest Rosz Hojdesz[?]? Jak się robi 'naftule'[?] (Havdalah)? Kiedy się liczy sfire (the Omer count)? Kiedy jest Jom Kipur (Yom Kippur)? Kiedy się idzie[?] do 'teszlich'[?] (Tashlikh)? Kiedy się robi 'brochim toirim boirim mine zemoigis'[?] (borei minei mezonot)? A kiedy 'mojce — lejchem min hamojcie'?"
Thus he torments me for whole days with other questions. Once he comes — I should show him how one fixes a "mezuzah" to the door, how one braids "cycełki w tałesu" [tzitzit in the tallit].
But my real defeat at his hands came on Passover eve. For a whole week he would not let go of me and kept asking:
— Panie Mendel, jak trzeba koszerować? [Mr Mendel, how does one kasher?]
— And when is one not allowed[?] to eat chomec?
— When are these sedery?
The Jankowa again asked my wife:
— Pani Mendlowa[?], jak trzeba koszerować kuchnię? [Mrs Mendel, how does one kasher the kitchen?]
But the real piece of work I had with him at the Seders.
For the first Seder he comes to me and begs:
— Panie Mendel, niech mnie pan nauczy robić the Seder. [Mr Mendel, teach me to do the Seder.]
So I went with him and gave him a lesson in how it is done, and he sat himself down at the head of the table and began to give orders:
— Małgosia, daj mi mięso[?] pieczone na zroa. [give me roast meat for the zeroa]
— Małgosia, jajko pieczone na bejcim. [a roast egg for the 'egg']
— Małgosia, garuszka[?] żale na moror. [... for the maror]
Następnie [next]: pietruszka na karpas, charoset i trochę chrzanu na chazeres. [parsley for karpas, charoset and a little horseradish for the chazeret]
Then he took the bit of "merchandise" and began to lay it out according to the "plan" of the Haggadah.
Instead of "Kiddush" he made a "hawdule"[?] (Havdalah). When the Jankowa started drinking the first cup, he raised a shout:
— Małgosia, na lechaim [—][?] się pije...
Then he broke off half a matzah and said to his wife:
— Małgosia, here, keep this for the afikojmen (afikoman).
Having finished the first "część" [part], he began to say: "Oto chleb nędzy" [Polish: this is the bread of poverty] (Ha lachma anya), and she, the Jankowa, began asking the "pytania" [questions] (the Four Questions).
"Ma sztanu[?] chalaile chaze mikol cha-lemt[?]" [a garbled 'Mah nishtanah'] — and Janek answered.
So it went on until the Plagues. At Rabbi Judah's mnemonic he "[—]"[?] [got stuck; Polish word unclear]; he could by no means make sense of the DeTzaKh, ADaSh, BeAHaV, and in the end he had to give up Rabbi Judah's mnemonic and move on.
At the drinking of the second cup he again raised a shout:
— Małgosia, na lechaim [—][?]!
I felt great pity for Janek at the "Korekh". Both of them grabbed the portions, choked, coughed and gasped; both had eyes swollen from the horseradish. The Jankowa coughed and groaned:
— Mój Boże, doprawdy nie [rozumiem?] tego [—]! [My God, I really don't (understand?) this …!]
The worst of it was with Elijah the Prophet's cup.
When it came to opening the door the Jankowa trembled with fear, her teeth chattered, she was white as the wall; Janek himself pretended it did not bother him, and when he opened the door he stammered:
— Shi... shi... shifakh[?] cha... cha... chamaski[?] [garbled 'Shfokh chamatkha'] — and remained standing as if paralysed. The Jankowa heard it and barely stammered out:
— We... we... witamy [welcome]... pa... pa... panie E... E... [—] [Elijah the Prophet?]..
Both of them, Janek and the Jankowa, stood pressed close[?] to one another and gazed with curious eyes at Elijah the Prophet's cup, to see whether it was getting any emptier[?].
And when the other closed the door, the Jankowa swore:
— [a Polish oath, unclear: '... by [my] health[?] ..., that it is ...']...
Janek too saw "that the glass moved[?]" — and the cup did stir.
Thus, with great effort, Janek conducted the first Seder.
I thought I was already off the hook — that on the second Seder night it would go for him "jak na masełko" [smooth as butter]; but it does not even begin. On the second Seder night there is a knock at the door.
— Kto tam? [Who's there?]
— Ja, sąsiad. [It's me, the neighbour.]
— What is it now?
He wants to know whether the second Seder begins with... Chad Gadya.
— What do you mean, with Chad Gadya? One begins exactly as on the first Seder night.
— Ale u mnie nie jest smak[?] [But mine doesn't taste right].
So I went in once more to have a look why with him it begins with Chad Gadya — and what do you think it was? A trifle: instead of opening at the first page, he had opened at the last.
Such a spoiled Passover I had because of the Seder and my neighbour Janek.
The Struggle of the Jewish Community against Luxury among Jews.

[Historical study — community and luxury.]
Mgr. Chaim Babad (President of the Jewish Community in Sosnowiec)
Introduction.
How often we have lately heard the reproach that we live in wealth and prosperity. We are reproached that we travel to spas at home and abroad, that we dress conspicuously, and there have even been found[?] such people as have held it against us[?] that we are a nation of idlers, because we have many holidays on which we sit with folded hands and do not lift a finger, and as the Roman proverb says: Nihil agendo, male agere discimus, i.e. "by doing nothing, we learn to do evil". "Idleness leads to boredom, and boredom to sin." We are also[?] constantly reproached that we live in luxury, and this incites the mob against us. And what do we do to prevent things coming to that? Where exactly is it written that a wedding at this or that "court" must be so conspicuous that it makes everyone's eyes pop and provokes the — to a certain extent justified — reproach that we live beyond our station?! In the past, when there was as yet no radio, when we did not yet have "kefitzat derakhim" [miraculous shortening of the road, i.e. fast travel], when our rabbis and the leaders of the generation were not yet "diplomats" and did not stand as candidates for the Sejm, our leaders and the great men of the generation then had more time to look into the affairs of this world and took care that there should be no desecration of God's Name. They endeavoured to regulate the day-to-day life of their community. When we leaf through the pinkasim [record books] of the communities, the regulations of the "Council of Four Lands" and various responsa, we find at every step prohibitions and bans whose aim was to combat the wild[?] luxury in the Jewish street. These regulations had a colossal influence on the day-to-day life of the Jewish street, because they touched the most intimate moments in the life of the Jewish family. They watched over the individual from the cradle, regulated the drive of life and gave it a direction that was desirable for the good of the community.
My treatise covers the period from the year 1220 to 1808 and takes into account[?] the cultural life of the Italian, Spanish, German, Czech and Polish Jews, and is based on printed and unprinted historical documents. I have also taken into account all the regulations against luxury issued by the Church, as well as those issued by the secular authorities, such as emperors and princes of various states. In doing so I have also striven to show the connection between the Jewish and non-Jewish regulations, which always had something in common.
Chapter One.
The struggle against luxury among the Christians in various European countries.
The struggle against luxury among the Christians appears in Europe only in the 12th century and lasts until the end of the 18th century, and it always depends on the financial order of one period or another. Until the 12th century barter trade prevails in Europe, i.e. trade based on the mutual exchange of products.
Under such a kind of trade the average person could satisfy only his most primitive needs, for in order to buy a product he had to pay the seller with another product that he had made himself. Under such conditions foreign trade was almost impossible, and where it existed on a small scale it was, after all, greatly limited by the means of transport of the time. Thus trade in those times was almost exclusively domestic. From this it follows that there was then no question of luxury, because the inhabitants of a country where, for example, there was no silk production of its own did not — apart from small exceptions — wear silk clothes, since no silk was brought in from abroad. In the 12th century, however, a tremendous change occurs in the money economy. The hitherto "barter trade" passes over into money trade, and this brings a tremendous change in the economic conditions of those times. Money is easier to carry from place to place, and this makes foreign trade possible. People begin to import foreign goods that had been entirely unknown until then. Various expensive articles appear, such as silk, velvet, costly furs, gold and silver jewellery set with precious stones, and people slowly grow accustomed to all these luxury objects, and "habit becomes second nature": in time one can no longer do without them. The money economy brings with it so-called "mercantilism"[?], which rests on the principle that every state strives to accumulate as much money as possible, which now represents the wealth of the country. And here the trouble begins. For luxury products such as velvet and silk the foreign merchants must be paid in real gold, in gold, and when the precious metal is taken out of the country, the country grows poor. The upshot of this combination is that people begin to prohibit the use of all these goods, in order to prevent the export of gold abroad and make it impossible.
The Church, too, joins the struggle against luxury, seeing in the use of various ornaments a survival of the idolatrous times.
The first restriction on the use of luxury objects appears in the year 1299 in Florence. A levy of 50 florins a year is imposed on those who wear precious stones, as well as other gold and silver jewellery, no matter whether the stones are genuine or false. Florence issues similar restrictions 5 times in the period from 1330 to 1396.
In the year 1453 the city council of Bologna issues a ban on wearing clothes containing silver threads, costly furs and other luxury garments. The inhabitants are thereby divided into three strata, each of which has different rules: 1) the wives and daughters of the old nobility; 2) the wives and daughters of the learned[?] and of the young nobility, to which only a person could belong who had not engaged in trade for 30 years; 3) the remaining inhabitants (see Weiss, Kostümkunde, vol. 2, p. 314).
The first anti-luxury ban in Spain appears in the decree of James I of Aragon in the year 1234 (see Weiss, Kostümkunde, vol. 2, p. 343). It forbids wearing clothes of so-called "estampado", i.e. printed coloured fabrics, and gold and silver ornaments. He also forbids holding large banquets and festivities. When Ferdinand of Castile conquers Andalusia, luxury begins to spread there too, and Alfonso the Tenth issues in the year 1256 a second decree in Seville, in which he repeats the decree of James I of 1234.
