Two Neighbours (An Erev-Pesach Picture)

[Fiction — an Erev-Pesach story.]
P. Blumenkranc (Częstochowa).
(An Erev-Pesach picture.)

In all five rooms of Yosef Gold's flat there is commotion.
The mistress of the house, a middle-aged Jewish woman, runs from one room to the other with the keys, giving orders.
Ever since Purim she has been tormenting the servants. Three times they had to drag the mattresses out into the yard and beat them under her supervision.
She stood over the servants like an overseer at forced labour.
— Balecze [?], that is not how one beats things at my place; that is how they clean at the Częstochowskis', where [?]. [?] — wallowing in dirt, and not at my place.
After 4 weeks of work, from which the maids got chapped hands and red eyes, Sarah Gold still does not rest. Now she is conducting a general review of the work; she bends down with difficulty (because of her fatness), wipes a finger across the floor and shouts:
— Balecze, just let Balecze come in [?] — this is called tidied? — she points with her finger — everywhere is full of "kurz" [dust]; one cannot rely on strangers. They only want to get it over with — she sighs as if to herself.
— Madame, that is from the street, the window was open.
— Then one does not open windows! I will wear myself out, and they will fling the windows open!
— But Madame told us to air out the flat.
— Balecze, you are already answering me back! You are not at the Wołkowiczes' [?], where a maid meddles in everything.
Leaving the maid a "mruke" [?], she runs on to take a look into the kitchen, where the cook has been standing since dawn stirring the big aluminium pots. Sarah scooped up a little fish broth, put the tip of the spoon to her mouth and shook herself as if from castor oil.
— Jadzia, put sugar in! You know my children love sweet things. One cannot rely [on anyone] [?] with the smallest trifle.
She runs on; she must get clothes ready for the children to put on.
At this moment, however, she hears her husband's steps. She hurries to the kitchen and shouts:
— Jadzia, the master is coming, get it to the table quicker, you may move a little faster. How she spares herself!
Jadzia can barely move from tiredness. A whole night making "pigess" [?] at the baker's; it is long since she has felt her hands [?]; since dawn at the oven, the heat has taken away her appetite. She would lie down right there in the middle of the room, her legs give way under her, but Madame's shouting rings in her tired head like an alarm bell. She takes the tray and drags her exhausted feet into the dining room.
She sets down the tray. Gold turns to the dishes and a pleasant smile floats on his lips; it is hard to guess even the reason, but evidently [?] he is pleased with himself. Perhaps yesterday's takings, which were not bad at all, are the cause, and perhaps also Jadzia, for he looks after her discreetly [printed "disret"] and the smile grows stronger on him...
• • •
In the same entrance, one floor higher, lives Yoel Stein. Gold and Stein have known each other for many years; they pray together, only a little apart: Gold stands by the Holy Ark and Stein — by the western wall.
A whole winter Stein made his living finishing "spinki" [clasps] taken home, working from dawn until evening together with his wife, and earned 2 zł. a day.
But lately he has lost the work. The manufacturer has goods in the warehouse. As bad luck would have it, he ended up without work just before Pesach.
So they both sit, Stein and his wife, on Erev Pesach at home. She has sat down on a low stool like a mourner and cannot look her husband in the eyes. Both are silent!
He had already, poor man [?], decided to turn to a charity society, but when he came closer and saw how in a long line children stand with little bags in their hands and a few kilos of matzah are poured [?] into them — he ran away. He is willing to go hungry, to eat only potatoes.
But something worse torments them. What will happen with the children, what will happen tomorrow, when all the children run out into the yard dressed up, and theirs will squeeze themselves, ashamed, into a corner.
Stein's wife remembers how a year ago her Yechezkele came home from [—], put his little hands under his chin [?] and was silent. On no account would he touch his food. She begged him and he burst out crying:
— Mama, I won't go to prayers, they laugh at me and point at the patches on my shoes.
Her mother's heart contracted; she wants to calm him:
— Better a [?] patch than a fine hole; you are young, my child, you will yet have and have.
— I won't go any more; David says to me: your father could have given you whole shoes, without patches!
The tears run down his childish face and she weeps along with him...
• • •
In the room it grows darker; the sun is already setting in the west.
Stein's wife sits in the same corner. He paces about the room, scrapes together the "szczerki" [?] lying on the floor and talks nervously.
— We haven't got a crumb of matzah for the holiday — she speaks up — I don't know what we will give the children to eat. Because of your false shame the children will go hungry, do you understand?
— Lost cause.
— What do you mean, lost cause?! You can do without, but you cannot demand it of a child. What kind of talk is this? Does a father talk like that? Your stubbornness will yet be the death of us.
He could no longer control himself. He planted himself in the middle of the room; the veins on his forehead began to dance.
— What do you know? You know nothing! You just chatter. Yesterday I went to the "Matan Beseter" society: a room full of people, Gold and five more chairmen sitting at a table, a young [?] fellow [?] stands at the door and shoves: "Don't push, you're not in a pigsty, manners!" Gold sits at the table and interrogates like an examining magistrate:
— What's your name, where do you live?
Then each one is asked how many children he has, while they crack tasteless jokes, and after all the questioning they order a check in a book, whether so-and-so, God forbid, hasn't smuggled himself into another institution in order to get another two kilos of matzot. You understand, I will not go to Gold for matzot any more!
— All right, then not — she wants to calm him — potatoes we have, and there will be coal too.
— If I didn't have potatoes either, I still wouldn't have stretched out my hand. I will not feed my children beggar's bread!
She remained sitting huddled in the corner. In the room it was already quite dark; he kept pacing up and down, nervously rubbing his forehead, as if he wanted to drive away a bad headache.
• • •
At the Golds' all five rooms are lit up; his wife is still giving orders; suddenly she runs to the bathroom.
— Yosef — she shouted in — Yosef, at Yoel Stein's absolutely nothing ["fartogne-gornisht", ?] is prepared for the holiday; the neighbour from across the way told me today.
— Well, what am I to do? Go and provide for them all. Let them work the way I work!
— You are not right. A neighbour you should have remembered. Everything depends [?] on you.
— You're talking nonsense. Can I remember all the poor people? Whatever the man of standing could get out of our society — surely one won't go running to the [—] "latayn" [?] poor people.
She went away from the door with a sigh and a smile. A sigh — out of pity, and a smile — because of the power, the "got-tsu-par" [?] and the cleverness of her Yosele. But she soon remembered her role and began bossing [?] the servants again.
Gold pondered for a moment, waved his hand as if he wanted to chase away a fly, and with pleasure dipped himself into the bathtub...
"Ha lachma anya"... (Passover Reflections)

[Essay — Passover reflections.] Yehuda Yafe
"Ha lachma anya" ("This is the bread of affliction")...
(Passover reflections).
(Specially for the "Zaglembier Tsaytung")

One need not be an adherent of the materialist conception of history, and yet one must[?] admit that certain factors in history do have a materialist background, a materialist driving force. Today more than ever we Jews can become acquainted with the doctrine that the great wheel[?] of history is driven by no idea, no spiritual force, but solely by coarse earthly power. On the other hand, however, it is [—] to deny that certain means of this [structure?] were forged solely out of that same materialism.
One of these means — and indeed a very important one — is human hatred. If you draw up a list of the authors who wrote that interesting book called "Human History", Her Majesty Hatred will take the top place. She, eternal hatred, stands at the cradle of every nation and at its grave.
And however far one may be from the materialist world-view, hatred must be conceded entirely to the materialists. Their doctrine applies to it best: not crippled, false idealism is its father, but materialism. I am something of a heretic regarding the saying "There is no hatred like religious[?] hatred": it seems to me that the worst hatred is the one that does not come under the mask of spirituality, but the one that shows itself in its naked[?], egoistic, materialistic face. Just as it is not entirely true, what people say, that an open enemy is better than a hidden one. Ah, you know[?], I am in fact more afraid of an open enemy. And the difference between the two hatreds mentioned is, after all, the difference between naked materialistic enmity and enmity covered with the fig leaves of a corrupted spirit.
* * *
What background did the first hatred have that the Jewish people had to endure? That hatred which became the greatest national memory, which serves as the foundation of most of the commandments and is mentioned fifty times in the Torah? — A purely economic, a purely materialist one. Of[?] religious or spiritual persecutions nothing is mentioned anywhere with Pharaoh. On the contrary — "Go, serve the Lord your God" — piety, spirituality — take as much as you like — only build[?] Pithom and Ramses for me, just knead bricks and carry clay, work for me, give me your bodies, your energy, and the spirit — that I leave to your God — said Pharaoh.
The scholars who have studied the ancient papyri establish that the word "Ivri" (Hebrew) was identical among the Egyptians with "brick-kneader" and clay-carrier, and nobody says[?] that "Ivri" was meant to be identical with "spiritually persecuted"; the Torah, too, tells only that God took us out "of the house of bondage", and nothing more.
Ramses II, as the Egyptologists portray him, wanted nothing more than to make his country rich. And indeed commerce flourished in his time. Egypt's prosperity rose, and for that the energy of a defenceless Semitic tribe had to be exploited. [—] him a reincarnation of an enemy — he built up a border city "Ramses"; never mind, the Jewish slaves can work. Besides these Jewish slaves there were many more Semitic tribes in the land — the Hyksos, and those Semites drove out the peasants. So the Egyptologists tell us. Egypt was then densely populated, the masses were starving; they formed an army[?] and drove out the Semites (see, e.g., Hermann Schneider: "The Ancient Egyptians", vol. 1). Only the Semitic tribe of Israel was hard to drive out — so it was enslaved economically, not spiritually.
* * *
And here we now[?] come to our heresy: that economic enslavement is far more dangerous than spiritual. In many countries Jews were spiritually even more enslaved than in Egypt, yet nowhere did they find themselves in the 49 gates of impurity except in Egypt; no exile brought the Jewish people to the 50th of the gates of impurity as did the Egyptian exile.
Because when our opponent[?] in the struggle is only a spiritual one — when we face a supposedly spiritual enemy — we have something to fight him with. It is different when we face a coarse enemy who does not touch our books, who wants only our bread: then one can truly sometimes fall into the 49 gates, into apathy[?] and despair; then the body is struck[?] and the soul — falls into despondency.
These two categories of hatred actually differ according to the pedigree[?] of their bearers. Both aim at the morsel from one's mouth, the "lachma anya". But a supposedly cultured nation writes on its antisemitic banner: spirit — though it means something else. A culturally lower collective, however, says openly: hand over the morsel from your mouth.
* * *
This economic struggle is indeed the hardest struggle. For which Passover is so symbolic: "This is the bread of affliction that our fathers ate in the land of Egypt." It is immensely harder. For a people as soft of body as the Jewish one it is much easier to wage a spiritual world war than a war for the bread of affliction. It is not a struggle suited to it.
And the only [consolation?] is that if the struggle is indeed a coarse, earthly one, unsuited to a fully[?] spiritual fighting people — there is nevertheless a great spiritual hope, the "Next year in the Land of Israel", which does not let one sink into the 50th of the gates of impurity, to which a miserable struggle for the bread of affliction leads[?].
The Festival of Freedom (Thoughts)

[Article — Passover.] By L. Goldsztajn.
...Do you remember the years of childhood? It is spring. The sun warms — a delight; on the meadows the snow has long since melted, on the trees the buds slowly creep out, and above all — no going to cheder. The rebbe said:
— Children, you're excused!...
...Do you remember how we suddenly became free? At home the mothers cleared out, washed and scrubbed — and we, like free little birds, dashed off to the fields and meadows; everything around us laughed and frolicked, everything around us sang and called:
— Freedom, freedom...
And slowly the greyness, the everyday drabness vanished from the home, and the dear festival little by little began to spread its white wings; father was getting ready to take over the kingdom, the rooms gleamed, everything around was so alive, and the child's little heart chirped[?] — a delight...
— And the Seder? No, there are not many experiences like the Seder night was for Jewish children.
Father straightened his back, and loud and proud rang his words:
— "Avadim hayinu" — We were slaves!... Yesterday we once were. But today, today we are free! We are no longer servants, we are citizens with equal rights — and the children's little minds fell into thought for a minute.
— How good, how beautiful this is! We are no longer servants, we are free, we sit at the Seder, we sing, we drink wine, we say the Haggadah, and father's voice rings ever stronger and stronger.
— "And thou shalt tell thy son"!... And we listen closely to the glorious story, the glorious, eternal legend...
* * *
— "And thou shalt tell thy son"!..
...And tell your son: We were once slaves, they tormented us with back-breaking labour; we built Pithom and Raamses, cities and towns, turned desert land into glorious oases, with our withered hands broke the hardest rocks, drained [—?] swamps and from them blessed fields arose; we ploughed and sowed, and full ears of grain sprouted[?] out of the wilderness — and yet the Egyptians tormented us, embittered our lives.
— "And they made their lives bitter." And deep, deep did the master's whip cut into our withered body, and persecutions and harassments poured down on our heads, and heavy taxes hounded and plagued us — until the miracle happened...
— The wonder above all wonders, the miracle of the Exodus from Egypt.
Forty years we wandered in the desert, without a day, without a path; desolate was life in the desert, without night and without day, no water, no meat — but with an iron will to free ourselves and firm trust in our hearts; girded with this[?] we marched forward through the desert with firm steps.
...And when a people no longer wants to be slaves! When a people wants to free itself, when a people wants air to breathe and [to leave] the nations behind it[?]! — it struggles to its last breath, it fights to the point of despair.
— "And thou shalt tell thy son"... So tell your son, and prepare him for a hard life, for a stubborn struggle.
* * *
— "Yom tov shel cherut" — a festival of freedom..
How beautiful is a festival of freedom, when the sun peeps out of its hiding place and announces to the world that dear spring is coming, that mankind is being set free, and everything turns green and blossoms, everything is full of hope.
And when today we sit at the Seder and tell the magical thousand-year-old legend, when today we sing the eternal song that tells us wonders of our people, that tells us of the thorny[?] road, the desert road, which our people wandered through, that tells us of the bloody struggle until a ray of sunlight reached it, that tells us how our forefathers leapt into the flames with a smile on their lips for the sake of their existence —
— Our people must exist, our people must be free.
In Honour of Passover

[For Passover — Torah sayings and folklore.] Passover Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes — collected and edited by Yehuda.

a) "This year here, next year in the Land of Israel. This year slaves, next year free men."
"Zion shall be redeemed with justice, and her returnees with righteousness" — first Zion will be redeemed, and only afterwards the enslaved Jews. The redemption of a people cannot come unless the redemption of the land comes first. And therefore first "next year in the Land of Israel," and only afterwards "next year free men."
The Vilna Gaon.
• • •
"Let all who are hungry come and eat" — because "next year in the Land of Israel," and then, when the Messiah comes, it will surely be "the penny gone from the purse": all will be equal, there will be no poor and rich, and therefore "let all who are hungry come and eat" — what is the point of collecting and hiding money?...
Birkat Hagir[?].

b) "Blessed is He who keeps His promise"
Earlier the author of the Haggadah says: "And I gave Esau Mount Seir to possess it" — to Esau the Master of the Universe gave at once everything He had promised him. At once — on the spot. Whereas — "Blessed is He who keeps His promise to Israel": with the promise to the Jews the Master of the Universe waits ("shomer" — to wait), "for the Holy One, blessed be He, calculated the end": the Master of the Universe calculates the End, does sums, and meanwhile the soul is going out of the few Jews...
R' Leibish Harif.

c) "As it is said: for there is no pasture [printed 'cave'] for the flocks of your servants"
The Egyptians regarded the occupation of tending sheep as something unworthy, "for every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians." Only Jews were admitted to this "unclean" livelihood. (Just as in other countries trade was regarded as unworthy and only Jews were admitted to it.) Later, when the Egyptians noticed that the Jews were making a fortune from this "unclean" occupation, he [Pharaoh] insisted that the Jews might leave Egypt but must leave behind the flocks and herds... To that Moses said: Not that! If we go — "with our flocks and with our herds we will go": we will take along these very "unclean" little sheep which you once regarded as unworthy and which you now have come to covet...
Rabbi David Avigdor.

d) "As it is said: Come, let us deal wisely with them, lest they multiply, and it come to pass that when war befalls us, they also join our enemies."
As is known, Egypt was for a time under the rule of the Hyksos, a Semitic tribe which ruled part of Egypt. The descent of Jacob and Joseph into Egypt falls in that period. Later Ramesses II drove out the Hyksos in hard wars, and therefore the words he said are understandable: "and it come to pass that when war befalls us, they also join our enemies" — fearing that in the struggle with the Hyksos the Jews would [side] with the latter as a Semitic brother-tribe...
Dr. Z. Jampel.

e) "Numerous, as it is said: And the children of Israel were fruitful and swarmed and multiplied..."
The Bible critics mocked the sages' homily on this verse, that "she bore six in one womb," and the new age shows[?] that it is not such an extraordinary thing at all. On 21 June 1838 a woman of thirty-three in Gaspel[?] gave birth to quintuplets, but they all died at once; and so the chronicle of recent times is full of such facts..
"Jerusalem" (Part Three).
Collector's note: lately there is talk in America of a case of quintuplets of whom all five children are alive..

f) "The heavens are the heavens of the Lord, but the earth He has given to the children of men"
"Hashamayim" — the heavens — "are the heavens of the Lord": the heavens were made and belong to God. "But the earth" — but to transform the earth into heaven, to make heaven out of the earth — that "He has given to the children of men": this God handed over to human beings, that they should make heaven out of the earth..
R' Moshe Leib Lentshner[?].

g) "I will rise now and go about the city, in the markets and in the streets" (Song of Songs 3:2)
A Masorah: the expression "and I will go about" occurs twice in the Bible — here, and in "I will wash my hands in innocence and go about Your altar, O Lord." Just as it is unworthy to bring robbery and theft to the altar, so too in the markets and the streets a person must guard himself against them. The street, the market, must be for a person like the precincts of the Temple, because God is everywhere...
Megillat Sefer.

g) [sic, for h)] "If the vine has blossomed... the pomegranates are in flower" (Song of Songs 7:13)
"The vine" symbolizes the scholars, and "pomegranates" — the empty ones who are full of mitzvot like a pomegranate. "If the vine has blossomed" — if the scholars flourish, if I see that the scholars are good and pious, then I know whether "the pomegranates are in flower," how the masses look — everything follows the head; all depends on the leaders...
Livyat Hen.
The Festival of Freedom.

[Passover essay — reflection.] By Y. Chigadzki [J. Chigadzki?].

"He brought us out from bondage to freedom,
... and from servitude to redemption."
(Haggadah).

The festival of Passover is, according to tradition, the symbol of freedom and liberation [?], from [?] the age-old times when the Jews were enslaved and subjugated under Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and after a hard and bitter struggle the Jews succeeded in freeing themselves from under the Egyptians' rule and in conquering the Land of Israel.

But is the festival of Passover, which we have been celebrating in exile for nearly two thousand years, nothing more than a remembrance of those age-old times, of the past? To this question we must answer with a great "No"!

Passover is for us not merely a remembrance, a sentiment of the past, but at the same time also a "lighthouse", a pillar of fire of hope, of expectation and consolation, and of striving for spiritual and physical freedom and redemption, which must and will come in the end.

That the opinion expressed here is the correct one is best shown by our traditional Haggadah, which we read every Passover night with so much mysticism, joy and enthusiasm, and on account of which the Jewish people has already sacrificed so many thousands of grievous victims. For the Passover night is, in the history of our martyrology, so rich in the most tragic blood libels and accusations. The Haggadah, which was actually composed and compiled on the basis of the verse "And thou shalt tell thy son etc. ... when I came forth out of Egypt", and which actually ought to concern itself only with the course of the events of the Exodus, has in truth been transformed into a stormy and roaring [?] scroll of protest against Jewish troubles and suffering, and into a mighty [?] and splendid, hopeful message of redemption, of consolation and hope for a better tomorrow — one that flows from a great spirit and from a strong and healthy people which, despite its sufferings and persecutions, does not give up its aspirations and strivings to become once again a healthy and normal people and to rebuild its ruined "Old-New Land", the Land of Israel.

If we consider the content of the "Haggadah", we see at once the first opening passage, "Ha lachma anya", which was composed in the Babylonian exile after the First Destruction and was therefore written not in "Hebrew" but in the language of the country, "Aramaic" — it already speaks of the present tragic situation and of the future redemption: "This year slaves, next year — free men." Although we are momentarily enslaved and in bondage — nevertheless we are sure that we shall again be a free people.

Then come the questions of "Ma nishtana" and the purely factual answer of "Avadim hayinu", which explains the content — why we celebrate the festival of Passover.

But immediately afterwards comes again the story of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva with their companions, who sat in the academy at Bnei Brak a whole night and talked about the miracles of the Exodus, until their students came and said to them: "Our masters, the time has come for the morning Shema." The whole story is in truth nothing more than a legend, for we must remember that this happened in those terrible and cruel times of the Roman despot-emperor Hadrian, who dared and set himself the goal of exterminating the Jewish people together with its religion. It was precisely then that the great men of Israel assembled, among whom the famous Tanna Rabbi Akiva occupied the place of honour, and they considered the dark Jewish situation "all that night" and deliberated on the means to be employed to free themselves from the despotic emperor Hadrian; and they took comfort in the events of the Exodus: however bad and sad the situation may be, one must nevertheless not lose heart and not be broken; one need only use the power of resilience and a strong will to liberation, and exploit the suitable and favourable moment. And during this serious [?] deliberation, which lasted the whole night, their students came in and said to them: "Our masters, the time has come" — the fitting and appropriate hour "of the morning" of a new dawn has arrived, which shall free us from troubles and suffering! And the result of this event is well known: Rabbi Akiva proclaims the uprising, declares the war-hero Bar Kokhba to be the Messiah, and his twenty-four thousand students — the proud national youth, ready to sacrifice themselves for the freedom of their people and land — fall like heroes on the battlefield, until Bar Kokhba is crowned as victor and saviour of the land of Judea.

Then comes the story of Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah: "Behold, I am like a man of seventy years etc.", which is absolutely incomprehensible: the great and famous Tanna and Nasi says: I am already seventy and nevertheless I did not merit to tell of the Exodus at night, until Ben Zoma expounded "all the days of thy life — the nights"! We must therefore understand this too as an allegory: Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah, the Nasi, was grieving and despairing because of the sufferings and persecutions that the Jewish people endured at that time. Ben Zoma, for his part, who was also a companion of the Tanna Rabbi Akiva, understood the harm to the uprising when so great a personality as the Nasi falls into despair and spiritual depression — therefore [?] Ben Zoma expounded "all the days of thy life — the nights": when troubles and suffering make our life very dark, like the night — then one must remember and keep in mind the redemption from Egypt, and thus [?] raise the courage and strengthen the spirit of the great Tanna and Nasi.

It would take up too much space if one were to interpret every sentence and comment on every saying; but it is enough to say that the whole Haggadah is a compilation of the Jewish persecutions, sufferings and torments, of their expression of sorrow and anger, and of an unshakable faith and hope in the future, and that the Egyptian exile is nothing more than a symbol, an allegory of the troubles and sufferings of the Jewish people in all generations, which find their strongest expression in the despairing cry of woe [?]: "For not only one has risen against us to destroy us, but in every generation they rise against us to destroy us."

Then come the expressions of hope and redemption for the future: "Raise up the congregation that none can count; soon lead the shoots of Your planting, redeemed, to Zion in joyous song" — raise up [—] [?] the people of Israel and lead them with song to Zion! And at the end, convinced and certain of the nearness of the redemption and full of hope for the rebuilding of the Land of Israel, he cries out in holy ecstasy: "Next year in Jerusalem!"

This, then, is the content of the Haggadah, and it is also important that every Jew should immerse himself during these Passover nights in the Haggadah and in the narratives of the Exodus, which are a symbol of the eternal Jewish suffering and of hope for the future redemption — let him draw fresh strength from invincible tenacity and endurance, until Passover is transformed into a true "Festival of Freedom", when the Jew will be able to say proudly:

"He brought us out from bondage to freedom and from servitude to redemption."
The Seder Nights!

How much has already been written to this day about Passover in general and about the Seder nights in particular. These two imposing, splendid, poetic nights, which bring joy into our homes, and above all into the homes where the light of the sun reaches but little. The two nights that strengthen our spirit, that we have been[?] and will remain an eternal people. The nights that strengthen our hope that tomorrow will be a better one, and [—] us so well, as [—] the redemption...

And more remarkable still is that we celebrate the Seder night on the threshold of spring, when nature, the world, awakens to fresh revival, to work, to gladden our people — the persecuted, languishing people, dreaming[?] of a home of its own.

These Seder nights, which all admire, become a symbol of national liberation. Without distinction, both the learned and the simple Jew, they unite[?] together the poor man as well as the rich[?], the orphans as well as the [—] and the sick. In this domain[?] the American Jew, the English and the Polish Jew are all united.

The Seder nights also remind us that out of a small family grew a great people, which the Egyptian ruler did not want to free, because he drew great benefit from this people — the opposite of the present day, when it is held [—]

“Raise up the congregation that none can count; soon lead the offshoots of Your planting, redeemed, to Zion in joyous song” [Hebrew quotation from the closing hymn of the Haggadah; printed with misprints] — puts the people of Israel on its feet and leads them with song to Zion! And at the end, convinced and certain of the nearness of the redemption and full of hope for the upbuilding of the Land of Israel, he calls out in holy ecstasy: Next year in Jerusalem!

This is the content of the

[...] would[?] be content if the slaves emigrated from the countries where they live.

It is therefore no wonder that the festival of freedom remains in the Jew's memory from the cradle to the grave, and it remained even among those who went away from us — among the Marranos, who conducted the Seder underground, in great fear, and paid for it with their lives.

Generations passed over the Marranos, but they still celebrated the Seders!

That is the instinct of the people!

And how many pogroms, blood libels and trials the Seder nights have brought us!

That is why we greet these nights with great joy, and they remain with us forever as a historic sign of deliverance, of freedom!

The freedom which we honestly earned by giving the world morality, ethics, on which all mankind has been nursed and from which it draws[?] comfort to this day...

Can there be a greater gift than to understand[?] or to hand on the divine voice[?]!

And with joy, with songs of praise, our Haggadah is full — written in prose, but its content is poetry.

The Haggadah records the immigration into Egypt as well as the exodus from Egypt, when the first stone was laid for building a worldwide moral fortress.

And the narrator of the Haggadah also tells us who the redeemer was: no angel, no messenger led us out of the Egyptian exile, but the Holy One, blessed be He, in His glory and in His own person!...

Herman Szer.
What we do not know.

a) Why such dearness?
In various newspapers all over the world there are reports printed in quite small type somewhere in a corner, although these reports are in fact very interesting.

Thus, for example, we learn from a statistic of the Leipzig fair that in the year 1936 two million „se-gn“[?] [unclear unit] of maize were burnt in South America. The locomotives of the local railways were heated with it, because people were afraid that as soon as the maize (corn) came onto the market it would have to be sold more cheaply and the price would be spoiled...

In South America last year six hundred thousand cows were slaughtered and the fields were manured with them, because there was a „danger“ that milk and butter would become cheaper... For the same reason more than two hundred thousand litres of milk were poured into the sea there every day...

Eight million sacks of coffee, that is more than half of the entire production, were thrown into the sea in Brazil last year, so that coffee should not fall in price... They have even invented such machines that destroy the coffee in the fields. It should grow[?] and one should save the work of pouring it into the sea...

In California in 1936 more than ten million oranges were thrown into the sea, so that they would not have to be sold cheaply.

For the same reason in Florida the strawberries (wild strawberries, poziomki) on more than ten thousand hectares of field were left to rot.

In Canada in 1936 about ten thousand tons of wheat were burnt, so that it should not, God forbid, spoil the price. In Australia the streets were paved with the local sheep's wool.

In Hungary in 1936 hundreds of thousands of kilograms of apricots („marillen“, „apricozen“) were left to rot, because people did not want to sell them more cheaply...

This is only an extract of those very great values that were destroyed in 1936 — at a time when hundreds of thousands of people in the world are dying of hunger.

b) How many people live off the automobile?
One of the greatest inventions of the nineteenth century was, without any doubt, the automobile. At the end of 1936, 36 million automobiles were registered in the whole world (of them only 7 million in Europe). How many people live off the automobiles? Statisticians have calculated that four people live off every car. There is no doubt of this when one counts first of all the miners who extract the ore, then the people who process it into steel and iron, the designers, the engineers, officials and workers in the car factories; in the factories that make the various parts of the cars, the dealers and further employees, the various workshops that repair the cars, the chauffeurs, the garages and further people, and a whole further series of people who are occupied with the automobile industry. If one counts all this together, one arrives at the conclusion that the figure of four people for every car is not too large.

c) How much is a billion?
People speak so lightly[?] of a billion. But how few people know how much a billion is. In the year 1937, which we are now counting, barely a billion minutes have passed. If someone, for example, had a billion dollars and spent a thousand dollars of it every day, he would have to live 2637 years to be able to spend the last thousand.. Fifty wagons[?] of maize (corn) make up a billion kernels. If someone wanted to count these kernels, he would need 57 years for it, working eight hours a day (even on Sabbaths and holidays).

A forest of a billion trees is as large as Holland, Belgium and Switzerland together. — A person who talks a lot would have to talk eight hours every day, very fast, to get through a billion words in 38 years...

And we say it so lightly: a billion...

Z. Haber, Vienna.
Under Arab Terror (A Letter from the Land of Israel)

M. Hampel (special to the „Tsaytung“[?]).
Are we once again on the eve of serious events in Eretz Israel? Will more needless victims fall? Again an „uprising“? — These are the questions that greatly occupy the Yishuv, and no doubt the Jewish Diaspora as well.
In truth I must say that the disturbances which broke out about a year ago have not ended to this day. For almost 12 months the Arab terror has already lasted, for 12 months the Yishuv has been under fire, for 12 months the struggle has gone on, and more than once it seems to us that these events will never come to an end at all, and that under such circumstances fate wills that we should win the land.
It is also true that less blood is being shed and fewer victims fall, but lawlessness is growing and the anti-Jewish terror movement is spreading considerably[?].
The Arab „emigration“ through the deserts and borders has not been shut off[?]; on the contrary — new murderers penetrate by the hundreds from the neighbouring Arab countries without the slightest hindrance on the part of the government. No faithful[?] guard is posted, a Jewish watch on the border is hardly to be found — and who is to stop them, and why should they not „immigrate“, when the borders are a no-man's land? The Arab newspapers do write: „Youth of Syria and Egypt, come to the help of your brothers in Palestine! Come to Eretz Israel, for here there are rich Jews with plenty of money and beautiful daughters“!
The Arab press has been turned into a kind of public arena from which people incite, organise, and call on the blind masses to arm, to mobilise and to the „holy“ war.
And the government censorship? It is very rigorous[?] and exacting[?] towards the Jewish press, yet it keeps silent about the Arab press, which poisons the souls and minds of its benighted readers. Thus, for example, this „press“ has invented new lies for its readers: in the Jaffa government hospital (where the two Jewish nurses perished) there is a single Jewish doctor who uses healing pills[?] and medicines that lead[?] to killing the Arab patients... And should such words not speak to the imagination of the half-savage Arab[?]? And should such a lie (one of dozens) remain without effect? The riots in Tiberias, the new victims in the Jezreel Valley: Dr. Yosef Leres[?] and the pioneer Chaim Bruck — that is the bitter sum total of the wild incitement and the Arab terror.
And „our“ Mufti? He too does not rest, and does his work quite nicely. He goes from village to village, summons the fellahin to the holy mosques, „teaches“ the Koran — which means: burn, kill, murder and rob. And when he also makes use of the legend about the holy Arab places that are supposedly in danger — he has certainly reached his goal, and his „work“ is finished and complete. You want to know the consequences of such a piece of work? Robbery and murder...
In the country chaos and disorder still reign, and the government does nothing to abolish the abnormal[?] situation, to make the atmosphere „healthy“[?]. To this day it has not uncovered the nest of the „murderers“, to this day it has not found those who go on brandishing[?] „liberation“[?], and punished them. The government is still ready to go in for compromises and negotiations with the Arabs, while us Jews it wants[?] to teach morals — that we should restrain ourselves and hide in holes when we are shot at... Is it any wonder, then, that our neighbours are full of arrogance and impudence? Is it any wonder that the events still go on?
The Yishuv is again wrapped in deep mourning, and once again we stand at the graves of our own Jewish victims. Doctor Yosef Leres[?], the only Jew in an Arab town, Beisan (Beit She'an), was known among the local Arab population as a good doctor who healed almost half for free. Friends advised him to leave the Arab town, but he heeded the voice of his heart: „I stay here among the suffering, where I have to fulfil the mission of a doctor“ — and here the murderous bullet struck him. He fell for his duty to man and for his love of the land.
On 11 Adar, on the 17th yahrzeit of Trumpeldor, on the day that symbolises Jewish heroism and élan — we again heard similar and, to us, well-known words: „It is good to die for the freedom of our people“! (Chaim Bruck of blessed memory). As then. From[?] the bloody days of Tel Hai to the bloody days of Tel Amal 17 years have passed, but our existence and defence have not been broken off, the will to build a land has not been destroyed, the pioneering spirit has not been crushed, and we are ready to give everything — our lives too — until the liberation comes!
The government „consoles“ us in our deep sorrow, it „reassures“ us that the bloody period belongs to the past, that calm has been restored in the country and that it controls the situation... Many troops have returned to London[?], the guarding of the roads has stopped, the Jewish supplementary police has been disarmed, and the saboteur again stands at the helm, and everything is a free-for-all, and no one knows who rules the country: the Mufti or the High Commissioner, the murderers or General Dill...
The „present“ tense situation in the country recalls those days before the outbreak of the disturbances, that poisoned air which caused the eruption. The same vile creatures are again busy fanning a new fire, and if the government continues to remain as „neutral“ as before — then who knows what the day may bring?
Day in, day out we warn and draw attention to the poison seeds being sown in the dark minds of the Arab masses, but the government neither hears nor sees.
We warn once again: the present „peace“ in the country bodes ill, the present „calm“ is a harbinger of new calamities. Will the government perhaps now at last learn a chapter in the ways of the world? Will our voice perhaps now at last not be a voice crying in the wilderness?
— Happy are the believers!
A Topical Matter

[Będzin — City council; municipal budget and Jewish education.] By City Councillor Ch. M. Zylberberg.

(Ahead of the budget sessions of the Będzin city council.)

Every budget, as is well known, is divided into two parts: revenues and expenditures. We Jews are everywhere made imposed "in-laws" of the first part of all budgets, because we take a very large share in the revenues of all budgets in general and municipal ones in particular; but when it comes to the second part of the budgets, the expenditures, then we are "forgotten" — worse, in the best case our needs are taken into account to so small a degree that it would really have been better to forgo everything altogether. The conclusion from this is that our representatives in the municipal bodies must vote against the budgets.

In connection with the latest budget deliberations of the Będzin city council, the writer of these lines wishes to touch precisely on a painful[?] matter that directly concerns Będzin's Jewish community, especially the people of no means.

As is well known, we have compulsory schooling for children aged 7 to 14. The state treasury does indeed spend enormous sums every year on schooling for children of that age; poor and rich alike, all are provided with a free school. The municipal bodies also take a small share in the budgets of the public (elementary) schools — by maintaining the premises for the schools and the teachers, school equipment etc.[?] — but even this small share costs this city of ours a sum of 156,200 zł a year (the budget for the year 1936-37), not counting the value of the rent for the schools housed in municipal buildings.

The total number of children attending the municipal public schools reaches 6789; that is to say, 1 child costs this city at least up to 23 zł a year.

And here one wishes precisely to deal with a matter, a specifically Jewish one. The question of education among Jews is well known. More than one father does not eat his fill so that he can pay tuition fees for his children, for the public school is by no means sufficient to give a Jewish education — especially, and all the more so, as regards the education of boys, as Maimonides of blessed memory rules, that "the education of sons is above one's means"; and poor fathers indeed give their last groszy for Jewish heders and schools, which have state rights and stand in for the official public schools, and in which the secular subjects are at a fairly high level, to which the inspector of all schools of the Sosnowiec school district bears witness.

In the said Jewish heders and schools about[?] 935 children study, for whom the city administration would have had to pay, reckoning 23 zł per pupil, around 22,000 zł a year. But how does the matter look in reality? Years ago, even under the rule of President [mayor] Sichel[?], the said Jewish schools got back, in the form of a subsidy, from 3 to 6 thousand zł a year. In the last years, by contrast, all the Jewish schools together receive the laughable sum of 600 zł a year, i.e. about 70 gr. per schoolchild. And the situation of the said schools is so[?] bitter — the teachers are literally starving and the parents give their last groszy. The question arises: should the magistrate rid itself of the matter with the small sum of 600 zł?

How does the matter look in other towns with a similar population structure? Take, for example, a town such as Białystok, whose population is barely 2 times that of Będzin and whose Jewish percentage equals Będzin's: last year it received 24 thousand zł for the same purpose, and when this year the subsidy was reduced to 18 thousand zł, the Jewish councillors decided not to vote for the budget. The same also on the question of the municipal loans — if the city administration does not restore the subsidy to [lit. "and"] its previous amount.

Of course the situation in this respect is, by comparison, better with us; but in any case we, the Jewish councillors, must deal with the budget question before the sessions, to talk it through among ourselves, so as not to be wronged in this area in the new budget.

We must also remember that last year the subvention was supposed to be in the amount of 1500 zł, and at the vote it was reduced to 600 zł.

On this occasion it is also worth mentioning the role of our "left-wing" Jewish councillors, who joined with the non-Jewish councillors, and all voted against raising the subsidy for the Jewish school system.

The writer of these lines, as vice-chairman of the audit committee, who has the opportunity to observe how the budgets are carried out, can assure with a clear conscience that a proper subsidy for the Jewish school system would not, God forbid, burden our barely 2-million municipal budget; but it depends on the awareness and sense of responsibility of the Jewish councillors.
“Zangen” — Supplement for Literature and Art. L. Szpigelman: Yes, One Must Look Deeper (Literature, Books, Readers)

[Literature — essay; “Zangen” supplement.]
[ZANGEN (“Ears of Grain”). Supplement for literature and art.]
L. Szpigelman.
Yes, one must look deeper (literature, books, readers).
In connection with the propaganda campaign for the Yiddish book, the editor Nachman Meisel declared that it is necessary to prevail upon the Jewish reader to spend a few guilders [złoty] on a Yiddish book. By this — the author concludes — the grave question of the crisis will not be answered at all.
Drawing a parallel with the sefer [the traditional religious book], which held such an honoured place in the Jewish home of old, where everyone found in his books spiritual nourishment that was later handed down from generation to generation, the book of today — which was supposed to replace the sefer of old — stands lonely in the Jewish home, because the children no longer read it. To them the whole complex of Yiddish literature, of Jewish problems, is foreign.
There are many national-minded Jewish homes, active public workers, where a Yiddish book and a newspaper have no foothold. Therefore — Mr. Meisel concludes — the matter of Yiddish literature must be understood much more deeply and broadly, and a fine place and an honoured position must be created for the Yiddish book.
Certainly, today's generation is not being brought up in the spirit of the Yiddish press and book, even though there are rare[?] achievements and one can well educate oneself on our literature. There are various reasons for the decline, and we blame first of all our little literary world, because there in Warsaw no attention was ever paid to the question of prestige; no one considered what is fitting and what is not, what does us honour and what degrades us in the reader's eyes.
As for people who still bought a book now and then, when they had the understanding to appreciate Yiddish literature — they were disappointed, seeing in what manner they were deceived by authorised agents.
We do not say, of course, that this entitles[?] the sympathiser to step aside, but he is left with an aftertaste from the deceptive[?] dealings, and this distances him from the Yiddish writer and book.
And indeed one has to state that the growing generation is not being brought up on Yiddish literature; but here we by no means blame the parents, for it is not they who are guilty if the surroundings and the people all around have changed[?]. On the other hand, guilty of this are our spokesmen, leaders and writers, those who have the press at their disposal, around whom the people gather, and to whom the Jew looks up with awe and reverence.
True, a good deal of irresponsibility (hefkeyres) has arisen in this field too, because of which trust in the printed word has weakened, and so one goes steadily downhill to the point of being unbearable. This degrades Jewish honour, and quite often[?] people begin to avoid anyone who has any connection with the Jewish people and with public life.
And then the question arises: did you, representatives of the printed word, not see with what impetus assimilation is breaking in on one side, and the boundless irresponsibility of “literature” on the other, and in parallel with this the Yiddish book is being mercilessly robbed[?]? Surely you watched this process — so why did you remain indifferent? Why did the PEN and literary clubs not react to it properly?
It is still far too little to find the reasons why Yiddish literature finds itself in an abnormal situation. Instead one must try with every possible means to bring it to full normality and to its proper height.
This problem must be taken up by our men of letters and poets and by all who know and have understanding for the Yiddish book, literature and education.
“Yung-Zaglembie” (Young Zagłębie)

[Literature — Zagłębie; the “Yung-Zaglembie” group.]
Zagłębie.
A rush of people, factories, mines, alleys, chimneys.
The Jewish poverty of shopkeepers and cobblers roars, sirens howl, chimneys spit red with soot and smoke.
Streets, alleys and slag-heaps.
“Rufers” [touts] drag customers in the alleys into the shops, jump out of their skins, bang keys on tin signboards, ring, drum; couples dance to the wild beat of hysterical jazz in pastry-cafés [cukiernie] and cabarets.
Zagłębie — the golden province.
Beneath the smoke-veiled face of the Zagłębie sky, in its coal-dust-polluted, pestilent, dense air, people live, people love, sing, birds chirp — the “Young Zaglembiers” sing[?], the quartet “Yung-Zaglembie” sings.
Four years, four [mipule — unclear word] years filled with torments, barely [enough] for anthology booklets.
Four years, four hard years of struggle with society — for society, sabotaged by the Jewish literary centres — have hardened and strengthened us.
Now we stand in enlarged ranks, ready for new, broadened work.
We are organising a circle of all young Jewish poets, in whatever language they may write — writers, musicians and artists in Zagłębie and Silesia.
We are building a centre of our own.
Y. Erb.
Poems by A. S. Pushkin

[Translated poetry — Pushkin.]
[Poems by A. S. Pushkin.]
To the Poet.
Poet, do not prize highly the people's love!
The great song of praise will soon vanish,
you will hear the judgment of the fool, the laughter of the mob;
but you, stay calm, hard, firm and cold.
You are a king: live alone. Go your free way
wherever your thought leads you.
Deepen your work, your dearest purpose in life,
and for your good deed demand no thanks.
It is within you — the highest judge, after all, is you yourself.
No one can value your work as you can.
Are you content, artist? Then let anyone, great and small,
revile, spit on the altar where your fire glows,
and with childish glee disturb your spirit[?].

Elegy.
I have seen death: he sat
by my quiet threshold,
I have seen a grave; a door opened:
and thither my hope flew in.
I shall die — and the empty traces of my youth
no one will notice.
And the beloved gaze will not be met
by the last gaze of my eyes.
— — — —
Forgive, sad world, where a dark path
lay before me over the abyss,
where life gave me no comfort,
where I loved, and was not allowed to love!
Skies pure and clear,
beloved mountains, merry rivers,
the bright early morning —
and you, joyful shadows of the mysterious forest and valley —
forgive, forgive for the last time.
From the Russian: B.[?] Sternberg.
S. Rotenberg's Illustrated Almanac of Jewish Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — literature and history; almanac.] S. Rotenberg has undertaken to publish an illustrated almanac of Jewish Zagłębie. The almanac will give expression — in pictures and in writing — to the whole social life of the Jews of Zagłębie in all its nuances[?].
It will shed light on the origins, development and activity of the kehillas, and of the cultural, professional, philanthropic, sports and other Jewish institutions in Zagłębie, as well as on the history of the Jews in this region.
In addition, the almanac will contain a section on Zagłębie Jews abroad, in which articles will be printed about the activity of the Zagłębie landsmanshaftn in the various countries, such as: America, Canada, England, France, etc.
The almanac, which will contain some 200 pages in magazine format, has a whole series of writers and historians taking part, among them also Prof. Bałaban, Dr. Ringelblum, Kantor-Mirski and others.
The first printed sheets lie before us, and we can assure that the publication will be a revolution in Jewish publishing, both as regards the material and the technical execution, which stand at a high cultural level. The work is being printed on the most expensive illustration paper, with over 100 artistic reproductions.
With this work a monument is being erected to Zagłębie Jewry, which has a 700-year history behind it, and it is certain that all strata of local society will know how to appreciate properly this colossal cultural-historical achievement.
Miniatures

[Literature — prose sketches; Sosnowiec.] By Heshl Dantsiger.
I.
Two laughs...
Against the background[?] of a dirty, sweaty face the whiteness of two rows of healthy teeth stands out — a healthy laugh rings out. On a human[?] calloused palm a silver coin sparkles...
His joy grows from moment to moment; who is happier than he now: he has earned with his own ten fingers, with his own sweat, enough to get through a day without worry — for himself and for his dear little children and his wife.
— Who is happier? Who can laugh louder, stronger? — — —
...Sopot. The casino hall. Around the long table sit men in stiffly starched[?] white, deeply décolleté ladies, faces masked with the greatest effort, flaming eyes and hands, uncontrolled hands, nervous, trembling, greedy, weeping[?], broken...
The roulette wheel turns. The little ball runs, jumps over, hops senselessly, lips whisper: rouge... noir...
Hands tremble.
— Lost. The mask falls off, it did not hold.
A chair tips over. A young man leaps up.
He has gambled away a whole fortune. Now he will no longer be able to throw money around, to spend on women. What is left is barely enough to live like a petty bourgeois; Sarlega[?] will run away from him,... others too. His face is terrible, the eyes bulging[?], and most terrible of all is his laugh — a crazed, broken laugh.
— Who is unhappier than he?
— Who can laugh more terribly? —
II.
Eve of Spring.
The earth lies cold, frozen — [?], under heavy leaden skies; at its head the yellow light of the wintry sun [?].
— And on the eve of spring hope is born, that:
the radiant messenger of nature will come — spring, and will revive the dead of humankind, which longs for spring — for the hope that carries within it the good tidings of reawakening nature.
Sosnowiec, 1937.
From the Book Table

[Literature — book review.] "Simfonishe gezangen" [Symphonic Songs] (poems, music and poems [poemes]) by Pinchas Jassinowsky. New York 1936.
The very name of the book already tells us that we are dealing here with a poet-musician, which among us Jews is a rarity; for that reason alone it is worth dwelling somewhat more broadly on the contents of the book.
The poet is enchanted by the symphony, by the wonder we call — "world". But he regrets that "people, armed[?], trample everything and torment themselves over life and death with the sword" ("A Night in the Mountains"), and further: "Hungry, hungry is the whole world, granaries full of grain; abundance of gold and money — not a cent for medicine" ("Hunger").
The poet believes, however, that a miracle will happen and the world's evil will perish... Meanwhile, though, we stand before a mystery! "Who can understand reality and fathom the secret of the world?" But the poet comes to the conclusion: "The more the days pass, the more comprehensible the secret becomes to me, the tracks lead to the Creator, to the foundation of 'One'" ("Philosophical Poems").
And since the poet is a great musician and composer, "he tightens his harp-string and sets about pondering with earnest intent the root of the mystery, with the help of a chord"! ("Thoughts").
And here the poet gives us ten songs with music, which sound very melodious and folk-like and are true pearls of musical literature. Especially outstanding is the song "Der royber" [The Robber], both for the beautiful content of its text and for its melodious, elegiac music. A pity that the poet translated[?] only half of the song into Hebrew and set it under the notes. The same happened also with the songs "Storm Winter", "Shabbat Kodesh", "Thoughts" and "For the Children"; but if in the other songs the matter is not so noticeable, in the song "Di royber" [The Robbers] it is an enormous[?] defect in the Hebrew text.
The poet is also strongly enchanted by Beethoven, and he dedicates to him "Symphonic Poems" over a full 36 pages with piano music to the Third and Fifth Symphonies.
How sad sounds the poem on the death of Beethoven, who in his lifetime depended on the charity of strangers; only some time after his death was he exhumed and brought for burial in the Vienna cemetery next to Franz Schubert: "And the spirit of these giants will forever bring us joy; never will the world forget their ringing words."
Finally it is worth noting that the book is very aesthetically produced and is worthy[?] to adorn with its splendour every better home.
Elchanan Zider.
