A town that is "Jew-free".
"Polonia" reports with satisfaction that the only Jewish family that had still remained in Pless-Bieruń [Pszczyna district] has also left, and that they are about [?] to have the closed synagogue dismantled.
Merger of both Jewish artisans' organizations.

[Katowice — artisans.]
On Sunday, in the "Concordia" halls, the festive act of the long-awaited fusion of the Jewish artisans' organizations existing in Katowice took place, i.e. of the German-Jewish one and the so-called Polish-Jewish one (affiliated with the Warsaw headquarters).
With a large number of participants, president Mr. S. Kaufman opens the meeting, explains its purpose and the agenda, and proposes to elect Mr. Markus as president of the united Katowice artisans' organization.
The latter is unanimously elected president and, taking the chair amid loud applause, Mr. Markus honours the deceased members, dedicating a few warm words and a minute of silence, all present standing.
President Markus then presents the programme of activity, calls for harmonious cooperation, and thanks president Kaufman for his successful efforts and for the sacrifice [?]. — Resigning as president, [Mr. Kaufman] also thanks Messrs. Kneler and Zucker and proposes to elect a united board, and the society's bodies are elected unanimously, consisting of Messrs. Kaufman, Kneler, Zucker, Milner, Lasnitzer, Schiller, Feltscher [?] and Prager. President Markus expresses his wish to elect as vice-president Mr. Kaufman, who has achieved much for the Jewish artisans of Katowice, being also a member of the Central Committee in Warsaw.
Several of those present also speak [?]; Mr. Kleiman proposes to elect a special commission for cultural activity.
Mr. Markus closes the meeting.
We wish the united Katowice artisans' organization fruitful activity.
Jewish soldiers at Judaic-studies lectures.

[Katowice — army and religion.]
After taking over the function of military rabbi, Rabbi Chameides "tsḥ. pnd." [?] organized lectures on Judaism for the Jewish soldiers of the Katowice garrison, who come [?] every Sunday morning to the Katowice synagogue.

It is desirable that the other military rabbis in Poland follow the very useful example of the rabbi full of initiative, Rabbi Chameides.

Stage and Variety

[Sosnowiec — theatre and culture review.]
I.
“The Runaway” and “Her Last Word”, staged by the Comedians' Theatre in Sosnowiec.
Neither play sins, God forbid, by too much literary quality. Both are imported from America and are cut to the generally accepted American pattern.
In every American operetta there must be an innocent condemned man whom the bride casts off because of a slander; meanwhile the bride loves, loves and longs, and it simply tears at your heart — but after two hours of weeping and singing the truth must come out like oil on water, and one goes home with a light heart.
* * *
Nevertheless the company of the young Comedians' Theatre deserves a few warm words for its serious attitude to the stage, and is admirable because there are several gifted actors among them.
First of all Moshe Zelwer [?] and Krasnow. One may have reservations about the former (especially when he plays a role that demands [—]); in the role of the runaway he was indeed weak, he did not bring out the transitions, did not convince, and at moments gave the impression of a beginner; on the other hand Zelwer was very good in the second piece, “Her Last Word”.
Almost the same can be said of Krasnow: he too was pale in “The Runaway” and played convincingly in “Her Last Word”.
Among the women, first place goes to Nadia [?] Rodina and Miriam Woronowecka [?]. The latter has very fine diction and was excellent in her character part in both productions.
But if one can have complaints about this likeable company regarding its larger productions, they are all in their element in the revue part.
Zelwer is a fine reciter. Lutzky's “Sasales” [?] were recited excellently, and he is also quite a decent monologist.
Krasnow, for his part, is a first-class singer. “Katerinka” as well as the Russian songs were performed by him very finely.
If we add that Nadia [?] Rodina dances not badly and that Abramow [?] performs the role of the compère quite decently, it becomes clear that the revue part is really very respectable.
* * *
The conclusion for us:
The comedians are a young company, but there are fine talents among them. They bring in something new, trying to combine in every performance a play and a revue — something which until now used to happen only at benefit performances and prize performances [?]. They do their work with seriousness and dedication. We, in turn, must help them develop, so that in time they can give polished and more valuable productions.
They deserve it.
II.
A Peretz Academy organised by the “Lira” in Sosnowiec.
On me, as a visitor from out of town, the initiative of the Sosnowiec “Lira” made a good impression. “Israel is not widowed” — that is to say, even in a town where there is not a single Jewish library, people remember a Jewish writer.
It is only a pity that Sosnowiec overestimates (for the better) its own powers. The lecture on Peretz turned out uninteresting. The lecturer, Dr. Liberman, did not dwell precisely on Peretz's work and his influence on the development of Yiddish literature, etc.
The artistic part already stood on a higher level. Although the recitations were weak (we mean those of the first amateurs), the dance stagings [?] on the other hand were very successful, especially “Bontshe Shvayg” (a pity that the finale came out pale for purely technical reasons).
Natan Blum recited “Monish” very finely (about his interpretation [?] as the defender in “Bontshe Shvayg” one may have serious reservations).
Also successful was “The Shabbes-Goy”, performed by N. Blum and the director of the drama studio in Sosnowiec, Sami Feder.
In short, an event in its proper place, although with a less [?] commercial calculation it could have turned out far more impressive.
Taking part were: Messrs. Sami Feder, Natan Blum, Stefa Wampel [?], the sisters G. Grendes [?], Fajgelbaum [?], Goldberg, Żelanka [?] and the tiny Fajgelbaum [?] brothers, who were rewarded with resounding applause.
P. Blumenkranc.
Public opinion must be heard.

[Będzin — rabbinate; opinion.]
(Concerning the rabbinate question in Będzin.)
The rabbinate question in Będzin has already "[—]" [—]; both sides have come out to fight and want to settle the question in this way.
It is very hard to speak about rabbinate questions in general, and about the Będzin one in particular.
The question actually arises: why has the matter suddenly become so topical, so burning, that even in the hardest days before Passover, when one must first of all care for the poor, for kimcha [de-Pischa, Passover flour relief], for the bread of affliction, for kashrut and other such festive matters, everything was put aside and people set out to solve the rabbinate question "on one foot" — a question they want to push through without any excuses?!
Simple people, naive citizens, ordinary householders all year round[?], who do not understand all sorts of over-clever schemes, cannot grasp what has suddenly happened here and how the above question stands.
Simple people do not know that, for our many sins, a town can be "blessed" with a rabbi when there is an opportune moment, when a chance turns up that favours this or that side — and as has happened now, or more precisely: the "Aguda" [Agudat Israel] is preparing itself for this "little piece of work"; it previously cleared out[?] Jews who were a "stumbling block", and, riding in the Jewish gmina [community board] on the kehilla nag, one must [?] understand what they are after[?] and for what purpose one actually sits[?] in the gmina.
That is the answer, the pure, sincere answer, why the question has become so burning and topical precisely in the days before Passover.
After all, today is not like the past, when a town had to elect a rabbi and the Jewish citizens decided such a matter with their votes. Now a few parnassim [community officials] are needed, and they alone decide for the community, for it is them, after all, whom we actually sent there to care for Jewish society and for our interests.
But we live in times of lawlessness and terrible demoralization, when representatives take no account of their voters nor of the postulates, but do as they please and as is convenient for them, so that under these conditions it was easy to "provide oneself" with an eastern-wall seat[?], and then one shows the community a fig and cries "crack nuts"...
That is roughly how the state of the rabbinate looks nowadays.
This time we are not taking a position on which candidate should occupy the Będzin rabbinical seat and who should not; at this moment that is not topical and also premature, because such an important question — we hold — must under no circumstances be disposed of, so to speak, on one foot, like a matter of chit-chat, even when one has the means to do so.
It concerns, after all, [—] a religious personality in the town, who must direct both the whole rabbinate system[?] and the religious affairs of the kehilla; so why should one not approach such an important problem with decorum and deliberation? True, the town does not have to elect a rabbi. So what — does that mean one need not ask the opinion of the town's householders, of the town's notables, of people whom the town costs[?] and who have an interest in religious representatives? Must one go over the heads of the town's personalities merely because the law does not require them? Need one not consult the town's people, Hasidim and non-Hasidim, when such an important matter is at stake?
And if there is no unity, if acts of violence are committed — will that bring good to the town, will peace and tranquillity reign then?!
We hold that the matter is not so burning at all, and one must not go over the heads of the citizens who maintain Judaism in Będzin; it does not matter, there is time to come together[?] and consult about this problem, and whatever is to be done must be with the consent of broader[?] circles, to whom the town is dear and precious and whose entire lives are, head and most, devoted to town affairs.
Yes, one must look at the question differently from those who are out to see that X or Y be provided with a lifelong livelihood; at this moment the concept is a much higher and more ambitious[?] one and must therefore not be regarded that way.
But if the party-interested people pay no heed to all this, if they stubbornly go on with their personal fight, then one can foresee[?] a long chain of disputes and quarrels, which will confound[?] and soil the [—] Jewish life, and God alone knows what that may lead to.
One recalls all this when casting a glance at the near future of Będzin's Jewish communal life[?]: one becomes pessimistic, and melancholy seizes the Będzin resident who will have to live in the [—] conditions.
The Jewish population here must therefore not remain indifferent to this question. And if a clique will by no means take public opinion into account, then the town's notables must come and say that their voice too must be heard; otherwise they too will bear responsibility for the deeds done — even if (and perhaps precisely because) they did not want to lend a hand to all this and stood at a distance watching Jews sow hatred and enmity among themselves — they will have helped bring about what is against their will and against their logical understanding.
The rabbinate question, or better said, the rabbinate fight, is already ripe, and without any excuse a position must be taken on how it should be finally settled in such a way that the town is not turned into hatred and disputes for generations to come.
This must be considered already now by people who seek the welfare of our citizens and the honour of its inhabitants.
R. Les.
Bill for a new guild (crafts) law

[Poland — crafts and artisans; legislation.]
The bill of the Union of Chambers of Crafts has been submitted to the Sejm by Sejm deputy Snopczyński [?]: the bill for a new guild law (crafts law).
The bill is meant to change the structure of the crafts and — in the opinion of its authors — put an end to "partactwo" [Polish: shoddy, unqualified workmanship]. All the artisans' problems which neither the guild law of the year 1927 nor the amendments ("novellas") with their countless clarifications, issued over the last few years, have been able to solve.
The most important provisions of the new bill are:
Everything that cannot be regarded as factory production is recognised as a craft. The principle is adopted that every industrial occupation, if it is not yet carried on in a factory manner, is automatically regarded as a craft.
To run an industrial workshop one will need, as until now, an artisan's card, to be issued by the chambers of crafts and not by the industrial authority.
All trades will be divided into 3 categories: licensed (concessioned), regulated and free.
The licensed ones are to include painting, carpentry (ciesielstwo) and the like [printed "eglikhe"]; the regulated ones — a large number of the crafts existing until now, as well as printing, milling and others. The free trades are to include part of the trades existing until now, among others glazing, brush-making, cap-making [?], hat-making (kapelusznictwo), photographers, ritual butchers, and sausage-makers, and besides that the whole of small industry. Artisans of the first 2 categories will be required to hold master's diplomas. Only on the basis of the diplomas will they obtain artisan's cards. The others will receive artisan's cards without any difficulties. Article 146 of the guild law, thanks to which artisan's cards could be obtained even by persons who held no journeyman's or master's diplomas, is abolished.
Every youth employed in a craft workshop is regarded as a "terminator" (apprentice). One will be admitted to the master's examination only at the age of 24, that is, after 5—6 years of practice as a journeyman.
Chałupnicy [home-workers], especially those who will employ outside people, will be regarded as artisans and will be subject to all the rulings of the new law.
M-n.
Just Like the "Shtibl" of Old

[Reportage — youth life; the tea-rooms ("herbaciarnie") as the new "shtiblekh".]
By Icchak Janasowicz.
(Reportage).
It is in the nature of every older person to lament times gone by.
An elderly pious Jew, sunk in worries about making a living, tells with a sigh about the old days, when he was still a boy.
"I tell you, young man," this Jew sighed deeply, "what once was will never be again. I am not talking about the fact that once there was a livelihood and today there isn't. I am not talking about the fact that once people knew nothing at all of all the good things one knows today — I am talking about the youngsters. What does today's youth know besides going to the 'clubs' and the 'dance halls'[?]? In the old days — you see, if you came into our 'shtibl' [small prayer house], you would have known what it means to live. Don't think that all one did there was sway over the Gemara. True, we studied too, but apart from that it was homely there; something drew you into the 'shtibl' like a magnet.."
I heard the Jew's words out and kept silent. Not only because I had nothing to answer him. I could have shown him that the old 'shtibl' life has not gone under at all; it has only taken on new forms. The peculiar type of the 'shtibl-bokher' has not disappeared either; time has merely recast the old and worn-out into a new form. Basically things have not changed — only the forms.
I would advise you to go into one of the many "herbaciarnie" [tea-rooms], sit there a little, and look and listen to everything that goes on there. After half an hour in such a tea-room it will seem to you that you have landed in an old-time 'shtibl' from which the Gemara volumes and all the other holy paraphernalia have been removed; the young people you see before you will look like yeshiva boys who have changed into "German" [modern] dress and shaved off their sidelocks.
Everything here is as in the old 'shtibl': people get heated, talk the Jewish way with their hands, hold each other by the lapels — only the subject matter of the conversation has changed. Instead of "two who hold a prayer-shawl" they talk about the "two who hold — Spain"; instead of studying the commentary on Gittin and Kiddushin, they study a commentary on the economic-political situation in France, on the Arab terror acts in Palestine, argue about the Moscow trials, and one is ready to tear the other to pieces over the question of dictatorship and democracy.
There are many such 'shtiblekh' in town that have been transmigrated into "herbaciarnie". I will pick one, located, let us say, on Sarbata[?] Street.
The outward look of this tea-room naturally attracts[?] no one, but inside the 'shtibl' is more than modest. Dark and smoke-filled, and in the air hangs a thick, curling[?] smell of cheap papirosy smoke. The little tables are even covered with oilcloth, but the oilcloth is torn in places and lets the raw wood show through. The oilcloth that is not torn is densely covered with pencilled figures and has long since lost its white colour.
The "guests" here are regulars, old-timers, and everyone knows everyone else well; here they spend the greater part of the day. There are even some who come here in the morning and go home only at night to sleep. No matter — they can afford it; their businesses won't run away in any case. So they sit, the unemployed young men, from morning till night, and for breakfast they eat — a discussion about the new kehilla and about the rabbinate question etc.[?]; and if someone is a great "glutton and drunkard", he snacks on a portion of news from the paper. There are also exceptional ones[?] here who allow themselves — no more and no less — to read right through "The History of the Great French Revolution" or "The Minimum Programme of the Mexican Syndicalists".
Everything here is as it once was in the 'shtibl': they tell one another about a good meal they ate in… a dream. Just as in the old days, the scholars are[?] absorbed today — not in Gemaras, but in thick crumpled booklets; and although they talk and debate so much about the reality of our time, they have nevertheless lost the feeling and the sense for real life — they have, as in the old days, crawled into the world of the book.
When I came into this tea-room I found quite a few young people; they were heated, waving their hands, and each wanted to out-shout and convince the other. The question was the absorptive capacity of the Land of Israel. Hottest of all was a fellow with a mop of hair long since ripe for the barber's clippers; he hurled figures, made ashes of his opponent and [—][?], and even the opponent regarded it with a certain respect, for comrade Mendel is not just anybody — he is a "masmid", who has studied "Capital" through, and a passage of Kautsky he will recite to you by heart, as a yeshiva boy of old would a passage of the Maharsha.
The crowd got heated and quarrelled, and the owner stood behind the buffet and yawned. Finally one of them, a short fellow whose throat had already gone dry from the discussions, spoke up:
"Fellows, we ought to have a bite of something."
The others got angry at him:
"Don't interrupt!" they shouted, boiling[?] with rage. "Why did you raise the spectre of hunger? You'll muddle an important point, and we still have to discuss Jabotinsky's appearance before the Royal Commission."
But little by little everyone grew tired and began to look at the door.
Meanwhile a strange young man came in and ordered a quarter kilo of bread and a marinated herring.
The fellows eyed the stranger and began a new discussion about the "Reich"[?] policy in Austria and in Hungary..
The Doctor's Well-Deserved Jubilee. Brief Character Sketches.

L. Szpigelman
Tomorrow the Jewry of Zagłębie in general, and that of Będzin in particular, gathers to celebrate the 40th jubilee of Dr. Weinzieher's public activity.
Eight years ago, when the jubilarian was dangerously ill and the Jewish population of the town was anxious about the doctor's condition, people asked in fear about the state of his health; and when the danger had passed, and we reported this to our readers, the joy was beyond measure: the telephone did not stop ringing, everyone wanted to know everything exactly, and whether the news about the prognosis[?] was true.
This small touch characterises how beloved the doctor is in the town.
40 years of public activity, 40 years of being occupied with the community, 40 years of engaging in the upbringing of forlorn little orphans and making human beings of them — that is no small thing, and all this under the worst and hardest conditions, for previously the orphans had no communal roof over their heads.
Does the public know with what patience, forbearance and endurance the past forty years have been bound up[?]? And these are, after all, the finest years of a human life. At the time[?] when people look around for ways to improve their situation, to make it softer — for which the doctor had every chance — he throws himself with all his zeal into[?] the people and puts himself at the disposal of society body and soul; for the doctor still belongs to the older generation and cannot understand how people can take public duties upon themselves and not fulfil them. He knows that as soon as one becomes president of an institution, one must carry the whole burden oneself. He is not one of those who merely want to get the title of president. In general the doctor hates with utter hatred the [—][?] public "work" which consists of ringing the bells, talking about this and that, while standing in one place, at a dead point.
• • •
Work looks quite different in the orphanage: there, calmly[?], quietly and modestly, grand things[?] are created; everything is carried out systematically and according to plan. A guest who comes to the orphanage from time to time sees improvement and enlargement on every occasion[?]; and when one examines[?] the budget that the institution needs and has at every moment, only then does one see that the town is far from fulfilling its obligations towards this colossal institution.
Dr. Weinzieher's ideal is the orphanage; his greatest happiness is seeing[?] children being brought up as good citizens and faithful sons of their people.
As we have already noted above, the doctor has achieved much for the public life of Będzin, which is without doubt of the greatest and most important significance; yet we firmly hold[?] that the doctor is lucky, otherwise it would be impossible to understand how admirers were found for the jubilee committee that has arisen[?]; because however much one may value and honour the achievements of the jubilarian, however dear and precious the person may be — he belongs to no party at all, and then[?] there is no one left to remember him. Therefore we hold that the doctor is lucky that, despite all the "shortcomings", he has not been forgotten... For, let us not fool ourselves: to whom does someone belong who wears no kalpak[?] (party cap), who does not know or does not want to distinguish between one human being and another?
• • •
It is characteristic: Dr. Weinzieher is not a Zionist, although Zionists gather around him; assimilated Jews group themselves around him, even though he is far from their views; and the same is true of pious Jews and democratic elements.
All listen with reverence to the doctor's words[?], whether in the City Council, where he speaks not only before Jews, or at a lecture, where a varied public hears him; all honour him and value his well-weighed[?] opinion. And this — so we hold — is because the man is honest and sincere; he has a heart that is very sensitive; he does not know how to distinguish between one person and another — his credo is to help and to understand all who are in need of help, excluding no one, whatever people and country they may belong to.
Instead of a toast, may we be permitted to wish the esteemed jubilarian long life, courage and energy in the public arena[?], which shall yield fruits of blessing and glory until the celebration of his 50th jubilee.
"Some Acquire Their World in a Single Hour"

[Będzin — Dr. Weinzieher's 40th jubilee; reminiscences.]
As I now move my pen across the paper to sketch a few lines and outlines about the person who is in our town [?] the central Jewish figure and occupies the first place on the eastern wall [the place of honour] of Jewish communal work — about the esteemed jubilarian Dr. [Salomon] Weinzieher — I truly do not know where to begin, for to enumerate and appraise his numerous deeds over the long period of his public activity one would have to write an entire book. I therefore wish to content myself, to pause and sketch only one single episode from the relatively distant past, [?] from a full 20 years ago, which until now has not only been absolutely unappreciated, but almost forgotten.
"Some acquire their world in a single hour," our Sages teach us. There are people who make themselves immortal and eternalise their name in one moment, through one single deed; and in such moments the person, the creator of that deed, grows beyond himself, beyond his own awareness — rather an unconscious [?], secret force drives him to it, and he feels an inner urge to act thus and not otherwise; and neither he himself nor his surroundings feel or know that something magnificent, something historic has been created.
And just such a deed, of the above-mentioned category, our esteemed jubilarian performed in our town.
But in order to make the matter stand out and to understand more clearly the importance of the event, one must first characterise Dr. Weinzieher's political biography and orientation.
From his earliest years Dr. Weinzieher was radically inclined, yet at the same time always a declared, ardent Polish patriot. How far his patriotism went is best attested by the following fact, which occurred immediately [?] after the outbreak of the war in 1914: as is well known, Russian was at that time obligatory in the schools as the language of instruction. Dr. Weinzieher made use of the favourable moment when the Russians had just left our town and demanded of Mrs. Szpicer [?] — then head of the elementary (people's) school — that she introduce Polish as the language of instruction, regardless of any consequences.
And another characteristic fact, which occurred three years later, in 1917, in that horrible and tragic time when the world was drowning in seas of blood and rivers of tears, when the German occupiers had subdued with iron tongs [?] and ruled the whole country — at that very time a certain great personage was specially delegated from Germany to influence Jewish society to introduce German as the language of instruction in its schools, and for this purpose a meeting of certain communal workers was convened. But in this case too it was none other than Dr. Weinzieher who came out against the proposal, pointing out that in the Polish school system no language other than Polish may prevail; and the result was that Dr. Weinzieher emerged as the victor and the personage capitulated.
And now to the main point, to the historic fact by which Dr. Weinzieher "acquired his world" [printed „קונה עלמו“]: in 1916 the German occupation authorities ordered free town-council elections. Two election committees were founded, a Christian one and a Jewish one headed by Dr. Weinzieher, and the following characteristic incident occurred: the Christian election committee demanded of the Jewish election committee that, since the Jews after all constituted [?] a majority and were therefore entitled to a majority of the mandates, the Jews should nevertheless voluntarily renounce their majority in favour of the Christian population. The demand naturally provoked a difference of opinion in the Jewish camp, but here the ardent Polish patriot Dr. Weinzieher revealed his Jewish national pride and declared in a categorical tone: No! We may not and will not renounce our civic rights, which we are fully entitled to enjoy together with all citizens. And at that very moment he acquired his world and sanctified the Name; by this decision he proved that one does not become a patriot through submission, servility and "mah yafit" [fawning] behaviour, but on the contrary: a more sincere patriot, who fulfils all his duties to the fatherland, can and must at the same time be a proud national Jew and have the courage and boldness to renounce [sic; evidently "not to renounce"] the rights that are naturally due to him as a citizen of his country.
The outcome [?] of those elections was such that a purely Jewish town council was elected, which was crowned with the historic name "Sanhedrin", with Eng. Gustaw [?] Weinzieher as president, and which existed for two full years, until the revival of the new Poland.
And that Dr. Weinzieher did not lose his Polish patriotism even after that historic event is best shown by the "Kościuszko celebration", which fell in 1917 and was carried out with the greatest success; it made an enormous impression on the whole population and brought honour and fame to the Jewish "Sanhedrin".
And now, on his 40th jubilee, as we wish him further fruitful public activity — may these memories give him fresh youthful courage and energy and remind him that "some acquire their world in a single hour".
Y. Wygodzki.
Dr. Salomon Weinzieher

As a physician and public worker.

There is [?] in human fate something like a lottery ticket, through which individuals are made fortunate.
The recognition of people's merits in the field of their scientific and social work is likewise like a lottery.
The first prizes go to great writers, poets, philosophers, composers, etc. [?]: so it is with literature, history and the press — that is truly a matter of fate. By contrast the lesser ones, for instance great mathematicians, astronomers, medical inventors, are remembered on the day of their birth, of their invention or at a jubilee celebration. How is this to be explained? Because poets, writers, historians, national [figures] [?] are esteemed more than the pioneers of technology, [?], architecture, medicine, pedagogy? To answer the question one must take into account the abstract thoughts of which our Sages say "if there is no flour there is no Torah". Bread and the body are 2 important factors without which mankind cannot exist; but precedence goes to hunger and illness — only then comes the spirit. And when that is [secured] [?], the road to culture is easier.
For example, is the director of a hospital who is at the same time a doctor, who sacrifices his whole life for the sick, not as useful a person as the poet, the painter and the like? Does he not deserve the same recognition from his society, from his fellow citizens?
Should a public representative, who gave up his private life and honestly and proudly defended our rights, be forgotten? 40 years as a physician and public worker, not striving for monetary wealth but serving the principle "I am for the people and not the people for me" — is that a small virtue?
Who defends our honour besides him? Who is a greater democrat, a defender of truth and an opponent of falsehood, than he? Who is a lecturer at the People's University and a teacher to his students in the hospital?
[?], such wreaths of splendid deeds must not be forgotten; the future historians will give our jubilarian his due honour in the history of the Jews of Poland, as also for his activity in the Polish parliament.
This, then, is our jubilarian — may he live to 120! This is our popular Dr. Weinzieher, who on the 10th of this month celebrates — and together with him all Jewish Zagłębie in general and Jewish Będzin in particular — his 40th jubilee in the field of his medical and social activity.
Most honoured jubilarian! May you be privileged to work for the common good for many long years. Be strong!
Your work is unforgettable for ever; it remains in the book of remembrance in golden letters! Together with all Jews and all people I wish you, and so do my children, your pupils, that you may live to have joy from your creations! Jewish medicine, Jewish Zagłębie and all Israel take pride in you.
Herman Szer.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Shemini)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Shemini
—o—
a) "And to the elders of Israel" (Lev. 9:1)
Once the son of the Rebbe of Lizhensk [Leżajsk], R' Shmelke, came to Ropshitz [Ropczyce] to try to obtain the rabbinical seat of Ropshitz, which had just become vacant, for his brother, the Rebbe R' Naftali. He called a meeting[?] of the heads of the community and gave them to understand that his brother was the most suitable candidate for rabbi of Ropshitz. One of the community leaders present remarked that R' Shmelke was speaking only out of personal interest, because he wanted his brother to be rabbi in Ropshitz.
Said R' Shmelke:
On the verse "and to the elders of Israel" the Midrash Tanhuma says: "The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: call the elders and anoint him, so that they should not say he made himself High Priest." That is, [God] ordered Aaron anointed in the presence of the elders, so that Aaron would not be suspected of having taken the priesthood for himself. The question arises: if people are going to suspect, they could just as well suspect Moses of having anointed his brother on his own initiative — but had Moses had selfish intentions, he would surely have taken the priesthood for himself, for whoever has personal interests exploits them sooner for himself than for his own brother; therefore Moses was not to be suspected of selfish intentions.
"So too — concludes R' Shmelke — if I were not concerned with the good of the cause but with my own benefit, I would surely be striving to become rabbi myself... and the fact that I am striving not for myself but for my brother, whom I consider fit for it, is the best sign that I mean the truth..."
—o—
b) "And make atonement for thyself and for the people" (ibid., 7)
The Netziv [R' Naftali Zvi Yehuda Berlin] was a childhood friend of the famous Haskalah writer Chaim Zelig Slonimski. Once Ch.Z.S. intervened with the government concerning[?] compulsory[?] government schools; the intervention stirred up the Orthodox world, and the Netziv rebuked him for it. Ch.Z.S. justified himself, saying that his intervention had only had a good intention and that he had been suspected for nothing. To this the Netziv said to him:
Of Aaron it is said "and make atonement for thyself", i.e. that he needed atonement for the sin of the Golden Calf; although Aaron meant it for the sake of Heaven, he still needed atonement, because — as the Yalkut says — by his deed with the calf he gave occasion for people to suspect him. Of the High Priest, too, it is said: "He turns aside and weeps and they turn aside and weep; he weeps — because they suspected him." So it is a bad sign if someone causes people to suspect him...
• • •
It is further told about the relations between the Netziv and Ch.Z.S.[?]: when the Volozhin [Wołożyn] yeshiva was closed, the Netziv came to Warsaw. While staying[?] as a guest in Warsaw, he was visited by educated people, rabbis, scholars, Hovevei Zion, maskilim, etc. Ch.Z.S. was living in Warsaw at the time and did not come to visit the Netziv. Once the Netziv met him in the street. The old friends embraced, and the Netziv asked him:
— Did you know that I was in Warsaw?
— Yes.
— Why then did you not visit me? Do you bear me some grudge?
— No, God forbid; but as I heard, you were in need of the goodwill of the Warsaw Hasidim, and I know the Warsaw Hasidim well. If Chaim Zelig Slonimski had visited the Netziv, they would at once have suspected him, and I did not want to be guilty of causing you to be suspected on my account...
The Netziv understood the allusion[?] to their former conversation and smiled.
—o—
c) "And they died before the Lord" (10:2)
R' Yehuda Aryeh of Modena [Leone da Modena], who in his books came out against making marriage a mitzvah, said in one of his sermons, as a witticism:
One of the reasons the Midrashim give for the death of Nadab and Abihu is "because they did not marry wives." The question arises: the verse says explicitly that their sin was "and they offered strange fire before the Lord, which He had not commanded them"? But in truth their sin was indeed because of the "strange fire" — only, had they had wives, the wives would have scoured away their sufferings: the wives themselves would already have been the greatest punishment for them...
—o—
d) "But let your brethren, the whole house of Israel, bewail the burning which the Lord hath kindled" (ibid., 6)
A person is indeed obliged to accept his sufferings with love — but only his own sufferings, not his fellow's. Therefore Aaron indeed had to keep silent and accept the tragic death of his sons, but his friends, the Jews, indeed had to grieve and weep: one may not accept a fellow's sufferings with love. Divrei Shaul.
• • •
"A prayer leader who errs is a bad sign for those who sent him" — and if Nadab and Abihu were punished, it is a bad sign for the whole house of Israel; therefore "let your brethren, the whole house of Israel, bewail the burning which the Lord hath kindled". Yalkut Yehuda.
—o—
f) "And their carcasses ye shall not touch" (11:8)
"And this is what they said: a person must purify himself on the festival." Rashi.
On the eve of a festival the Rabbi of Lissa [Leszno] (author of "Chavat Da'at") came to Warsaw on an urgent matter. When R' Shlomo Eiger heard of it, he came at once to welcome him. In the course of conversation the Rabbi of Lissa hears R' Shlomo Eiger call him "Rebbe", and says to him jestingly[?]:
— If you held me to be a rebbe, you would have come to welcome me only tomorrow, on the festival, as it is said: "A person must greet his teacher on the festival"; and since you come on the eve of the festival, it is a sign that you consider me barely an "eve-of-a-rebbe"...
R' Shlomo Eiger answered him:
— By the expression "on the festival" the Talmud means the eve of the festival: when it says "a person must purify himself on the festival", it cannot mean on the holy day itself, since one has to purify oneself on the eve of the holiday; therefore here too it means the eve of the festival..
What Will the English Coronation Cost?

There is today no newspaper in the world that does not bring sensations every day about the coronation of the English king [George VI], which will take place on 12 May of this year. All papers are full of reports on various matters of the coronation. It is already known today how many guests will come from Australia and how many from the Indian princely courts, because these guests from the distant places have already left home, and it is almost known, too, how many foreigners there will be altogether during the coronation in London.
The official bodies reckon with about 160 thousand foreign guests, among them about half from "sebr lis"[?] [unclear word] and the other half from the great European states. Of course the hotels and restaurants are counting on it; they are raising prices and preparing all good things, so that the guests will feel well with them.
The greatest worry of all this, however, falls on the head chef ["Ober-Koch"] of the English court. More than 8 thousand people from the four corners of the world have been invited to the "wedding". Kings and princes from everywhere will have to be provided for for about 2 weeks — dependent[?] on the king's table. One can imagine that this is no easy matter, especially since among these guests there are thousands of Australian persons who must be fed according to their custom, according to the customs[?] and dishes they are used to eating at home; surely one needs a real "minister's head" for it, so that it can be carried out properly and [unclear words: "smon kore"[?]].
But however great the expenses of the English state during the coronation, they cannot be compared with the sum of expenses the guests themselves will have; everyone will have to bring along a hefty "mortgage" [i.e. a considerable sum], if he is invited to the "wedding".
First of all, clothing. There is an exact description of what everyone has to wear to the "wedding canopy" and to the meal, and everyone must be dressed exactly as the ceremonial prescribes.
The most money will be spent on the ladies' toilettes. An ordinary lady — of whom only very few are invited — wears a dress trimmed with ermine two and a half centimetres wide (it may not have more).
Such a dress of a better fabric costs at least 240 pounds. But non-genuine ermines (made of Chinese hares) are also permitted[?]; such a dress costs only 122 pounds. Baronesses, peeresses[?], viscountesses, countesses and duchesses must wear genuine ermine. For them, too, it is prescribed quite exactly how wide the ermine border must be.
The duchess must wear an ermine collar over the dress, which alone costs 320 pounds; in addition the dress 60 pounds, the girdle 5 pounds, the crown 20 pounds; gloves, shoes, stockings — all in all one can reckon with 430 pounds that every duchess will have to spend.
The men, too, will have to spend a fortune, if they have not kept the garments from the last coronation: velvet breeches, a three-cornered hat, a sabre, shoes, gloves — all costing, according to the rank of the guest, from 70 to 140 pounds.
Added to this are the various articles that everyone buys as a souvenir. In the archive of the Leipzig Fair there is a list of the articles which various countries sold at the last coronations.
There is no article in which pictures of the crowned couple were not stitched in or worked; all countries of the world were invited to manufacture fine articles and sell them as souvenirs at the coronation. It was wanted that all industries of the whole world should "do good business". For the present coronation, too, all industrial articles from all countries that produce souvenir articles for the coronation have been admitted without limit of number, and everywhere people likewise hope to do good business at this greatest show of the last 25[?] years, which — as experts assure — will bring in more than twenty million pounds to the commercial world of all the countries of the whole world.
Z. Haber, Vienna
The Jubilarian About Himself

[Będzin — personalities; interview.] A conversation, as[?] reported by S. Lewkowicz.
I found him at a "solid"[?] (calm) hour; he was cheerful, though[?] this time without the ever-pessimistic look of Dr. Weinzieher; and indeed, when I tell him the purpose of my visit, he bursts into hearty laughter and says:
— You can write my biography in a few lines, short and to the point: I was born (that, after all, is beyond doubt...), studied, did things, but more for others than for myself, and the main thing —
— I go on living.
— But, excuse me, Doctor, your most devoted[?] friends, from [—] the large number of readers of our paper, would like details of your so[?] rich life.
Then the esteemed doctor turns serious, his broad forehead stands out more, and he says:
— True, my life has indeed been rich; quite[?] strange and remarkable it is that the richness of life stands in fact[?] in inverse proportion to material wealth: the richer life is, the smaller the material wealth; the poorer life is — the more one enjoys material wealth. When I am asked what I would want if I were to start again from "Bereshit", to begin living anew — to be rich, or to be poor but to go through a life of emotions and strivings to improve the general condition of all humanity — I would choose the second.
Let us leave aside[?] — says the jubilarian — the philosophical system, and turn back[?] to the so-called "story of my life".
I went through my gymnasium studies in the era when the Tsarist government wanted with all its might to carry out the Russification of the Polish intelligentsia; not to speak of the lessons — even uttering a Polish word was treyf. In the Piotrków gymnasium where I studied there were notices that it was forbidden to speak Polish, but the repressions brought a negative result, because the repressions bound the Jewish students even more to Polish ideals and Polish culture and to the Polish great spirits: Kościuszko, Mickiewicz and others. "We learned Polish among ourselves and studied Polish literature; it was characteristic that the best Polonists were Jews; in general, relations among the student youth were quite different from today...
The first time I felt the "yellow patch" on myself — that I am a Jew — was in 1888, when on the basis of the percentage norm the Tsarist universities were closed to Jews; the decrees robbed me of almost two years, and only after a sharp telegram to the then Minister of Education (who, incidentally, threatened me with exile) was I privileged[?] to be admitted to Warsaw University. There I took an active part in revolutionary work, which later caused me, together with other students, to be expelled from the university — again a year lost.
After going through various experiences I finished my studies some time later. In 1997 [sic; read 1897] I arrived in Będzin, where I began[?] to occupy myself with political, social and philanthropic affairs. I founded a number of societies and institutions, Jewish and non-Jewish, in which I made a name for myself, and indeed during the elections to the First Duma I was put forward as a candidate by the Polish Democracy.
And the work was colossal, because one must bear in mind — says Dr. Weinzieher — that Będzin 40 years ago was very poor in the cultural, social and political field. The first society I founded is the "Dobroczynność" [charity society], of which I am president to this day; then — an important economic institution, the Mutual Credit Society, which brought great benefit to Jewish merchants; I am also one of the founders of the Polish real school that still exists today — but who is able, and to what end, to enumerate all of that; I am altogether far from any public self-advertisement.
— It seems that you, Doctor, were president of the kehilla?
— Those "unpleasant" memories I wish to avoid entirely. Precisely when I was elected a Sejm deputy for the second time, I became head of the Będzin kehilla, but I managed to free myself from that office.
An important date in this jubilee is played by the jubilarian's role in hospital affairs. In 1921 Dr. Weinzieher was elected director of the Będzin General Hospital, but when "new times" arrived, things became too tight for him there...
In 1929 he takes the post of director of the Sosnowiec Jewish Hospital, which stands[?] firm thanks to the management of this tenacious public worker.
— I had intended — says the jubilarian — to withdraw from public work, but the hard Jewish situation, which grows worse from day to day, compels me to stand at my post and defend Jewish honour and Jewish rights.
The Living Dead Man

A. Zaglembier
The Living Dead Man
(A most thrilling novel of Jewish life in Zagłębie before and after the World War.)
(3

Summary of the beginning of the novel.
One winter evening before the World War, when two Cossacks were about to transfer the dangerous bandit "Szmulek Łapka" to the Piotrków prison, they were suddenly attacked on the way to the Będzin station by two disguised "strażniks" (guards) — Łapka's helpers. At dawn the Cossacks were found lying bound with their mouths gagged, and Szmulek "Łapka", set free, had fled to the [—] road and hidden himself somewhere[?].
That same evening, and almost at the very same hour, the universally known, respectable debt-collector Yosl Wertheim — a father of three children — suddenly disappeared. His wife Sarahtshe runs about the town terribly desperate, searching for him in every possible hiding place in all of Zagłębie. But Yosl Wertheim vanished like a stone in water...
At the same time the police were energetically searching for the thief Łapka, for whom wanted notices (Steckbriefe) had been sent out everywhere; but Szmulek Łapka too vanished like a stone in water. Then this mysterious affair was taken up by police inspector Charecki[?], a specialist in this field.
Now read on.
Charecki himself had of course known the vanished young man as a very serious[?] and respectable person. According to the statements of his wife, friends and acquaintances, Yosl had never had any conflict or quarrel with anyone, and, as was established, he had no money of the firm on him at the time either. It may well be possible that the murderer was mistaken, thinking that Yosl did have money on him, and that was why he was killed.
But if so, where did his dead body go? Not a single plot of ground in all of Zagłębie and beyond had been left unsearched. And the trained police dogs had still[?], in the best case[?], never misled and had always discovered the murderer, or the murdered, and in "many" cases — both together...
All the work[?] was taken in hand[?] by police inspector Charecki himself.
Soon, however, he had to admit to himself that to a s k is much easier than to give an a n s w e r. Still, he did not, like others, at once drop his hands and remain helpless. No, he caught every sound, every turn, in the thought that perhaps the truth would unexpectedly leap out from there...
And at last, on the fifth day after the tragic disappearance of Yosl Wertheim, it looked as though some ray of light had suddenly begun to break into the thick darkness...
For the strange, tragic story, which happened at a time when people were not yet used to such cruel crimes as today — had already become known far and wide. The Warsaw and Petersburg newspapers too wrote about the disappearance of Yosl Wertheim, and there was not a single Jewish home — especially where Yosl had been known — that did not at times weep[?] over the unfortunate Sarahtshe.
And everyone was ready to do something, to help clear up the terrible riddle.
Where, after all, had he gone, Yosl Wertheim?
If he had really been murdered, why is his body not found? If he is alive — then why did he vanish so without a trace?..
And out of pity for the unfortunate Sarahtshe, various people turned up who came and told: that on that day they had seen Yosl here and there; but no one could point out[?] the exact place and hour. Nor did anyone remember whether Yosl Wertheim had then gone alone or with someone else, and whether he had been carrying something with him or had empty hands...
Did it then occur to them that they were seeing Yosl for the last time in their lives?..
Nevertheless police inspector Charecki heard out all the witnesses very attentively and seriously and recorded their statements exactly.
Nor was he too lazy to go himself, or to drive with the witnesses, to the place in question where Yosl had been seen for the last time... On the spot he might orient himself better and find out something more...
So the police inspector, together with an old Będzin merchant, drove out especially to Sosnowiec. The latter led him to a side street where he had then seen Yosl. But at which house number this had happened, the merchant did not remember.
With a second Jew Charecki went to Pogoń[?]. All these inspections, however, had so far brought no tangible result whatsoever.
Until at last, on the fifth day, when the police inspector was sitting at his writing desk, just busy with another matter, the young steelworks (huta) worker Wacek entered his office — an ugly, pock-marked gentile lad with big ears and a somewhat crooked nose. Wacek, however, was an honest man. He stayed standing timidly by the door, crumpling his cap in his hands.
"Good morning," said Wacek, and gave a little cough, thinking[?] that the police inspector had not even heard him come in.
"Good morning," answered Charecki, giving Wacek a look with his deep, piercing eyes. "Whom do you want?"
"You."
"Me?" Charecki wonders.
"Yes."
"About what?"
Wacek stays silent a while, as if he had still not overcome[?] the thought he had been wrestling with for several days... But now he saw that backing out was no longer possible. After all, he had come especially to tell everything... So he made up his mind quickly[?] and began:
"I have come about the disappearance of the Jewish collector Yosl Wertheim..."
"What? You?!" Charecki jumped up from his seat, greatly astonished, for this was the first Christian witness to come forward of his own accord. "Please, sit down."
And when Wacek had sat down opposite the inspector, still timidly glancing around the office, Charecki went on questioning him, writing down at once everything the pock-marked man said:
"And who are you?"
The pock-marked Wacek gave his first name, surname and address.
"Do you know Yosl Wertheim personally?" the inspector asks further.
"Not personally. But I have seen him many times..."
"And when did you see him for the last time?"
"Last week."
"On which[?] day, last week?"
"It was Wednesday."
The police inspector began looking at Wacek even more piercingly. It was precisely on Wednesday, the tragic day, that Yosl had not come home any more to his wife and children. But the new witness's manner struck Charecki as something very strange... and he suddenly asked:
"When did you learn that Wertheim had disappeared?"
"Right the next morning."
"How?"
"Everyone was talking about it."
"Where? At your place, in the works (huta)?"
"No," — Wacek became very confused — "in our courtyard. We live among Jews on the Grobla[?]. Afterwards I also read it in the newspaper."
"Then why didn't you come right the next morning to report it?"
The question confused Wacek still more and he did not know what to answer. The police inspector noticed his great embarrassment at that moment, and his clear mind at once whispered to him that if this really was a witness from whom[?] he was to obtain important information, he must conduct the interrogation so that Wacek would not become flustered and lose his head.

Sefirah Season

[Der Kokh-Lefl — humour.] The Sefirah (counting) season in Poland is in full blaze[?]; in this field there is, for instance, no unemployment.
The "rabbinate-seekers" in Będzin count how many [?] one must bribe...
The new kehilla leaders in Sosnowiec — count how many złoty[?] the commissioner left behind.
The butchers — count how many "pieces" they still have left of the cattle quota.
The pickets — count how many Jewish shops must[?] close[?] on every street.
The "loshnikes"[?] — count how many meetings they hold each month.
The Keren Hayesod activists in Sosnowiec — count on their fingers the number of Zionist declarants...
The Dąbrowa parnassim — count the days until there will again be some business dealing...
The dacha[?] wives — are already counting the weeks until the holidays...
And at the Jewish philanthropic societies one counts... the poverty.
And I count the advertisements of Jewish firms in the Jew-baiting press...
He Loves the Endek Press...

[Der Kokh-Lefl — humour.] On a tram a Jew is reading the Endek newspaper "ABC". Opposite him sits an Endek [National Democrat], who cannot bear the outrage, and he turns to the Jew with the complaint:
— You have your own newspapers, so why do you grab at our press?
— In the Jewish newspapers — answers the Jew — I find only Jewish troubles. In the Endek newspaper, on the other hand, they write only about Jewish wealth, Jewish prosperity, from which I get great pleasure.
Communiqué from the "Shomrei Shabbat"

[Der Kokh-Lefl — humour.] The "Kokh-Lefl" is asked to publish:
Five minutes before candle-lighting one may no longer give the customer change.
After candle-lighting every iron object is muktzeh, and the wife must use exclusively wooden objects for throwing[?] at the husband[?].
Scratching counts as forbidden labour; it must be carried out by the janitor (stróż).
Putting out the light must be done by the governess — in French.
Manufacturers who are pious Jews may not see how their Jewish workers work on the Sabbath, as well as on weekdays, like donkeys[?], because it is written "that thine ox may rest"...
Women's Hair / The Wise Son Does Not Give

[Der Kokh-Lefl — humour.]
1.
Wife: I found a long black hair on your coat. Tell the truth — are you having an affair with a woman with black hair?
He: Don't talk nonsense, Zoshe[?], that's one of your own hairs, from before you became a blonde.

The Wise Son Does Not Give
[Sosnowiec — humour.] Delegates who were collecting[?] for kimcha [Passover flour for the poor] went in to a well-known Sosnowiec miser to ask for kimcha for the poor for Passover.
The rich man received them nicely and said to them: I think highly of the mitzvah of giving for kimcha, since it corresponds to the Four Sons, the 4 sons mentioned in the Haggadah — and he takes out 3 gulden and gives it to them.
— How's that — say the delegates — there are 4 sons, so why do you give only for three?
— The Wise Son does not give — answered the rich man.

— What is the difference between a loan and counting the Omer?

What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 28 Nisan 5697 — piątek 9 kwietnia 937 [Friday, 9 April 1937].)
Będzin
The Ger–Radomsk „Match“ Is Wobbling...
As our readers know, an agreement was concluded between the Ger and the Radomsk Hasidim, under which the „firms“[?] [i.e. factions] of both sides are obliged to vote for the candidacy of R' Mendel Lewin as rabbi and for R' Dawid Halberstam as „podrabin“ [deputy rabbi].
But, as we are informed, things are close to the „match“ being called off, because the Radomsk side has little trust in the assurance that Halberstam will afterwards be elected „podrabin“, and instead demands that first of all Halberstam be elected moreh hora'ah [rabbinic decisor].
The proposal has aroused discontent on the Ger side, and work is going on on all „fronts“ so that the match should not be spoiled over these „trifles“.
She Gave the Bill to the „Right Landlord“

[Będzin — swindle.]
The baker's worker Judel[?] Fajman (Sandruszewska[?] Street 44) went off to work, leaving with his wife a bill of exchange for 56 złoty, which she was to give the landlord as rent.
At about 11 o'clock at night, when Mrs. F. was already in bed, she heard knocking at the door.
Thinking that the landlord had come to collect the bill, she went to the door and asked: „You surely want the bill?“ — and hearing the answer „Yes“, she handed the bill through the half-open door and went to sleep.
The next morning, when the real landlord came and demanded the bill, it only then became clear to Mrs. F. that she had been tricked.

On the Memorandum of „Agudas Yisroel“.

In this connection the national dozors have turned with a memorandum in which the whole rabbinate affair is set out factually. Among other things it is also stressed that Rabbi Khamayres[?] is properly fulfilling the functions of acting rabbi.

Next Tuesday at 8.30 in the evening a recitation evening will take place in the WIZO premises (Sanczewska[?] Street 13) with the participation of the artist Natan Blum, who will perform a new programme.

Drunken Beggar Smashed a Pane
A drunk came into the jewellery shop of A. D. Balimazski[?] and demanded alms. When he went out without the alms he had demanded, he smashed a pane of the entrance door out of revenge. The police drew up a report against the drunk.

Tea for the „Orphanage“
Was donated for the holiday by the representative of „Wissotzky“, Mr. J. S. Gancwajch[?], and by the firm S. Wajsbart.
Children of Today...

[Będzin — children; runaway.]
Szalom Szpigelman, 12 years old, a pupil of the „Yesodei ha-Torah“ cheder, left home on Sunday afternoon saying he was going to cheder, but instead of the cheder he went into „Orbis“ [the travel bureau] and bought a ticket to Gdynia[?]. Before departure he took provisions for the journey with him, which he bought at Dyszkin's branch shop, and so on[?]...
And so that his parents should not know where he had gone, he made his own friend Szmul Szpigelman give him a handshake-pledge that he would not tell.
Naturally, the parents, seeing that it was already late in the evening and the innocent little Shloyml had still not come home, became uneasy and a search began, but without result. Their agitation grew still greater when the next day too there was no trace of him. Only on the third day was a telegram received from Gdynia[?] from a certain Mr. Wachs, saying that the „gem“ was there.
As it turns out, the boy had long been dreaming[?] of the journey. For this purpose he had saved up 52 zł. in a savings book for travel expenses.
They Went to „View“ a Bride and Met „Bridegrooms“

[Będzin — matchmaking; police.]
Mrs. S. travelled with her brother-in-law Mr. Plawner[?] to Strzemieszyce to „view“ a bride. On arriving there they went to a woman they knew in order to obtain information about the match. Just then a [police] search was taking place in the acquaintance's flat, and on coming in they too were detained. The city administration has decided to engage a psychiatrist for the madhouse in Buszowice[?], so that[?] from now on[?] the mentally ill will at last be under the control of a „rector“ [sic; read: doctor].
Sosnowiec — General Meeting of “Bikur Cholim”

[Sosnowiec — charitable institutions.] On Sunday [?] a general meeting of the members of “Bikur Cholim” took place in the beth midrash in Old [?] Sosnowiec. With about 60 members present, the president, Mr. Reuven Binensztok, opens the meeting and proposes Mr. Rajchman as chairman, to which those assembled agree.
Invited to the presidium are Messrs. the feldsher Jakub Zajchner [?], the vice-president of “Linat HaCholim” Bunem Szpiler, editor S. Lewkowicz, the delegate of “Tomchei Cholim” in Szelce—Słabecki [?], and Bezalel Terens [?] as secretary.
After the reading of the minutes of the last general meeting, the treasury report of Mr. Kornfeld is heard. It turns out that nearly 50 per cent of the income is spent on medical aid; over 2000 zł. was paid for medicines, and the society also provides a great many important medical appliances and the like [?]. Unfortunately the attitude of the Jewish population is a very weak one, as a result of which a large number of needy people cannot be provided for.
The activity report is given by the president, Mr. Binensztok. This time the report is an original one: instead of recounting signs and wonders, Mr. Binensztok accuses himself and also the board of having done nothing with regard to what needs to be done — but who is the greatest culprit? — The members, because of the 600 “reklarired” [?] members barely about 250 pay.
Then a discussion begins. The dozór [kehilla board] member Mr. Reuven Czapnik accuses the board of having conducted a frivolous [?] activity, on account of which the report is a pale one. The board did not turn to the broad strata, but always to the rich, and it is, after all, a rule that “the rich don't want to give”...
Also speaking are Messrs. Sendyszew, Kac, Zajchner, Bekerman, Goldenrat [?], Kasirer, Spiler, Klajman, Platek and Czapnik. The last declares that the new kehilla board has in its programme to concentrate all philanthropic institutions under its authority.
Then Mr. Binensztok speaks on the question of creating a “Beit Lechem” at the “Bikur Cholim” society. After the explanations of editor S. Lewkowicz, as vice-president of the Będzin “Beit Lechem”, it is decided that “Bikur Cholim” will extend its activity to the field of supporting convalescents with food products.
By acclamation the following board is elected: Reuven Czapnik, J. M. Kornfeld, R. Binensztok, H. A. Wajstuch [?], A. Rajchman, H. Ajzenberg, M. Dajczman [?], B. Lauren [?], H. Waksman, A. Englard, J. M. Ginzburg, M. Czechowski, J. Wajcberg and M. Rajzman [?].

Later part of the new board gathered in the apartment of Mr. Czapnik, where over a glass of “Carmel” a series of questions concerning the further activity of the institution was discussed.
If the Train “Made a Mistake”, the Groom Is Not to Blame...

[Sosnowiec — local story.] The story happened during the past Chol HaMoed Pesach. A groom from Kraków came to a local [?] Orthodox family. When the groom's father learned that the groom had travelled to Sosnowiec to his bride, he demanded by telegram that he come home, so that he would not remain in Sosnowiec for the second days of the holiday.
The groom, poor fellow, had no desire to go home, but — when father orders, you go.
The bride's side, however, absolutely wanted the groom to spend the holiday with them. So they hit upon such [?] a ruse: they escorted him as far as Szopienice and, instead of travelling on to Kraków, they so “misled” him that he went back by train to Sosnowiec. And the bride's side calmed him, saying that a “mistake” had happened with the train, and since it was too late to travel to Kraków, he stayed with the bride.
“Pure” Maccabists Back in Power

[Sport — “Maccabi”.] In Maccabi's own premises a members' meeting took place for the fourth [?] time, at which the fusion with the “Gurdia” [?] was rejected and a board of “pure” Maccabists was elected.
Elected were: Wilhelm Szwajcer (president), Kronenberg and M. Liberman (vice-presidents), Litman (treasurer), Kimelman (secretary), Mendelewicz, Łęczycer, Komrad and Cytryn (“gos-hadarosh” [?], probably “gospodarz” — steward).
The new board organized a ping-pong match with the participation of the vice world champion Mr. Ehrlich and the candidate for world champion Mr. Bukiet (Sosnowiec), who came out the winner.
The board has also set about organizing a propaganda month for Jewish sport; for this purpose a series of events will take place.
Pigeons Before the Judge's Bench...

[Court — local.] An interesting trial took place last Tuesday in the local municipal court.
In the dock sat 2 young Christians, who had been charged with keeping [?] carrier pigeons.
— Do you plead guilty to the charge? — the judge asks the first of the accused.
— I am innocent — answers the accused — and the proof: I have brought along a pigeon, and one can establish at once whether it is a carrier pigeon.
The same statement is made by the second accused as well; he too has brought along a living “witness” — a pigeon.
Merriment in the hall is aroused by the statement of the witness, who indeed has a carrier pigeon with him in order to establish whether the charge is well-founded.
Then the opinion of an expert is heard, who was specially summoned to this trial from Katowice.
The expert and the judges as well examine the carrier pigeons and the ordinary pigeons. It turns out that the pigeons which the accused own and the carrier pigeons of the witness are two different “races”. On this basis the accused are acquitted.
Meeting of Bookkeepers.

[Professional associations.] In the premises of the Small Traders' Association a meeting of bookkeepers took place, in connection with legalizing the branch of the Bookkeepers' Association in our town.
It was decided to carry out a recruitment of members. For this purpose a representative is on duty every day and registers the members.
The first examinations in Jewish studies at the Jewish gymnasium

[Będzin — education.] At the local Jewish gymnasium, examinations in Jewish studies ("limudim") were held in the eighth gymnasium class. All the pupils who finish the school this year sat the examination. This year's eighth class is the last one of the former girls' gymnasium, which later went over to co-education. Even though most of the examined graduating girls ("abiturientki") have been pupils of the gymnasium for only 2—3 years, they nevertheless showed great proficiency in the Judaic studies; this is owed to the strenuous and energetic work of the management and of the teachers. The pupils were examined in the Hebrew language in: religion, Tanakh (Bible), Hebrew literature and Jewish history.
It is worth noting that the examinations had a purely internal, not official, character, since these were the first since the gymnasium has existed. The Hebrew matura, however, which will take place in a year's time, will be an official one, and the pupils will receive Hebrew certificates.

Festive Farewell Evening at the Soldiers’ Kitchen

[Kielce — kehilla, Jewish soldiers.]
On the night after the last day of Passover a festive farewell evening took place at the soldiers’ kitchen which the kehilla had arranged in the premises of “Maccabi”.
The evening was conducted by Rabbi Rapaport, who delivered to the soldiers an inspiring speech about their role as loyal citizens of the Polish state, towards which they fulfil their civic duty, and as future military men in the Jewish army in Eretz Israel. Rabbi Rapaport took leave of the soldiers with the blessing that he might meet with them, together with all Jews, in the land of our fathers.
The soldier Militau [?] of Przemyśl thanked, on behalf of the soldiers, the kehilla headed by its president Piotrkowski for the painstaking work in organising the Passover kitchen and for the meticulous [?] treatment and the very good board during the 9 days of the holiday, which they spent together pleasantly.
After a photograph was taken, the soldiers sang the Polish and the Jewish anthems and took a hearty leave of the kehilla representatives present.
Celebration of the Beginning of the Book at the “Toras Chesed” Yeshiva

[Kielce — religion and education.]
Next Sunday, at 6 in the evening, an impressive celebration of the beginning of the [Torah] scroll of the “Toras Chesed” yeshiva will take place in the “Linas Halaylo” [?] beis medrash. Taking part in the celebration were [so in the original, past tense] the Kielce rabbinate, all the Kielce Admorim [Hasidic rebbes], kehilla dozors [board members] and parnasim, as well as representatives of all organisations. The festive prayer was led by cantor Górnicki with the choir.
Great Success of the Keren Hayesod Campaign

[Kielce — Zionism.]
The Keren Hayesod campaign is being conducted with great success. In the course of eight days nearly 150 declarations [pledges] for a very considerable sum have been collected. Very many declarations from new contributors have also come in. The collectors are received everywhere with a friendly welcome.
It is now already certain that the campaign will be concluded with brilliant success.

Second Yahrzeit of Shimon Kajzer of Blessed Memory

[Kielce — Zionism, memorial.]
Tomorrow, Saturday, falls the second yahrzeit of the well-known Zionist activist Shimon Kajzer of blessed memory. In connection with this, on Sunday, the 11th of this month, at half past three in the afternoon, a memorial gathering will take place at the Kielce cemetery, in which friends and comrades of the deceased will also [?] take part.

[Kielce — Zionism.]
This Sabbath the well-known Zionist activist, member of the party court of the Zionist Organisation in Poland, Adv. Trepman, will stay in Kielce; at a meeting of the representatives of the Zionist groupings he will proclaim this year’s [Zionist] shekel campaign in our town.

Meeting in the synagogue about the F.O.N. (National Defence Fund)

With the participation of Prosecutor Olig.
On the Sabbath, the last day of Passover, between the Shacharit and Musaf prayers, the president of the F.O.N. committee, Prosecutor Olig, gave a lecture in the municipal synagogue about the F.O.N., calling on the Jewish population to contribute en masse[?] to the Fund for the Defence of the State. Prosecutor Olig's lecture was introduced[?] by the Kielce rabbi, Rabbi Rapaport. Cantor Górnicki recited a special prayer for the army of the Polish Republic, and afterwards he sang, together with the choir, the Polish and the Jewish anthems.
The numerous audience resolved to support the proclaimed F.O.N. campaign. A temporary committee was elected, to which belong the representatives of the Kielce Jewish community, headed by Rabbi Rapaport.

Land of Israel slide pictures

Today, Friday, at 8 in the evening, interesting pictures of the Land of Israel will be shown with a projector at the Zionist premises. There will be shown: the growing[?] Jewish city, Tel Aviv, Transjordan[?], Purim celebrations, Herzl, Zionist congresses, etc.
At each picture the emissary of the Head Directorate of the Keren Kayemet in the Land of Israel, Mr. M. Karger[?], will give a series of explanations.
The said pictures will also be shown tomorrow, Sabbath, at 6 in the evening for children and at 9 in the evening for activists, at the premises of the Keren Kayemet (Wesoła 28).

The quota for kosher meat reduced.
The quota for the April—June quarter for the Jewish population has been reduced. Instead of 227 thousand kilos, only 101 thousand have been allotted.
Reception in honour of Rabbi Grossman in Będzin

Yesterday, by the midday[?] train, at[?] 16:16 [as printed], the candidate for the Będzin rabbinate, the Grajewo rabbi, Rabbi Yitzchak Eizik Grossman, arrived in Będzin.
Hundreds of people from all strata of the Jewish population had gathered at the railway station. A large crowd travelled to Ząbkowice to await[?] the esteemed rabbi.
The rabbi is staying with the well-known Mizrachi activist R. Meshulam Lejzer[?].
As we are informed, R. Icze Meir Lewin telephoned the above-mentioned rabbi yesterday, telling him to withdraw his candidacy as Będzin rabbi.
Today, at Kabbalat Shabbat, the rabbi will pray in the municipal Beit Midrash; the next morning — in the Great Synagogue, where he will deliver a sermon. The rabbi will spend Seudah Shlishit at the Mizrachi, where he will take part in the Oneg Shabbat.
On Sunday morning the rabbi will appear with a public lecture in one of the local cinemas.
Tomorrow the Keren Hayesod campaign will be proclaimed in Dąbrowa

A great academy (gala assembly) with the participation of Gross-Zimmermann.
This coming Saturday night a great academy will take place in the “Janus”[?] hall in Dąbrowa in connection with the proclamation of the “Keren Hayesod” campaign.
At the academy the well-known writer and brilliant speaker Mr. Moshe Gross-Zimmermann will give a lecture on the subject “Exile and Palestine”.
The academy has aroused strong interest in Jewish circles in Dąbrowa.
Advocate Landau — acquitted

Behind closed doors, the trial of advocate Landau, who had been suspected of immoral acts, took place at the Sosnowiec district court.
After the court proceedings the court handed down a verdict of acquittal.
“Don't come with complaints against others — first make peace among yourselves”

Says the director of the Kielce Chamber of Crafts.
This week the director of the Chamber of Crafts in Kielce, Mr. Okcentowicz, stayed in Zagłębie and held conferences with Christian and Jewish craftsmen — in connection with the amendment which deputy Samoczyński[?] has introduced to the industrial law.
On Tuesday evening a conference took place at the premises of the Craftsmen's Union in Będzin (Kołłątaja 45) with the participation of Dir. Okcentowicz, the representative of the starosty Mgr. Mikadski[?], Handels-Ratmaner[?], Dir. Mazur, Szyluszak, Goldsztajn, Kilszak, and also representatives of the craftsmen's associations in Zagłębie.
The conference was opened by the vice-president Mr. Fersztenfeld with a declaration in which he expressed regret that the conferences do not take place together with the Christian craftsmen: we have — he said — common interests in the problems of the crafts.
Then the presidium was elected: Alderman Wilberszlag (chairman), Sabkadski[?] (secretary) and the above-mentioned guests.
Dir. Mazur explained that with the separate conferences they had wanted to avoid an incident such as the one that took place at that time[?]. The representative of the starosty, too, declared that in future joint conferences will take place.
Then Director Okcentowicz gave a lecture, in which he touched in passing, at length, on the question of the fragmentation and the quarrels among the Jewish artisan masses. “Before you come with complaints to others, first make peace among yourselves.”
During the discussion, with the participation of Goldsztajn, Siluszek, Barankiewicz, Brasl, Dreksler, Szrajber, Magla[?], Jarszyk[?], Tuchszniajder and others, a number of craftsmen's questions were raised, which the director, in his reply, promised to settle favourably.

Lecture by Prof. Zaderecki in Katowice.
This coming Sunday[?] at 8.30 in the evening, in the "Powstańców" hall in Katowice, the well-known Christian Talmud expert Prof. Dr. Tadeusz Zaderecki will give a lecture on the topic "If people knew the Talmud".
The lecture has aroused great interest.

On Monday a group of schoolboys in Katowice amused themselves: they posted themselves near the railway station and blocked[?] the way of Jewish passers-by.
When they saw a policeman coming, they ran away.

(K.S.) On Saturday night, the 17th of this month, at half past 8, the annual general meeting of the Katowice Zionist Organisation will take place in its own premises, 3-go Maja 29.

The Revisionists' Celebration in Katowice

[Katowice — Revisionists.] Last Sunday the "Brit HaChayal" in Katowice celebrated the festival of its four years of existence. Taking part in the celebration were delegates from Upper Silesia, Zagłębie and from the leadership in the persons of Eng. Szeskin (Eretz Israel), Secretary-General Teker[?] and Com. Chrust.
At 10 o'clock in the morning a conference of all the delegates took place in the "Loża", at which they gave reports on their activity.
The main celebration took place in the afternoon, during which the decorations were distributed to the deserving members.
About 100 uniformed members took part in the ceremony, with their banners at their head. Decorations of merit were received by members Wachs and Ehrlich; a larger number received diplomas.
During the decoration, greetings were delivered by: the president of the N.Z.O. in Katowice, Mr. Kitzlinger, and the rabbis Chameides and Vogelman. The latter ended his greeting by saying that "the time will come when the whole Jewish people will greet one another with the watchword: — Tel Chai!
In the evening a reception (raut) took place.
He Worked on All "Fronts"

[Katowice — court; antisemitism.] A characteristic trial before the Katowice court.
Last Saturday a trial took place before the municipal court in Katowice that characterises the antisemitic ground.
In the dock sat a certain Aleksander Starzyk, accused of committing a series of swindles.
In the light of the court proceedings the following emerges: Starzyk, the editor of the Jew-devouring newspaper in Poznań called "Pająk"[?], came to Upper Silesia last year and, introducing himself to the Christian organisations as vice-president of the Endeks in Poznań, declared that he had come with the aim of leading the boycott campaign against Jews.
To this end he managed to obtain larger sums in the form of subsidies or for advertisements for his newspaper.
When he had "worked over" the Christian merchants enough, he then turned to the Jewish merchants, to whom he offered, for a certain reward, to fight the boycott campaign.
But this did not succeed, and the matter reached the police, who arrested him.
The epilogue took place in court, and after the hearing of witnesses the court sentenced him to 10 months' unconditional imprisonment.
