At a Summer Residence.

(A sketch)
By Chaim Wysocki.

Tsila received the first letter from her friend Ida, who is staying at a summer residence in a village in the Beskids. Ida describes everything to her with wholly[?] heartfelt friendship[?], the enthusiasm[?] over the beautiful and merry rest[?]; she tells of each thing separately and, above all, that she should not forget and, without further[?] excuses, come over immediately.
Tsila, who for certain reasons could not travel at once with her friend, did indeed arrange[?] that Ida should see to[?] everything and that she would come afterwards.
For a whole day Tsila had already been in a strange, agitated mood; although she could by now actually leave[?], the strenuous "travel preparations" had exhausted her terribly, and [—] about really so many little things to provide for.
By evening the big packed suitcase was already simply overfilled with everything that could fit in, and, strained and tired, at about twelve o'clock she barely got[?] into an overcrowded carriage.
It was rather[?] dark; from the melting tallow[?] candle above the window there dripped[?] [—][?], mixed with a [—] village smell of makhorka[?], which burned in the throat and choked one to tears.
After the hopeful thoughts that she would come to her dear friend in the so intimate, fragrant little room with windows onto the pine forest, as Ida had described it, [these] sweetened[?] her whole vision[?].
The train stopped at a dimly lit wooden building[?]. She barely found someone to carry out her big suitcase.
Under the [—], in the dark, a couple of broad-shouldered silhouettes with [—] bass[?] voices were already quarrelling over her suitcase, until one of them finally[?] hurled the heavy suitcase like a ball into the droshky. Then she too got in. The droshky began to toss back and forth on the uneven, [—] road, so that her heart nearly jumped out.
"Not a big '[—]'; in about 10 minutes we'll be at the villa," the coachman answered her in his indifferent voice during[?] the ride...
With a clatter the droshky drove into the first lane, which lay sunk in sleep. A strange[?], dense darkness cut the eyes; from somewhere dogs were barking so menacingly[?], and[?] now the wheels are already rattling with a clatter over the highway itself[?]; past them run low, dark house-shadows, as if hunched up, pressed together from fright. [—] in the [—] and in the darkness of the four-cornered market a drawn-out s-p-r-r-r could already be heard!
The droshky stopped beside a fine, adorned[?] wooden villa; from all the windows there burst [—] a strong, bright light. Broken, with an extraordinary headache, she barely got out of the droshky. She opened the door – but this she had not expected at all.
Several big lamps struck her in the eyes. A mixture of voices, an uproar around a long laid table on which [—] leftovers of fancy town dishes; bottles, carafes with sparkling drinks of various colours gleamed among plates and glassware, and the crowd – young, dandyish, town-like – festively dressed up.
Tsila was a little at a loss, thought it perhaps a mistake, but out of the noisy crowd Ida suddenly shot forth, smiling quite[?] merrily, flushed and with shining eyes.
"Oh, Tsila! Good that you've come now[?]! Oh, how good! Just in time! We're having a 'wieczorek' [an evening party] today. Well, come, Tsila, I must[?] introduce you."
And before Tsila even had a chance to object[?], fingers – broad[?], stiff and softish[?], perfumed with manicure – were already pressing her hands. Men's eyes, a little tipsy, cut so insolently into hers, and from all of them came a [—] smell of alcohol mixed with perfume and powder.
Ida wildly pulled the coat off her. It did not help that Tsila pleaded she was not properly dressed; the other shouted even more wildly [—] that it doesn't matter[?] – our own people, dacha folk. They poured[?] little glasses for her by force. She insisted she couldn't now, but nobody listened to her. Little glasses would tip over on the gleaming-white tablecloth, and others would be filled.
Tsila's head ached even more; it knocked in her temples as if with hammers. If only she could lean somewhere on a sofa[?] – but, as if to spite her, a group of young people with goggling[?], shining, feverish eyes had sprawled out[?] there on the divan in the corner. She wants to turn to Ida – but the latter is already sitting so tipsily[?] among the crowd on the divan...
Once[?] a place at the edge of the divan suddenly became free. She quickly jumped up onto it. Leaning against the high [?] wall – in the other corner Ida sat with a couple of young men, so intimately.
Tsila looked at her piercingly and meanwhile thought: this is the same always reserved[?] friend. And she already felt a hatred toward everyone around, [—] dried-out eyes, and toward Ida, too, a disgust...
Suddenly she felt around her bare neck a firm male[?] hand, and a mixed smell of cigarettes and alcohol struck her nose. With a powerful[?], hasty impulse she pushed someone away from her, and[?] a male figure stretched out at full length on the floor, somehow so foolishly, senselessly[?].
In the commotion that[?] suddenly arose, she was already in the yard, out of the gate, straight onto the road leading to the forest.
The sky had already [—] toward day, and in the forest there was a smell of morning dew and conifers. On a hillock, under a broad, branching canopy-roof, she let herself down [—], gazing "thoughtlessly"[?] into the ever-brightening horizon.
From afar, from the fine, adorned wooden villa, noisy voices still rang out, echoing like a distant echo amid the pious[?] morning stillness.
The World Is Not Coming to an End. — Travelling Around the Provinces

[Feuilleton — impressions of a journey through the provinces.] If I were a doctor, I would advise all our pessimists and gloom-mongers who spend their time in the spas and summer resorts that they would do better to travel to the remote, forsaken provinces — there, among wild, spacious fields and forests, rivers and mountains, in an environment of simplicity, they might sooner than anywhere else be cured of their gloom and pessimism, which shortens their years...
The remote province is something quite different — here everything is simple, big-hearted, like the nature around it. Here "modern culture" has not yet set its seal, and everything still looks as it has since the six days of Creation... Even the people here have remained "backward"; they know nothing[?] of any "stragan" [Polish: market stall — an allusion to the boycott campaign for Polish stalls], and still think in the old categories of the pre-Hitlerism[?] era...
I met some Jewish provincial merchants with whom I travelled in the railway carriage: how does the boycott look? They looked at me rather strangely, just as if I had come from another world. After a short conversation with them I learned that the only thing that interests them is — that there should only be a good harvest. About the "Rolniks" [farmers' associations] and the "spółdzielnie" [cooperatives] that have multiplied in the provinces they ask nothing at all — why should things be any worse[?]! For even now, after all the agitation, the peasant prefers to trade with the Jew, and sells him the grain and the flax 5 groszy cheaper than to the "Rolnik".
After reading day after day in the newspapers about what goes on in certain provincial districts, one can hardly believe it, and it all looks like a dream. But it is no dream and no fantasy, only reality itself, which bears witness that[?] the peasant, and the village person in general, does not want to know of all these new theories that all sorts of poison-mixers want to inoculate him with.
I myself had the opportunity to learn of a fact that shows how the peasants regard the fashionable "straganism" conducted by a certain sort of Polish newspapers. A well-to-do peasant (whose name and village I do not want to mention, for understandable reasons), while still alive divided his land, consisting of several dozen hectares of good soil with rich equipment, among his sons, and himself remained with a fine farm. In a short time his sons set up farms of their own, with buildings and considerable dead and live inventory, and lived like the squires...
Not long ago, however, certain persons talked his eldest son into coming to town and opening a shop here, promising him mountains and hills. The young peasant let himself be persuaded, leased out his land for several years, sold off his equipment and buildings, and with a sizeable mortgage of a few tens of thousands of gulden [złoty] came into town and opened a shop here. Naturally, business at the new shopkeeper's did not go very brilliantly, and in a short time he liquidated his shop. He was then advised to use the money he had still managed to save from his liquidated business to set up a mobile cinema and travel with it around the province.
Since[?] he lacked money for this business at once[?], the peasant came to his father to lend him some. But the father would not even let him across the threshold. Now the outcast peasant sits and does not know what to do. The lease on his land will end only in a few years, the money he has eaten up, and [—] his father [—] toward him [reading doubtful], because he does not want — he says — such a son, who is eager for "żydowskie" ["Jewish"] livelihoods...
This fact resounds through the whole surrounding district and is the best argument against all the "stall preachers"[?] in the village.
And, as it turns out[?], there where the peasant lives in peace with the Jew, no antisemites and agitators are at all frightening; even those who have come from the big cities suddenly change their skin here, and it is no rarity to find die-hard supporters of the "left benches" [the ghetto benches] at the universities cheerfully playing handball with Jews.
That is how the healthy village atmosphere works here on the sick guests from the over-politicised town...
Sh.-Z.
What All Happens in the World in One Hour?

[Science & miscellany — world statistics.] It is not so easy to answer this question. One must first of all have the data on what happens in the world in general; only then can one divide the data into months, days and hours, and only then can one say clearly what all happens in the world in the course of one hour.
Of course one can only reckon with those events that occur day in, day out. Things that happen only from time to time, not constantly without pause, cannot be counted at all, because one cannot estimate their amount[?] in an hour, since one does not know exactly whether the same will happen in the next hour too.
A statistic of the Leipzig Fair gives an answer to the question of what happens in the world in the space of one hour.
In the whole world twelve hundred weddings are concluded in one hour. According to an exact count, 5,440 children are born in the whole world in one hour.
Since only 4630 people die in one hour in the whole world, one can calculate from this that the world gains 810 new people every hour.
These statistical figures cover, of course, only the civilised countries of the world, where exact records are kept of who is born and who dies. Those people who are born or die among the wild tribes are not recorded here.
In one hour a billion and 200 million letters and telegrams arrive and depart. The stamps and fees for these letters and telegrams of one single hour cost some 70 million gold francs, a sum with which much good could be done, if people would only stop writing, dispatching and receiving letters by post for one hour.
This does not include those letters that arrive or depart by various special ships or aeroplanes, since these are only individual consignments which naturally cannot be included in exact statistics.
In one hour 190 wagons of paper for writing and for newspapers are produced in the world.
No smaller is the work people do in one hour for their clothes. Thanks to modern machines, no less than ten thousand double-centners [quintals] of cotton and three thousand double-centners of wool are now processed in one hour.
In one hour 1700 double-centners of tobacco are consumed.
In one hour two million dollars' worth of tobacco goes up in smoke.
In one hour fifty kilometres of film are produced in the whole world, costing a hefty fortune; exact figures on this cannot be given.
In one hour 2500 various crimes are committed in the whole world, of which only a part are dealt with in court, because the other criminals cannot be caught.
In one hour eight murders take place in the world, of which only six succeed in being caught, because two murderers vanish and cannot be caught.
As one sees, a good deal of work is done in the whole world in the course of one single hour, which with us mostly passes so quickly that we do not even notice it...
Z. Haber, Vienna.
She Doesn't Like the "Porządek" [Order]...

[Humour — feuilleton; summer-resort life.] The Troubles of a Summer Visitor ["letnik"].
By Y. Oberżanek [?].
You know women, you say? If you say so, you are a braggart; you don't even begin to know them.
Take, for example, such an expert in the women's line ["branża"] as me: however much I have studied, they have remained a secret to me. The more I have researched them, the more I have become convinced that the "fair sex" is and will remain a riddle for male humanity.
I will tell you what happened to me myself.
I'm walking once [?] in the street, and somebody stops me:
— Is that Mrs. Y ["Igrek"] with her granddaughter?
I stood there embarrassed:
— Which one is the grandmother and which the granddaughter? After all, both wear short dresses and fitted [?] men's jackets ["marynarki"], short boyish bobs ["chłopczyca"], both have blood-red lips like fire, shaved eyebrows, black circles like half-moons around the eyes. Well, go and tell who is the grandmother and who the granddaughter!..
Or such a fact:
An acquaintance of mine suffered for years from "harenshtshek vshulpshakhi" [?] [unclear term, apparently a nervous/imaginary ailment], and her husband was fed up [lit. his gall overflowed]; he took her to doctors, and also [?]... to "good Jews" [rebbes] and to "pney rush" [?] — the "haretshek" [?] would not budge!
Suddenly a miracle happened: she found [?] a doctor, a "specialist", who took the "haretshek" in hand, and thanks to him she became a different person; she became a young [?] "na placu" [?], no longer got any "fits" ["napady"], no longer needed compresses or "injections" [?] ["szczepienia"] — she became as healthy as a fish.
Do you want to know who the doctor was? — A doctor of philosophy!
Well, isn't that a miracle? Men, when they have "haretshkes" [?], even a doctor of medicine can't help them, while with women even a doctor of philosophy is a "specialist"...
— So, I ask you, can one be wise about the "fair sex"? If you say you are a connoisseur of women, you are a braggart; they have been and will remain a riddle for male humanity.
Why do I say this precisely now? Because of an affair with my own wife; she too is a riddle to me. For 17 years we have lived under one roof, and still I don't know her; however hard I try to figure her out, I don't succeed.
In earlier times she had complaints against me:
— You call yourself a man? A "khorets" [?] [unclear insult] you were created, not a man. Just look how other husbands behave, learn from our neighbour: when he comes home, he gives her a kiss, she asks [sic]: how are you, "saltshele" [?] [term of endearment], how do you feel? Every day he brings home parcels and "presents" ["podarunki"] from town; he never comes home empty-handed — and you? Some husband I have, for all I care [?]!
Now, at the summer lodging [?], I had a hard time of it [lit. "roasted troubles"], every time the same refrain:
— Every husband, when he comes to visit, brings his wife something to gladden her heart, and you come flying in empty-handed; it's a disgrace and a shame for me before the other wives; I'm bursting with jealousy ["zazdrość"]...
So I realised that my missus was right: why indeed shouldn't I bring my little wife something to gladden her heart? Other husbands, when they come to the summer resort ["letnisko"], kiss their wives and ask: what's new, how are you; why should I be the exception? Why should I be the exception? Why shouldn't I do as all the others do, why? So I decided this year to do as other husbands do, and let my missus not burst with "jealousy".
The first Friday, as soon as I arrived at the resort, I embraced my summer-lady ["letniczka"] and kissed her heartily like a bridegroom with a bride, no comparison intended; at the same time I handed her a whole bunch of parcels and "tishlekh" [?], and as [?] I noticed the "jealous" ["zazdrosne"] looks of the other summer-ladies, I started questioning her:
— How are you, "saltshele"? Are you at least well? And I told her how I had been counting the days, the hours, that every [?] evening [?] I went home at 9 o'clock, and by [?] 11 o'clock I was already lying in bed.
The second Friday, again the same kissing, the same parcels, the same questioning and the same stories.
So I was sure that my little wife was in seventh heaven that I was behaving so, that the summer-ladies would burst with "jealousy"; so I thought — and it turned out to be something quite different.
The third Friday, when I began carrying out my "programme", I noticed that my wife was somehow clouded over ["pochmurna"]... Outwardly she takes the parcels and "tishlekh" [?] to gladden her heart, she pretends to be pleased, but somehow it isn't the real thing. So I ask her:
— "Saltshele", what has happened? Are you, God forbid, not quite all right [?] [lit. "not with everyone"]?
She lowered her eyes and said in a [—] voice:
— I'll tell you the truth, Yosl, I don't like this business.
— What business?
— That... that you have suddenly become so "tender" ["czuły"] to me... I don't like the parcels and "tishlekh" [?] you bring me every Friday, I don't like your "hearty" ["serdeczne"] kisses, I don't like your early [—] sleeping — the whole business, Yosele my crown, I don't like; the business is somehow not kosher... Who knows what you, "Józiu" [?], have on your conscience!...
Here I really stood bewildered: when I didn't do as other husbands do, I was a "khorets" [?] created, and she burst with jealousy; and now, when I do everything by the book, again it's no good — to her the business isn't kosher.
But all this is still nothing; listen to what else happened:
This week, on an ordinary Wednesday at dawn, I was still sleeping sweetly when suddenly the doorbell rings. I run to the door, open it, and who, do you think, was it? She, my "saltshele".
— What has happened? Why so suddenly?
She answered nothing, took off her coat and began to search.
First in the kitchen, then in the room, and finally in the bedroom, in the wardrobes, in the drawers; after the "search" ["rewizja"] she sat down at the table and started putting questions to me:
— Tell me, Yosele, since when is it with you that when I'm not here — such "order" ["porządek"]? Once, when I wasn't at home, everything was head down and feet up, and now suddenly such a "Warsaw [?] order" [perhaps "wzorowy porządek", model order]!.. Everything stands in its place, everything gleams, the beds freshly made, the floors ["podłogi"] swept, not a scrap of cobweb on the walls — where do you get such "order" from? You won't make me believe you do it with your own hands!. Yes, and for whom did you set out the vase ["wazon"] with flowers on the table?
— Now everything has become clear to me, now I understand why you became so "tender" to me; I understood at once that the business wasn't kosher, I understood at once that you had something on your conscience... Now I can see the "order" in the house when I'm not at home, I can see the vase of flowers on the table — now I know everything.
In short, gentlemen: the "fair sex" has been and will forever remain a riddle for male humanity...
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Ekev)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Ekev.
—o—
a) "And the lovingkindness which He swore unto thy fathers" (7:12)
"Master of the Universe! — so R. Moshe Leib of Sasów pleaded, as it were, with God — had You done all the good You do with us by strict justice alone, according to what is due to us, You would be right that with our forefathers You did good, because they were worthy of it, while we are sinful and do not deserve Your goodness. But in truth, 'and the lovingkindness which He swore unto thy fathers' — even with our forefathers You did good only out of lovingkindness; and if it is lovingkindness anyway, then lovingkindness is due to us too, since we are more sinful than our forefathers..."
—o—
b) "For that will be a snare unto thee" (ibid., 16)
If you live together with the foreign nations, you will be made to stumble through them.
And that is the meaning of the juxtaposition in King David's earlier words, "Who can discern errors?... keep back Thy servant also from presumptuous sins": if you find yourself in the neighbourhood of the wicked, you will already stumble into errors, into unnoticed sins... Pnei Yafot.
—o—
c) "A land wherein thou shalt eat bread without scarceness" (8:9)
1.
The Land of Israel has this virtue, that there one is[?] never poor; one is content with what one has, for "thou shalt not lack any thing in it" — nobody lacks anything, and when nothing is lacking, one is already rich... R. Leibish Charif.
* * *
"Give me neither poverty nor riches."
One can be a poor man and a rich man at the same time, for "he who has a hundred wants two hundred." It follows that the one who owns a thousand złoty is poorer than the one who owns nothing: for the one who owns nothing needs a thousand złoty, while the one who owns a thousand lacks two thousand. That is "poverty and riches" — poverty and wealth at the same time... Maharam Schiff.
2.
"Whoever engages in building becomes poor" — building, construction work, makes one poor; and that is the blessing "and hast built goodly houses": you will build houses in the Land of Israel, and "thou shalt eat bread without scarceness" — from building houses in the Land of Israel you will not become poor...
R. Yosef Shaul Nathanson.
* * *
"One who builds — how much must he build to be liable (chayav)?" — whoever builds, how much must he build in order to remain in debt? — so R. Zalman Pozner[?] explained the Gemara in tractate "Shabbat" — to which the Gemara answers, "one who builds anything at all": whoever builds even a little must[?] already remain a debtor...
—o—
d) "Then thy heart be lifted up, and thou forget the Lord thy God" (ibid., 14)
"Every man who has a haughty spirit is as though he worshipped idols."
For idolatry one is punished even for a thought, even when one does not actually worship idols but only in thought; for pride, too, one is punished for a mere thought — for puffing oneself up with the idea that one is great. For pride one need not do anything at all: only [—] oneself and think: I am great, enormously great... Imrei Chen.
* * *
In the Zohar, portion Bereshit, folio 23, there is a wonderful passage:
When Rabbi Shimon heard a voice calling him, "Shimon! Shimon!", he said: it is none other than God, blessed be He, Himself.
One asks: is that possible? It looks[?], God forbid, like pride — that R. Shimon bar Yochai was sure that no one born of woman would[?] call him "Shimon" except the Holy One, blessed be He, Himself.
But the plain meaning is different: R. Shimon meant to say by this that the whole world is mistaken about him, it cannot see [printed: "be"] his true lowliness, and therefore he is called "Rabbi"; but the voice that called him by his bare name, Shimon, must be God's voice, for only the Blessed Name knows him and knows "that I am only a Shimon and not a Rabbi Shimon"...
* * *
"How much we are obliged to thank the Creator of the world — R. Naftali of [—] (printed "Berszed"[?]) used to say — for commanding us to conduct ourselves in humility. What would we have done had He commanded us to hold ourselves great — how could we have managed it? Well, on the contrary: let Naftali just try to persuade himself that he is a great man..."
* * *
"How great pride is in man — R. Yehuda Aryeh of Modena used to say — can be seen from tombstone inscriptions: the smallest praise I ever found[?] on a tombstone was 'a man perfect and upright, one that feared God and eschewed evil' — which was said of Job, and our Sages say that Job's praise is greater than the praise of Abraham our father..."
—o—
e) "Wherefore Levi hath no part nor inheritance with his brethren; the Lord is his inheritance" (10:9)
"The Lord is his inheritance" — the lot of the tribe of Levi is like the lot of the Blessed Name, who also has no place in the world. "Where is the place of His glory?" — ask the angels.
R. Uri of Strzeliska.
—o—
f) "And now, what doth the Lord thy God require of thee, but to fear"
"Is the fear of Heaven then a small thing [printed 'Vetu' for 'Atu']? Yes — for Moses it is a small thing."
For humility leads to the fear of Heaven (Sotah), and Moses was, after all, the humblest of all men. And "for Moses" — all those who found themselves in Moses' surroundings had to be humble, for how could one hold oneself great in front of Moses? So for them, too, it was easy to be God-fearing.
[—]omer.
"Nothing Has Changed"

[Feuilleton — Bystra, summer resort; series, sketch 4.]
Little pictures from the "Line". 4.
By S. Libason.

Before midnight.
"When the evil angel, the bad angel who accompanies every Jew home from synagogue on Friday night, sees in the Jew's house the festiveness in honour of the Sabbath, he says Amen against his will; conversely, when the good angels see the bad conduct of Jews, they must, with lowered heads, also agree with the bad angel."
We too, unfortunately, are forced this time to stand in the ranks of the bad angel and "agree" to the plan[?] which stings[?] the eyes [?] ... through the various "pregurehniks" [?] and so on.
— It is, after all, a "well-known" thing that the Jews have "grabbed" everything into their hands: commerce, industry, the market stall [stragan] and even — dance halls.
Not only in the towns, but also in the summer[?] resorts the dance halls are being "occupied" by "alien elements".
And among the "grabbed" places is also — Bystra. Indeed (in the expression of the guests, who speak only German) Bystra has this year become "verjudet"; there are no "slavrushnos" [?] — the fair sex complains to me; the young people have packed off [?] elsewhere; but since, as it were, there is no [?] creature at all [?], the young people's place is filled by others, literally: this year the "older people" [Polish starsi ludzie; ?] dance too, so that the hall where people dance is always full. Especially on Saturday nights after the Sabbath, when it is, after all, a mitzvah to dance.
And if our brethren the Children of Israel dance on Tisha be-Av, how much more so on the night after Shabbat Nachamu, and especially this year, when "the Jewish people has found consolation in the favours of the English government"...
So the hall was indeed well "filled" by the "strangers", and "our own" had, poor things, no way out.
But among those displeased with "Jewish chutzpah" there was one who, as it turns out[?], was soaked[?] in the "Aryan paragraph", and he called out:
— Gentlemen [Polish Panowie; ?], now the orchestra is playing a tango, but "for kho-runkies" [?] — only Aryans may dance...
That our "salatshes" [?] and "yunks" [?] no longer danced to this "kosher tango" goes without saying; but one felt bitter pity for them, because right in the middle of the "blaze" their joy was disturbed and they, poor things, had to leave
— before midnight...

The "holy" villa.
"The Jews are the most beloved people of all seventy nations, Jerusalem is the holiest city, and of all villas the holiest is Villa 'Maria'."
All rivers fall into the sea, and all "pious and good people" receive their spiritual nourishment at Villa "Maria".
In the villa is concentrated the "olive oil" [the cream] of the "litenikes" [?] in Bystra; the whole building is enveloped in pure holiness and... flirting.
The first part[?] is influenced by the bearded[?] men of our circle, and the second[?] — young "litenikes" [?] "pan Warszawske-poy" [?], little-bearded yeshiva lads in long kapotes, their heads "covered" with small round caps. During prayer they clap their hands with fervour, and [—] they flirt[?] with smiles.
The flirting is not done modestly, but precisely on the "deptak" [promenade]. We — say the Hasidic young men — behave like your "Polish" Hasidic boys, who live within their narrow four cubits; to stroll with a girl[?] in the street is, God forbid to mention it — "[?] other people"...
And the "other people" become very[?] popular: when one hears in the evening singing of a composition by Yossele Rosenblatt [the cantor], or simply Hasidic tunes, accompanied by loud voices — everyone knows it comes from Villa "Maria". Even when a "datshnitse" [?; perhaps a summer-cottage landlady or a cook] runs into a mishap — the gizzard of the "nogn" [?; perhaps the goose] is somehow not quite in order — she runs to ask a rabbinic question at Villa "Maria", because Villa "Maria" has been crowned with the name
— the "holy" villa.

"Gourmets".
In the field of "gourmandise" nothing has yet changed among our "Moshkes" [a Polish slur for Jews]; apparently the lessons about the domestic and foreign antisemitic "production" have to this day not penetrated their heads, and they still cannot stand the "żydowski smell", the[?] "żydowska kuchnia" [Jewish cuisine].
— Why do you avoid the Jewish guesthouses? — I ask a Jewish house-owner I know from Sosnowiec.
— "Panie szanowny" [Dear sir] — I cannot suspect myself of being an antisemite, but Jewish dishes don't appeal to me. With Jews — he gives me to understand — all dishes are cooked with schmaltz. A lot of fat; once I ate a piece of "yaptshak" [?] at a relative of mine and ruined my stomach. With them [the gentiles] they cook with butter, so the dishes are "light to digest"...
And truly we can have no complaints against our "gourmet": how is he to blame, poor man, that he has acquired a "goyish stomach", which cannot digest the dishes of a "żydowska kuchnia"? So naturally he must avoid the Jewish guesthouses; and by the way, perhaps he even managed to acquire a goyish head too — then he will really be well off.
— A question: what else can still happen?...
The Living Dead Man (19)

[Serialized novel — "A most thrilling novel of Jewish life in Zagłębie before and during the World War"; installment 19.]
A. Zaglembier [pen name].

— Have you ever heard such stories — may it not happen to me or to you — that people suddenly vanish and nobody knows where their bones have ended up?..
Yosl's heart begins to pound even harder; the bite sticks in his throat.
— Where? Where did this happen? — asks the curious crowd.
— What do you mean, where? Right here at home, in Zagłębie. I tell you, a young man — may all Jewish children be like him — I think I even knew him myself, and he suddenly vanished. I tell you, it cuts your heart to look at the wife with the children. They say bandits murdered him and buried him somewhere — what can't happen nowadays?..
— Well, well?
— When I left, they were still searching for him everywhere. They arrested some shiksa, called Jakasz [?], because she had supposedly been seen with that Jew... So she made up some slander about the missing man that is a disgrace to repeat.
— And nobody knows where he is?
The ground is already beginning to burn under Yosl. It is him they mean, after all... And perhaps he should talk to the Jew? Perhaps he could help him?.. Meanwhile, though, he hears the Jew go on telling:
— In short, she denies it flatly ["denies stone and bone"], and only today did I learn the truth.
— And what is it?
— Here, read the newspaper, here you have the whole story: they found the young man dragged out of the river, [—] [?]... Oy, oy, he left home fresh and healthy, and today they are already sitting shiva for him...
— Terrible! Terrible! One has truly never heard of such murders!
Someone began to read aloud. Yosl hears his name being called out, but he is so dazed [?] and agitated that he does not understand a single word. Only when the newspaper is laid aside does Yosl go over and ask in a dry voice:
— May I have a look at the newspaper?
— Please, by all means.
With a trembling hand he takes the paper, sits down again in his former place and begins to read.
He does not believe his own eyes. The blood rushes to his face; he turns towards the wall so that no one will notice his agitation.
And again he reads over that last meeting with Wanda [printed in the inflected form "Vandan"], and then the few tragic hours in the forest with the dangerous bandit...
Actually he could have been satisfied with the outcome of the sad affair, but how can he let his wife and children live in such a terrible error? And at the very time when he is alive and well, they are sure that he is rotting in the grave... and they have already wept and mourned for him.
— No, no, he cannot bear it...
After all, he has committed a terrible crime — no matter how and under what circumstances, he did kill a man... True, a lucky fate has played into his hands; the very thing he himself had not believed in before has happened: to the world he is already dead, deceased — but may he pass as such in the eyes of his beloved wife and children too?..
— No, no — he says to himself — they must know the truth, and above all they must know that he is alive. They must not mourn him, for after all they buried a stranger, a bandit.
But Yosl Wertheim also takes into account what will happen if Saratshe [a pet form of Sarah] suddenly learns that he is alive.
And what if she does not believe it? Has anyone ever heard of a dead man writing a letter from "the other world"?
And Yosl knows his Saratshe well: if she cannot keep the terrible secret, she will show his letter to someone, the truth will come out like oil on water, and they will even start hunting for him as a murderer?..
No, he must still think it over well — how to act, and find the best way to let Saratshe know about him.
But here, in the cheap eatery [garkikh], it is impossible for him to do it; his temples are pounding too hard. He is still too stunned by what he has read about himself in the newspaper.
He pays and goes out into the street.
He walks to the park; the wind from the sea refreshes him a little, his head becomes clearer, and he begins once more to look for a way out of his painful situation.
At moments he is overcome by the thought of throwing [himself] into the sea. That would be, thinks Yosl Wertheim, the easiest and most convenient way out, since he is in any case already counted among the dead...
But when he remembers his wife and children, his heart begins to ache. Why should he orphan such young lambs? What are they guilty of?..
And hope — which is indeed quite often "the mother of fools" — begins to paint a plan for him, so lovely and smooth, without any stumbling-blocks...
With money one can get anything — thinks Yosl — why shouldn't he obtain bought documents and become again like other people? Are there few people living on false documents?
And to Saratshe he will indeed write a letter this very day or tomorrow. In his mind he is already composing a draft of how to write the letter so that Saratshe will believe that it is really he, Yosl, her husband, who is writing to her; but at the beginning he will first write that apart from her no one at all may know about the letter, not even father and mother on both sides, nor the children either.
And only after that will he write out the whole truth to her, even what he had to [?] hide from her for a long time — the story with Wanda... And he is sure, Yosl, that Saratshe will forgive him, pardon him.. She will do it — if not so much for his sake, then for the children's sake, so that they will know their father is alive... And he will take up work here — a man does not get lost — and afterwards he will bring them over here to himself. The main thing, though, is that she should keep the secret the whole time, and that everyone should indeed believe that he is no longer alive, until the terrible story is forgotten...
But when the whole plan is already complete in Yosl's mind, he suddenly asks himself:
— And what if Saratshe will no longer want to live with me, with such a husband?..
It weighs on his heart, but he can no longer give up this plan...
He must do his part [?] and have a clear conscience, come what may; Saratshe surely won't hand him over to the police.
And just as he decided, so he indeed did.
And because nothing but his own affair interested Yosl that day, nor could interest him — he did not know that the whole world was already standing in flames and that a terrible conflagration was about to break out, one that nobody had reckoned with...
He had noticed how the last emigrants were running to the port, like people trying to save themselves from death.
He had even heard something about people everywhere talking of an outbreak of war, but just like others, it had not occurred to him either that it was already so near.
And precisely at that same time, when Yosl sat for hours on end writing the letter to Saratshe and confessing to her the painful [?], terrible secret — precisely at that time all the borders of Germany were closed, and from one end to the other the dreadful cry resounded:
— War!.. Mobilization!..
And Yosl learned of it only when he hurried to the post office and wanted to send the registered letter to Saratshe. The postal clerk looked at him in astonishment and said with a smile:
— Unfortunately, sir, yesterday you could still have sent the letter, but today it is too late — war!.
Yosl stood rooted to the spot, as if he had suddenly received a blow to the head, and asked himself:
— Is there no possibility at all any more?
The postal clerk, who had heard his question, answered him:
— The possibility is this: if you yourself see to delivering the letter...

(A little song of sorts).

So I'm a young fellow
without any worry,
I take my little suitcase
and off I go to Zoppot [Sopot].

There I meet Madame Chrane [?]
and her daughter Freyde,
and Madame has a governess
prettier than both of them.

The mother has a lot of money
and the daughter — years;
so I marry the governess — done with it:
oh, how I've been had!!!

I'm no longer a young fellow,
oh, what a worry!
I pack my little suitcase
and run away from Zoppot...

The Jewish State

[Humour — the "Kokh-lefl" page; the Peel partition plan.]
Who — and what he says:
In the little-town study-house sit three Jews, one a little tailor, the second a little shoemaker and the third a little baker.
Says the little tailor:
— Nicely, upon my life, has the Englishman cut out the Jewish State — no [cut?], no even shoulders, one trouser-leg [?] shorter and the other longer. From top to bottom [basting?] stitches — a botched piece of work, as sure as you see me a tailor!...
Says the little shoemaker:
— Hee... hee... hee... how do you like the cut of the State? May I have as much luck as the Englishman is a [?] craftsman. It's not sewn [?], not [?], not even [?], pulled over the last, a patch slapped on a patch and that's it! And then he went and made two left shoes... No, that's no guild-standard piece of work!...
Says the little baker:
— A [fine?] leaven the Englishman has fermented: it's not rolled, not kneaded through, not baked through — just taken and shoved into the oven. So many years of kneading a dough, and it's stayed raw...
Twenty-three years ago.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Members of the Kehilla Board Demand Elections for a New Council and Kehilla Board.

[Będzin — kehilla.]
The national councillors, Messrs. Pe-nele[?], Goldsztajn, Gimperk[?] and Waspal[?], have submitted the following appeal[?] to the kehilla board:
We, the undersigned members of the board of the Jewish kehilla in Będzin, hereby turn to the kehilla board to call elections for a new council and board of the kehilla in Będzin.
We base this proposal of ours on the fact that the term of the present kehilla ends in the month of August of this year. According to the regulations, new elections must be called 2 months before the term expires.

[Będzin — housing.]

Public Auction of Confiscated Goods.

[Będzin — commerce.]
The board of the local Merchants' Association draws the attention of interested circles to the fact that on 9 August [sierpień], at 10 a.m., public[?] [?]-day auctions of various confiscated foreign goods will begin at the customs office in Katowice.

At the Right Time...

[Będzin — religious life.]
In honour of Shabbat Nachamu a larger number of worshippers came to the town synagogue [the Shtot-shul] to enjoy the prayers. It is, after all, Shabbat Nachamu, but the choir also used the opportunity and, in honour of the Sabbath, went on strike[?].

From the Wedding to the Hospital.

[Będzin area — incident.]
In a village beyond Oytse[?] a wedding took place. During the dancing a quarrel broke out between the bride's brother-in-law and a guest who also felt like dancing together with the closest family; from words they passed to deeds with [?] ['bangesn'], and the end of it was that two of the guests were taken to the hospital in a serious condition.
Accident to a Jewish Butcher.

[Będzin — accident.]
On Saturday night, when Mr. Fersztenfeld wanted to take down a 'side' of meat from the wall in his butcher's shop, an accident occurred.
The hook on which the meat was hanging was torn out of the wall, and the meat fell on Fersztenfeld and badly injured his right hand.
How Is the Relief Campaign for Brisk Going?

On Monday evening[?] a meeting of the relief committee for Brisk was held in the kehilla offices. The report given shows that there are still many Jews, among them well-to-do ones, who have refused to give the sum assessed on them, and in general people are indifferent to the Brisk campaign.
To date a total of 5000 zł. has been collected, but donations from the house collections still have to come in.
It was decided to call on the house delegates, and the authorised collectors in particular, to intensify their work so that the Brisk campaign can be wound up.
On a Tunnel under the Railway Crossing

The municipal administration has approached the railway directorate in Warsaw with a petition on the question of building a tunnel under[?] the railway crossing (przejazd) opposite the local railway station. The municipal administration supported the petition with a series of arguments about the necessity of building the tunnel. One of the main arguments is that the crossing is closed about 80 times a day because of the passing trains. It has been calculated that 15 thousand people pass through the crossing daily.
A memorandum on the matter has also been submitted to the D.O.K.P.[?] (District Directorate of the State Railways) in Kraków.

There Will Be No Export Premium on Grain.

We learn from well-informed circles that in the new economic year no premiums will be given for exporting grain, such as wheat, rye etc.; the government has already decided so.
It is only planned to make an exception and to give an export premium for the export of pulses, peas and rapeseed.
The export of bran and of the cheaper grades of flour will not be permitted.
The export of wheat, rye and the most expensive grades of flour will be permitted.
The government wants[?] by all means that the local grain prices should be supported by the prices abroad.

My Sympathy to the Radom Patron of the Two Ignorant Little Souls of Kielce

[Kielce — press polemic.] There is truly nothing left but to pity and to feel sorry for the people from whom the demon of earning one more złoty has already robbed common sense, leading them astray onto wild, crooked paths where they wallow [?] in deep mud.
[—] [?] about the talk [?]
Against the personal savageries directed at my address, which found a comfortable [?] place [?] in "[—] Serk" [?] and in "Radomer Lebn" ["Radom Life"] (a Radom Jew asks: does such a "life" really exist [—]).

Ch. Zieloni [?].
He — 10, and She — 11.

[Kielce region — everyday life.]
Sensational betrothal between young children, and a tale of a divorcé and a divorcée.
The neighbouring little town of P. near Kielce is now in an uproar. The sensation is a match that was concluded these days, and the groom and bride are both together 21 years old.
This match was concluded under very interesting circumstances.
In the little town the shopkeeper G., a divorcé, made the acquaintance of a divorcée. At the very first "look" she caught his eye, and they decided to marry. The only obstacle was that both have [?] children: he has a little daughter of 10, and she has a little son of 11.
"Everything would have been fine," the divorcé said to the divorcée, "but the children... There will be 'mine' and 'yours'; my little daughter will scrap with your little son, and when, on top of 'yours' and 'mine', 'our' children come along too — it will be sheer hell at home."
"Well [?], do you know what has occurred to me?" the divorcée said to the divorcé.
"Namely, what has occurred to you?"
"It occurred to me that we should make a match. My Balczele will sign the betrothal contract with your Josele, and so we shall be both in-laws and husband and wife. What do you say to my plan?"
The divorcé wrinkled his forehead, scratched under his chin and finally said:
"Yes, you are right, that is a plan. We'll write tnoim: first my Balczele with your Josele, and then me with you."
They both shook hands, wished each other mazel tov, called in the children and said to them:
"Children, give each other your little hands and wish each other mazel tov — you have become bride and groom."
Hearing the news, the children began to jump for joy. "She" grabbed "him" by the coat-tails and set off running [?], while the "groom" then grabbed the "bride's" "little cap" [?] and ran off through the street:
"Folks, wish us mazel tov, I'm a groom and Balczele is my bride!..."
That same evening the betrothal took place at the bride's mother's. The news spread quickly through the town and among the summer visitors who stay there in summer lodgings, and the whole notability of the town, with the rabbi at its head, came to the betrothal. Also many guests from among the summer visitors, and in a lucky hour the 10-year-old Balczele and the 11-year-old Josele became bride and groom.
After the betrothal the in-law says to the bride:
"Balczele, in 10 years' time, God willing, your wedding will be."
The bride stamped her little foot and answered:
"[?] 10 years? Only 8 years! At 18 one may already marry!..."
At that she goes up to the groom and strokes him on the chin:
"You'll see, Josele, I'll play the lottery, I'll win the million, and we'll be millionaires too — you'll see, Josele!"
The company celebrated until late in the evening, and now the wedding of father and mother is to take place.
Well, is it any wonder that the town is in an uproar over this match?

The Moratorium on Mortgage Debts Will Be Extended and the Law on Cheaper Rent Will Remain in Force

Well-informed circles explain that abolishing the moratorium on mortgage debts is bound up with a great and highly complicated preparation of new laws on how to liquidate the mortgage debts gradually.
It is impossible simply to abolish the mortgage moratorium, because that would provoke an enormous crisis, with a wave of auctions of houses. There would be so many house auctions that even a small part of them could not take place and be auctioned.
It is clear that before abolishing the moratorium one must create a law which on the one hand will further extend the moratorium and on the other hand will at the same time compel [debtors] to proceed to[?] pay the debts in small instalments. It is not believed that in the present situation on the money market the house-owners will be able to pay instalments on the mortgage debts, especially as it is impossible to obtain borrowed money on a mortgage.
In order to abolish the mortgage moratorium one must first create the proper conditions for it, so that[?] no complications arise that could have a very bad effect on economic life. That is now difficult and simply not feasible.
There will therefore [be] no other way out than to extend the mortgage moratorium for another year.
If the moratorium on mortgage debts is extended, there is no doubt that the law on cheap rent for flats of 2 and 3 rooms will also be extended further.
In general one must know that the 2 matters — the mortgage moratorium and the reduction of cheap rent — are connected and depend on one another.
A Summer-Resort Story That Nearly Ended Tragically

The Kielce holidaymakers who have just come back from Zoppot [Sopot][?] tell the following story, which nearly ended tragically.
A Jewish student and a Jewish merchant both fell in love with the Kielce summer-holidaymaker S. A.; they[?] spent time together everywhere: on the beach, by the water, at the „dancing“, in the woods. But the two lovers were jealous of one another.
Once the young men had a frank talk between themselves and both came to the decision that it could not go on like this — one of them had to withdraw.
Both young men, themselves sportsmen, decided on a duel... in swimming. The one who won the swimming race would be allowed to court the holidaymaker; the one who did not swim to the finish had to withdraw.
Neither was a great swimmer, and both strained their last strength to achieve victory. Both also overrated their strength, and before they had swum to the beach one of them began to drown.
The other wanted to save him and also began to go under.
The swimming „duel“ would have ended tragically had not, luckily, a small boat come by and rescued them.
Thus a shared love for a summer holidaymaker nearly cost the lives of two people.

A tram disaster averted

Yesterday at 5 in the afternoon a tram disaster was averted in Będzin. At the corner of Kołłątaja and Małachowskiego [streets] stood a platform wagon loaded with furniture; at a certain moment a tram arrived from Małachowskiego street, at which the horses took fright and backed[?] towards the tram, but thanks to the quick presence of mind of the motorman, who instantly stopped the tram, the disaster was averted.
If you lose a bond of the National Loan

A new circular has now been issued by the Ministry of Finance, explaining what to do when one loses a bond of the National Loan. One must report it in writing to the special Office for State Debts in Warsaw, stating the number and series of the bond, when and under what circumstances it was lost, and request that the bond be cancelled and a new one issued. The office publishes notices about it in „Monitor Polski“, and after 3 months (if nobody comes forward) one receives a new one.
The fee is: from 50 zł. — 8 zł.; up to 200 zł. — 11 zł.; up to 300 — 13 zł.; up to 400 — 14 zł.; up to 500 — 17 zł.

The writer of these lines, in order to be able to bring the parents a living[?] greeting from their children, travelled to Rabka to the colony of the Chorzów children.
The colony, which bears the name “Miriam Franklowa”[?], lies in the midst of beautiful dense forests and has 2 large, beautiful and comfortable pavilions, one pavilion for girls and one for boys; each pavilion has 5 halls, each hall is beautiful, high, airy and sunny, with 4 windows.

The colony operates for 3 months in 3 turns of 230 children. So the parents should feel happy that their children are at the colony in Rabka. The parents of the children in Chorzów ought to express thanks to the management for the courteous and motherly treatment, as well as their deepest thanks to the holiday committee at the Jewish community in Chorzów.

Young Merchants and Commercial Employees — Enrol in the Supplementary Courses

[Zagłębie — commerce; appeal of the merchants' associations.] We live in a time when every day the possibilities of preserving the sources of livelihood, which were the source of Jewish earnings, grow ever narrower. The restriction on the institutions of higher learning, the guild law, the licences for peddlers, the tax burden on retail trade and handicraft — these are measures that have a very close [printed 'gur'] bearing on Jewish livelihood.
The Jewish merchant, too, has not been spared, although there are as yet no special regulations (apart from [?] a census for merchants already instituted by the Sejm) that would legally hinder one from engaging in commerce. But the slogan of tearing trade out of Jewish hands has gripped a large part of the Christian population. Laws are also already being prepared that will be directed against the Jewish merchant.
Standing face to face with what awaits the Jewish merchant, we must find the ways and means to preserve our economic positions.
Every single merchant must know and be familiar with all the regulations and laws being created for him. The Jewish merchant, who until now has played the most important role in developing trade in our country, must continue to stand on guard, so that no one can reproach him that by modern standards he is not qualified to engage in trade.
For present-day times, inherited qualities, personal abilities and character are too little; one must also take into account the changed economic structure, and consequently one must also become acquainted with the commercial [?] knowledge required of the modern merchant, and above all of young merchants and commercial employees, who face a bitter struggle for bread, for their existence.
We therefore call on all young merchants and commercial employees to complete a systematic commercial course. All those, however, who for various reasons have no possibility of completing a systematic commercial course should enrol in supplementary courses, where one will be able to obtain all the necessary knowledge required of a modern merchant. Such courses are being organized with the help of the economic institutions of Zagłębie: the Będzin Merchants' Association, the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association in Sosnowiec, and the Central Small Traders' Association, Będzin and Sosnowiec branches.
Remember your own future, remember that your fate depends only on yourselves, and all of you enrol in the supplementary courses through the above-mentioned associations.

Artisan and Merchant Questions

[Economy — artisans and merchants.] Vocational training of the artisan youth.
The Industrial Law of 1927 introduced the regulation of the crafts in Poland. In order to practise independently a trade that falls under the concept of a "craft" (melokhe), one must hold an artisan's card, which is issued by the competent industrial authority on the basis of a certificate of qualification.
As a certificate of qualification, which makes it possible to run an artisan workshop independently, the law recognises first and foremost the possession of a certificate of completion of the apprenticeship in the relevant craft and of having passed the journeyman's examination (journeyman's diploma), and in addition the possession of 3 years of journeyman's practice.
This is the normal and lawful path by which the artisan youth could attain the rank of an independent master artisan with full rights.
In accordance with the relevant provisions of the Industrial Law, the apprenticeship in a craft can be completed in the workshop of a certified master, on the basis of an apprenticeship contract, which must be registered with the Chamber of Crafts; alternatively it can be completed in a vocational school for artisans.
It is therefore understandable that the existence and growth of the Jewish artisan in Poland depends in the first place on the number of Jewish apprentices who will receive their vocational training in accordance with the binding regulations, both in the artisan workshops and in the artisan schools. This artisan youth forms the element that will in future have the opportunity to engage independently in the crafts.
To have a clear picture of the prospects of Jewish crafts even in the nearest future, one need only point to the following proportion:
During the years 1932—1935, 2164 Christian apprentices were registered with the Warsaw Chamber of Crafts, whereas Jewish apprentices registered numbered altogether one hundred and twelve. As to the fact that the number of Jewish pupils in the state and municipal vocational schools for artisans is negligible —
it is superfluous to point this out, since every one of us knows how far access to the said schools is restricted for Jewish youth. The number of private Jewish artisan schools that have the right to examine their graduates for the journeyman's grade is, however, almost negligible.
The same is true in Zagłębie and elsewhere.
From the above it can be seen how far the growth of Jewish artisanry is threatened: this situation may no longer be tolerated; we must realise that the crafts are almost the only field of productive work and of a healthy economic base for the Jewish population in Poland.
The artisan youth, which is to form the future cadres of independent artisans, is interested in this first and foremost; it must not rely on miracles. In caring for its economic existence in the future, it must first of all adapt itself to the requirements of the Industrial Law, according to which apprentices must undergo vocational training.
The parents of young people undergoing vocational training in the workshops of certified masters must make every effort, as quickly as possible, to have contracts concluded with the apprentices and registered with the competent Chambers of Crafts; at the same time these apprentices must attend the supplementary vocational schools.
Likewise every certified master individually who employs apprentices and has not yet concluded the contract has a sacred duty to carry out as quickly as possible the formalities connected with registering the apprentices.
At this point we wish to add that, in caring for the existence of Jewish crafts, we must strive to have as large a number as possible of artisans entitled to keep apprentices in their workshops, because, as we have already pointed out above, the artisan workshop is today almost the only school where a young Jew can receive vocational training in accordance with the provisions of the law.
Jewish artisans should therefore make use of the new concession granted by the Ministry of Industry and Commerce, under which artisans who employed apprentices before 16.12.1927 may, after completing certain formalities, also obtain the right to keep apprentices in future.
M. Kac.
