Show Positive Deeds.

[Dąbrowa — economy and relief; interest-free loan fund; editorial article.]
(On the revival of the Gemilut Chesed fund in Dąbrowa)
At last the activity of the Gemilut Chesed fund has been renewed in Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza] — or, as it is called, the interest-free fund for needy small traders and artisans.
The lack of such a fund had long been felt in the local Jewish street, especially in the present hard crisis years, when a small credit is able to keep a whole family going.
Admittedly the People's Bank [Volksbank] did no small amount to maintain the weak Jewish economic positions; with the convenient loan at the People's Bank, a small trader and artisan had the possibility of sustaining his livelihood more calmly.
Thousands of Jewish families, however, need credit without interest, because their incomes are not able to cover any interest.
The interest-free funds are in the highest sense a humanitarian act toward the economically weak Jew, who borrows a certain sum of money without losing anything on the sum[?].
Here too it must be mentioned that the "Joint" helped a great deal in founding the said bank.
At first, in the hard crisis years, the "rescue committees" arose, which, true, accomplished much and saved many Jewish families from ruin, but which in a certain sense bore a philanthropic character and therefore did not have the broad scope of large-scale social help.
The interest-free funds open a wide field of work and help for thousands of Jewish families from the poorest strata, in an honourable way, without the special aftertaste of the charity box.
This is help through credit in a dignified way, in which the borrower takes the loan with an open face, as in any other bank.
As regards the Dąbrowa interest-free fund, it is now setting about a broad campaign in this matter.
Dąbrowa's Jewish public must take a deep interest in this newly established institution, which is so important for the broadest strata of the Jewish population.
It must be said here that the interest-free funds serve[?] with credit not only the poorest part of the population but also families who, for one reason or another, find themselves in temporary financial difficulties.
It goes without saying that every important body[?] must be supported by the public; there is no doubt that Dąbrowa took part in the founding and consolidation of the interest-free fund.
The fund must already begin to issue loans, and in the future this will broaden its activity.
The whole development of the fund depends on how Dąbrowa's Jewish public relates to it.
One must bear in mind that the "Joint" will undoubtedly take part in financing the fund. The "Joint", however, demands that the community itself also do something for its institutions. The Joint's means are thus dependent on the help that Dąbrowa itself will create.
Every well-to-do Jew in Dąbrowa must therefore respond warmly to the appeal of the board of the interest-free fund and take an important[?] part in developing its activity.
Throughout the whole territory of the Polish Republic interest-free funds are now being created. Dąbrowa too, as one of the cities that have suffered, should and must have such a credit institution.
We warmly greet the new board, the initiators of the enterprise, and it is to be hoped that with the help of the Jewish public, and especially of the town's notables, they will succeed in carrying out their difficult but useful work for the needy Jewish population.
Dalet.
When May a Landlord Detain Belongings

[Law — tenancy; landlords and tenants.]
As soon as the new Code of Obligations [Kodeks zobowiązań] was published, we pointed out at once that the provision under which a landlord has the right to detain a departing tenant's belongings on account of rent owed — without a court judgment and without a bailiff [komornik] — would demoralise a section of the landlords, and especially their [—] and [—]; that they would abuse the aforementioned[?] strange provision, and that it would expose tenants to all sorts of harassment.
Practice shows that our concerns[?] were justified. Belongings are detained not only on account of overdue rent, but also for not giving notice of leaving the flat in advance, or even on account of an entirely different debt — for example: the landlord runs a grocery shop and the tenant owes him for goods taken, and he already dares[?] to detain as well. Not only household goods, but also work [in the tenant's hands], when the tenant had to deliver it to a customer or a warehouse-keeper; likewise belongings the tenant wanted to take to a rented summer dwelling; what is more, even sub-tenants had their belongings detained on account of the tenant's debt.
No arguments or pleas helped; those whose things were detained were forced to comply with all the landlords' demands, or remained stuck in the predicament.
True, the injured parties[?] could later bring[?] lawsuits against the strongmen and claim monetary compensation from them for the damages suffered; but such lawsuits drag on endlessly[?] and involve considerable costs, which a tenant can rarely afford.
Consequently the landlords could freely apply these home-made means of execution against the tenants.
The measure[?] of injustice must evidently have overflowed, if the Ministry of Justice found it necessary to publish a clarification that will[?] curb the landlords' actions somewhat.
According to the aforementioned[?] clarification, based incidentally on the latest rulings of the Supreme Court, the landlord may himself detain belongings only on account of overdue rent, and not on account of future rent or because of some other claim.
Thus, if a tenant moves out of the flat on 30 September or earlier and shows a receipt that he has paid rent up to 1 October, the landlord may not detain his belongings. The landlord's claim for failure to give earlier notice of termination of the [lease] agreement[?] must be pursued through the courts, and in no way belongs among the debts that are indisputable and which the landlord may therefore enforce himself.
As stated, the landlord's right to detain belongings himself applies only to debts for overdue rent, but not to claims for another debt, for example for goods taken in the landlord's shop, and not even for damage the tenant caused in the flat while he lived there. All these claims fall within the competence of the court, and meanwhile the landlord may not detain the tenant's belongings on their account.
Likewise the landlord may not detain the sub-tenant's belongings on account of the tenant's debt.
The landlord may detain only household goods and business equipment, but not work [in hand], especially when the materials were entrusted to the tenant by a customer or a warehouse-keeper.
The landlord may detain the tenant's belongings regardless of whether he vacates the whole flat or takes out only part of his things.
The same rules that govern relations between landlord and tenant also apply to the relationship between a tenant and a sub-tenant; likewise it makes no difference in this case whether the tenant's flat is covered by the tenant-protection law [ustawa o ochronie lokatorów] or not.
Y. A.
Quiet Tragedies.

[Feuilleton — sketch from the series "Come with Me".] By Y. Vaynshteyn [J. Wajnsztajn].
(From the series "Come with Me").

And now, my companion said to me, we will pay a few visits to the houses of the rich. You think[?] that only in the little houses of the poor[?] are sad scenes of life played out. In the so-called "wealthy" houses, too, tragedies take place, but they are of a quite different sort, of a quite different sort...

The tragedies of the rich are mostly quiet ones, not heart-rending, but they are tragedies all the same, and perhaps there is more sorrow in them than in those that strike everyone's eye.

A house — a man come down in the world...

Yes, houses too fall into various categories, just like people. There are houses that live quietly, modestly, according to certain traditions which pass down by inheritance from generation to generation. The wall clock hangs in its place for decades, the bookcase stands in its place for years and generations, and it would occur to no one to move it to another place. In the street revolutions, upheavals have taken place — but in the house everything stays as it once was. Some invisible hand maintains with its strength the long-existing order in the house and permits no changes.

There are, on the other hand, houses that change every three months; they know of no traditions, of no stability, of no definite style; they swim in an endless colourlessness[?] and stylelessness.

The house in which we paid our visit[?] belonged to the first category.

Spirits of past generations hovered over the massive hanging chandeliers cast of old bronze and over the old-fashioned furniture. The table told in its mute language of the rich feasts of former times that had been held on it; the chairs, although already badly worn and here and there with holed upholstery from which aged[?] straw peeped out, stood with a special kind of pride [— doubtful reading] with their noble lineage and looked with disdain upon the present time, which had strayed in here. From the bookcase thick spines peeped out, but torn with age; the once-gilded letters on them had already rubbed off, and only faint traces of them could barely be made out. The Shas [Talmud] had here[?] befriended "Tsilim"[?] and a few concordances.

And a few portraits of geonim [great rabbinic sages] looked sadly[?] down from the walls, and it seemed as if they had deliberately remained frozen[?] in their places in order to see what the end of this rich man's house would be.

In the house we found two living souls, which flickered[?] in dried-up[?] bodies and recalled the picture of age and decline in the house. Two lonely, gloomy souls — R' Yoel Itshes and... a cat.

It was between day and night. Thick shadows clung stubbornly to the corners of the furniture, to the edges of the crystal-cut glass on the sideboard, and quietly waged a struggle with the descending[?] darkness.

"How are you, R' Yoel Itshes?" I asked, just like that, the impoverished rich man, who had once "cracked the big whip" [i.e. wielded power].

R' Yoel Itshes — not yet[?] such a very old man, but already worn out by the last hard years of want — at first tried to let a faint little smile out of the dark cellar of his soul, but the little smile[?] immediately turned back again, and in its place a grimace twisted his emaciated face.

"What can one do? Feh, one lives, thank God; of course it's hard lately, but what can one do? We'll drag on like this to the last station..."

"Where is your wife?"

"My wife? With her there is a very great misfortune. Have you heard nothing[?] of our calamity?"

And R' Yoel Itshes told a story, perhaps quite an ordinary one in our days, but within the four walls of this rich man's house it sounded strange.

They have only one child, an only daughter, [on whom they doted — doubtful reading]; among the schoolgirls she was the best; besides that[?] she was simply an outstanding child: beautiful, clever, very well-read[?], of brilliant character; she would never [printed "amol", apparently for "keynmol", never] let us sense that she suffered from our poverty. And you must know that only ten years ago I was still a rich Jew[?], and our daughter, may she live, spent her childhood years in great luxury.

R' Yoel Itshes paused[?] for a while, listened to a rustle that could be heard from another room, and at once said to us:

"Wait a moment, I'll be right in."

He went off into a side room, and after a few minutes he came out with his old wife.

"She," he says[?], "has gone deaf and almost blind in the last couple of years, since the calamity with our daughter happened; it struck us both like an axe over the head. Who could have expected that such a thing would happen in my house — that my own[?] child would take up[?] with some cobbler's boy and disappear with him."

So she sits around[?] — it is already almost two years — silent, shrunken, full of grief and troubles, and... strokes the little flower.

This little flower, which she holds in her hands even now, we received in a little letter from our daughter: "I send this little flower to my dear, beloved Mama, for the suffering I have caused her."

So she carries the little flower around with her, kisses it, sleeps with it, does not part from it even for a moment, and all her motherly tenderness, all her mother's grief and pain she puts into the withered little plant her daughter sent her...

— — — — —

When we were already standing at the door, ready to leave this house, R' Yoel Itshes came up very close to me and whispered a secret... a secret that came out from between his lips as if from red fire set[?] upon black glowing coals:

"And on top of all the troubles, people are saying that he is a gentile..."

The silence swallowed the secret, as the sea swallows raindrops... "And on top of all these troubles, people are saying that he is a gentile..."
The Jews in Danzig

(Impressions)
Every Jew travelling to Danzig by way of Zoppot [Sopot] is interested first of all in the question: what does Hitlerism look like in practice with regard to the Jew in the Free City? Is the situation really such as some newspapers portray it?
True, in most German shops the Hitlerite emblem hangs in the shop window as the sign of an Aryan business.
On entering Zoppot, for example, the newcomer receives a very unpleasant impression from the Hitlerite flags that flutter along the whole main street; the mole (pier) too is hung, besides the official Free City flag, with the swastika flags.
And the swastika meets you wherever you turn; even on the beach [?] the Hitlerites stick little swastika flags into the sand.
But the first impression is without doubt more unpleasant than the real situation.
First of all it must be said in praise of [unclear word] the Danzigers that the ordinary man, though he wears the Hitlerite emblem with the whole rattling paraphernalia [?], possesses tact and manners.
I happened to ask various people about a street or a firm, among them Hitlerites with the swastika in the lapel, and if one could not give an exact answer, he stood embarrassed and was sorry that he could not give me an exact answer.
It is true that Jews try to explain this truly impressive courtesy by the fact that the Zoppot residents, for example, are good businessmen; possibly the commercial sense dictates to them to be polite, possibly they think that the Jew is treyf, but his money is kosher...
* * *
We talked with many Danzig Jews, and none of them complained about the attitude toward Jews there.
True, the authorities pursue an anti-Jewish policy, which expresses itself in not employing Jews in official posts, but beyond that one does not feel it.
The law that one may not open a shop without a permit must — according to the explanations of the local Jews — not be understood as a regulation aimed [?] against Jews, but as a means of holding back the surplus of shops, which can create unwanted competition.
In the same way one must understand the authorities' attitude to the peddlers, who unfortunately consist in great majority of Jews.
The peddlers, paying no taxes, thereby create competition for the merchant class, which has larger administrative expenses. But in general the Danzig Jew lives not too badly.
* * *
And one can easily convince oneself that the Jews there feel free.
We are not speaking in this case of Zoppot, because in most resorts, even elsewhere, it is quiet; but one can easily see it in Danzig itself.
In Danzig, for example, the traditional "Dominik" [St. Dominic's Fair] took place during the last two weeks, that is, a fair together with a Luna Park.
The amusements at the Dominik are organised by German firms; the Dominik gathers every evening thousands and even tens of thousands of people. As is the custom, the masses go to such amusements, yet there was not a single case of anyone accosting a Jew. Jews, individuals among thousands of Germans, not only feel fine but are drawn into the great din and enjoy themselves together with the thousand-headed crowd.
And here it is worth bringing a fact that the owner of a shoe shop in Danzig told me.
A German bought a pair of children's shoes from her; the soles came off [?]; the woman took his complaint into account and asked him to come later, as she wanted to put the shoes in order.
The German began to talk loudly and unpacked an antisemitic sermon. It was Saturday, when the takings are big; the surrounding customers, Germans, hearing his words, began to protest strongly, and they simply carried the German out of the shop.
* * *
It goes without saying that we have, God forbid, no intention of glorifying the local Germans' infatuation with Hitler and singing praises because they do not beat the Jews.
But the Jews there have a bit of comfort in the fact that, despite the official anti-Jewish policy of the government and despite all the propaganda, the masses are not yet poisoned as they are portrayed. Evidently the Goethes and Schillers still had an influence on the shaping of the people's soul.
The owner of a colonial-goods (grocery) shop in Danzig told me that although he lives among Hitlerites, he lives nicely. If they cannot come themselves, they send the children, and all the neighbours behave this way; each one is only wary of the other.
The Jews there can be somewhat lighter at heart: let them poison the people [?] — a few days after such special trial [?] incitements they go about with drooping [?] noses, and afterwards they forget and go back to the Jew.
So the Jews there relate, smiling as they do so, and one of ours [?], a Jew, shrugs his shoulders in amazement and envy:
— What does it mean: the "[unclear word]" orders them to give the Jew a pinch [?], and nothing [?] — truly incomprehensible..
How can an ordinary goy have such an "evil inclination" and not fulfil this commandment, when he is explicitly told to oppress the Jew?
It is hard for him to understand this.
P. Blumenkranc (Częstochowa [?]).
Trifles.

[World — economics and figures; "Trifles" column.]
a) How much money is there in the world?
Today it is hard to give a clear answer to that. Because of the great foreign-currency ["devizn"] difficulties that dominate almost the whole world, it cannot be said precisely today how much money there is in the world.
The latest report that we have [?] on this, from the Leipzig Trade Fair Office [Leipziger Messeamt], dates from the year 1929. One can, however, safely say that the state of money compared with 1929 has remained the same. Only the owner has changed. It may be that Europe or America has less or more today compared with 1929, but the total has remained the same to this day.
In the whole world there is money amounting to 35 billion and 16 million dollars. Of this, about forty percent is in gold, and for the remaining sixty percent there is paper money in all the countries of the whole world.
About seventeen billion dollars are in Europe, nine billion dollars are in all the countries of America, Asia holds seven billion dollars, one billion dollars is in Africa, and Australia holds about a third of a billion dollars.
In the United States of North America alone lies money amounting to five billion dollars. In 1929 France held three billion dollars. England then had "only" two billion dollars.
As one can see, a nice bit of cash...

b) How long are the railways of the world?
According to a report from 1927, there are railways in the whole world with rails ("relsn", "shines") of a length of one and a quarter million kilometres. The longest railways belong to North America, with 403 thousand kilometres; that is as much as all of Europe together [?].
If one calculates the length of the railways against the length [sic; meaning area] of the country, the longest railways belong to Belgium, which has 37 kilometres of railway for every hundred square kilometres; next comes Switzerland with fifteen kilometres, and England with 14 kilometres of railway per hundred square kilometres of land.

c) How much coal is there in the world?
Fearful people always ask: how many years will we still be able to mine coal in the world? These people can be answered calmly: another 3 300 years, if we mine as much as was mined according to a statistic in the year 1929.
In America there are 344 thousand tons of coal, Asia holds 68 thousand tons of coal, Europe 66 thousand tons, Africa 23 thousand and Australia 15 thousand tons of coal. That is, we have today altogether a quarter of half a million [sic] tons of coal in the world. Not counted here are the quantities of coal that are constantly being found in new coal mines around the world.
North America alone has about half of all the coal in the world; next comes Canada with 67 thousand tons, Russia with 42 thousand tons and China with 22 thousand tons of coal.
As one can see, we will not, God forbid, suffer any shortage of coal in the last [sic; i.e. coming] few thousand years.
Z. Haber, Vienna.
„Nothing Has Changed”

[Feuilleton — summer-resort life; antisemitism.] From the series „Pictures from the ‘Line’” [the railway line of summer resorts]. By Sh. Libaszon[?].

With a tanned face and... raspberry juice.
If you ask Jewish women why they go to the dacha [summer cottage], ninety percent will answer you that they never had any intention of going. And[?] if they did go after all, it is only because of the children. What doesn’t one do nowadays for the children? Because of the children one becomes „European”, because of the children one keeps a treyf kitchen, and what not. Everything because of the children.
But there are also specific dacha „articles” that concern the female holiday-makers themselves. These are: „tanning” and raspberry juice.
To be at the dacha and not bring home a few baskets of juice (plenty, no evil eye[?]), besides other preserves (for which there are special „kenerins”[?]..), is like a [—] pig eating matzos on Passover..
In „pressing season”, i.e. when one buys up the raspberries for pressing, I happened to overhear the following conversation between 2 women:
— Have you already pressed anything[?]?
— A fine question, upon my life. I already pressed last week, and I’m sending it home with my husband, who comes for the Sabbath. Because I’m afraid it might go mouldy[?]...
— And I’ll get down to pressing on Sunday, when my husband will[?] be here. Do I have the strength to press? May my enemies have[?] my strength. Let the husband press[?] — he has to[?] carry it home. What a business I have with all that juice..
And when the weeks of „back home” draw near, one sees[?] how the poor husbands drag the filled baskets or the bottles of juices that the wife, the capable housewife, made at the resort.
And the husbands are very careful, guarding the „juice” the way a pious Jew guards a fine etrog. The wife ordered him to „keep it upright”, not to give it a knock, God forbid, for they went, true, because of the children, but for „the world” one must come home with a tanned face and with raspberry juice...

He is to blame..
I met him sulking, irritated[?], angry at the whole world in general and in particular at whoever „invented” the dacha fashion. Like a herring I would tear him apart — he says.
— May one know why you are so angry? — I ask him.
— Why, you ask? Because of the dacha fashion and because of my wife.
— Well... it’s not a matter of life and death[?], upon my life.
— On the contrary, it’s easy for you to say: well, not a matter of life and death, because you are not in my situation. Just imagine: I came here in such a downpour and find the door of my flat locked.
— Where is your wife?
— That is the whole trouble, that I don’t know where she is. The neighbours tell me she went off with some acquaintance to Szczyrk..
— Never mind, she surely hasn’t „settled down” in Szczyrk with the „stranger” — I try to console the desperate grass widower, and my „prophecy” came true. A week later his wife came back, and here the epilogue begins.
„She”, on seeing her husband, came out with a retort: How is it possible?! How can one be so „impudent”[?] as to write „I can’t come” and in the end come after all..
After that „speech” the husband was left speechless and willy-nilly had to admit that his little wife is as pure as an angel: since he had written to her „I can’t come”, she went off with „some acquaintance” to pass the time. Yes, yes, yes.
— He is to blame...

The „orphaned” villa.
The dacha season is drawing to a close. Our brethren, the children of Israel, have carried off millions of złotys and „brought back” fresh air. Hundreds of „villas” are again being taken over by their owners until the new dacha season; only one villa has, poor thing, been orphaned: the „Shekhinah” has departed[?] from it. This is the villa „Maria”, which through the writer of these lines became known as the „holy villa”.
All season long the villa hummed like a beehive. A stranger from the street who came into the villa even on an ordinary Wednesday got the impression of being at an international congress where one hears seventy languages spoken...
In the villa they sang from evening till morning. In the villa grooms and brides „courted”[?], played cards and, lehavdil, prayed with a minyan every day. Not to speak of when the Sabbath came — then the villa was wrapped in sheer holiness. But now the crowd has dispersed, „gone is its glory, gone its splendour”, and the last Mohicans pass by and shake their heads in pity at the „orphaned” villa...

„Something has changed after all.”
Drawing up the total, we come to the conclusion that „something has changed after all”, and the dacha place we are writing about is also somewhat polluted with the Aryan air. Once the Jewish holiday-maker was a welcome[?] guest; young and old greeted him with a smiling „dzień dobry”, but today everything is as if [—]: not, God forbid, beating or harassing, but „silence, too, is as good as speech”...
The system of taking money from the holiday-makers has also changed. Formerly every holiday-maker paid a „Kurtaxe” (spa tax); this year, however, everyone paid a certain percentage of his „letnie mieszkanie” (summer flat) and in return received a bigger portion of.. dust.
— Yes. It has changed.
A Word in Season.

(For the attention of Jewish parents).
Jewish parents must, in times like these, think deeply about the fate and the prospects of their children. For have you ever taken stock of the predicament they find themselves in today with their matura certificates and foreign diplomas? Have you [—] [—] the old tradition of making your children doctors, engineers, chemists and so on, when the road to the free professions is severely restricted and your children are left standing at a crossroads, without a future, without means of living, and later[?] remain a burden on your shoulders? Do you know the sufferings of your children who are abroad — how they go hungry, crushed in spirit[?], [—] in spirit[?], embittered[?], estranged from home, exposed to various illnesses and misfortunes, drifting from one place to another, in a foreign environment, in a foreign language — only for the sake of the diploma, which afterwards has no real value at all? And how “easy” it is today to keep children abroad, the Jewish parents surely know — among them are those who literally give away the last bite from their mouths to keep their children there; and later a tragic picture presents itself, with the great question: what did I torment myself for, all those long years, suffering only to arrive at the conviction that the diploma is a document that has no value whatsoever for a Jew in the practical sense of life, since all sources of livelihood are closed to me?
And so, with these words on their lips and the diplomas in their pockets, they are after all “unproductive”[?]... for that is what the spirit of the present time dictates...
This is how, in reality, the end of Jewish studies looks today — a black[?] wound both for the parents and for the child.
On this question we must take precise stock; we must adapt ourselves to the spirit of the time and lead the children onto new practical paths, more realistic, productive, so that they become self-reliant.
Let the advertisement in a Warsaw Yiddish newspaper that I read these days serve Jewish parents as a moral:
“A doctor of medicine with a foreign diploma seeks employment of any kind; also commands[?] foreign languages.”
This is how a doctor with a foreign diploma looks today — often envying the man who paves the streets, because the latter earns his bread while he goes hungry.
Our youth must train itself as first-class craftsmen, and also as European-style commercial employees.
To a trade — that is the way henceforth to maintain our positions in the countries of the Diaspora.
Herman Szer.

End of the month.

Today there are other Selichot.

The wooden hammer of the Selichot-waker is replaced today by stones flying into windows — and not on a dark night, but even in the middle of broad daylight.

Fritz Lang, the Film Director Who Fled Hitler’s Germany.

Who does not know the name of Fritz Lang — the famous German film director? There is, it seems, not a single film lover in the whole world to whom this name is unknown. With Fritz (formerly Friedrich) Lang the history of German film is bound up until Hitler’s coming to power.
It is interesting: precisely the Jew Fritz Lang managed to create the genuinely German film, both in its character and in its content. That is the famous film “Nibelungen” in two parts, which is in and of itself German through and through. It fully reflects the genuinely Germanic Nibelungen work of the master Richard Wagner.
Then came a series of various films, of which “Metropolis” must be especially mentioned. Here it is no longer so much the human being that plays the part, but the modern machine. This film made an impression on the world. Later came the film “A Woman on the Moon”, then “The Murderer”, which was no average film.
When Hitler came to power, Lang had to leave Germany. His Aryan wife Thea von Harbou officially broke with him and remained in Germany. Lang goes to Hollywood, where he creates the film “I Am Innocent” with Sylvia Sidney in the female lead. Now he is making a second film with the same actress. The film will be called “You and Me”. Sylvia’s partner is the actor George[?] Raft. A true artist is never lost anywhere.
On a Summer Sabbath Evening

[Poetry — Sabbath in the shtetl; Sosnowiec, 1929.]
L. Kerner.
On a summer Sabbath evening
the sun still stands high in the sky,
looks down on the bustle of the little town —
as if lost in Sabbath-holy thought!...
• • •
On a summer Sabbath evening —
a breeze blows with a taste[?] of Paradise...
In the material world — weekday worries, sufferings,
the Sabbath has made everyone forget them all;
fathers, like children, come outside
to breathe in from the rye and the flowers
the scent of the earth — reviving, which the wind
has brought[?] and carried from the distances,
as if wanting[?] to say to everyone thereby:
— Refresh yourselves for the whole
week, now!...
• • •
On a summer Sabbath evening —
with young girlish smiles, laughter
on[?] their faces — grace — Jewish daughters,
like princesses in Sabbath splendour, —
stroll with their mothers — delicate queens,
lost in dreams, pampered...
In side alleys[?] girls flit[?],
meet the young lads' glances,
which, lustful[?] and longing, delight[?]
in girlish charm and rosy[?] grace...
They hurry back — bathed in rays,
their breasts heave... their hair dishevelled...
They blush! — it seems he smiled
at them! —
they lower their charming eyes,
nestle against their mothers, like lulled[?]
children who confide, who hide a secret...
• • •
On a summer Sabbath evening —
a quiet longing strides through the town,
like a gnawing twilight prayer
after a day spent in holiness —
and somehow one so does not want to part
from the Sabbath spent in joy!...
— — — — — — — —
On a summer Sabbath evening...
Sosnowiec — 1929.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Ki Tavo)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Ki Tavo
—o—
a) "I have not eaten thereof in my mourning" (Deut. 26:14)
"I have not eaten thereof in my mourning, nor given thereof for the dead" — I have not kept Judaism like a dead cult[?], like certain Jews who hold to Judaism only during the period before a burial, during mourning after a death — "Kaddish- and yortsayt-Jews"...
Drashot el ami.
• • •
R' Hershele Bialoshiger[?] was once abroad in a big city. Coming to the synagogue on the Sabbath, he hears all the worshippers saying Kaddish. R' Hershele was a great wit[?], and he asks the shammes:
— Is there[?], God forbid, an epidemic here? Are all the worshippers orphans, or what?..
The shammes laughs and explains to him:
— In our city only Kaddish-sayers come to pray.
Says R' Hershele then:
— Now I finally understand the verse "Wherefore I praised the dead which are already dead more than the living which are yet alive." I value the dead more than the living, because the living fathers are not able to bring their children into the synagogue, and the dead fathers do manage it...
• • •
Someone once asked the chief rabbi of New York, R' Yaakov Yosef:
— Our Sages say that on Rosh Hashanah "the books of the living and the books of the dead are open." The question arises: granted, the books of the living are opened on Rosh Hashanah to examine their deeds, but why open the books of the dead? Their balance has long been settled!
R' Yaakov Yosef answered in jest:
— Apparently this means the "yortsayt-Jews." As is well known, every Jew has each year a special book in Heaven with 365 pages, according to the number of days in the year, and on Rosh Hashanah an angel looks through each person's book to see whether he has not once missed praying, putting on tefillin and the like. But when it comes to these "yortsayt-Jews," the angel thinks: why should I trouble myself in vain and for nothing and leaf through these 365 little pages in order to find on which day he prayed, when I can find this out in a much easier way: I need to look in the "books of the dead" to see when his father or mother died, and thus I know when he prayed...
—o—
b) "And now, behold, I have brought" (ibid., 10)
R' Eliyahu Chaim Meisel once asked a well-known Łódź magnate for a donation. The man began to complain that his business was going badly and that he himself was poor and destitute; he spoke with bitterness and even had grievances against R' Eliyahu Chaim, as though he were to blame for it.
Some time later it became known in Łódź that the said magnate had become enormously[?] rich through a business deal[?], and when R' Eliyahu Chaim met him and asked him how things were with him now[?], he answered under his breath:
— So-so...
Says R' Eliyahu Chaim to him:
On the verse "And now, behold, I have brought," the Midrash says: It was taught, R' Shimon bar Yochai says: a person says his own praise in a low voice and his own disgrace in a loud voice. His praise in a low voice — from the confession of tithes; his disgrace in a loud voice — from the recitation of the first fruits. That is just how man is: when things go well for him — "his praise" — he answers in a low voice: eh, not bad; "his disgrace" — when things go badly for him, he shouts in a loud voice...
—o—
c) "And all these blessings shall come upon thee, and overtake thee" (28:2)
It is a special blessing that after all the blessings — "and overtake thee": they will find you the same person; you will not become different on receiving all these blessings...
Mei Shiloach.
—o—
d) "Because thou servedst not the Lord thy God with joyfulness" (ibid., 47)
Joy is the greatest protective wall; when one has joy, one is protected from everything. Not even any rebuke [curse] can have power, and the whole rebuke can strike only "because thou servedst not the Lord thy God with joyfulness"; if you are joyful — the rebuke cannot take effect upon you...
R' Nachman of Bratslav.

[Serial novel.] (A highly gripping novel of Jewish life in Zagłębie before and during the World War.)
After all, he had already met prettier, more alluring women, but none of them had so inflamed [?] his heart and soul as this one... Ah, if only she would consent [?], his life would gain a new meaning and he himself would become as if renewed...
But even happier was Blumke, though she tried hard not to show it. She was afraid to tell her relatives about it, not wanting them to misinterpret Mister Plank's special affection for her.
But in herself she was happy, and also felt more uplifted in her loneliness.
A whole night afterwards she could not sleep and thought without stop about what the boss had told her.
She had already heard a few compliments from men and young fellows back in her old home, but nobody had yet spoken to her the way he did. She herself could not account for it, but somehow she had the impression that this man was much closer to her than all the others... Somehow it also seemed to her that even his voice was so familiar to her, as if she had already heard that voice once, but very long ago...
And with every day they grew closer and closer to each other. Blumke was no longer afraid of him, and when one evening he again invited her to his house, she no longer looked for [?] any excuses; she went with him knowing that this man, whose eyes behind the dark glasses she had not even seen yet, would do her no harm...
And there, already in "Mister Plank's" apartment, something happened once that Blumke had in fact often thought about, but had not reckoned it would come so soon...
Sitting at a finely set table with refreshing, expensive drinks, "Mister Plank" suddenly moved closer to her, lightly put his arm around her and said:
— Miss Betty...
— What?..
— I have long wanted to tell you this; surely you sense it yourself...
Blumke's face flares up like a blazing fire; she pretends not to understand, and he goes on:
— True, I am no longer a young man, I am already in my fifties, but believe me, under this breast there still beats a healthy young heart, dear Miss Betty. With me you will be the happiest woman in the world. I don't want you to give me your word right away; think it over, because I would like you, just like me, to mean it seriously, and since I truly mean your happiness seriously, I would like you to consider it well before you give me an answer.
— Good...
— I would gladly introduce you to my family, but unfortunately I have no one in the world; I am all alone.
— I too am all alone, lonely as a stone.
— You have no parents?
— No.
— And brothers, sisters?
— No one, all alone...
— And family?
— Family — yes, the relatives did bring me over here, but you know how it is: relatives and cold fire [a saying: relatives are like a fire that gives no warmth]...
— Very true; nevertheless I would like to meet them, if possible...
— Oh, it will be the greatest honour for them if Mister Plank will consent [?].
— For me too it will be an honour.
When he saw her home he already had feelings toward her like those of a bridegroom for his bride. He was also pleased that he had invited her relatives; he meant by this not only to show off his wealth before them, but also wanted to talk with them about his future wife, because deep in his heart he somehow felt that this beautiful, clever Betty was hiding something from him... He had noticed it in some of her smiles, in the sudden breaking-off in the middle of her words when she told him something about her life...
But at the same time he no longer made a secret to anyone of his feelings for Betty, and he is preparing to marry his beautiful employee. Betty all at once grew in the business as if by ten heads; everyone began to flatter her, wanting to win her confidence, because she was already regarded as the future mistress of the house... "Mister Plank" had even entrusted the cash box to her, and she was allowed to do as she wished.
And then came the Saturday evening when "Mister Plank" had invited Betty's relatives to his home. "Betty" invited the closest and finest members of her family, so that she would have someone to show off with — people who had already been in the country for twenty-odd years and spoke fine English. In fact, "Mister Plank" wanted that evening also to hold a "vort" [engagement ceremony] in the old Jewish manner, when bride and groom get acquainted and one starts to talk about the "tna'im" [betrothal terms]...
And [?] indeed a finely set table was prepared for the guests; the neighbours wondered, because for the first time one saw guests and a merry mood at "Mister Plank's".
But already at the greeting and the introductions to "Betty's" relatives, "Mister Plank" was surprised again and again on hearing their names, which somehow rang so familiar in his [printed: "her"?] ears...
And "Mister Plank" was even more astonished and surprised when some of them began to speak Yiddish, and in just the way he himself used to speak...
And of the closest relative, who sat next to him at the table, "Mister Plank" suddenly asked:
— Tell me, from which region of Poland do you come?
— From Zagłębie; hasn't "Betty" told you yet?
— Yes — the eyes under his dark glasses began to sparkle somewhat more strongly — I even had acquaintances in Zagłębie..
— Oh? You also come from our area?
— No, I was there only a short time, passing through. Nevertheless I still remember to this day some family names, for example your name...
— Wow, wow, you have a good memory.
— Yes, for that I must praise myself. Possibly, perhaps, I also knew my Betty's parents. But her family, "Grinwald"... I can't recall...
Here "Mister Plank" noticed that the relative was trying to turn [?] the conversation to something else. To [?] explain why Blumke is called "Betty Grinwald", he would also have had to [?] tell the tragic story of Blumke's father, who once had an affair with a shikse [a non-Jewish girl] and [?] perished unhappily.. That could have spoiled the celebration, it might perhaps have become a blemish in "Mister Plank's" eyes... Better as he knows it: she is an orphan, and that's that — her parents perished in the war.
But when it was already shortly before the wedding, something strange suddenly happened.
While making all the necessary preparations and also the wedding documents, "Mister Plank" said to Betty:
— Dear, you once told me that your relatives brought you over to America on someone else's papers; they could not do it otherwise.
— Yes.
— Well then, now that you will be officially registered as my wife, you can also get back your maiden name — would you like that?
— Oh, very much! I'll be very grateful to you; even though it has been such a long time, I still haven't got used to my new name.
— Well then, tell me exactly what your name is, because right now I need [?] to prepare our documents.
— My real name is Blumke Wertheim.
She did not notice how his hand, which was in the middle of writing down the name, suddenly gave a strong tremble, but she did notice how his face all at once became as if frozen.
— What's the matter with you? — Blumke asks, frightened.
— Your name is Blumke Wertheim? — he asks as if stunned [?], and begins to look at her piercingly.
— And you come from Zagłębie?
— Yes; why are you so frightened?
— Oh, nothing — he catches [?] himself back [—]
— Tell me, dear, what's the matter with you? Do you feel unwell?
— No... Blumke Wertheim is your name?
And suddenly he also asks the thing he feared most: And your mother's name is?
— Sarah; they called her "the beautiful Sarahtshe".
"Mister Plank" grabs hold of the table as if afraid of falling down, and asks in one breath:
— And what was your father's name?
— Yosl Wertheim — but what has happened to you, Willy [?]?
"Mister Plank" snatches the dark glasses from his eyes and cries out with joy and grief together:
— Blumke.. my daughter.. why, it's me, Yosl Wertheim.. How little you were when I saw you for the last time! Tell me, do you recognise your daddy?!
Blumke gave a terrible scream like a [—]; she would have expected anything, but not such a thing... But looking now into his eyes, she recognised him at last, and instinctively something pushed her into her father's outstretched arms.
— My father! Is it you, whom we mourned so much?..
— Yes, daughter, so life willed it, my fate. I am myself to blame, but the punishment [?] has been enough for me [?]...
— And my heart too always somehow...
— Yes, a heart [—] [?], my daughter! We have found each other, I am happy! Unfortunately I must still live under a false name; when I tell you, you will understand how unhappily your father has lived for so many years — but not now; now let us rejoice and savour the great happiness that life has sent us.
And they held each other long, heart to heart, unable to tear themselves apart...
— The End —
“To the Chief Musician on Neginoth, a Psalm, a Song...”

(On the 1st “yortsayt” [anniversary] of the kehilla elections in Sosnowiec).
Mazel tov, Jews of Sosnowiec! “This day have I rolled away the reproach of Egypt”!
At last you have lived to see a year since you elected a new kehilla “board”[?].
No doubt you remember that day,
on which you threw off yourselves the plague
and the shame —
of “with a mighty hand will I rule over you” — with a strong hand..
I mean the “commissarial kehilla” of R' Dov;
well, thank God, it has now been a year since — “and he was not, for [God] took him”, done with, an end
(may we never again be tried[?] with such grief, God forbid...)
So[?] now you already have an “own” kehilla,
where your communal representatives,
if you'll pardon the expression...
do not rule over you with fear and dread and with arrogance[?],
but with “democracy”, a plausible notion too,
as the word has gone out in town.
Now they are going to lighten for you the heavy yoke
of the town and of other things.
(What won't your representatives do for you!.)
For that purpose they will appoint over you judges and rabbis,
so that you may have a decent face before the world..
as is proper —
and what most of you have strongly[?] desired[?]...
they are putting up for you a hygienic mikveh
and also all the “nalipvukes”[?] will set up the “chazakit”[?]...
by my life, a question!
The kehilla is, after all, now already [—] a “national” one!
In general the “government”[?] on “Modrzejowska”[?] street already acts with sense and tact,
as Warszawski says: “Thus said the P'eus[?]”...
Never mind, first on the P'eus[?], then on the “vibe”[?] clock — on Leguzmen[?] Meir[?]
you can rely, just as on your
own good sense,
and they will lead you into the “aspkurirte”[?] camp...
• • •
Jewish people of Sosnowiec, don't worry — head held high!
He who always helps you will probably help you this time too...
Libele.
A Proclamation in the Będzin Synagogue.

In the Będzin synagogue the matters that have a connection with “history” are very carefully preserved (perhaps that is why the synagogue is situated next door to the castle), so that to this very day no change whatsoever has taken place in the synagogue (except for [a ...][?] of the choir, which strikes 11 months a year).
Nor has the custom changed of proclaiming and announcing every Sabbath after the Torah reading various bits of news: which couple is standing under the chuppah, on which leg of the goose the little kashrut seal must be found, and the like; and when it happens that the shammes errs and mixes everything up, the following is announced:
The young man, the bridegroom Getzl Plokushiser, takes the bride Mrs.[?] Tsertl[?] Ploymeniukh, who may not be used[?], because the meat is from a shot animal; the town mikveh is open again and one must take care that the seal is on the right leg, otherwise the goose is forbidden for any benefit; the men too should pay attention to this, because about the utensils, too, one must ask a rabbinic question.
—o—
That's What Mummy Says.
Father[?] (to the child): Moyshele, do you want to travel with me to Warsaw?
Child: Yes, but how will Daddy travel?
Father[?]: What do you mean?
Child: Mummy says you are already an “angeforener” [one who has “arrived” / done for].
—o—
Precisely[?].
— Which month is a “well-wished” one for Jews?
— The month of Tishri: people send each other greeting cards.
• • •
— Which knocks does a Jew not fear?
— Those with which the shammes knocks for Selichot.
Socrates.
—o—
A Wife Who Is a Teacher.
— Tell me, Chaniek, whom did you marry?
— A gymnasium teacher.
— And how do you feel after the wedding?
— I feel as though I had married an encyclopaedia.
Changes in the Municipal Budget / Subsidy for Private Jewish Schools Reduced to 600 zł.

[Będzin — Municipality; Education.]
In the municipal budget, which was approved by the Kielce voivodeship office, a series of changes were made in the expenditure sections. Among other things, the amount of the subsidy for the Jewish private schools was also changed, from 1,500 to 600 zł.
As is known, at the time a part of the Jewish councillors voted for the proposal that the budget be adopted en bloc, in order to obtain the subsidy sum for the private schools, which had been raised from 600 to 1500 złoty.
In the Commercial School of the Small Traders' Association Classes Are to Be Held 6 Days a Week / So Ordered by the School Curatorium

[Będzin — Education; Commerce.]
The School Curatorium in Kraków has ordered that in the commercial school of the local Small Traders' Association classes shall be held 6 days a week (until now classes were held only 5 days).
The order may cause material damage to the school, because, as is known, there are in the school about 30 percent non-Jewish pupils, who will certainly not be able to continue studying because the lessons will take place on Sunday.
Report Meeting on the Small Traders' Convention

[Będzin — Commerce.]
Last Sunday there took place in Częstochowa a convention of all small traders' organisations in the Kielce voivodeship; the chairman was Mr. D. Gutensztajn.
On behalf of the local association the speakers were: Łaźnik N., Rechnic, D. Gutensztajn and M. Kaner.
From Sosnowiec: S. Honigman, M. Federman and Igusz. Mogil.
Next Sunday, at 4 in the afternoon, a report meeting will take place in the premises of the local small traders.
A Tahara House Will Be Built

[Będzin — Kehilla.]
In the coming days work begins on building a tahara house (for the ritual washing of the dead) on the model of the tahara house in Katowice.
The costs of the construction are covered by the firm of Yaakov Gutman.
A Tragic Accident to a Worker

[Będzin — Accidents.]
While carrying out work on the walls of the town synagogue (the "Shtotishe Shul"), a worker fell down and was seriously injured.
Suicide of a Poor Jewish Craftsman

[Będzin — Incidents.]
On Friday towards evening the 40-year-old carpenter B. committed (attempted) suicide by drinking denatured spirit.
The cause of the desperate step is want, hunger and family suffering.
B. is in the municipal hospital.
From the Town Board

[Będzin — Municipality; Education.]
At the last meeting of the town board it was resolved to elect a commission which is to inspect the renovation carried out in the Jewish public (powszechne) schools, because this year each school separately received a certain sum from the magistrate for renovation purposes.
The commission will include Messrs. Łaźnik[?], Rechnic and Moris.
To Lock the Gates at 11 p.m.

[Będzin — Commerce.]
At the last meeting of the board of the Merchants' Association it was resolved to intervene with the competent circles so that in the winter months the gates should also be locked at 11 in the evening.
It is desirable that the small traders' and artisans' associations should join in this action, so that the intervention may bring the desired result.
The Poultry Dealers Refuse to Agree to Maintain Supervisors

[Będzin — kashrut.] As we have already written, a sharp dispute has broken out between the rabbinate and the poultry dealers over the matter of maintaining ne'emanim [kashrut supervisors], to which the dealers do not want to agree.
In connection with this the rabbinate has issued a public proclamation (kol kore) in which the poultry bought from the local poultry dealers is declared forbidden. The ban, however, has sharpened the situation even more, because [?] the poultry dealers have united [?] not to comply with the rabbinate's demand.
Officials' Petition on Tenant Protection and on Keeping Rents Low

[Poland — officials and housing.] The Union of State Officials has approached the government with a petition in which they express the necessity of further extending the law concerning the prices [?] of 2- and 3-room apartments, so that the same rents [?] as now will continue to be paid.
The officials point out that their salaries [printed „pensiyes“ — pay/pensions] have not increased, the high cost of all articles of daily use has grown further, and if rents [?] for apartments were raised again by 10–15 per cent, the latter would fall into a difficult situation.
It is to be hoped that the government will meet this just [?] demand.
A Christian Alarms Jewish Residents

[Sosnowiec — odd incident.] That they should conduct the prayer at the bedside of a dying Jew.
In Jewish circles in Old Sosnowiec [Stary Sosnowiec] [?] people are seething over the story that happened there this week.
In the middle of the day an unknown Christian ran into several Jewish homes [?] and alarmed them, saying that Mr. G., who lies in his death throes, asks that a minyan of Jews come up to him and recite with him the „ninth“ [?] chapter of Psalms before he dies.
The Jews, on hearing this, found themselves in a quandary, for only 2 days earlier Mr. G. had been healthy and strolling in the street; but one does not question a fact — perhaps he had suddenly fallen ill? It was decided that one of the Chevra Kadisha [burial society] should go to the dying man...
When the Chevra Kadisha man entered Mr. G.'s apartment, he found the „dying man“ sitting at the table eating breakfast...
— So, what do you say, anything new? — the „dying man“ asks the Chevra Kadisha man.
— No news at all. I just came to pay you a visit.
The story soon spread, and everyone is curious to know who the person was who sent the Christian on this concocted [?] errand.
If the Back-Room Slaughterers Do Not Stop Their Work, They Will Be Sent to Bereza

[Sosnowiec — kehilla and shechita.] As we have already written, the kehilla board intervened with the supervisory authority concerning the „winkl-shochtim“ [unlicensed private ritual slaughterers], who slaughter illegally and cause material damage to the kehilla treasury.
On the basis of this intervention the starosta, Mr. Weniar [?], summoned the back-room slaughterers, Messrs. Herszkowicz [?], Poznański [?], Noach Rot [?] and Szwarc, on Tuesday morning and declared to them that if they did not stop the illegal slaughtering they would be arrested and sent away to Bereza [Bereza Kartuska detention camp].
Mr. Szwarc did not come, but sent his wife, who declared that „her husband is ill“.
After this sharp warning the back-room slaughterers promised that they would no longer occupy themselves with the „holy“ work.
Which Kehilla Budget Will Be Approved — the Board's or the Council's?

[Sosnowiec — kehilla.] This will be decided in the Ministry.
As is known, both kehilla budgets, that of the board and that of the council, were sent to the supervisory authority. Because of this the supervisory authority has sent both budgets to Warsaw, to the Ministry for kehilla affairs, where the fate of both budgets will be decided.
Father Demands 10,600 Złoty for His Child's Hand

[Sosnowiec — courts.] In the civil division of the local district court the case was heard against the chauffeur Sosparek [?], who ran over a 6-year-old girl and broke her right hand. The child's father came forward with a claim against the bus company to which the car belongs, for a sum of 10,600 zł.
Before issuing the verdict the court decided to make a site inspection at the place where the accident occurred and to hear the opinion of a doctor concerning the child's incapacity to work.
—o—
Flag campaign of „Brit HaChayal“.
[Sosnowiec — Revisionist Zionism.] The leadership of the local „Brit HaChayal“ is starting a fund-raising campaign for the flag that the organisation is having made. The unveiling of the flag is to take place during Jabotinsky's visit to Sosnowiec.
—o—
Dr. Czapnik resigns as steward of the synagogue.
[Sosnowiec — kehilla.] This week Dr. Reuven Czapnik sent the kehilla board a letter in which he announces that for certain reasons he is resigning as „wirtschaftler“ [steward/administrator] of the synagogue in Old Sosnowiec [Stary Sosnowiec].
—o—
Intervention for permission to trade on the Sundays before the holidays.
[Sosnowiec — trade.] The board of the local small traders' association has intervened with the supervisory authority for permission to sell food articles on the Sundays that fall on the eves of the holidays, from 8 to 10 in the morning.
The result of this intervention is not yet known.
—o—
From „Chalutz Ba'al Melacha“.
[Sosnowiec — organisations.] The committee of „Chalutz Ba'al Melacha“ [Pioneer Artisan] is conducting intensified activity; every Shabbat members' meetings take place with lectures on literary and social topics. It has also succeeded in organising for the members of „Chalutz Ba'al Melacha“ medical and legal aid under the direction of Dr. S. Meladiste [?] and the lawyer Dr. Kapelski [?] at a reduced fee.
The secretariat is open daily except Shabbat and holidays from 6 to 10 in the evening.
—o—
The Radomsker Rebbe in Krynica.
[Hasidism.] The Radomsker Rebbe, who has gone through a serious illness, has travelled on doctors' orders to Krynica, where he will stay over the High Holidays (Yamim Nora'im).
Not „An Eye for an Eye“, Only 4 Years in Prison

[Sosnowiec — courts.] Trial [printed „prolog“] over a brawl between competitors before the district court.
In wintertime Mr. Yaakov Wajcman was attacked on Dęblińska Street by the Wajsman brothers, who had business scores [?] to settle with Wajcman; they struck him so hard in the eye that he had to be taken to the Jewish hospital, where the necessary operation was performed.
The trial over the brawl took place in the local district court. In the dock sat Shmuel Leib, Chaim Wolf and Yisrael Wajsman. The main culprit was Shmuel Leib Wajsman, who had wanted to be the leader of the brawl.
After the court proceedings, which lasted several hours, the court delivered its verdict, according to which Shmuel Leib Wajsman is sentenced to 3 years' imprisonment [so in the body; the headline says 4]; the other accused will be committed to a house of correction if within 3 years they commit any offence again.
Conference on the Tobacco Trade

[Zagłębie — trade.] On Tuesday a conference was held in the Chamber of Commerce concerning the draft regulation on the tobacco trade. At the conference, in which representatives of the merchants' associations in Zagłębie took part, as well as the tobacco sections, a number of proposals on the said question were discussed. A lengthy discussion developed around the proposal that the small traders be obliged to buy the tobacco articles at the so-called „semi-wholesale depots“ [printed „por-hurtownies“; perhaps półhurtownie] [?]; after the discussion it was decided that in this field there should be free trade, i.e. the trader may buy wherever he wishes.
As we have already written, the Ministry of Finance has already drafted the text of a new decree on the trade in tobacco and cigarettes.
The Ministry of Finance wants to introduce strict control over the trade in the articles of the cigarette monopoly [?].
All who will trade in cigarettes — wholesalers, semi-wholesalers and also the retail sellers of cigarettes — will have to obtain licences.
The Ministry of Finance has sent the text of the decree to the merchants' organisations for their opinion; the associations are against introducing licences for retail sellers, because owing to the introduction of licences many retail traders will not receive any licence and will therefore stop trading in them.
5-Year-Old Girl Under a Motorcycle

[Dąbrowa — Accident.]
5-year-old girl under a motorcycle.
On Friday a terrible accident occurred in Dąbrowa [Górnicza] on Legionów Street, which cost the life of 5-year-old Krystyna Adamus.
The child wanted to run across the street; at that moment she fell[?] under a motorcycle, which dragged her about 10 metres.
In serious condition the child was taken to hospital, where an operation was performed.
Grodziec

[Grodziec — Community; Grodziec — Antisemitism.]
Grodziec.
On a subsidy for the Gemilut Chesed (interest-free loan) fund.
On behalf of the local G"Ch fund, a delegation of Messrs. Drożdżak[?], Kesner[?] and Ehrlich intervened with the kehilla president, Mr. Rubinlicht, regarding the granting of a subsidy to the G"Ch fund in the amount of 1,000 zł.
During the intervention Mr. Perlig described the sad economic situation of the local Jews, and that only with the help of the fund can a number of Jewish livelihoods be maintained.
Hooliganism.
A group of underage hooligans (łobuzy), [unclear words][?], wounded Mr. Israel Dawid[?] Hejnrig[?] with a stone.
J. Perlig.
Great Political Trial over the Events in Racławice.

[Kielce and district — Courts.] As we are informed, on the 13th [month illegible] the great trial over the events in Racławice will begin.
The trial will take place in Miechów, in the large hall of the firemen, at an away session [?] of the Kielce District Court, under the chairmanship of the vice-president of the Kielce District Court, Judge Wysocki [?].
62 persons from the Peasant Party will sit in the dock. About 200 witnesses have been summoned [?] to the trial.
15 of the greatest lawyers will appear at the trial.
Kraków Court of Appeal Increases the Sentence of Chaim Opatowski.

[Kielce — Courts.] As was reported in our paper at the time, the Kielce District Court sentenced the Kielce resident Chaim Opatowski to 4 months' imprisonment; he was accused of actively resisting the police, as well as of "insulting" the Polish nation, during a mutual clash with Endek [National Democrat] hooligans who had attacked the funeral of the tragically murdered Jewish merchant Baruch Mangurten [?], of blessed memory.
Both the prosecutor and the convicted man appealed against the verdict of the Kielce District Court.
A few days ago the case was heard by the Kraków Court of Appeal. The court acquitted Opatowski of the charge of insulting the Polish nation; on the other hand, the Court of Appeal increased his sentence from 4 to 6 months for actively resisting the police.
Delegation of the Kielce Small Traders' Association at the Kielce Starosta over the Endek Pickets.

[Kielce — Economic boycott.] A delegation of the Small Traders' Association in Kielce, Messrs.: Adv. Manele [?], chairman Arnold [?] M. K. [?], councillor of the Chamber of Commerce Chaim Fachel [?] and G. Górski, visited the new Kielce starosta [district head], Mr. Wojciechowski, and asked him to take measures against those who picket the Jewish shops and conduct a boycott campaign.
The starosta promised the delegation to take sharp measures against the [?] pickets and against the Endek "Fachgruppists" [?].
Intensified Boycott Agitation.

[Kielce — Economic boycott.] The anti-Jewish boycott agitation is intensifying from day to day.
On Wednesday evening the Nara men [ONR, National-Radical Camp] sent around the town a good number of young fellows who photographed the Christian customers going into Jewish shops to buy.
Some of them took up position in front of the shop of Mr. Strasberg ("Kateta" [?]) and simply terrorised the Christian customers who wanted to enter the said shop.
The police, on arriving, drove the fellows away.
10 Months' Prison for Violating the Foreign-Currency Law.

[Kielce — Courts.] Last Saturday the Kielce District Court heard the case against Mr. Wendel [?] Taiman [?], who was accused of violating the foreign-currency law. The court sentenced him to 10 months' imprisonment. The convicted man was released from custody on bail of 200 zł.
Paint Factory Burnt Down in Skarżysko.
[Kielce district — Fire.] A fire broke out in the chemical paint factory of Mr. Rosenbaum in Skarżysko. A considerable part of the machinery was destroyed. The damage amounts to about 20 thousand zł.
Round of Dinners for the Kielce Old-Age Home.

[Kielce — Charity; old-age home.] The following persons have provided meals for the Kielce old-age home, and the management thanks them:
Last week:
Sunday, dinner — Moshe [?] Eisenberg and sister, on the yahrzeit of their father R' Eli' [?], of blessed memory; Monday, dinner — Yosl Kan and wife, on the wedding of their daughter Ch. T. [?]; Tuesday, breakfast — Elimelech Süssholz, on the yahrzeit of his mother-in-law Gnendl, of blessed memory; dinner — Chaim Berner; Wednesday, breakfast — Dr. St. Silberszlak; Thursday, dinner — Shlomo Feigenblat [?]; Saturday, dinner — Natan Grinberg.
This week:
Sunday, dinner — Meir Eliezer Gross and wife, on the yahrzeit of his mother Chana Sara, of blessed memory; Monday, breakfast and supper — Dr. Fleszler [?], on the yahrzeit of his wife Sonia [?], of blessed memory; dinner — Zalman Waksman, on the yahrzeit of his father, of blessed memory; Tuesday, a whole day — Yechezkel Sztulpewicz [?]; Wednesday, dinner — Wolwil [?] Szklarsz [?] and wife, on the wedding of their son; Thursday, dinner — Yaakov Goldszmit [?]; Saturday, dinner — Shlomo Lagran [?].

The New Number Plates Must Be Exchanged by the 1st of [—].
Until the 1st of [—] one can exchange, without any fee, the number plates for the new type [?] on cars and motorcycles.
After this deadline one will have to pay 10 zł. for a plate for a car and 6.50 zł. for a motorcycle.
—o—
Bees Sting a 2-Year-Old Boy to Death.
In the village of Wola Libertowska near Kielce [?] bees stung a little boy so badly that on the way to [—] [?] he died in terrible agony.
—o—
[Kielce — Brisk relief committee; appeal.]
Jews of Kielce!
Support the fund-raising campaign of the
Brisk (Brześć) Relief Committee.
Donate en masse for the benefit of the unfortunate Jews of Brisk!
"The 20th Zionist Congress and the Founding of the Jewish State". A Lecture by Dr. Kleinbaum.

[Kielce — Zionism.] In the coming days the vice-president of the Zionist Central Committee, Dr. [Moshe] Kleinbaum, will come to Kielce and will deliver a most interesting lecture on the subject "The Twentieth Zionist Congress and the Founding of the Jewish State".
Dr. Kleinbaum's lecture has understandably aroused great interest in all circles of Jewish Kielce.
The Tishri Campaign of the Keren Kayemet LeIsrael

[Zagłębie — Zionism / JNF.] On Sunday the 29th of this month the great Tishri campaign of the KKL [Keren Kayemet LeIsrael – Jewish National Fund] begins in Zagłębie, with the distribution of an artistically designed Shana Tova (New Year) card illustrating the achievements and tasks of the KKL; pocket calendars of the KKL will also be distributed.
One may trust that the Jews of Zagłębie will support the redemption of the Land generously, and that the campaign will be crowned with great success.
R' Mendel Ferens, of blessed memory

[Będzin — Obituary / Chevra Kadisha.] On Wednesday, at the age of 68, there died one of the most distinguished householders of Będzin, the long-time chief gabbai and president of the Chevra Kadisha (burial society), R' Mendel Ferens, of blessed memory.
On the same day, in the evening, the board of the Chevra Kadisha in Będzin held a mourning session in the kehilla premises, at which Messrs. Rubinlicht, Rechnitz and Plessner recounted the virtues of the deceased.
The funeral, which took place yesterday, was attended by a very large crowd from all walks of life. The deceased was carried into the municipal beit midrash, where hakafot (circuits) were made. Eulogies were delivered by the dayan (moreh tzedek) Frajberg and Rabbi Chamaides[?].
At the cemetery the eulogy was given by the head of the "Keter Torah" yeshiva, R' Yashe.
May his soul be bound up in the bond of life.
Imprint (Colophon)

[Colophon.] Editor and publisher L. Szpigelman, Będzin. — Printed in its own printing house.
Editor-in-chief and publisher L. Szpigelman; responsible editor Sz. Lewkowicz.

A Zionist Academy

(L. S.) Last Saturday night the Katowice Zionist youth organisation “Akiba” arranged, in the large “Powstańców” [?] hall, a festive academy (already a tradition with the organisation).
On the beautifully decorated platform a choir sings “Hatikvah”, and Rabbi Chameides delivers a short speech rich in content. He says, among other things, that Jewish youth no longer has any illusions in the Exile, at a time when the insane chauvinism of the nations persecutes Jewry. Why Is Nothing Further Being Done?

[Będzin — artisans — opinion.] (On uniting the artisans' organisations in Będzin).
Anyone who knows the history of the negotiations to unite the Jewish artisans in Będzin will admit that things had already reached the point where the negotiations were about to break a record; but, as it turned out, the talks ended in nothing. There were meetings, conferences and so on[?], and in the end... everything remained... as before.
People did believe, and everyone was sure, that the union was an accomplished fact. Unfortunately, however, the sad truth is that nothing further has come of the union, although nobody wants to believe what[?] is being said[?]; when two Jewish craftsmen meet, the first question is: what about the union, has it come about? Everyone is sure that the talks between the sides are still being conducted.
And it is indeed no wonder that nobody wants to believe any more that the union has remained, for the future too, a utopia. Even those who conducted the negotiations took the matter seriously, because they knew that the question can no longer be handled as it once was, that the union can no longer be a game for fooling somebody; everyone knows that the union of the Jewish craftsmen has now become a question of Jewish craft in Poland.
The so strongly organised Endek [National-Democratic] antisemitism has created a united front against the Jewish economic positions.
Day after day one hears more cries from the ruined Jewish artisan workshops in the provinces.
Hundreds of Jewish artisan workshops are forced to liquidate, and their owners with their families come into the town[?] to starve.
From all sides calls for help arrive at the Jewish artisans' organisation, and one is at a loss[?] how to help: can an organisation that is itself broken and splintered accomplish anything for the community? Can such an organisation have any outward influence whatsoever?
And yet, all the more[?], the question: how could it again be allowed that the union of the Jewish artisans in Zagłębie, which was supposed to serve as a motive for consolidation, should again come to nothing? Especially at a time when one sees[?] that the Christian artisans' organisations in the country have organised themselves into a single organisation, and that solely in order to create the front against the Jewish craftsman.
As it is explained to us, the union has not come about now because of fear. One organisation was afraid that the other would snatch the primacy from it, because they would carry[?] into it[?] — take over — the party influence.
For anyone who knows the situation of the Jewish craftsman at the present day, and who seriously intends to find the way out by which to improve it, this motive (and unfortunately it is the true one) is a ridiculous one, because, first, today, when any question whatsoever of the Jewish craftsman is being dealt with, the party question can no longer come into consideration; in this case only one party comes into consideration — the Jews in Poland.
The antisemitic wave makes no exception between the artisan who is a Zionist, a Folkist or of some other party affiliation, and therefore — in creating the general artisans' organisation — the party element can no longer come into consideration.
The fear of the primacy being seized is also almost[?] an excuse — greatly exaggerated, for who wants to take anything from whom, and who can here, if one may say so, gain or lose, and what? It is a simple question of Jewish craftsmen uniting, artisans with artisans, who have workshops and belong to two Jewish organisations, which likewise have nothing that anyone would want to take from them; or is it perhaps a matter of great fortunes that one wants to take from the other!
And therefore the negotiations must be continued, all the motives that hinder the work must be removed, and with a little seriousness and good will the union can be realised.
The Jewish Artisans' Union in Będzin, as one of the first in Poland, must continue to set the tone for good organisation, and the union in Będzin, too, will surely serve as an example and give the impetus for the union of all Jewish economic organisations in Zagłębie.
***
Union of the Two Merchants' Organisations

[Będzin — merchants — opinion.]
More than once we have touched, in the columns of our newspaper, on the question of the necessity of both Jewish merchants' organisations in Będzin. We hold that such a phenomenon is harmful in general, and particularly now, at a time of Endek [National Democratic] assault on the very existence of the Jewish merchant class — then a uniform line of union of all the active forces is surely absolutely necessary.
If the existence of two merchants' organisations perhaps still had some justification at the time when the tax commissions were active, to which both organisations sent their members and thus enlarged the representation of the merchant class on the commissions — that system has now been abolished, and the members of the appeal commissions are, after all, not sent by the merchants' organisations but are appointed by the Chamber of Commerce; thus this argument now falls away entirely.
There remain, then, other considerations which are, in our opinion, second-rate in comparison with the main task that such an organisation has to fulfil now.
Surely we cannot justify the existence of two organisations merely on account of the independent appearances at the various elections — beginning with the Sejm, the Chamber of Commerce, municipal self-government, the kehillas — or on account of ambition for representation, or interventions [?], or on account of second-rate motives. Surely the union of the economic interests of the merchant class, which forms so large a part of Polish Jewry, must not be put in the shade because of these personal ambitions — particularly now, at a time when the merchant class must fight against the means that threaten its existence.
This question is surely clear to everyone, and the fussing over the "darling son" only serves to diminish the role of the Jewish merchant class.
Besides, we have after all seen with our own eyes (on the 8th of this month, on the Day of the Polish Merchant) in Sosnowiec [?] the big Polish merchant marching together in one rank with the owner of the small shop, and the common intentions [?] of the two of them are surely so clear that they need no explanation; and indeed it was then that the question stood before us in all its nakedness: and now, too, shall the curse of disunity still reign among us?
This is not the time to look for the guilty; besides, such a search would not bring us nearer to the goal but, on the contrary, take us further from it.
One thing, however, is clear to us: never yet has the necessity of a union of the two merchants' organisations been as urgent as now, and therefore we want the leaders of the Jewish merchant class in Będzin to remember well that in unity lies strength.
Y. B.
